When will Poundland shops close? Five key questions answered

BBC News Thu, 26 Nov 2026 17:21:21 GMT

Poundland has collapsed into administration, leaving the jobs of its 11,000 staff in doubt in the run-up to Christmas.

The company has appointed consultancy Alix Partners to oversee a sale of part or all of the discount retailer, with questions remaining about the future of the company.

This is the question that is most difficult to answer.

Poundland shops will remain open as usual for now. The firm collapsing has acted as a reset in the process of selling it.

Administrators are looking to either sell the business as a whole, or to break it up, which is the more likely outcome.

When Poundland was still a going concern, Irish property firm Martin Property Group made an offer for it. But a source said the group was now "unlikely" to make a fresh bid due to "irreparable harm" to the brand from the administration process.

Before the collapse, Fortress, which owns rival budget chain Poundstretcher, was interested in buying about 200 of the stores, and wanted to keep those trading under the Poundland brand.

But Fortress's position at the moment is unclear. The BBC understands it is considering selling Poundstretcher, a move first reported by Bloomberg.

A decision on Poundstretcher could come before the end of this week. However, Fortress has declined to comment.

That depends on who you ask.

When the chain was sold by Pepco last year for £1 it was struggling. It suffered a £68m loss that year.

Poundland's managing director Barry Williams said Poundland had been seeing a "strong recovery" and recorded a profit by one measure in the first nine months of this year.

Poundland's management paint a picture of a retailer that was turning a corner until the owner, US investment firm Gordon Brothers, pulled the plug on funding for day-to-day expenses such as buying stock.

The Usdaw union, which represents shopworkers, claim the owners forced Poundland into administration.

Labour MP Antonia Bance said she was "pretty appalled" by the conduct of Gordon Brothers over the past few weeks, and that it was going to make much bigger profits by breaking up the business rather than by keeping it going.

However, Gordon Brothers insisted the business was only turning a profit on paper, and had missed budget forecasts.

A spokeswoman said while the management team had made £100m in cost reductions, the business had moved from a £70m loss to "around break-even".

"Break-even is different from generating the cash needed to buy stock, invest, and withstand increasing economic pressures," the spokeswoman said. "A few good weeks do not make a turnaround."

Poundland repeatedly missed budget targets over the year, the spokeswoman added.

Gordon Brothers was concerned that as inflation goes up next year, those pressures would have helped to make the business unviable, it said.

And Julie Palmer, managing partner at insolvency agency Begbies Traynor, said Poundland's collapse "seemed somehow inevitable" due to challenges facing retailers - including higher costs to employ staff.

Stores are still trading while the administrators work out if the business is viable.

The funds locked up by Gordon Brothers - at the last count about £70m - have now been released by the administrators.

This has turned the taps back on, so staff will continue to be paid in the run-up to Christmas, and so will suppliers.

But here's the catch: the administrators have a legal obligation to maximise value for "secured" creditors. It means the owners, Gordon Brothers, are at the head of the queue for being paid back the loans that were stumbling blocks in the negotiations.

But more importantly for staff, if the administrators can get more value by breaking up the business than by selling it as a whole, then that is what they have to do, even if the business would be viable.

If the business is broken up and its stores are sold off, the new owners would not be obliged to keep staff on.

In the short term, yes.

From 26 November you will not get a refund for goods if you change your mind about the purchase. If the item is faulty you will still get a refund.

The immediate reason Poundland collapsed was that Gordon Brothers locked up funds for the day-to-day running of the business, including to pay suppliers.

This meant that stock was running low at Poundland.

But those funds have now been unlocked, meaning suppliers can be paid, and supply chains can be re-established, at least in the short term.

If an item is on the shelves, then shoppers can buy it.

That depends on what happens next.

Administrators will have to get the best value for creditors, which could mean selling the business as it stands.

But if Poundland is broken up, administrators could sell the brand without the stores, or the brand along with some of the stores, or the stores without the Poundland brand, to other retailers.

As a result there could be fewer discount stores on the High Street, providing less incentive for other retailers to keep prices down.

"Poundland is a place they go on the High Street to get bargains and... given the cost of living challenges we face, that is of concern to us in government," Wes Streeting, the defence secretary, told the BBC on Thursday.

Poundland's customers may well turn to rival budget retailers in the hunt for bargains.

Nearly 100 Labour MPs including ministerial aides oppose Rosebank oil field

BBC News Thu, 26 Nov 2026 16:29:54 GMT

Ministerial aides are among nearly 100 Labour MPs who have signed a letter to the prime minister to express their opposition to the Rosebank oil field.

The government could also face resignations from junior ranks if the project goes ahead, the BBC has been told.

Energy Secretary Miatta Fahnbulleh is due to make a decision on whether to give the go-ahead for drilling in the oil field off the north-west coast of Shetland within weeks.

The government has remained tight-lipped - both publicly and privately - about what it is likely to do.

Those close to the energy secretary insist that she has not yet made her decision.

But 92 Labour MPs have signed a letter, sent to the prime minister today, urging him not to allow the project to go ahead. Ministerial aides - the most junior rank of government - are among the signatures.

The MP who organised the letter, Catherine Fookes, said: "If Rosebank is approved, champagne corks will pop in the offices of oil companies - but it will not make an iota of difference to my constituents' energy bills.

"The oil belongs to private companies, and will only be shipped overseas to the highest bidder.

"What it will do, however, is accelerate the climate crisis, which is already pushing up food bills, causing devastating winter floods like those we saw in Monmouthshire last year, and fuelling wildfires across our green landscapes in summer."

It's the most visible demonstration yet of the deep divides in the Labour Party over the issue.

The decision about whether to approve Rosebank involves a legal process which technically lies solely with the energy secretary.

Fahnbulleh has, in the past, been regarded as someone personally opposed to the oil field.

Others in the cabinet, including Chancellor John Healey, have let it be known that they would like to see the project given the go-ahead; while the prime minister has repeatedly said he wants to take a "pragmatic" approach to North Sea oil and gas.

But Fahnbulleh insisted last month that she alone would make the final decision and claimed the courts would ultimately side with her if colleagues attempted to overrule her.

Influential pro-Rosebank voices suggested that senior ministers had toned down vocal support as the decision draws closer.

They suggested this wasn't a sign that Rosebank would be vetoed, but because any obvious attempts to pressure the energy secretary might mean her final decision would be subject to a legal challenge.

A number of MPs say they have heard conflicting claims - with both outcomes being predicted.

What is clearer is that the government's decision will be controversial, whichever way it goes. There is a private and public battle playing out.

Backers of the scheme argue approving it would provide an economic boost. The Conservatives also say it would enhance energy security.

But oil is traded internationally – and the energy secretary has said approving the scheme will not help with immediate cost of living pressures. Rosebank would also be more polluting than Jackdaw, a gas field, which was approved last month.

A fortnight ago, backers of the field were confident it would be approved.

They believed the chancellor's language on energy bills at the Budget, coupled with the lack of political jeopardy that materialised from the approval of the Jackdaw gas field, had made their case stronger.

The same group of MPs believe it would be difficult to reject Rosebank around the same time the prime minister is set to deliver a 10-year plan focused on reindustrialisation.

The government has said oil and gas would be part of the energy mix for many years to come and sources in the trade union movement have suggested that if Rosebank doesn't go ahead, existing inward investment in the North Sea would be put at risk.

While Labour's manifesto upon entering power in 2024 pledged not to "issue new licences to explore new fields", it does pledge to honour existing ones.

In 2023, the then Conservative UK government granted a licence for Rosebank and a legal challenge followed.

The Court of Session in Edinburgh ruled last year that the government had made the approval unlawfully, leaving the current Labour government to make a new decision on whether to give the go-ahead.

The mood among some pro-Rosebank MPs changed this week, with several who back approval telling the BBC they were now worried it would be blocked.

The BBC has spoken privately to Labour MPs involved in the debate, before the letter was sent to the prime minister, to get a sense of how divisive it is proving.

One ministerial aide said: "There are quite a few of us who are considering our positions. I'm in that group. We want to see leadership on climate change."

Another aide who said they might quit added: "There a group of us for whom we became Labour MPs because of climate change. It is the issue that motivated us into politics."

Other aides – known in Westminster as parliamentary private secretaries – told the BBC they were opposed, but would stay in their jobs if it went ahead.

Another said they thought there were increasing signs the prime minister would not be able to carry his party with him if the scheme was given the thumbs up.

And another said the energy secretary might have to resign if it goes ahead, given her scepticism about the project.

It has been reported in recent weeks that members of her team are encouraging opponents to make their feelings known. The BBC has been told the same.

One MP, who backs Rosebank, said the behind-the-scenes operation had been so effective, the scheme was up in the air again.

That has led to some anger at the energy secretary.

One minister says: "Miatta has boxed herself in with how she's handled Rosebank. It's outrageous if she's encouraging MPs to speak up over Rosebank. We should get on and do it."

Like the decision itself, the exact timeframe is unclear. But some opposition figures expect it mid-December.

Whatever happens, it will be controversial and has already exposed splits in the Labour Party.

Princess of Wales drops in on arts project in the Borders

BBC News Thu, 26 Nov 2026 16:18:33 GMT

The Princess of Wales has been in the Scottish Borders to see the work of an arts organisation that is helping to support projects across the UK.

It was her first engagement since two men were charged with trying to steal cufflinks and a clock from the royal couple's country home in Norfolk.

The Hugo Burge Foundation (HBF) which has three bases in the region - one of them on the Marchmont Estate near Duns - carries the name of the internet entrepreneur and philanthropist who died in 2023 aged 51.

The princess - who is known as the Duchess of Rothesay while in Scotland - got a glimpse of the work being carried out by the group.

She was welcomed by Lucy Brown, HBF chief executive, and learned more about its work supporting creativity and craftsmanship.

She also spent time talking to head gardener Toby Loveday and creative director James Fox during her time in the Borders.

The HBF offers grants, prizes, residencies and studio spaces to artists and craftspeople and provides funding to arts organisations and community groups.

It also funds major public art projects with the goal of "permanently enriching Britain's cultural landscape".

Established in 2022, last year it distributed more than £400,000 of grant funding to individuals, communities, organisations and projects.

Across its three locations, it offers a range of workspaces including a community pottery studio, a state-of-the-art silversmithing workshop, a printmaking studio, and a traditional chairmaking workshop.

It also safeguards a nationally important collection of modern British art.

On its main campus it offers funded residencies throughout the year and cares for a walled garden.

In 2026, it opened Rhymer's Works, a new creative hub in the town of Earlston that offers subsidised studios and community spaces.

Violent knifeman told doctor his psychosis drugs weren't working days before train attack

BBC News Thu, 26 Nov 2026 15:38:38 GMT

Hurtling along at more than 120mph, passengers on an East Coast Mainline train bound for London King's Cross found themselves caught up in one of the worst acts of violence on Britain's rail network in recent times.

Anthony Williams stabbed 10 people in five minutes on board the train last November, near Huntingdon, in Cambridgeshire, leaving some seriously injured. On Thursday, a jury found him guilty of 14 counts of attempted murder.

It has now emerged that, in the month before that attack, the knifeman had twice contacted his GP to say the anti-psychosis drugs he was taking for schizophrenia were not working.

But he never saw a doctor and did not receive additional mental health treatment.

Now his trial at Cambridge Crown Court is over, BBC News can also report his long history of violent criminality, revealed through old court transcripts we have obtained.

It stretched back two decades. In his teens Williams robbed people at knife point, including on a train. Even after he had started his 25-hour rampage, culminating in the Huntingdon attack, there were potential opportunities to arrest him.

Williams, who was born Anthony Abiola Oluwatuyi in London in 1993, first arrived on the police radar aged 12, when he was excluded from school for arson after setting fire to the toilets.

One acquaintance from the time - who would only speak on condition of anonymity - told BBC News Williams would "turn people's pockets inside out just because he wanted to". They said: "He was a thug who brought a knife to class."

Over the next seven years, he was convicted of 14 further offences, including five thefts, three robberies, and two offences of possession of a knife.

In October 2012, aged 19, he robbed two fellow teenagers of their smartphones at knife point on a train, warning them: "If you tell, I will come back and find you."

When he was sentenced for that at Wood Green Crown Court to three and a half years detention in March 2013, the judge referred to his "sorry record of previous convictions".

Williams' barrister, Victoria Kerly, told the court he had mental health problems, adding: "They are things that I have myself experienced with him and they do raise some concerns for me."

By the time Williams appeared at St Albans Crown Court in February 2020 he was a crack cocaine and heroin addict, as well as a drug dealer.

He had been arrested the previous year in possession of heroin, crack cocaine and cannabis, as well as a pair of scales and 12 "burner" phones. Asked about his drug dealing, he told police: "If I don't do it, not good things will happen to me."

He was sentenced to four years in prison, where he was sectioned and held in a psychiatric hospital until his release.

Upon release, he moved to Peterborough to live with his mother and stepfather. At this stage it is unclear exactly what mental health treatment he received there, but the BBC understands that, following last year's train attack, Cambridgeshire and Peterborough NHS Foundation Trust launched an internal review.

On 30 September 2025 - a month before the Huntingdon attack - Williams contacted his GP online about what he described as his "deteriorating mental state", saying his drugs were not working.

Contains some upsetting scenes.

The doctor told him he should be taking 200mg of the Quetiapine he had been prescribed to treat his paranoid schizophrenia, but he was only taking 100mg.

The GP invited him to a meeting on 14 October which he did not attend. Williams contacted the doctor again on 23 October, again saying the medication was ineffective - but he did not respond when the GP tried to get back to him.

In a phone call with a taxi firm on 31 October, the night before the train attack, Williams can be heard apparently speaking to voices in his head, saying things like "devil wanna play", and making strange noises, before then resuming the conversation normally.

Following the attack, Williams told psychiatrists "things were bad" in the days before it.

"I was paranoid people were going to attack me. They were coming for me. I was hearing a lot of voices, feeling a lot of fear," he said. "I just needed to protect myself. It was me or them."

Psychiatrists who assessed Williams after the attack concluded he had been "acutely psychotic".

Dr Bernard Chin said Williams was suffering from "paranoid persecutory delusions" that he was the focus of "an organised conspiracy that came about because of the machinations of the devil".

Following the guilty verdicts, NHS England's East of England division said it would commission an independent investigation into the healthcare provided to Williams "to help identify any opportunities for learning and improvement".

A month before the Huntingdon attack, a man was attacked close to Williams' home.

Two officers from Cambridgeshire Police now face a gross misconduct hearing over their handling of the alleged assault. The Independent Office for Police Conduct said one of the officers allegedly failed to conduct appropriate inquiries and both officers were alleged to have concealed this by falsely claiming no CCTV was available.

Having been in and out of court for two decades, Williams, now 33, continued his violence before boarding the train.

The day before the train attack, on 31 October, Williams carried out three knife attacks in Peterborough, injuring one person. None were recorded on CCTV.

He then went into Ritzy's Barbers in the city, threatening those inside with a knife. That incident was caught on camera. It was reported to police two hours later, but officers did not collect the CCTV until three days later - two days after the Huntingdon train stabbings.

On the morning of the Huntingdon attack, on 1 November, Williams stabbed a teenager on a Docklands Light Railway (DLR) train near Pontoon Dock station, in east London. British Transport Police (BTP) said initial CCTV of the attack was of poor quality.

However, the force tracked the knifeman to nearby Poplar DLR station where officers obtained clearer CCTV images.

Using reactive facial recognition software they generated a match with Williams, who had two addresses recorded on police systems - one in Waltham Cross, in Hertfordshire, the other in Peterborough.

Officers prioritised the Waltham Cross address because there was a "recent financial trace" to it, and it was closer to the DLR attack.

At 6:48pm that day, BTP officers turned up at the address to arrest Williams. But half an hour earlier, at 6:16pm, Williams had left his actual home - in Peterborough - to travel to the station and launch his stabbing spree on a London North Eastern Railway (LNER) train.

BTP Deputy Chief Constable Stuart Cundy said "it was certainly not for want of trying by the officers who responded and commenced our investigation immediately after the attack on the train at Pontoon Dock".

But when it comes to other incidents during Williams' chequered past, whether criminal or health-related, various authorities will now have to assess whether anything could have been done before he boarded that LNER train.

Additional reporting by Robbie Kalus

How the Huntingdon train attack unfolded - carriage by carriage

BBC News Thu, 26 Nov 2026 15:25:57 GMT

Contains some upsetting scenes.

Footballer Jonathan Gjoshe, 22, was on the 18:25 train from Doncaster to London King's Cross on 1 November last year.

Just weeks into his first season at Scunthorpe United, Gjoshe was travelling to his home in London alongside 150 other passengers.

He was sitting at a table seat in Coach J when a figure appeared over his shoulder. The figure, dressed in black, was Anthony Williams, who had boarded the train moments earlier at Peterborough at 19:26.

CCTV captured the horror of what happened next.

The London-bound train was on time, travelling through Cambridgeshire at about 122mph (196km/h), when Williams began to walk through the carriages, stabbing people with a kitchen knife.

Gjoshe was the first person to be attacked. In the ensuing terror, passengers darted for cover, hiding in locked toilets, bike racks or under seats. Others tried to flee.

When they could run no further, some tried to defend themselves as well as other passengers by using frying pans and even throwing toasters.

Williams, who has schizophrenia, has now been found guilty of 14 counts of attempted murder.

Using court testimony and first-hand accounts from the victims, this is the story of what happened during five terrifying minutes on the train.

At 19:37, Williams walked into Coach J, where Gjoshe was sitting.

The footballer was leaning slightly into the aisle when Williams appeared over his shoulder. The pair briefly made eye contact before Williams, clutching a large kitchen knife, stabbed Gjoshe seven times, including to the shoulder and bicep.

Gjoshe's adrenaline kicked in and he jumped over the table before shouting: "I've been stabbed – run!" He later told police some passengers thought he was joking and remained seated.

Sitting across from him was Dinaria Soares, who, seeing the attack, jumped to her feet and ran towards the front of the train, away from Williams.

Two rows away was 29-year-old Sachin Balakrishnan, who had been on his way to see friends. He had his headphones on and was speaking to his partner. Hearing the screaming, he stood up to see what was happening.

Williams stabbed him in the forearm and the chest. The knife passed just centimetres away from his heart, puncturing a lung. In a desperate attempt to flee he said he then "runs and runs".

David Presland, 73, was also in Coach J. In the chaos, he fell to his hands and knees in the middle of the aisle.

Williams, now standing over him, stabbed him multiple times. Presland said he was left thinking he was going to die.

Williams ignored other passengers, including a woman and child, as he moved through the carriage.

Scott Bletcher, 50, who was sitting in a far corner seat of Coach J, was on his way home to Letchworth Garden City. He had been Christmas shopping in Newark and said he had been looking forward to eating the tapas he had bought.

He presumed there had been some sort of fight or disagreement when he saw people running down the aisle. Then Williams moved in front of him. Neither of them said a word before Williams stabbed him six times to his arm and body and moved on.

Bletcher called 999, but while he was on the phone to police he told them: "Oh my God, he's coming back." Bleeding, he managed to hide in a bike rack.

William's attack in Coach J lasted just 40 seconds. In that time, at least 15 wounds had been inflicted.

Scott Green was sitting a few seats into Coach H with his cockapoo, Poppy, who had been restless as fireworks exploded outside. It was four days before Bonfire Night.

Like Bletcher, the 52-year-old initially thought a fight had broken out. Then he felt a sudden jab to his side as Williams stabbed him.

Green tried to grab the blade but was unable to take it from Williams, who he said appeared dead in the eyes.

Poppy, his dog, went into attack mode, barking at Williams who continued down the train.

Green then picked up his bag and was thrown into a toilet by a woman. Amid the chaos, came a moment of levity.

"I don't usually get in with men I've just met," she told him.

When the attack began, Kevin Deely, 58, had his earphones in and was watching a video on his phone. He tried to help an injured David Presland and later remembered telling Williams: "You don't have to do this."

Deely threw a piece of luggage as Williams continued his attack, before he too was stabbed while trying to protect another passenger, Maisie Harrison.

The first alarm on the train was pulled at 19:38. At first, the driver, Andrew Johnson, had assumed someone was messing around.

But suddenly there was banging on his cab door and a voice on the intercom shouted: "There's a knifeman stabbing people."

Johnson had just 10 seconds to decide what to do next, quickly switching the train to the slow line towards Huntingdon.

Many of the passengers on board were returning from a football match between Nottingham Forest and Manchester United. One of them was Forest fan Stephen Crean, 61, who was sitting near the buffet car. He had just bought himself a £6 meal deal.

The carriage quickly filled around him as people were running for their lives through the train carriages, including some of those who were already injured.

Crean suddenly found himself at the door, with nothing between him and the vestibule between Coach H and G.

Faced with Williams, he began to grapple with the knifeman.

He said Williams seemed to be "on a mission". As they wrestled, Williams asked him: "Do you want to die?"

During the tussle, Crean's phone fell to the floor. Williams told him to pick it up.

Williams then continued into Coach G, where passenger James Tomlinson heard him say: "You're all going to die today."

Williams then turned around and headed towards the front of the train, passing through Coach L where CCTV showed him swigging from a bottle of fortified tonic wine.

Now hiding inside a toilet, Crean also called 999. "I'm scared," he told the operator.

With nowhere else to go, passengers in first-class Coach M were preparing to defend themselves. Staff member Samir Zitouni, 48, had managed to collect frying pans from the kitchen area to use as weapons. He also placed a walking frame in the aisle in an attempt to slow Williams down.

As Williams entered the carriage, Christina Jones, who also boarded the train at Peterborough, said she would throw her hot drink at him. "He's coming this way," someone else shouted.

Car delivery driver Raza Aslam, 44, who was travelling for work, said he had thought about taking shelter in a toilet when the attack began but decided he would not be able to live with himself if he did - especially as others were injured.

For protection, he stuffed a plastic bag with an empty coffee cup down the front of his jacket and told himself: "Better than nothing."

He was handed a frying pan by Zitouni to defend himself with - but he was quickly stabbed by Williams. He said he was in disbelief at how fast the attack had happened.

By now, the first-class carriage was full of people trying to flee from Williams.

Michael Paffett, 34, one of the few passengers in the first-class section prior to the attack, suffered a fracture to his cheekbone when Williams slashed his face.

As the chaos continued, Zitouni told Williams: "We love you, we can help you." He said he thought that was a better strategy than swearing at him.

He then tried to knock the knife out of Williams's hand.

Williams launched a "prolonged, persistent and brutal" attack, stabbing him multiple times. Medics who later treated Zitouni worried for his life.

Behind Zitouni was passenger Michael Gawthorpe, who told Williams: "Please stop - we've got kids." He remembered how Williams had said: "They're trying to kill me."

Gawthorpe had been handed a toaster from the kitchen, which he threw at Williams. He said the knifeman looked back at him and he later remembered thinking: "That was me done - I've made a mistake here." He said his mind turned to his wife and daughter.

Suddenly, the train abruptly stopped.

After 15 seconds, the doors opened and passengers flooded out on to the platform at Huntingdon train station.

Zitouni walked down the platform with his white shirt stained red and collapsed, falling through the gap between the train and the platform.

Williams, now standing in a doorway, threw a bottle of tonic wine he had been swigging from.

Leaving the train, he jumped over a fence into the railway station car park.

Armed police arrived within minutes and Williams was shot with a baton gun, tasered and handcuffed.

His violent attack was brought to an end at 19:50.

Police had initially been told that nine people would likely die as a result of the attack. Yet all the victims survived.

Each had their evidence heard in court as Williams was convicted. His trial heard how Williams had "brought terror" to the train.

However, many of those onboard had tried to fend him off, putting themselves in harm's way to protect strangers.

They had, the court was told, shown extraordinary bravery.

New UK-EU treaty has 10-year termination clause

BBC News Thu, 26 Nov 2026 15:23:17 GMT

The government and the EU have published the texts of two treaties agreed last week as part of a post-Brexit reset.

The treaties were published on Thursday afternoon, alongside legislation designed to enact the bulk of the deal.

The deal covering food exports has a 10-year termination clause that would mean if one party ended the agreement, they would have to pay "reasonable and proportionate costs" to rebuild border checks infrastructure, which will be significantly scaled back as part of the new deal.

Opposition leader Kemi Badenoch has said she would scrap the deal while Reform UK's Nigel Farage has suggested he would refuse to pay.

The Brexit reset deal has already sparked debate about its benefits, its costs, and a wider discussion on the future of the UK-EU relationship.

The deal covers British food exports, emissions trading and a youth experience scheme.

Two of the three legal texts were released on Thursday, covering the food trade and emissions trading scheme deals, alongside the government's cost-cutting bill to enact the deal.

A new assessment of the impact of the deal on different sectors and regions of the country was also released.

Under the deal, food exporters will be significant beneficiaries from the scrapping of considerable red tape and checks, and dismantling of border facilities. An internal analysis forecasts a 16% boost the export of major agricultural commodities.

The industry and government hope the reduction in costs for food producers and sellers will be passed on to customers, but there may be no clear visible impact at the checkout.

Privately, industry insiders told the BBC earlier this week that there are too many moving parts in the world economy, in particular the energy price shock resulting from war in the Middle East.

Regarding the fine detail in the text of one of the treaties relating to the 10-year termination clause, European affairs minister Hamish Falconer said: "The Cutting Costs Bill allows us to implement two major trade agreements."

"It allows us to eliminate paperwork for our food and drink traders, protect billions of pounds worth of British exports from carbon taxes, and make doing business with our largest trading partner cheaper and easier."

A plan to link British and European emissions trading schemes will see more coverage across the UK's aviation and maritime industries.

The treaty text also contains finer detail of how the UK will observe, shape but not vote on relevant EU rules. The UK will be invited to attend European Commission meetings and expert groups as an observer, as well as taking part in emergency food security planning.

However, the UK will not be given voting rights.

Plans to use secondary legislation, including granting direct so-called "Henry VIII powers" to ministers to align UK and EU laws, are detailed in the legislation.

Such powers will enable ministers to make changes to bills with less Parliamentary scrutiny.

Outlining the agreement with the EU to MPs earlier this week, the prime minister said new agreements with the EU are "pragmatic" and "not a prelude to anything".

Andy Burnham also said it would be "unthinkable" for the UK to rejoin the bloc without a referendum.

Several former prime ministers have urged him not to reopen the Brexit debate. Burnham said they are "stuck in the past" and later claimed there would be "no banging on about Europe" from Labour.

Badenoch said Burnham has "oversold" the deal and was "trying to take Britain back to 2015".

UK net migration at lowest level since 1997 as asylum claims also fall

BBC News Thu, 26 Nov 2026 14:55:16 GMT

Net migration to the UK has fallen to 77,000 in the year to the end of June - the lowest level this century, other than during the pandemic, Office for National Statistics (ONS) figures show.

Excluding the limited movements of people during the worldwide travel restrictions in 2020, the figures show the number of people arriving in the UK, minus those leaving, tumbled 92% from the record high of 944,000 in the year to March 2023.

The ONS said this was the lowest net migration since 1997.

Net migration is a measure of how many extra people are added to the population in a given year.

Prime Minister Andy Burnham said the figures showed there was now "a sufficient degree of control" over the migration system.

The prime minister went on to say: "I'm not going to say all of the work is done, and I don't want to appear complacent, but I think we're finally as a country getting into the position that the public has long wanted to see."

The underlying official statistics show that an estimated 738,000 people immigrated to the UK in the year to June while 661,000 emigrated.

Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood said the figures showed that Labour had "delivered" after Conservative failures - but Chris Philp, her Tory shadow, said restrictions introduced by his party before the 2024 General Election were behind the falls.

The 77,000 figure is also the first time the UK has seen net migration in the tens of thousands since former PM David Cameron's controversial pledge 16 years ago to reach such a level.

The biggest factors in Thursday's record low were falls in the arrivals of people coming from outside Europe in three major categories of migration: The number of people coming to the UK to work fell by 45,000, asylum claims fell by 19,000 and the total number of students fell by 33,000.

These number had been expected to fall because of the tightening of visas rules that began under the previous Conservative government which was then continued by Labour from July 2024.

The effect of those policies, plus emigration from the UK, has meant that while net migration had already begun to fall, it more than halved in the last 12 months alone.

Mahmood said the figures showed the government had "restored control".

"We have brought net migration to 77,000, down 92% from its peak under the Conservatives," she said. "Where they failed, we have delivered for the British people."

This is a reference to the so-called "Boriswave" after Brexit. When the UK left the EU and its freedom of movement rules, Boris Johnson's government allowed in many more people to work and study from other parts of the world.

That led to the record-breaking arrivals in the year to March 2023. Johnson's successor, Rishi Sunak, introduced major restrictions on visas in the last months of his government.

Shadow home secretary Chris Philp said the falls were a result of those changes.

In a post on X, he called for an "annual legally binding inward migration cap, set by Parliament, at far lower levels".

Dr Ben Brindle of Oxford University's Migration Observatory, an impartial expert body, said: "We are entering an unusual period where immigration has come down and may still have further to fall - but we still have relatively high emigration, at least for the time being.

"Most of those emigrants are non-citizens, including people who arrived a few years ago when immigration was very high. That could push the net migration figures down even further next year, but the downwards blip is unlikely to last forever."

In the year to June some 73,000 people arriving in the UK seeking asylum - down from 93,000 the previous year.

As of September, the number of people who were waiting for a decision was 41,000, down 49% on the previous year.

The Home Office said that these changes were driven by speeding up the system in taking decisions and a fall in the arrivals of new claimants via "illegal entry routes" - largely meaning English Channel small boats.

As a result, the number of people accommodated in September by the Home Office was 93,000 - 16% lower than the year before. Some 52 hotels that had been dedicated to asylum seekers have been emptied this year. While some 140 are still in use the total number of people in hotels has fallen 64% to 13,000.

Responding to the latest statistics, Reform UK's home affairs spokesman Zia Yusuf said the figures were "no cause for celebration".

"This population explosion is why British people struggle to get a GP appointment, can't get housing and our prisons are overwhelmed."

Liberal Democrat asylum and immigration spokesperson Paul Kohler said: "Britain faces serious demographic and economic challenges, and urgently needs a proper immigration plan to support our economy and public services."

A spokesperson for the Green Party added: "Creating a harsh environment for migrants and people seeking asylum is not a measure of success. The British people are overwhelmingly compassionate and will not be taken in by the dangerous and opportunistic narratives of the far right."

French film actor Gérard Depardieu is to stand trial for the alleged rape of actress Charlotte Arnould, a Paris appeals court has confirmed.

Arnould, who was 22 at the time, had reported the alleged rape several days after going to his house in Paris to rehearse a play.

She has waived her right to anonymity and her lawyer said Thursday's ruling was a "first" and the forthcoming trial would be historic.

Depardieu, 77, had contested his indictment on two counts of rape. In a letter published in Le Figaro in 2023, Depardieu strongly denied Arnould's allegations, saying "there was never any coercion or violence between us".

Depardieu was for decades a leading figure in French and international cinema for roles in Green Card, The Man in the Iron Mask and the Asterix films. He was awarded France's Légion d'honneur in 1996.

But in recent years a series of allegations have been made against him over his conduct on film sets and elsewhere in the wake of France's #MeToo movement, known as balance ton porc (call out your pig).

Last year, he was given an 18-month suspended jail term after he was found guilty of sexually assaulting two women on a film set in Paris in May. He was also placed on the sex offenders register and ordered to pay compensation.

He dropped his appeal against the ruling last week and offered "sincere apologies" for his behaviour on the set of director Jean Becker's 2021 film Les Volets Verts (The Green Shutters).

Depardieu had been a friend of Charlotte Arnould's father and on 7 August 2018 she had gone to his home, where much of what happened was captured on the actor's own CCTV.

Arnould's case was initially dismissed for insufficient evidence, but after she filed a civil complaint, a judicial investigation was opened in the summer of 2020.

Speaking outside the Paris appeal court on Thursday, her lawyer Carine Durrieu Diebolt said the ruling was a victory for her client for whom it was "genuinely a relief".

The appeal court said that while Depardieu should stand trial for what took place on that day, he would not be tried for a further alleged rape at a hotel six days later.

Millions of people to see average monthly mortgage payments rise by £100

BBC News Thu, 26 Nov 2026 14:00:20 GMT

More people face higher mortgage repayments when they roll off a fixed deal than previously estimated, new figures from the the Bank of England show.

About 6.5 million owners are forecast to see their monthly repayment jump by £100 on average when they move onto their next deal by the end of 2029, new data in its Financial Stability Report reveals.

That is more the double the £45-a-month hike that the Bank estimated in its last report in July.

In the shorter term, about one million of those homeowners, who are on mortgage rates below 3% and due to refinance by the end of next year, will see an average £200 increase in their monthly repayments.

For borrowers, the interest rate on a fixed mortgage does not change until it expires, usually after two or five years, and a new one is chosen to replace it. The vast majority of homeowners and buyers have this kind of mortgage.

Since the Iran war began, global economic uncertainty has been pushing up the cost of deals, with the average rates on two and five year fixed mortgages at their highest for about three years.

On Thursday, the average rate on a two-year deal was 5.99%, and at 6% for a five-year deal, according to the financial information service Moneyfacts.

Analysts have described the situation as "brutal" for homeowners coming to the end of their fixed deals.

However, the Bank's report points out that the average £100 increase in monthly repayments was half the rise experienced by those refinancing during 2023 and 2024.

Dawn Fazackerley-King is a Pilates instructor who lives near Ipswich and has previously spoken to the BBC about her struggles with the cost of living.

She was on a five-year fixed deal at 1.4%, which she took out in January 2022. But the mother-of-two is about to refix for two years and the best deal she can find is a 5.69% loan. That will push her costs up by about £200 a month.

She is far from alone, with one million homeowners facing a similar increase often because they are coming off deals that were agreed before interest rates began rising in 2022.

The Bank's report said that households facing higher payments "may need to reduce discretionary spending or draw down savings as higher energy and other essential costs feed through".

Most had savings buffers but lower-income households, including renters, had less wriggle room owing to spending a greater proportion of their income on essentials.

Early in November, the Bank raised the benchmark interest rate, which influences borrowing costs for individuals and businesses, for the first time in more than three years, from 3.75% to 4%.

The numbers could change were mortgage rates to fall, primarily if international economic volatility eased.

Even so, the Bank said around 350,000 were already projected to see monthly mortgage repayments fall when they fixed their next deal within three years.

The report also suggested there were no signs of an increase in borrowers defaulting on their loans, while UK households remained resilient.

"We have not seen the scale of mortgage arrears that we saw if you go back to earlier periods, the early 90s, the early 80s, actually even the financial crisis. And we are not seeing the scale of house repossessions, and that has to be a good thing," said the Bank's governor, Andrew Bailey.

However, separately, the Bank warned that cyber attacks had become a more prominent threat to the UK's financial stability.

Financial firms needed to "keep pace with the growing scale and sophistication of cyber threats", the report said.

Number of young people out of work or training still stubbornly high, data shows

BBC News Thu, 26 Nov 2026 13:55:02 GMT

There were just under one million young people aged 16 to 24 not in employment, education or training (Neet) in the UK in the three months to September, according to new data.

Thursday's figures from the Office for National Statistics (ONS) recorded 959,000 people who were Neet in that time, a very slight increase on the same period a year ago, though the number of women who were Neet was at its highest in a decade.

The data comes a week after a major review by former government minister Alan Milburn set out a series of recommendations to bring the numbers down.

Work and Pensions Secretary Pat McFadden said the government was "fundamentally reforming how we support young people".

Thursday's figures from the ONS suggest there were 17,000 more young people who were not earning or learning this summer compared to the same period last year.

The overall number of 959,000 young people who were Neet this summer represents 12.7% - about one in eight - of the whole UK population aged 16 to 24.

The rate has dropped slightly, by 0.3 percentage points, compared to earlier in the year, with 22,000 fewer young people recorded as Neet between July and September than in April to June.

The Neets data tends to fluctuate across the year with seasonal hiring patterns and academic summer holidays.

The changes in the latest figures are also within the margin of error of the Labour Force Survey which the stats are based on.

In his long-awaited report into youth employment, published earlier this month, Milburn set out proposals aimed at bringing the Neet rate down to 5% over the next decade.

If successful, that would put the UK in line with some of the lowest rates in Europe. Currently, only Romania has a higher Neet rate than the UK.

Milburn called for a "whole system reset" across education, health and welfare to achieve that. It would include an overhaul of the benefits system for under-25s, new legal rights to work and training opportunities and plans to expand college places and double the number of young people taking up apprenticeships.

The government has broadly accepted Milburn's proposals, but is yet to respond to all the plans in detail.

In the data, Neets can be categorised as either unemployed - which means they are actively seeking work - or economically inactive - meaning they are not seeking work, which could be because of illness or caring responsibilities.

Most young people who are Neet fall into the economically inactive category, with 596,000 young people economically inactive in the latest stats, compared to 363,000 who were unemployed.

Overall, there are still more young men who are Neet (483,000) but the number of young women who are Neet is at its highest level in a decade, at 476,000.

Ben Harrison, from the Work Foundation at Lancaster University, says the higher number of women out of work could be partly down to the loss of a "significant" number of jobs in retail, a sector in which "historically, many young women have taken their first steps into work".

Responding to the latest Neets figures, McFadden said "every one" of the young people out of education, employment or training "deserves better".

"That's why we're fundamentally reforming how we support young people to grow up in this country," he said.

He said the government was "building a new settlement that invests in young people's success instead of paying for failure" in the wake of the Milburn review.

"That includes a Jobs Guarantee offering eligible young people on universal credit a fully funded six-month job, as well as thousands more work experience placements, and youth hubs bringing employment, health, and skills support under one roof."

BBC News Thu, 26 Nov 2026 13:24:22 GMT

The Ministry of Defence has written to ex-military personnel to check their contact details and skills against the backdrop of a rising "threat environment", Defence Secretary Wes Streeting has said.

It comes after The Times and the Telegraph reported that reservists who previously served in the Armed Forces have received letters telling them to prepare to be called up for war.

Streeting told BBC Radio 4's Today programme that this meant should they ever be needed "either for a national disaster here at home or for a more serious threat or conflict elsewhere" then they would "know where our strategic reserve is" and what their skills were.

"I want the country to be alert, not alarmed," he said.

"You can't not look at what's going on in Europe and not be concerned about a threat environment which has deteriorated in recent years and is sadly increasing," Streeting told Today.

"We saw last Friday a very serious incident – the incursion into Polish airspace by Russian missiles, we've seen state-sponsored terrorism waged by Russia across Europe, we've obviously had incidents concerning Iran around RAF bases here in the UK.

"And so against that backdrop, against that threat environment, the government and the country has to be ready to face down those risks."

He added: "Because the more ready we are the less likely we are to find ourselves in a conflict, in a war, that is my goal, that is the goal of this government."

Streeting told BBC Breakfast that "if, God forbid, this country did find itself at war" and there was then an inquiry, the Ministry of Defence would be criticised if the government had not kept its records up-to-date."

The Telegraph reported that the letters offered opportunities to volunteer for training and exercises.

This is not a case of pressing the panic button for imminent war, but more one of good housekeeping.

When Britain went to war in Iraq in 2003 the MoD had a poor grasp of who might be available to serve, what current skills they had and what their up-to-date contact details were. So they obviously don't want to be in that situation if there is a national crisis in the future that triggers a mobilisation.

Twenty three years on, the Ukraine war has changed everything. It's brought a hot war to the very borders of Nato, it's exposed the dangers of having too few troops available, but most of all it has changed the nature of warfare.

People who have spent their adult lives never touching a weapon can turn out to be extraordinarily skilled drone operators, those with a talent for electronics, radio and signals work have a vital role to play in electronic warfare.

So this exercise by the government, probably long overdue, is about knowing who can do what and where they can be contacted.

Justin Crump, a former Army officer and now CEO of the business intelligence firm Sibylline, told the BBC: "Ukraine has shown us the importance of mobilising civilian skills and approaches in modern warfare. This is a first step, and an overdue one in many ways, with the effort likely to increase through early 2027. [It is] very much a part of deterrence and not an intention to use people".

He said veterans - a sometimes misleading term for men and women who are often in peak physical shape and fitness - that he has contacted have generally responded positively to the move. "After all", he said, "they signed up to help before, but want to make sure their enhanced skills and talents are valued".

The MoD's decision to contact ex-military personnel comes after news that the UK has signed an £8bn contract to upgrade its nuclear submarine fleet, which the defence secretary said would help get the country "warfighting ready".

Meanwhile, Streeting also praised the Duke of Sussex's "patriotic spirit" after the former Army officer said he would rejoin the armed forces again if needed.

Asked whether there could be a role for Harry, the defence secretary told Today: "I'm always happy to talk to him about how we can work together, whether that's through his Invictus Games, which does a brilliant job supporting our veterans and giving them opportunities to take part in those amazing and inspiring competitive sporting events, but he does have experience to bring to bear."

Streeting praised the "service he's given to our country" and the fact he had spoken about his "willingness and readiness to serve".

"I think that's exactly the sort of patriotic spirit we're looking for," he said.

"I think it's that sort of patriotic spirit we'll find throughout our strategic reserve."

Last week, Harry, who spent a decade in the forces and served on the front line in Afghanistan, said: "If asked to sign up again, if the need is there, then I will 100% be there to serve my country, alongside my fellow veterans and service personnel."

'Laughing gas has ended careers' - so how common is it in football?

BBC News Thu, 26 Nov 2026 06:18:30 GMT

This video can not be played

Watch: Moment Raheem Sterling arrested after car crash

It is known as laughing gas but the impact nitrous oxide can have on a professional footballer's body is anything but funny.

"I'm not going to name names but I have colleagues who know Premier League footballers who are no longer playing as a direct result of nitrous oxide [use]," said Dr David Nicholl.

Nicholl, a clinical lead in neurology with Sandwell and West Birmingham NHS Trust, was speaking after former Manchester City, Chelsea, Liverpool and England forward Raheem Sterling was handed a suspended jail term after pleading guilty to dangerous driving.

A key part of the case was that Sterling had been inhaling nitrous oxide from a balloon while driving.

His Lamborghini was seen veering across a motorway and later crashed into a metal gate. Sterling, 31, was arrested at the scene and found with six gas canisters in his car.

He disclosed to custody staff "he had a problem with nitrous oxide", the court was told.

Defending Sterling, Jason Bartfeld KC said his client "recognised the various unhealthy coping mechanisms that brought him to this position" and that he has "sought to address" these in the "most positive and effective way and with some success".

So, what is nitrous oxide, how does it affect those who take it and is its use more common in footballers than the wider population?

This video can not be played

Footage was released of the footballer driving dangerously

Nitrous oxide's original use was as a sedative that healthcare providers like dentists could use to keep patients comfortable during procedures.

It is now legally sold for catering, medical and industrial purposes, but is frequently used as a recreational drug and is commonly known as laughing gas.

This can be abused by inhaling the gas via a balloon, leading to a short-term high causing symptoms such as brief euphoria, mild perceptual changes and uncontrollable laughter, external.

Nitrous oxide also slows brain and body responses and can displace oxygen in the lungs and bloodstream, contributing to dizziness, confusion or fainting.

It is thought long-term or excessive use can have disastrous effects on the body, from neurological harms to nerve and spinal cord damage which could lead to permanent disability.

According to medical journal The Lancet, it is now the third most commonly used drug after cannabis and cocaine in the UK, with use highest among people aged 16–24 years.

It has been increasing in popularity as a recreational drug over the past decade.

This prompted it to be reclassified as a Class C drug in 2023 after a government consultation.

This video can not be played

Does football have a nitrous oxide problem?

BBC Sport has been told the abuse of so-called laughing gas has been widespread among professional footballers for a long time.

Former player Drewe Broughton is now a human performance coach, working with Premier League footballers and clubs around the world.

He said laughing gas was seen by some as a release.

"I think the use of nitrous oxide is really common," he added.

"It's something that can be done in private. It's something that can be hidden. You can't smell it on their clothes or the breath. It's an underground thing."

Broughton said he had been in the company of professional players when they had been using 'balloons'.

"I remember sitting in a players' house on the outskirts of Manchester, and these canisters were all over the floor," he added.

"I was from a world where people drank or they gambled or went to pubs and nightclubs. That was my first exposure to it."

Broughton has developed an app to help tackle issues with mental health and under-performance in football.

He said the reasons to use nitrous oxide had always been there: pressure on players to perform leaves them searching for an escape.

But Broughton has concerns about the toll nitrous oxide can take.

"I don't think there's the same awareness around nitrous oxide and damage to the body as there would be around alcohol or other drugs," he said.

BBC Sport has been told that some footballers see laughing gas as an alternative to harder substances because it does not stay in the body's system for more than a few hours.

Luci Hanmer, who works with Lancashire drugs and alcohol support charity 'We Are With You', said a substance like nitrous oxide was hard to detect.

She said: "Anything that you're inhaling, the effects that you're going to feel happen very soon.

"So if you are looking for that escapism, the effects are going to be quick.

"Once ingested, it doesn't last very long within your body compared to some of the other substances which can be detected for quite a number of days.

"So if you're getting a drugs test the next day for example, that won't show up."

Sterling given suspended sentence for dangerous driving

Former Manchester City defender Nedum Onuoha said more support was needed, particularly for players like Sterling who break through young.

Sterling made his debut for Liverpool and England at just 17 - before going on to win four Premier League titles at Manchester City and 82 caps for his country, including the Euro 2020 final at Wembley.

"Look at what's happened to Raheem," he said. "Look at how this led to this moment, a moment which I'm sure he's hugely embarrassed about, because I'm sure he can see how dangerous that was to not just his life, but the lives of so many people who are on the road at the same time.

"But I just don't feel like football is in a position where they think it's important to support people who have issues with nitrous oxide."

The BBC Radio 5 live pundit said the use of nitrous oxide in professional footballing circles was very common.

"I think the difference from when I was younger is that people would openly party in certain places," he said.

"Now they party where they're harder to spot. That's why you don't really see on a week-to-week basis now the scandal of somebody that's been out drinking.

"The players are doing it, but it's more sophisticated in terms of how they do it, the locations, and this is an example here with nitrous oxide."

Neurologist Dr Nicholl has been working with patients who have abused nitrous oxide for years and issued a warning to others.

"It certainly is being used by footballers, but it's pretty much the worst thing that you want to be using if you're a professional sportsperson," he said.

"It damages your spinal cord and the spinal cord is a bit like an electrical cable, where the insulation - the outside of that cable - gets stripped away.

"So what patients will complain of is difficulty with feeling on their hands or feet, or unable to walk at all.

"So, in effect, it's like a spinal cord injury. But they can also get blood clots, deep vein thrombosis, pulmonary emboli, and some patients have died."

Desperate appeals from women on death row in Iran after protests

BBC News Thu, 26 Nov 2026 06:01:58 GMT

Taraneh Rahimi is on death row in Iran.

In recent weeks, the 21-year-old has been unable to walk properly after her legs were beaten, and an ear-infection caused by an untreated head injury has affected her balance, her cousin says.

She is "keeping her spirits up" but "there are days she breaks down in tears," Masoud Nourmohammadi tells BBC News Persian.

He says Taraneh and her twin sister Romina were arrested after joining the anti-government protests that swept the country in January.

When the twins' mother first saw them in prison, their faces were so swollen and bruised, and their hair pulled out, that she could only recognise them by their voices, Nourmohammadi says, speaking from the US.

He says Taraneh signed a confession after interrogators threatened that her sister would be raped in front of her.

Taraneh is one of six women who have been sentenced to death this year in connection with the January protests, according to the UN's human rights rapporteur for Iran, Mai Sato.

The figure for men is much higher. However, women protesters and dissidents are being sentenced to death in numbers not seen for decades, as part of a "horrific rise" in politically motivated executions, Amnesty International's Iran researcher Raha Bahreini says.

The Iranian embassy in London told the BBC that claims of an increase in the use of the death penalty in protest-related cases were "misleading".

It categorically rejected allegations of the use of torture and any allegations that the death penalty has been imposed solely for peaceful protest, which it said is a "legitimate, and protected right".

It said death sentences in relation to the "riot in January 2026" were issued in cases involving "intentional murder" or "Moharebeh (the taking up of weapons with the intent to threaten or wreck the people's lives or property)".

The twins were seized in late January, Nourmohammadi says.

It was two weeks after the end of the protests, which began in late December over economic grievances and grew to become Iran's largest against the clerical establishment since the 1979 Islamic Revolution.

The US-based Human Rights Activists News Agency (Hrana) says it has identified more than 7,000 people killed in the crackdown that followed, most of them protesters, but believes the true figure is much higher.

The Iranian government accuses the US and Israel of fomenting the unrest, blaming "terrorists" and "rioters" for the deaths, which it says totalled 3,117 including some members of the security forces.

The twins' family did not find out where they were being held for more than three months, their cousin says. They were tried over protests in Isfahan, in an area of the city where a member of the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) security force was killed.

Court documents have not been published, but the BBC has seen part of a sentencing document which says Taraneh was convicted of moharebeh, which is a capital offence under Iran's Islamic Penal Code. The offence included "drawing a bladed weapon with the intent to endanger people's lives", according to the document.

Romina was sentenced to 25 years in jail for the lesser charge of aiding and abetting moharebeh, according to Sato, the UN rapporteur.

Nourmohammadi, who has been in contact with relatives and others in Iran familiar with the case, says both women deny all the charges against them and that there is no evidence Taraneh had a "bladed weapon".

Sato says the sisters were part of a case in which 10 people were sentenced to death, but that there was "no clarification of the acts attributed to each individual".

According to sources familiar with the case, the twins' lawyers have submitted a complaint alleging they were tortured and sexually abused during interrogation, but the investigation into it is being overseen by an official they accuse of torture.

Voice messages from other women on death row contain a mixture of desperation and defiance.

Mahboubeh Shabani - widely reported to be 33 and a civil engineer - was sentenced to death in September under Iran's espionage law after transporting injured protesters, according to rights groups.

She called for help for herself and other prisoners from jail in the city of Mashhad in north-eastern Iran: "Everyone is in a terrible place mentally, especially those whose sentences have been finalised," she said.

Also jailed in Mashhad is Najmeh Amini, reported to be 23, who was initially arrested in the wake of the January protests, and later sentenced to death after being convicted of committing blasphemy in a social media post, according to rights groups.

"As long as I am alive, I have one hope, and that is to see a free and prosperous Iran before my life ends by the noose," a voice message attributed to her says.

In addition, Mojdeh Hashemi Bazargani - reported to be aged 27 - is also facing execution, according to rights groups. They say she was convicted of charges including "espionage", after being arrested in April, during the current war between Iran and Israel and the US.

The US-based Iranian rights group Tavaana has shared audio it says is of a phone call she made from prison, describing being beaten in the head, neck and body and made to sign a confession.

The woman in the recording says: "They accused me of espionage. They say you've been paid for it. If I had been paid for espionage, I would have a car or a house. I have nothing."

Amnesty International describes the charges in all three of these cases and also the twins as "politically motivated".

In response to the BBC's questions, the Iranian Embassy in London said "any allegations of the use of torture in connection with the mentioned cases are categorically rejected". It did not comment further on individual cases, but said "confessions obtained under duress have no legal validity".

At least 39 people have already been executed in connection with the January protests, according to Sato.

She notes a "sharp" increase in arrests and sentences across both men and women, and sees the rise in death sentences for women as an "escalation and expansion" of an "established pattern of repression".

Iranian human rights lawyer Musa Barzin, who is based in Turkey, says "it appears that factors such as gender or age now carry less weight in determining the severity of punishment".

Official detail on cases is often scant and some may go unreported.

However, Sato says as well as the six women she identified as being arrested in connection with protests, a further three have received death sentences this year - for "blasphemy" and "corruption on Earth charges, in relation to the war in March" and "espionage and moharebeh".

In comparison, these nine sentences are more than Hrana recorded for women for similar offences over the whole decade to 2025 - with no more than three in any one year.

The death sentences in three of the cases Sato identified as being linked to the protests have since been overturned – though two of those have been sent for retrial. She says she is concerned by an "increasingly frequent pattern" where overturned death sentences are later "reimposed by a parallel branch of the judiciary once public attention has subsided".

Sato says there was a "turning point" for women in Iran during the 2022 protests over the death of Mahsa Amini, who died in custody after being detained over an alleged breach of Iran's dress code.

Women "were at the forefront of challenging state policies and structures of control," says Sato. "Their political agency, visibility and leadership have made them targets of state repression."

The Iranian embassy said judicial proceedings in Iran are conducted in accordance with the Constitution and rule of law. It adds: "Cases involving the death penalty have included charges such as serious criminal offences, violence, terrorism, espionage, cooperation with hostile intelligence services and Moharebeh."

Iran executes more people per head of population than any other country, according to UN experts. Human rights groups say last year saw the highest number in decades.

Hrana recorded 2,003 executions in the year to October 2026. The vast majority - including 47 women - were for crimes such as murder and drug trafficking.

Nourmohammadi says the family are trying as best they can to support the twins.

Romina enjoys music and often asks relatives to play songs over the phone, he says.

Taraneh loves horses and has always wanted to set up a horse breeding centre, he says, and they tell her they plan to help her do so in the future: "That's how we try to give her hope."

When Scott Peden thinks of the night his family died in a fire caused by an e-bike battery, he has one overriding regret: "That I lived, and they didn't."

An inquest recorded conclusions of death by misadventure.

Lilly, he says, was "the cheekiest little girl you've ever met" while "Oliver loved his motorbikes, he loved his cars and, most of all, he loved his sister.

"They had such an amazing relationship. It's unlike any siblings I've ever seen. Most siblings argue and fight, but these two just didn't."

Peden bought the e-bike in order to travel to and from his job in retail.

It had been plugged in under the stairs to recharge.

He says the night of the fire at their Sackville Close home was "just a normal night", but about 45 minutes before his early-morning alarm for work was due to go off, the family were woken by a bang.

He went out of the bedroom to see what was happening and was confronted by flames.

"The only way I could describe it is an old World War Two scene where they've got flame-throwers. It was just shooting up the stairs with such ferocity," he says.

It appeared the walls were "dripping fire" and he ran to the window to call for help.

"I looked back and Gemma was panicking trying to get the kids together and I told her I'll be right back," he said.

"I didn't realise how bad it was."

He jumped out of the window, went through the back door and saw the house engulfed in flames.

When he got to the bike, he says he "realised there's no way I can put this out".

He was unable to get it out of the building and even tried to kick the charger out of the wall.

But realising "there's nothing I can do", he called to Germeney to jump.

"I never heard from them again," he says.

Peden, who broke an ankle jumping from the window and also suffered burns, was placed in an induced coma for four weeks and woke to be told that his family and their two dogs had been killed.

In that moment, he says, he felt "lost".

"I'd been in a relationship with Gemma for 14 years and we were talking about marriage. She was the one."

He is still dealing with the physical effects of the fire and says: "I'm not the same person that jumped out that window. That person has died.

"The person I am now is a nerve-stricken mess. Work have to let me know every time they are doing a fire drill because if I hear a fire alarm, my heart starts jumping."

On the purchase of the e-bike, Peden says he feels he has been "punished for three years for trying to make my life a little bit easier".

The inquest heard it had been modified and the battery was a second-hand replacement, but the coroner said there was insufficient evidence for her to find that repairs done to the battery had caused the blaze.

Prior to the inquest, Cambridgeshire Fire and Rescue Service wrote to the coroner, requesting they push for better regulation of online sales of e-bike batteries.

Assistant chief fire officer Stuart Smith told the BBC he had the same concerns about the secondhand market in lithium ion batteries.

He said there also needed to be "a cultural change", particularly around charging phones, tablets and other devices overnight.

"The advice from us, really, is please follow the manufacturer's guidance and only use the charging device supplied with the battery," he explained.

"Make sure you are alert and awake so you are able to switch it off when it is 100% charged, and can keep an eye on the temperature, and think about where you are charging them, should something happen."

Since the fire, Peden has campaigned for tighter regulations, highlighting the death of Elisha Brabin and three of her children in Bootle, Merseyside, last month, caused by an e-scooter lithium-ion battery that was on charge at the time.

"It seems like no-one's learnt a thing in the three years since," he says.

He is fundraising to cover the cost of his legal representation at the inquest, saying: "I'm just so determined that this doesn't get swept under the rug as another tragic accident. I won't allow it. And I won't stop."

Speaking after the inquest concluded, he welcomed coroner Elizabeth Gray's request for submissions about a possible prevention of future deaths report.

"We need this... report to come out and the government and the Secretary of State [for Business] to actually pay attention this time," he said.

Seabird ‘spies’ could help spot ships that aren’t broadcasting their location

New Scientist November 25, 2026

Audio from seabirds fitted with mini recording devices and GPS trackers has been used by researchers to show that marine life can record encounters with vessels that are otherwise difficult to track.

Many large vessels are now legally required to carry automatic identification systems broadcasting their identity and location at regular intervals. Although this has allowed interactions between animals and fisheries to be studied at scale, there are enormous gaps in coverage.

In fact, recent research suggests that three-quarters of industrial fishing vessels don’t use the technology, says Jonathan Rutter at the University of Oxford. This is partly because regulations on the types of vessels that are required to share data vary by country. Large satellite ‘blind spots’ also contribute to the problem, he says, and so does subterfuge for the purpose of illegal, unreported and unregulated fishing (IUU).

Advertisement

Most large fishing boats go untracked as ‘dark vessels’

Rutter says that being caught as bycatch in fishing is one of the greatest risks to seabird populations, but if fishing vessels are only tracked “with conventional methods, such footprints of risk may be strikingly incomplete”.

The team analysed audio collected from devices attached to seven northern gannets (Morus bassanus) and found that one third of the audio detections couldn’t be matched with vessel tracking data – mostly off the UK coast.

Overall, 12 per cent of the vessel detections made by the four critically endangered Balearic shearwaters (Puffinus mauretanicus) included in the study couldn’t be matched to public data. But given the high vessel density where they were – off the Catalan coast – the researchers estimated that up to 20 per cent of the vessels detected by the four birds weren’t broadcasting their identity.

Tammy Davies at BirdLife International – a global partnership of non-governmental organisations – who wasn’t involved in the study, says the research could “give us a more complete picture of the risks seabirds face at sea” and “ultimately, this could contribute to better assessments of bycatch risk and help identify fisheries and areas where conservation measures are most needed”.

Peter Ejbye-Ernst at the Netherlands Institute for the Study of Crime and Law Enforcement (NSCR), describes the study as “fascinating” from a green criminology point of view, too.

“What this study is somewhat proposing is that we can also look outside of humans for witnesses too,” he says, which overcomes a key barrier in observing crime at sea.

In terms of its applications for cracking down on IUU, he says: “There’s a fine line between trying to understand something better and document it and then trying to control it and surveil it.”

There are caveats, as the study has a small sample size and records both false-negatives and false-positives. It also gives very little information on the type of activity vessels were carrying out. But, while the research isn’t a solution to the problem of IUU, it is “part of the toolbox” for understanding what is happening at sea, says Ejbye-Ernst.

The study didn’t differentiate between the size of vessels, but Rutter and his colleagues say this would be a good area for future research.

Photographer Nicole Tung captures the tough world facing South-East Asia’s fishers and their families in this series of images, which won her the Carmignac Photojournalism Award for fieldwork

“Animal-borne audio recorders could potentially be used to investigate other ecological interactions and human activities that are difficult to observe directly, particularly in the marine environment,” says team member Ana Bertoldi Carneiro, also at BirdLife International.

Hugo Tagholm at the charity Oceana says it is shocking that so many of the interactions were with unseen vessels, but he is concerned about attaching devices to seabirds on a broader scale to track this.

“Seabirds are already grappling with the harm caused by overfishing and climate breakdown, we don’t want to put them at even greater risk from vessel operators acting illegally,” he says.

“What we need is mandatory remote electronic monitoring across all fishing vessels, clear and effective laws and catch limits to protect and restore our seas, and truly deterrent sanctions for those breaking the law.”

Science Advances DOI: 10.1126/sciadv. aeh2224
