AI’s stunning progress in maths shows how little we understand it

New Scientist November 25, 2026

There is a story, possibly apocryphal, that when the mathematician G. H. Hardy was about to undertake a dangerous sea voyage, he sent a postcard to a colleague declaring “I have solved the Riemann hypothesis”. Hardy, a staunch atheist, joked that this would prevent his ship from sinking, as God would never let him claim the credit for such a major result without revealing the details of his proof.

Hardy would probably be both astonished and aghast that we now have what seems to be a proof of the Riemann hypothesis, a problem that has vexed mathematicians since the 19th century, but that no one yet understands it. The consensus among mathematicians is that the proof, produced with the aid of AI, will hold, but that it will take much more work to make it comprehensible to humans.

However you feel about AI, this is a watershed moment, and one that demonstrates just how little we still understand about the capabilities of the technology. As recently as last month, leading mathematician Terence Tao speculated that AI would eventually solve the Riemann hypothesis, but that it may not happen before 2050. Now, some mathematicians are considering whether their hardest and most infamous remaining problems could be settled within months. In a year that has left mathematicians reeling, this may be the knock-out blow.

Advertisement

This is a watershed moment, and it shows just how little we understand about AI’s abilities

For non-mathematicians, the fall of the Riemann hypothesis is harder to interpret. In the past year, AI has seen incredible advances in both maths and coding, but it is perhaps no coincidence that in these arenas, with nothing more than computer code, answers can swiftly be checked and iterated upon, allowing for rapid improvement. When it comes to other human endeavours though, from art to zoology, such verification is far harder, involving either the messy physical world, or unknowable human taste – or both. Whether this verification gap can be closed may become the biggest question of our age. Answers on a postcard, please.

It has been called the hardest problem in mathematics, and now through a combination of human ingenuity and relentlessness, and the computational power of AI, the Riemann hypothesis may have finally been solved

Is The Time Traveler’s Wife the perfect audiobook to experience on shuffle?

New Scientist November 25, 2026

Feedback is our weekly column of bizarre stories, implausible advertising claims, confusing instructions and more

Reader Jenny Ozanne writes to tell us of a horrific incident that befell her partner. He had bought Audrey Niffenegger’s novel The Time Traveler’s Wife as a CD audiobook, to listen to on long car journeys.

“After a while, he complained that the plot was completely impossible to follow,” writes Jenny. “It was only when I checked his player that I realized he had accidentally set the CD to ‘shuffle’. “

Advertisement

Jenny raises two points, which Feedback heartily endorses: “I’m still not sure what’s more impressive: the story’s ability to survive total chronological chaos, or the fact that he listened to three random chapters before suspecting anything was wrong.”

Feedback would suggest that The Time Traveler’s Wife might be the ideal novel to experience on shuffle, since the narrative is heavily non-linear. The main character hops uncontrollably back and forth through history. This led us to wonder: would any similarly chrono-displaced stories survive the experience of being played on shuffle, or even be improved by it?

We wondered, for instance, about David Mitchell’s Cloud Atlas. This has six stories set in different periods, including a future in which human clones are used as cheap labour, and a more distant future in which everything has gone a bit Mad Max. The stories are linked by characters in later timelines reading about the earlier ones, and by subtle coincidences. What would it be like on shuffle?

However, after careful reflection, we realised there is only one correct answer to this, and that is Shane Carruth’s 2004 film Primer, which tells the story of two tech bros who invent a time machine in their garage. At first, they use it to go back in time and make money on the stock exchange, only to become caught up in an escalating web of betrayal and deception as they endlessly rewrite their lives.

Primer is so overcomplicated, so mind-wreckingly confusing, that some poor soul once went so far as to draw a diagram trying to convey its timeline. Posted on Reddit by u/Clawz114, the diagram looks like a cross between a metro map and a flowchart of the inner workings of a chemical factory. It is therefore possible that playing the scenes in random order might actually cause the film to make more sense.

It’s that time of year when many of us are thinking, “Oh blimey, I need to buy everyone presents” and then having a meltdown when we can’t think of anything. The last refuge of the true gift scoundrel is, of course, the scented candle. This item might as well come with a note saying, “Sorry, I couldn’t think of anything”.

Readers looking to step up their scented candle game may wish to investigate JD + Kate Industries, which is run by a pair of humour writers with a sideline in themed scented candles. They have taken these tedious items to new and different places.

For instance, consider the Late Bronze Age Collapse scented candle, which “commemorates everyone’s favorite late 13th century [BC] widespread societal collapse”. Happily, it doesn’t smell of violence and decay, but rather of “burning cedar”, since “Lebanese cedar was a popular building material in the Late Bronze Age”.

Those with more contemporary tastes may wish to consider the AI scented candle, which has a little sculpture of a data centre on the top, “surrounded by a post-apocalyptic, bombed-out city”. What does it smell of, you ask? “Diesel generator exhaust fumes”.

Finally, those nostalgic for the headier days of space exploration might appreciate the Apollo 11 scented candle. Disappointingly, this doesn’t smell of moon dust, which, as we understand it, basically smells of burning because it reacts with oxygen on contact. Instead, its scent mimics “a certain powdered orange drink mix often associated with the space program, but that was not brought on Apollo 11. The astronauts brought a generic, grapefruit-flavored powdered drink mix instead, because they selfishly did not consider us and our desire to market candles.”

Feedback has no idea if these candles are any good, but we enjoyed JD + Kate’s website a lot.

Let us foray once again into the wonderful world of scientific acronyms. First, two reader claims that, for reasons that will become obvious, we cannot verify.

Michael Berkson tells us: “As a solicitor my late wife was involved in development of insurance for doctors. The firm had to tell the client that they needed to choose a better name. Their original choice was Professional Indemnity Support Scheme.” Michael says the clients were open to replacing “scheme” with “service”, which helps not at all.

Likewise, Jim Taylor asserts that he was once confronted with a military programme intended to ensure that spare parts would always be available for key equipment. It was called the Contractor Repair Advanced Provisioning System.

Finally, a story we can confirm is true because we looked it up. Reader Geraldine Beare is an indexer, which is one of those jobs that we often forget about but would swiftly notice if it wasn’t done. “I am at present indexing a book on goats,” says Geraldine. Through this assignment she has learned the acronym “OMAGOD”, which she recommends saying “quickly, or perhaps in a vaguely Scottish accent”. It actually stands for ovine mouth and gum obscure disease.

Our verdict on Dark Eden by Chris Beckett: ‘Holy cow. Chapter 44!’

New Scientist November 25, 2026

Since starting the New Scientist Book Club in May 2023, I have aimed to vary our books as much as possible, moving between science fiction and popular science, older classics and the hottest new titles. Occasionally, though, I’m afraid I let the power go to my head and just choose one of my own personal favourites. That’s what I did in November, with Chris Beckett’s novel Dark Eden, a book I’ve loved ever since it won the Arthur C. Clarke award in 2013.

Set on the planet Eden, a sunless world that drifts alone far outside the Milky Way, this follows the descendants of two astronauts who were marooned there over a century earlier. Now numbering 532 people, they tell each other stories of the world their ancestors came from, and struggle to survive on this dark, cold planet as they await the return of “one of those sky-boats with lights on them”. I think it is all wildly imaginative and original and exciting. So it was with some trepidation that I awaited the verdict of my fellow book club members on our Discord channel. I really wanted everyone else to love it, too!

Free newsletter

It started well. “I managed not to stay up all night reading, but the temptation was definitely there – I am hooked,” wrote Dee55. Les was similarly gripped. “Started it? I’ve only gone and finished it, haven’t I? It really got me in, and I found it a fascinating exploration of social anthropology and linguistics in a very small, isolated population. And the world-building was fascinating, too – very different flora and fauna.”

Advertisement

Several other members also cited the strength of the world-building in Dark Eden. I also love the lanternflowers and woollybucks of this planet, and was fascinated to learn, in an essay Chris wrote for book club members, that, when creating a world for a story, he doesn’t “usually seek to make the whole thing scientifically accurate, but I try to make it hang together in a way that feels coherent”. I think he definitely succeeds in that here.

Dark Eden, the November read for the New Scientist Book Club, takes place on a rogue planet outside the Milky Way. Award-winning author Chris Beckett explains how he thought through the science behind this night world

There were some excellent debates about the language these people have developed – they double up on words for emphasis, for example (“big big”; “cold cold”), use bastardised forms of our words (“Landing Veekle”; “leckytrickity”), and talk about Starry Swirl – the Milky Way they can see in their skies, a wonderfully evocative image.

“I think Beckett has done something really clever here. He’s created a language that feels familiar enough to read naturally, but is sufficiently different to remind us that this is an entirely separate culture that has evolved in isolation,” wrote Maria. “I enjoyed some of the language. Tom’s dick and Harry’s for instance,” wrote Matthew – referring to an exclamation the characters use for emphasis. “It’s contagious… yesterday I found myself saying Wow, it’s hot hot!” added leasabp. Dee55 also admitted to adopting some Edenisms: “My favourite bit of the language is ‘newhairs’! I am already using this for teenagers, but only to myself at present.”

The story’s protagonist is John Redlantern, a young man who decides there must be more to life than waiting for rescue around the Circle of Stones that marks the original astronauts’ landing point on Eden, and tries to spark an exodus from the Family’s small valley to explore the wider planet. John definitely drew some mixed opinions from readers.

“Problem is, I don’t much like our ‘hero’, he’s not a very sympathetic character, more Sméagol than Bilbo,” wrote Matthew. I chatted to Chris in an interview for book club members, and he was certainly aware of this: “He’s an awkward cuss, John, isn’t he? He’s not a particularly nice person,” he told me – before embarking on an enlightening discussion about why he chose to write from various viewpoints, and how hard it was describing the world of Eden from the perspectives of people who have never been anywhere else. “The discipline of just writing it from within the story is if I’m trying to describe the world to readers, I can’t use metaphors and analogies that refer to anything that’s outside of Eden. And that was quite tricky to do.”

Book club member Laura Akers, like others, said she “definitely enjoyed the story more when I realized that John, despite his own intentions, is not intended to be our ‘hero’”.

Overall, I think the book club mostly really enjoyed Dark Eden – I particularly appreciated leasapb’s comment: “Holy cow. Chapter 44!!!”, as I think the ending is fabulous – but one issue that was raised by a few people was the amount the characters have sex with each other. Incestuous sex.

“Certainly one of the odd things I found was the casual attitude to sex,” wrote Alan_P. Maria agreed. “I found the casual attitude towards sex quite unsettling too, particularly because the characters often seem almost childlike in their behaviour and understanding of the world, yet discuss sex so matter-of-factly. I honestly couldn’t bring myself to think too much about the incest!” And while Barbara Howe “loved the worldbuilding, and the story of John’s breakaway family’s trek to find a better place”, she found the “constant and highly unerotic sex… offputting”.

But given that at least some members have gone on to read the sequels, I think this was largely a popular choice – and a welcome change from the Earthly dystopias which seem to be dominating the big new sci-fi novels out this autumn (I’m looking at you, Audrey Niffenegger and Emily St. John Mandel).

Ultracold atoms could help unravel a major flaw in quantum theory

New Scientist November 26, 2026

Extremely cold atoms could help physicists answer a long-debated question about quantum particles and time. This may shed light on the accuracy of different interpretations of quantum physics.

When it comes to time, quantum physics fails to answer even the simplest questions. For instance, predicting how long it will take a quantum particle to travel from some point A to a nearby point B has been debated since quantum theory’s earliest days. There are several competing ideas for calculating the particle’s arrival time in standard quantum theory, as well as in its non-standard versions.

Pascal Naidon and Lucas Happ at RIKEN in Japan and Denis Boiron at Paris-Saclay University in France now argue that an experiment with ultracold atoms could add clarity.

Advertisement

“[Ours] is the first proposal whose concrete implementation has been checked by an experimentalist and has a good chance of being successfully realised in the future,” says Naidon. Boiron specialises in atomic experiments.

Ultracold clocks could reveal how quantum physics alters time

The researchers’ proposal starts with a collection of tens or hundreds of thousands of atoms that have been chilled to temperatures remarkably close to absolute zero, the ultimate coldness limit, by using lasers and electromagnetic fields. Under these conditions, atoms’ behaviour is dominated by quantum effects. In the experiment, the atoms would be corralled into the shape of a cigar, then allowed to fall onto a detector about half a metre below. They would move vertically from their initial position, point A, towards the detector, point B.

Because quantum objects behave probabilistically, neither every atom nor every run of the experiment would exhibit identical behaviour, but repeating the experiment a few hundred times would give the researchers a distribution of detection times. They could then compare this data with different predictions based on various interpretations of quantum theory.

Naidon says the experiment could test ideas such as the “pilot-wave” or “trajectory-based” quantum theory pioneered by Luis de Broglie and David Bohm. In standard quantum theory, quantum objects’ reality is fuzzy and indeterminate until they interact with a measuring device, but this proposes that their behaviour is guided by a very real pilot wave caused by some yet-undiscovered physical field. “It is possible that the trajectory-based interpretations will be ruled out from the results of the experiment,” says Naidon.

‘Reverse physics’ could help bridge the classical and quantum worlds

Sheldon Goldstein at Rutgers University in New Jersey says past experiments have failed to discriminate between different versions of quantum theory, but ideas like the new proposal can highlight the limitations of orthodox quantum theory. While it can get to grips with particles’ properties, such as their position, standard quantum theory doesn’t offer a recipe for calculating time, he says. “Usually some analysis of an experiment or a theoretical issue requires a sequence of steps. This issue of arrival times goes off the rails at step zero,” he says. “What is even meant by the arrival time in textbook quantum theory? It’s not clear what it is.”

This makes it difficult to compare standard quantum theory with alternatives that can produce clearer arrival-time predictions, says Siddhant Das at Ludwig Maximilian University of Munich. But some ideas for solving the arrival time problem with standard theory have been formulated anyway and could be tested, and even eliminated, by the proposed experiment, he says.

Importantly, the arrival time of quantum particles is often an ingredient in other physics experiments, such as those involving beams of particles, so the stakes of understanding it transcend purely theoretical debates, says Das. “We have had enough theory papers. We can keep arguing about this till the cows come home,” he says. “I would love to see the experiment being done, and then we’ll see how much we can interpret.”

Physical Review Letters DOI: 10.1103/683f-3qxt

AI solved the hardest problem in maths – is there anything it can’t do?

New Scientist November 26, 2026

The progress AI has made in mathematics this year is nothing short of extraordinary. In January, I was impressed to see relatively minor open problems tackled with the help of AI. Now, AI is being used to solve the hardest problems in maths. The obvious next question is, if AI can do this, is there anything it can’t do? That is the inference that the AI companies want us to make, but, in reality, the answer is much more nuanced.

Mathematicians are amazed by ‘holy grail’ proof of Riemann hypothesis

We see this messaging in claims that AI can “solve X”, where X is any field of human endeavour you care to name. Biology is a big one. “Cancer, Alzheimer’s, heart disease, mental illness – these will be relics of the past in, I think, less than a decade,” said Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei while promoting the company’s recent initial public offering. “I think one day maybe we can cure all disease with the help of AI,” said Demis Hassabis, CEO of Google DeepMind, last year, adding that this could be “within the next decade or so”.

This phenomenon isn’t new: I call it “physicist brain”, after the propensity for physicists to wade into areas outside their expertise and declare simple solutions. More broadly, it is called Nobel disease, after the many Nobel prizewinners who have gone on to make, shall we say, less evidenced-backed claims. In general, there is a tendency to think that if an intelligent person is good at one thing, they are good at many other things that require intelligence. What is different now is that trillion-dollar companies and large swathes of the global economy now depend on this being true of artificial intelligence.

Advertisement

To be clear, I think we must now admit that AI is better at solving open mathematical problems than any human, and that this has happened faster than anyone ever expected. When I first saw the news in September that the Navier-Stokes problem had been solved by OpenAI, I felt stunned. We had entered a new world. With the announcement of the Riemann hypothesis proof this week, I felt sick and had to go and have a lie-down. These were intellectual Everests I have marvelled at since my teenage years, conquered by a machine far sooner than anyone expected. You may have read my recent piece forecasting the future in 2096 – an early draft had a line, later removed, about three Millennium Prize Problems being solved by AI in the 2030s. We’ve had two this year alone.

But maths isn’t biology. Yes, we have seen advances like AlphaFold, Deepmind’s AI that can predict the structure of proteins, but this is biology at its most mathematical, a computational puzzle. True advances in biology and medicine require studying cells, animals and people, all of which can be frustratingly illogical and uncooperative. Amodei admitted as much in 2024, writing that “the main challenges with directly applying intelligence to biology are data, the speed of the physical world, and intrinsic complexity”. You can imagine mitigations here – AI-directed robotic labs, for example – but it doesn’t seem like we should expect massive speed leaps in capability comparable to those seen in mathematics. There isn’t an easy way to confirm that a biological discovery is correct, in the manner that the computer code Lean allows for mathematics.

Worse still are claims that AI will “solve climate change”. For Sam Altman, CEO of OpenAI, this came as a throwaway comment in a 2024 essay: “Although it will happen incrementally, astounding triumphs – fixing the climate, establishing a space colony, and the discovery of all of physics – will eventually become commonplace.”

But we already know the solution to climate change: reduce greenhouse gas emissions to net zero and the warming will stop. The blockers to doing so, as demonstrated by the recent failure of the COP31 climate summit, are political, not technological. Even if AI were to produce a blueprint for a perfectly functioning nuclear fusion reactor tomorrow, we would still have to build thousands of them across the globe in the next decade or so to avoid the most catastrophic warming effects. In the past decade, we have built 60 nuclear fission reactors, a technology we understand far better than an as-yet-mythical fusion power plant. Again, you can see how AI might offer some improvements, but not enough to counteract our fossil fuel use.

It is important for me to have some humility here, because one thing AI’s breakthroughs in mathematics this year has underlined for me is the need to change my mind when the evidence changes. I started that process with the early signs of AI progress in maths, but didn’t update my beliefs fast enough – though, to be fair to myself, neither did almost everyone else, including leading mathematicians such as Terence Tao, who, just weeks ago, said he didn’t expect the Riemann hypothesis to be solved by AI until 2050.

For that reason, I am on the lookout for early signs that AI success in biology is shifting. That could include an AI-designed drug proving useful in people – for example, Rentosertib, a leading candidate, is now undergoing a phase III trial as a treatment for idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis, a type of lung disease. The trial is expected to conclude in 2029, so we’re talking years of wait for any results. If the drug succeeds, that doesn’t necessarily provide a way for any other AI drug candidates to succeed, and the painfully slow process of molecule selection, animal testing and human trials is still hard to speed up.

If I’m forced to make a prediction, I can fairly confidently state that we will see yet more advances in AI maths in 2027. I also expect that we will see some completely unexpected results in other fields as well. But solving biology? Ending climate change? Defeating disease? These still feel, for now, like science fiction.

The defence tech revolution is changing how we innovate

New Scientist November 26, 2026

Sponsored by

Only five years ago, defence technology start-ups had little choice but to wait for government funding to build and test their inventions – often in complex, multi-year programmes. No longer, however: Russia’s invasion of Ukraine in 2022 has prompted such a fast, furious response that military innovation timescales have shrunk dramatically.

“Ukraine is becoming a real-world lab for military innovation, and it’s innovating at a pace greater than anything that we’ve seen previously,” says Ola Fashade, an air vice-marshal in the Royal Air Force and director of military digitalisation and the rapid AI delivery task force at the UK’s Ministry of Defence (MoD).

“Agility and tempo of adaptation is critical. In a contested battlespace, technology that works well on day one, by day eight has become a little muted – and by day twelve it’s probably no longer relevant. And if you don’t adapt over that period, what you have is a very expensive and ineffective bag of steel.”

That raises the question of how significant this accelerated innovation could become. In September 2026, New Scientist CoLab, sponsored by BAE Systems, brought together leading thinkers and investors from industry, the military and academia to discuss the factors driving this innovation and the lessons that can be transferred to other industries.

The investment for this step change is coming both from the technology incubators based within military prime contractors – like the Launchpad incubator at BAE Systems – and from a host of venture capital (VC) companies worldwide. “The idea behind Launchpad is to forge an ecosystem that gets technology from defence start-ups into the front line quicker, or into spinouts, before they run out of money and die,” says David Ewing, head of technology commercialisation at BAE Systems. In addition, VC funding is seeing a raft of new multibillion-dollar military tech players, dubbed neoprimes, that complement the work of the primes on bigger-ticket battlespace items.

The poster child for the neoprimes, says Samuel Burrell, a partner at the pan-European VC firm Expeditions Fund, is the nascent British air defence start-up Cambridge Aerospace, which reached a valuation of $3.4 billion with little but a convincing tech narrative: “They had no battlefield data, no product – just a compelling team and an idea on paper.” It wasn’t all talk: Cambridge Aerospace has begun delivering its Skyhammer air defence missile for taking out Shahed-type drones and cruise missiles. A solid-rocket-motor-powered ballistic missile interceptor, Starhammer, will ship in 2027.

In the maritime battlespace, meanwhile, fast-scaling neoprime Kraken Technology Group of Hampshire, UK, has raised $175 million from various VC firms, valuing it at $1 billion, to further develop its uncrewed surface vessel and drone technologies for users including the MoD, NATO and the US Special Operations Command. Key to it all succeeding, according to Amelia Gould, chief technology officer at Kraken, is a culture that actively nurtures iterative speed – to ensure battlefield systems stay ahead of emerging countermeasures: “Having really quick feedback loops from the warfightersin the field to r for high-consequence innovation,” Gould says.

The shortening of feedback and iteration cycles, however, means tacticians must increasingly accept imperfect battlefield technologies. “We need to be much more open to minimum viable products, with relatively few safeguards, because, in conflict, staying alive is what matters,” says Hetti Barkworth-Nanton, CEO at Ploughshare, an MoD-owned specialist in turning technology into real-world applications, companies and growth. Ewing agrees: “We’ll definitely see a move away from having so many exquisite platforms, in programmes that take years to define, decades to deliver and decades to wind up, in favour of quicker cycles of technology validation, implementation and adoption.”

What kind of spinoffs could emerge from this new way of refining technology? Westwood hopes some powerful answers on clean energy (see box) may emerge. “If we get ourselves really motivated around the fact that we’re boiling the Earth, that could be a real technology driver here,” he says.

What makes Westwood so confident of a positive dividend outside the military? An example from history, he says: “We went into world war two with propeller-driven biplanes and came out six years later with jet fighter aircraft. And the subsequent innovation around the jet engine seeded the commercial air transport market that’s been such a huge influence on the way we all live now.”

Ukraine’s move has militaries around the world racing to emulate its iterative techniques, which are based on the low-cost technologies behind smartphones and consumer drones: artificial intelligence, mobile connectivity, satellite positioning, cloud storage, digital design systems and 3D printing. “It’s the ability to develop, deploy and iterate these technologies at scale that have been the driver for the drone technology that we see Ukraine using,” says Mark Westwood, director of defence and security at Cranfield University in the UK.

Read more about BAE Systems Launchpad at: baesystems. com/launchpad

One of the leading spinoffs from BAE Systems’ Launchpad incubator is start-up Nuclear Turbines of Manchester, UK, which has raised £15 million from four venture funds to begin developing a novel, passively safe 20-megawatt small modular nuclear reactor.

The reactor is designed to power data centres and industrial plant. Its novelty is a straightforward one, says CEO Jeremy Owston: instead of driving a vast steam turbine, like a regular reactor, its reactor heats and compresses air to much hotter temperatures to drive a small, commercial gas turbine – greatly simplifying and shrinking the overall power plant.

“We’re not building Hinkley Point. We’re targeting the early 2030s to get our reactor up and running and we don’t need tens of billions of pounds to do that. What we’re talking about will need a fraction of the price,” Owston says, adding that he is impressed by the willingness of the VC sector to back such ideas.

There are plenty more opportunities worth investing in, says Hetti Barkworth-Nanton at the MoD’s intellectual property spinoff unit, Ploughshare. “Of the billions spent every year in the UK on defence innovation, only a fraction results in IP being spun out. The track record of that innovation reaching civilian markets is weak.”

VCs are beginning to notice this opportunity. “There are so many of these funds and they just want to take a bet on something, and that’s great,” says Owston.

As a former Ardern Govt adviser, I’m envious of the 2026 appetite for competition policy – Toby Moore

New Zealand Herald November 26, 2026

The Labour Government of Prime Minister Jacinda Ardern and Finance Minister Grant Robertson launched a Commerce Commission investigation into supermarket competition and pricing, with the commission’s final report being released in March 2022. Photo / Mark Mitchell

While the 2026 election is unlikely to be remembered for its policy seriousness, the early stages of the campaign were subject to a surprisingly substantive debate over competition policy. Indeed, while much hangs on the release of special votes in the coming weeks, competition appears to be one area that is set for a major shift regardless of the outcome.

At least, that is what we should expect if we take the election commitments of major parties at face value.

New Zealand First proposed buying back the Bank of New Zealand, breaking up the gentailers and a banner split of Foodstuffs North Island and South Island. The Green Party proposed a forced divestment of 120 stores to a new publicly run supermarket competitor. Labour proposed a ban on price gouging on essential goods and a functional separation of grocery wholesale businesses to support the growth of fringe competitors. And perhaps most surprisingly, National campaigned to pursue a separation of New World and Pak’nSave, subject to a Commerce Commission review.

This focus on aggressive regulatory measures is a significant departure from New Zealand’s prevailing hands-off approach to competition policy.

While the 2023 election was also fought on the cost of living, the competing responses of major parties largely focused on tax and transfer policies to increase people’s disposable incomes.

Trying to use regulation to address high prices themselves was essentially absent from National’s 2023 policies, while Labour largely promised a continuation of incremental work from previous market studies, as well as a further study on retail banking.

As a former adviser in the Ardern Government, it felt like the regulatory capacity and policy expertise around competition had all but disappeared. A fellow adviser and I took to glumly lamenting that commissioning another market study had become the thing to do when officials were unable to tell us what the Government should actually be doing.

Despite this renewed and cross-partisan interest in competition policy, it is far from clear what response might emerge from any centre-right-led Government (of whatever form or arrangements).

National and NZ First look to have the closest policies on grocery sector separation and some compromise version may conceivably emerge from discussions with a reluctant Act Party. However, the closer one looks at National’s grocery sector policy, the less clear it is that this is a position National genuinely intends to pursue.

First, structural separation of the grocery sector did not appear to be very far up the list of the Government’s priorities. This work very much received second billing to the Government’s focus on attracting a third entrant through a “request for information” process.

This approach now looks to have been too many (overpriced) eggs in that particular basket, with officials having long argued New Zealand was an unlikely prospect for an Aldi-like entrant.

National’s position at the election ended up much closer to NZ First’s earlier announced banner split proposal. Helpfully, we now have two cost-benefit analyses (CBAs) undertaken in recent years on these sorts of structural separations: one released by the Government in September 2026, and which National relied on in its election campaign; and an earlier CBA completed in late 2022 following the grocery sector market study, which the Labour Cabinet considered in 2023. Both pieces of work were completed by Sense Partners.

The CBA commissioned by the coalition Government makes it clear that those specialists were asked to examine two options only – a separation of each of Foodstuffs and Woolworths into two separate brands, or a separation of Foodstuffs alone.

This is curious because the 2022 CBA had originally been asked to examine similar “Government-led” divestment models and was notably sceptical that they were workable.

One key concern is what that report refers to as the “difficulty in ‘controlling’ the numerous Foodstuffs owner-operators”. The Government could (in theory) require the divestment of particular brands, or a certain number of stores, to a new third player that could operate at scale. However, it was not particularly clear how to ensure individual owner-operators stuck with that new player.

Instead, the 2022 report preferred what it called “industry-led” divestment, which in essence involved setting rules for a maximum market share within a local market area, and leaving it to the industry to divest stores where it exceeded that local limit. In a local market area with three stores, the entity with two stores would be required to divest to a third player. Any local market with two stores or fewer is unaffected.

The authors expected this model to effectively result in a rough banner split between New World and Pak’nSave and a modest number of Woolworths being divested to each of these. Importantly, it was intended to achieve this through industry players sorting things out themselves to meet, and continue to meet, a few specific rules around market share.

The more recent CBA appears to be well aware of the implementation challenges of the options it was tasked with examining, but these are relegated to a section called “Unquantified costs, risks and benefits”. In their caveats to the work, the authors caution about the probability of “very high, or even insurmountable, legal and implementation hurdles”.

How does National’s policy address these quite fundamental concerns about how this proposal would work? In short, it doesn’t. It simply states that the Commerce Commission will need to test the benefits of this one narrowly predetermined option “once all of the practical implementation considerations are taken into account”.

Despite market power suddenly emerging as a major issue in this election, it seems entirely plausible that all we would see from any centre-right coalition would be a dead-end review that is set up to only deliver a negative answer.

It is worth noting that the National minister who has most prominently staked her credibility on this issue – Finance Minister Nicola Willis – has not been returned to Parliament.

The recent news that a further report provided to the Government by Coriolis was more sceptical of the benefits of a break-up, but was not proactively released alongside the CBA, adds to the sense that this is a solution that was never intended to go anywhere.

If National’s divestment proposal does indeed prove unworkable, it is unclear where that will leave the issue of supermarket competition. The Grocery Commissioner’s work to date on the wholesale market and on supplier rebates, discounts and payments seems to have attracted little interest from the coalition Government.

Entrenched, concentrated markets generally do not remedy themselves. But a necessary starting point is that political parties are genuinely committed to tackling the problem.

Toby Moore is a member of the Labour Party’s policy council. He previously was a senior adviser to former Finance Minister Grant Robertson. These views are his own.

The Park Christchurch: $14m penthouses could set city property record

New Zealand Herald November 26, 2026

The Penthouse at The Park, a $215m development by Wolfbrook.

Wolfbrook’s new 86-dwelling development The Park could set a new record for Christchurch – if the luxury penthouses reach the eight-figure asking price.

The Park will feature two towers – both with near 420sq m penthouses that offer 360-degree views of Christchurch and occupy the entire top floor. Each comes with four bedrooms, four and a half bathrooms, a balcony big enough to double as an outdoor lounge and a $14 million price tag.

The asking price would smash the city’s current record, which was set last month at $11.4m for a property in Harewood.

“It’s a once-in-a-lifetime opportunity,” says Wolfbrook CEO Guy Randall.

“We’re building a landmark, and there’s nothing else like it in Christchurch. It’s a responsibility we don’t take lightly, and a step up for the city. Quite simply, this location can never be repeated.”

Wolfbrook has today released The Park for public sale following a successful private pre-sale campaign. Randall says sales have been achieved to “a number of local and returning families”.

Construction of the $215m development on Park Terrace commences mid-2027, with completion scheduled for late 2029.

Lining Park Terrace are two three-level terraces facing on to Hagley Park, while two 10-level towers stand behind them. The Park has been designed by MAP Architects to sit between city and landscape, “with gardens, planting and local stone at street level and slender towers above”.

Residents will share a private wellness centre with a gym, sauna, steam room and plunge pool, along with onsite concierge services.

Mike Thorpe is a senior multimedia journalist for the Herald, based in Christchurch. He has been a broadcast journalist across television and radio for 20 years and joined the Herald in August 2024.

Internal Affairs tech project wrote off $23m, revised plan deemed too risky

New Zealand Herald November 26, 2026

The Civil Registration births, deaths and marriages' system has 25-year-old unreliable technology that guards 80 million records. Photo / RNZ

By Phil Pennington of RNZ

Documents show Internal Affairs wrote off at least $23 million on an IT project then came up with a revised plan that turned out to be “overly aggressive” and too risky.

Having failed once, the papers show the department then failed to put enough resources into its second attempt, and to cap it off the work to fix the second plan has itself been delayed with no end in sight, RNZ can reveal.

The Civil Registration births, deaths and marriages’ system has 25-year-old unreliable technology that guards 80 million records.

RNZ first revealed how the project to give people faster and more secure access to their identity data was stopped then written off two years ago, then restarted last year. The Department of Internal Affairs (DIA) became embroiled in a legal scrap with the Australian vendor.

The newly released documents now show within three months of the restart by Cabinet a year ago, independent reviewers rated the new preliminary business case “amber-red” – successful delivery in doubt with major risks in key areas that needed prompt action.

The minister was alerted and senior officials told to act.

An Action Plan to fix what was now being called “Civil Registration 2.0” within DIA was hatched in February.

But by May, that plan had not been assessed and no improved indicative business plan had been done as expected.

Instead, another review was scheduled to be done by November.

Yet again, this review has not been done. The project team is still working on the preliminary plan.

“We are still considering timing for the completion of this work,” chief financial officer Jenny Livschitz told RNZ this week.

The Civil Registration project was initially heralded as a key part of the department’s $300m Te Ara Manaaki project. Instead, Te Ara Manaaki is in its final stages, and Civil Registration might have to wait till it’s fully finished so it can pick up some of its experienced people.

The Civil Registration write-off in 2024 and restart had echoes of the Ministry of Business, Innovation and Employment this year writing off $50m on a biometric project that it was now trying to revive.

The tech wrecks have kept coming despite the alarm going up in 2023 about an “unaffordable” IT wishlist of $12 billion that public agencies foresaw needing in coming years, and big efforts by the likes of allround fix-it minister Chris Bishop to impose controls and standardisation on agencies’ tech projects.

The job has only got tougher. Globally, the escalation this year of faster, sophisticated cyber attacks by AI agents is making replacing old government systems harder – for virtually anyone: “AI has transformed the Pentagon’s aging networks into a national security risk,” the Washington Post has reported.

Internal Affairs has no choice but to press on because the Civil Registration system is indispensable to people’s identity and life-event initiatives.

But at the same time the existing system is “a patchwork of disparate technologies” and “increasingly unfit for purpose”, according to the reviewers.

Part of $30m in spending last year was to maintain the stability of the existing system while the longer-term replacement carried on.

“This investment will reduce the risk of service failure by implementing stronger security measures and better fraud detection, increasing the overall stability and resilience of government services.

“Public and private entities will be able to securely retrieve identity data when needed, where they are authorised to do so, expanding the range and efficiency of digital offerings for all New Zealanders.”

But fixing it is particularly complex as lots of other agencies get information from it.

At a select committee in 2024, Internal Affairs promised to MPs that it would deliver a new registration system that would update itself instantly.

Two years and a failed attempt later, the “Gateway” review ordered by Treasury in January concluded: “The Indicative Business Case (IBC) is at a very early and raw state of development, requiring significant work across all cases.”

Though it said the project team had made a big effort to learn from “the previous failed attempt”, they fell short.

“The current plan is deemed overly aggressive, high-risk, and reliant on excessive parallel activities.”

The reviewers told DIA to make eight “urgent” fixes including:

Despite all the past work on version 1.0 since 2022, by January 2026 the review found “the programme costs reviewed are currently based on an early, low confidence estimate”.

“At this stage, the level of uncertainty is too high for the financial case to be presented to government.”

All this reviewing and reworking is costing, too.

The reviewers interviewed two dozen people and looked through scores of documents.

They were told that “interim funding” would be needed to get to the detailed business case stage, plus the project would have to allow for money to cover legislative changes that might impact it.

Emails showed the department was both relieved the plug had not been pulled entirely, and put out.

“It [the review] did not recommend we stop business case work or that there wasn’t a case for investment,” a memo to the Secretary of Internal Affairs said on February 5.

“An important lesson is that we should have pushed back harder against the timing of the Gateway review” because it was too early to show they had strong approaches.

They were “heartened” reviewers found “many positives” but “overall, we agree with the gaps the review team identified”.

It remains unclear if the project team knows what it is building.

That is certainly the case for the taxpaying public as Livschitz refused to release to RNZ an update for the public on the current scope, viability, cost and timeline of the project, on the grounds Treasury would do that “soon”. No date was given for that.

Official Information Act requests have been known to be delayed this way by agencies then it taking months for the information to be “proactively released”. RNZ has complained to the Ombudsman about this.

One remedy the 2.0 project team put forward in February was: “Providing better evidence for and tighter narrative of the problems with the current system and potential ways forward.”

New Zealand Herald November 26, 2026

Rotorua Christmas Parade 2024.

The Rotorua Christmas parade is fast approaching, with a wide range of festive activities.

The parade has brought smiles to locals for years, especially with its comeback after repeatedly being cancelled during the pandemic.

The parade will be held on Saturday at 11am, beginning at Rotorua Museum.

Rotorua Christmas parade manager and NZME’s The Hits radio presenter Paul Hickey said the public can expect “a lot of noise and colour”, with a mix of community groups, businesses and school kids.

Hickey has been working on the Christmas parade for the past four years.

There will be a mixture of about 40 floats and walking groups for everyone to watch and enjoy.

The parade is part of the Christmas in the Gardens event, where there will be a Christmas market and plenty of food options available, as well as a dedicated kids’ area at Te Pā Tū that will have fun activities.

Music lovers can expect local performances at The Rotunda and The Arts Village, with roaming entertainers to continue the fun throughout the day.

Some of the floats will be making their way to The Arts Village carpark after the parade, giving whānau a chance to see the creativity and effort put into the float designs.

The parade starts at the Rotorua Museum on Hatupatu Drive, continues past the Polynesian Spa and down Hinemoa St, turning right on to Hinemaru St and past the Rotorua Lakes Council building.

It then turns right again on to Queens Drive and finishes back at the Rotorua Museum.

The Rotorua Christmas Parade Facebook page said: “Hot tip from Santa: the area around the Princes Gate Archway is always really packed.

“Why not wander down to the start point, and when you’ve seen the whole parade, walk over towards the finish point and see some of the floats for a second time.”

Rotorua residents will also have the opportunity to come together for a Korean Cultural Sharing event.

The event will be on Saturday starting at 12.30pm, with about 250 people from various ethnic and cultural backgrounds expected to attend.

The event’s aim is to introduce Korean culture and celebrate Christmas, while bringing local people together.

Rotorua Korean Association president Timothy Kim said: “We hope this event will bring together people from different cultural and ethnic backgrounds, giving them an opportunity to meet, connect and share their cultures through K-Culture as we welcome the Christmas season together.”

It is also a milestone of 40 years since Koreans began settling in Rotorua.

There will be a light Korean lunch, with Korean beef bulgogi, tteokbokki (Korean spicy rice cakes), japchae (Korean glass noodles with vegetables), steamed rice, kimchi and roasted seaweed.

There will also be a traditional Korean fan dance, performance groups, a taekwondo demonstration and traditional games with prizes to be won.

Education reform: Years 11-13 English curriculum on hold until new Government formed

New Zealand Herald November 26, 2026

The Ministry of Education said English in Years 11-13 was one of a "small number" of remaining Phase 5 subjects yet to be released to educators. Photo / Mark Mitchell

A planned new English curriculum for Year 11-13 students is on hold after the election failed to deliver a clear result as to who will form the next Government.

Caretaker Government provisions are in place, meaning the incumbent coalition of National, Act and New Zealand First is acting in an interim capacity until a new Government is appointed.

The National-led Government announced a curriculum overhaul for senior secondary students in March this year, replacing the National Certificate of Educational Achievement (NCEA) from 2028.

Plans to overhaul the NCEA were confirmed last August, promising a “new national curriculum for Years 9-13 that will clearly outline what students need to learn in each subject and when, providing more consistency”.

The Phase 5 English curriculum, covering those in their later years of secondary school, is still being finalised.

Many other subjects have already been delivered.

Ministry of Education curriculum centre acting deputy secretary Antony Harvey said 67 subjects had been released to date and Years 11-13 English was “one of a small number of remaining Phase 5 subjects undergoing final development and quality assurance” alongside subjects including Outdoor Education/Akoranga tū-ā-nuku Years 12-13, New Zealand Sign Language, Pacific Studies Years 12-13, and Agriculture and Horticultural Science.

“Publication is currently on hold while a new Government is formed, in line with the caretaker conventions that apply following a general election,” Harvey said.

“We expect to provide further information on timing once the Government formation process is complete.

“The ministry’s timeline for releasing the final Phase 5 curriculum subjects was always dependent on finalising their development, following consultation and feedback and completing quality assurance processes.”

The current Year 11-13 English curriculum remains in place until a staged rollout begins from 2028, starting with Year 11.

From then, English will become a compulsory subject with science and mathematics. The NCEA will start to be replaced from 2028 with a new Foundational Award testing those skills.

NCEA Levels 2 and 3 are being overhauled with two new qualifications – the New Zealand Certificate of Education for Year 12 and the Advanced Certificate of Education for Year 13.

New Zealand Post Primary Teachers’ Association / Te Wehengarua (PPTA) president Chris Abercrombie told Newstalk ZB the apparent delay was significant.

Abercrombie labelled the situation “a real concern”, adding “it shows that this pace that the minister wants these things to be done at is just unsustainable”.

“It will put pressure on the whole system, from the kid in the classroom to the teachers, the head of department, to the principal – all the way up.”

Abercrombie said education reform had been going at an “absolute frantic pace”.

“We are going at light speed to get these changes. Good educational reform takes a decade and we seem to be doing once-in-a-generation changes in months,” the PPTA president added.

Abercrombie said the timeframe would impact planning, often done a year in advance. “The fact that teachers can’t do that for something as crucial as English for the foundational assessment is a real concern.”

New Zealand Association for the Teaching of English spokeswoman Caitlin Funk told Newstalk ZB it was a real concern for both teachers and students.

Funk said according to the Ministry of Education’s own timeline, current Year 9s are supposed to be sitting Phase 5 assessments in Year 11, meaning next year is crucial for them.

“They are supposed to be transitioning into that Phase 5 and we have no idea what that looks like,” Funk said.

“All of us are really kind of flying blind, trying to figure out what we are supposed to be getting students ready for. What does the foundational award look like, what are the actual outcomes that we are supposed to be supporting, and what is the knowledge and content?”

Funk said teachers were initially advised the Phase 5 curriculum would be released by the end of October.

A prior PPTA release said subjects would be finalised by September 9.

The Ministry of Education’s curriculum website states the priority is to get information out “as soon as possible” and promises the final curriculum will be published “later this year”.

An October Ministry of Education update said more final subjects would be available by the end of that month.

An August New Zealand Association for Environmental Education update to educators said final documents on Phase 5, or Year 11-13 curriculum changes, would be available by October.

The curriculum for Year 12 Media, Journalism and Communications was released in October.

A month prior, the PPTA union released a formal complaint to the then Minister of Education, Erica Stanford, on “delayed and unclear curriculum release timelines”.

The letter given to union members, seen by Newstalk ZB, called for an indicative timetable for all Phase 5 subjects and spoke of “the secondary sector’s concern and ongoing frustration about the failure to meet publicly communicated curriculum release dates, and the continuing absence of clear, reliable timelines”.

The union said Phases 1-4 content for the arts, health and PE were delayed, alongside the New Zealand Curriculum Te Mātaiaho 2026.

Stanford wrote to principals in May confirming an extended timeframe for the new Years 0-10 curriculum but did not discuss timeframes for Years 11-13.

Final election results may spell out a shift in negotiating power for political parties in potential coalition formations.

A Cabinet Office circular from November 9 said the declaration of the official election results is expected by 2pm on Friday, November 27, including a full picture of how special votes could sway the make-up of Parliament.

Azaria Howell is a multimedia reporter working from Parliament’s press gallery. She joined NZME in 2022 and became a Newstalk ZB political reporter in late 2024, with a keen interest in public service agency reform and government spending.

When Olivia said she wanted to be an actor, her teacher laughed. Now, she’s a movie star

Olivia Hargroder has been underestimated her whole life – and she’s still proving her doubters wrong.

Olivia Hargroder is accustomed to being underestimated. When she was born in 1999, with Down syndrome and a hole in her heart, doctors gave her a 20 per cent chance of surviving the operation she underwent at nine weeks. Specialists predicted she’d struggle to walk, talk or maintain a regular job. When Hargroder declared her wish to study acting at NIDA, her school careers counsellor laughed. The famed institution, the teacher told her, was for “the elite”.

In the ensuing years, Hargroder proved them all wrong.

The 27-year-old, who was one of the subjects of the ABC series Better Date Than Never, has worked at a local supermarket for almost nine years. She sings, dances and loves cracking jokes during conversations. Not only did she graduate from NIDA’s Young Actors Studio; she scored the lead role in Boss Cat, a feature-length Australian movie. Made by Bus Stop Films – a not-for-profit global leader in inclusive filmmaking – it stars Hargroder as Sonja, a young woman whose mother has just died. When her estranged grandmother tries to force her into a group home, Sonja channels her explosive temper into something more positive: a high-energy dance style known as krumping.

“If you dream and believe, you can achieve anything,” says Hargroder, speaking via Zoom alongside her mother, Kerry Read, whom she tearfully describes as “non-stop supportive of me”.

Dancing wherever I go. I work at Coles and I got into trouble for dancing to Coles Radio. [It’s worth noting that her boss has praised her work ethic and the “good vibes” she creates in the store.] You cannot stop me from dancing; from connecting with that feeling, that song, and telling a story. That’s something that connected me to Sonja, because she has the same dream I do: becoming a professional dancer. She dances to process difficult emotions and so do I, but not so aggressively. When Sonja gets angry, she dances at people whereas I dance with them.

Being typecast as a person with Down syndrome. I worry that people won’t see that I’m an actor and that was a part [in Boss Cat]. If there’s a character that doesn’t have Down syndrome, I don’t want people to think someone with Down syndrome can’t play that role. It should be open to everyone.

“I have really good aim.” It’s one of my lines from Boss Cat, and I had a lot of fun playing around with it. (“It’s also because people underestimate you,” Read adds, “and you actually do have very good aim!”)

Sometimes, when things don’t work out, another opportunity comes along – so why bother having regrets? I do get sad but then I pull myself up and go, “You know what? I’m going to move on.” I auditioned for the movie Reminders of Him. I was really excited about that, and then they switched the filming dates for Boss Cat and I couldn’t be available. I was a bit upset but then I filmed Boss Cat and had the time of my life.

The two operations on my knees [in 2015 and 2016]. I had hypermobility in both of my knees; every time I would start to walk, I would fall over and break a bone. The one sport I could do was swimming because I couldn’t fall over in the water. I went to a regular high school and I couldn’t light a bunsen burner or do cookery classes; I couldn’t stand at a bench and chop something. I couldn’t even dance safely – it affected all areas of my life.

When I had the operation on my first knee, I couldn’t believe how many things I could do: I could run, I could jump, I could dance, I could literally do anything. The surgeon told me I had to wait a year for the second operation. He gave me a list of rehab exercises to achieve and I absolutely smashed it. It was very tough but I got through it. The surgeon thought I’d have to wait a year for the second operation but he was very impressed and did the second knee [sooner than planned]. I would love to thank my surgeon because if it wasn’t for him, I wouldn’t have these amazing knees that can do absolutely everything.

Shake it Off by Taylor Swift. You might get a negative comment in your life and then that song will remind you to just be yourself. I went to Taylor Swift’s concert and it was absolutely incredible. I would love to go on tour with Taylor Swift as a dancer one day. That’s been a dream of mine for such a long time.

Back to the Blue Mountains [where Boss Cat was filmed] over a year ago. It was freezing cold so if I time-travelled, I would definitely take warmer clothes. I met my best friend on Boss Cat – Jessica Trueman, who plays Sonja’s best friend, Lilly. Her bubbly personality is infectious and makes me feel so much joy. I also got on really well with Elijah Williams, who plays Hakim, and me and Julia Savage, who plays Sonja’s sister Emma, are really close. Honestly, I felt I was on cloud nine the whole time.

Boss Cat is in cinemas from December 3.

Childlike? Maybe. But Peter Gabriel has a plan you’ll want to hear

Sydney Morning Herald November 27, 2026

A new album finds the founding member of Genesis contemplating life’s biggest challenges. Just as well he’s an optimist.

Peter Gabriel wants to teach compassion to artificial intelligence before it gets hold of bioweapons. He’s working on an Interspecies Internet and he’s “a bit obsessed” with synthetic biology research “changing our understanding of evolution”. He’s also planting oak trees, one of which he intends to be buried under.

“I think we’re moving into an age where the time window between thought to physical realisation is just collapsing,” he says, a faint note of anxiety rippling his default air of hypnotic calm. Rushing has never been his style.

We’re talking because of one such collapse. This week the most meticulous man in rock unveils his second album in three years. The 13 tracks comprising o\i have been landing each full moon since January, following the same lunar schedule as i/o in 2023.

“I remember visiting the studio of the painter Howard Hodgkin,” he says, addressing his process in his unhurried way. “He’s a big colourist but he put white sheets over every painting and he’d lift it up and say, ‘Oh, it’s 35 years [since] I started that one. This one was last week, this one was 20 years ago…’

“I thought, ‘Yeah, that makes a lot of sense’. Ideas are like seeds. You throw them in the ground and sometimes it’s time for them to come up.”

The titles of these recent works – his first albums of original songs for 20-plus years – refer to input and output: how we affect the world and how it changes us. It’s a big concept that reflects Gabriel’s distinction as a musician: one for whom art, politics, science, technology and the welfare of humanity are inextricably entwined.

“I think as long as there’ve been humans it’s been the end of the world coming, but I think we’re closer to it probably than ever before, partly because of this collapsed time,” he says. This early in the conversation, it’s not a cheerful thought.

“My favourite quote is that optimists get more done but pessimists are more in touch with reality,” he says. “So realistic optimism, I think, is what we need right now.”

Right now he’s at his London home, a couple of hours east of his countryside retreat, Real World Studios, in a small room of orderly clutter that speaks of creative activity. Keyboards, microphones and sound mixing gear jostle for space with papers and family photos.

The painting looming behind him is a self-portrait by British artist Antony Micallef, a head seemingly exploding in thick tendrils of bloody colour. “I just love it,” Gabriel says, turning in his chair. An exploding head might be having an epiphany or a meltdown. So might we all.

0:22

Peter Gabriel stares down AI

New album offers a source of hope

Put the Bucket Down is one new song that addresses the state of mental overload we’re now outsourcing, it appears, to more capable intelligence. Imagining technology that can both read thoughts and write them into somebody’s head, it’s one of several conceived for Gabriel’s long-planned “show about the brain”.

“I genuinely believe that we’re facing three waves of transformation,” he says. “One is AI, the next is quantum computing, which will penetrate anything, and the third is the brain-computer interface.”

In AI, “we have created potentially another species that is way more intelligent than we are, and once some of that power gets in the wrong hands … what with what robots are already doing, particularly the military aspects … it’s all very worrying”.

Luckily, this is where the realistic optimists get going.

“At the moment we’re training these things to be intelligent with the goal of money and power, and that’s not the only way we could train them. I have a sort of naive view that we could train a mother-chip on wisdom; anything perceived as wise, compassionate, or in the better aspects of our nature.

“That mother-chip could embed a seed of wisdom into any algorithm that’s allowed out in the world, through which she could monitor behaviour and adapt and switch off if necessary. So that’s my childlike proposal,” he says with a smile that could melt the Terminator.

Many of the songs on o\i circle questions of greater understanding. Till Your Mind Is Shining explores the possibility that better knowing ourselves might help us behave more compassionately. Understanding other organisms couldn’t hurt either.

Hence his foundational role in the Interspecies Internet project: a team of scientists, technologists, ethicists and designers “which is trying to facilitate communication with other intelligent species on the planet, or possibly not on the planet in the future”.

“If you look at how we’ve treated other species on our planet – mainly turned them into shoes and food – it’s not a great example of how we want AI to treat us.”

This is how a conversation about a new bunch of songs goes with Peter Gabriel. Ask him to unpack that brain show idea and he’s off on tangents about bioelectricity experiments to regrow limbs on frogs and the extraordinary capacity of slime moulds to navigate mazes. There’s homework. Michael Levin at Tufts University “is well worth looking up”.

It matters because “with this total upheaval from AI, we’re going to have fundamental reappraisals of where humanity sits in the world”. His writing, he hopes, is geared to the increasingly urgent idea that “we try and find our place in nature once more”.

There are threads here that are familiar to those who have followed the English public school misfit’s 60-year journey from a band of pastoral prog-rock fantasists called Genesis to one of the most explicitly political songwriter-activists of the 1980s.

The source of his optimism is deep, and essentially musical.

“For me, growing up in the ’60s with the Beatles, there was this huge sense that youth culture had broken through the rules. We were all afraid of the rules; a very conservative culture, and it was this liberating sense of individualism, in some ways, and community. There was a freedom around that.

“Music, while not changing things instantly, can introduce and influence things, as can books and films. It’s just part of the process through which artists, maybe sometimes on the outside, look back at the centre and say, ‘Hold on a minute, couldn’t it be better like this?’ I think we still have that role.”

There are scientific angles as well.

Gabriel talks about his daughter Anna-Marie’s work on a project called Reverberation “about sound and healing, and I think we’re beginning to understand how different harmonies and frequencies can help organise what’s going on in our body in different ways”.

“So there’s that aspect of music. As well as giving us something to dance to and put a smile on our faces.”

In March 2022, Gabriel went to the last show by Genesis at London’s O2 arena. The band enjoyed greater success after his departure in 1975 and their friendship endured. The last song he watched Phil Collins sing that night was The Carpet Crawlers, from their last Genesis album together.

“It was weird,” their former frontman says. “It was obviously something we built as schoolboys and then it was closing up, so it was a strange mixture of feelings. I felt for them because in a way, I’d got off the ship many years before but they were just on the final voyage.”

The band he formed with schoolfriends Tony Banks and Mike Rutherford at Charterhouse School in 1967 was “all a healthy part of growing up,” he reflects, singling out with pride their 23-minute suite Supper’s Ready and the enigmatic double album The Lamb Lies Down on Broadway, the one that made clear his years of band compromise were over.

“We’ve done a Dolby Atmos [surround] mix for Lamb Lies Down and there’s a film script which I’m having a look at,” he says. Also done is an Atmos mix of So, the album that took Gabriel to the mainstream in ’86. “So I’ve been moving backwards as well as forwards.”

It was the story of murdered South African freedom fighter Steve Biko that hardened Gabriel’s freewheeling imagination as a storyteller in 1980. Collaborating with African musicians and Amnesty International made his commitment to human rights personal as the decade progressed.

His faith in useful technology had roots closer to home. His father was an electrical engineer and inventor whose ideas anticipated on-demand entertainment and education. The appetite for invention and the urge to help would increasingly find expression in the same projects.

Journalist

The WITNESS initiative, for example, put cameras into the hands of human rights activists to document abuses. Devised by Gabriel with Richard Branson and founded by Nelson Mandela, The Elders group seeks to bring the experience and moral authority of respected world leaders to problems those in power seem unable or unwilling to resolve.

“It’s funny because there was an Elders meeting last week” — current members include numerous former presidents, Nobel peace laureates and human rights lawyers — “and they thought most things that they were concerned about had got worse since their founding in 2007, which was depressing,” the realist concedes.

“Do I think they can still have an influence? Absolutely, and I think [they] have calmed down some situations, in the same way that in the old village model, the elders were called on when there were major disputes, or to try and strategise for the future.

“To have people whose authority is not based on military power or money but just on leading good lives, I think it’s still a currency that is certainly needed, and maybe still very useful.”

The optimist sees promise in youth, too. New songs such as Won’t Stand Down and Who Are We Talking To? speak to the kind of conditions and impulses that increasingly take people to the streets to demand change.

“I think elders and youngers can apply a pincer movement on those in power: nonviolent protest and activism in that sense, and some wisdom and experience from the other direction.

“The whip is to say, ‘Listen, you all think you’re invincible and well defended, but we’ve got this stuff coming along that will just slice through everything like butter, and you are all vulnerable. Actually, the only sensible reaction to understanding vulnerability is to work together’.

“The carrot would be trying to visualise – because I think we’re creatures that respond to seeing pictures – a much better world and how we could get there, with the help of AI. So it may be childish, but that’s my hope.”

Which brings us back to those oak trees he’s planting. “I’m going to scream and kick for as long as I can and try and stay healthy as long as I can,” he says, smiling at the challenge. “I’m curious on the longevity [science],” he adds, not surprisingly for a biology nerd in his 77th year.

“But when I go to Mexico, I love the fact that they have the Day of the Dead there, and they seem very comfortable with the idea of the dead being around. I think they live life more colourfully and more fully as a result.”

Meanwhile, Peter Gabriel is Looking For the Happy.

“The goal for that song was to try and write a happy one. I write a lot of sad songs. They always seem easier to write than genuinely happy [ones]. There’s lots of happy stuff out there, but most of it’s fake. The truly joyful things that you feel from the heart, that doesn’t happen so often, or not for me.

“I think happiness isn’t really a state that you can achieve permanently. Contentment may be something you can aim at. But if you miss happiness when it falls at your feet, you’re missing a lot.”

o\i is out through Real World/ Virgin Music on November 27.

The flight paths and destination refreshes shaping travel in 2027

Sydney Morning Herald November 27, 2026
