Fresh new experiences in familiar destinations, and exciting new flight paths are redrawing our travel maps for 2027. It’s time to look beyond the usual suspects for deeper, slower and more surprising elements of classic holiday spots – and jump on non-stop routes that make far-flung destinations feel closer and easier than ever.

GREECE … ALONNISOS

During peak summer months on Greece’s two most visited islands, Santorini and Mykonos, tourists outnumber locals by about 200 to one. Need we say more – in 2027 go further afield to, say, Alonnisos. While Alonnisos is a quiet alternative, it’s not dead quiet – there are enough visitors, with enough local tavernas, to give the island a festive atmosphere. Its old town, Chora, is a hill-top medieval village with car-free cobblestone lanes and 360-degree sunset views. Isn’t that what we go to Santorini for?

The island is better known for being at the heart of the Alonnisos and Northern Sporades Marine National Park, Europe’s largest marine-protected area. You’ll find the best diving and snorkelling in Greece, with creatures you won’t see anywhere else, such as the Mediterranean monk seal. There’s also 20 known beaches and coves, which include Agios Dimitrios, where crystal-clear water drops down into deep blue beside a crescent-shaped stretch of white sand. Or there’s Leftos Gialos if you want lively beach bars.

Sign up for the Traveller Deals newsletter

Get exclusive travel deals delivered straight to your inbox. Sign up now.

But the best reason for making Alonnisos your 2027 Greek island of choice is that unlike other Greek Island destinations, it feels like a place where tourism fits around island life, rather than island life revolving entirely around tourism. And for 2027, the best Greek island is likely to be the one hardly anyone’s posting about.- Craig Tansley

GREECE … THE PELOPONNESE

Travellers to Greece looking for a slower, richer, more immersive experience are discovering the Peloponnese, the southernmost part of mainland Greece, which is connected to the mainland by bridges over the Corinth Canal. Mountainous in the interior, it has four peninsulas with sparkling beaches and harbours that rival the islands, yet with fewer crowds. The rural interior of farmhouses and rolling hills can feel like Tuscany. In the west, flanking the Ionian Sea, it has the sparse beauty of Sicily.

Its tranquillity belies centuries of conflict, from the Peloponnesian War between Athens and Sparta in 431 BC to 404 BC to the Battle of Kalamata in 1941 when 300 Anzacs lost their lives. Unlike the islands, which involve transport by ferries, visitors can drive to the peninsula or take a train.

History buffs will love visiting the ancient sites for which the region is known, among them Sparta, Mycenae, Olympia, Mystras and the Sanctuary of Asklepios at Epidaurus, home of the most celebrated healing centre in the classical world. Some of Greece’s most beautiful cities and towns are also found there, including the Byzantine fortress town of Monemvasia, which is one of the oldest continually inhabited fortified towns in Europe, Kalamata, a seaside city famous for its olives, and Nafplio, a charming harbour city with bougainvillea-draped streets.

This is “authentic” Greece, full of vineyards, olive groves, magnificent ruins, fishing villages and staggering ocean views from rocky coastlines. It’s less expensive than the islands and the pace is slow enough to savour it all while getting to know the welcoming locals.- Lee Tulloch

JAPAN ... CRUISING BOOM

The number of Australians heading to Japan each year has soared to just shy of 1 million, driven in part by a booming cruising industry. International cruising to Japanese ports grew 20 per cent to 1.8 million visitors in 2025 thanks to a surge in port calls from foreign cruise liners and fly-cruise packages.

The Japanese government hopes to draw 1 million cruise travellers by 2030 and to help reach this goal it has renovated Tokyo’s dual cruise terminal and expanded capacity at ports in Kyushu, including Nagasaki and Fukuoka (Hakata). A new terminal is under construction in Okinawa.

New voyages are on offer, from Okinawa in the south to itineraries linking the northern prefecture of Hokkaido to South Korea. Most departures take place in April while others set sail to coincide with summer festivals, such as the Gion Festival in July and Aomori lantern festival in August.

Princess Cruises has invested heavily in Japan, with 50 itineraries in 2027 aboard Diamond Princess and Sapphire Princess, rising to 52 in 2028. These include a mix of shorter sailings, such as a nine-day return Tokyo voyage taking in Kochi and Hiroshima, to a month-long circumnavigation of the country.- Justin Meneguzzi

JAPAN ... STAR TRAINS

Powder hounds know about Hokkaido, Japan’s northernmost island, thanks to the prodigious snow that blankets resorts such as Niseko. For everyone else, the country’s second-largest island remains something of a mystery. Rail operator JR Hokkaido hopes to change that with two new tourist train services next year.

The Red Star service will debut first, and offers a two-day round trip between Sapporo and Abashiri in February to see the spectacular drift ice in the Sea of Okhotsk. From April to July, it will shift to a daily coast-to-coast sightseeing service from Kushiro to Shiretoko-Shari.

Then comes the Blue Star, which will run from Asahikawa to Furano from June to September to coincide with Hokkaido’s lavender season, when the countryside around Biei becomes a blaze of purple blooms. Returning in winter 2028, it will offer a twice-daily coastal service between Abashiri and Shiretoko-Shari for the drift ice.

Both trains are designed by Eiji Mitooka, the creator of Kyushu’s Seven Stars luxury sleeper. The Red Star will feature a tatami-mat tea room while Blue Star carriages will have glass-walled observation rooms. Schedules and pricing are being finalised, so check for updates. See jrhokkaido. co. jp - Rob McFarland

REGIONAL JAPAN

Now you’ve crossed the obvious attractions off your must-see list, 2027 is about venturing beyond, to Japan’s lesser-known parts. The good news is the country has an abundance of off-the-beaten-track regions, easily accessible via train.

Kanazawa, dubbed “mini-Kyoto”, is located on the north-western coast of Japan’s main island of Honshu. It is 2½ hours from Tokyo by Shinkansen and is worth visiting for its traditional architecture, with a 400-year-old castle town layout from Japan’s Edo period, including its perfectly preserved Nagamachi samurai district and geisha quarters. There’s only a fraction of the crowds of Kyoto and there is also the opportunity to visit Kenrokuen, ranked among one of Japan’s three most beautiful gardens. Escape tourists altogether in nearby Toyama, home to a World Heritage-listed traditional village of Gokayama, hot springs and one of Japan’s best scenic drives that weaves through the northern Japanese Alps along the Tateyama Kurobe Alpine Route.

Meanwhile, Australian skiers and snowboarders can branch out to more than 400 ski resorts in Japan. Nearly half of all snowsport enthusiasts who visited Japan last year went to Niseko in Hokkaido, while only 35 per cent went to the Hakuba region on Honshu’s west coast. There’s a lot of untracked powder snow waiting beyond these two resorts.- CT

INDONESIA … AN ARCHIPELAGO TO DISCOVER

Bali might be Australians’ favourite Indonesian island, but it needn’t be the extent of our acquaintance with the country. A new generation of resorts and small-ship journeys is giving us reasons to venture further into the archipelago where familiar comforts await the adventurous.

On Sumba, Cap Karoso combines sophisticated accommodation and visiting chefs with an organic farm and excursions led by Sumbanese guides. Beyond the pool are villages, ikat weaving and the island’s distinctive traditions. Flights from Bali take about an hour, making it an achievable addition to a familiar holiday.

Nihi, whose Sumba resort helped establish the island’s luxury credentials, has now opened on Rote. Its 21 villas and estates sit on Bo’a Beach, with surfing, mangrove paddleboarding and lagoon excursions on offer. A hospitality academy trains local young people alongside the resort’s operations.

For an island-hopping holiday, Rascal Voyages’ new yacht Rogue will launch in 2027. Built using Indonesia’s traditional phinisi craftsmanship, it extends the company’s floating-villa approach to exploring the islands. Existing voyages range from Komodo to Raja Ampat and the Spice Islands, with selected departures bookable by the cabin. Keep Bali’s restaurants and favourite villa in the itinerary. Just leave room for more. See indonesia. travel- Julietta Jameson

SRI LANKA ROARS BACK

After a period of economic and political instability, Sri Lanka is in the spotlight, and its key drawcards – ancient cultural sights, tropical beaches and wildlife safaris – await visitors.

Giving the country a leg-up are Jetstar’s new non-stop flights three times a week from Melbourne to the capital, Colombo. Launched in August, the 10.5-hour route is also a perfect way to reach southern India. From Colombo, it’s a 90-minute flight to Male, the Maldives’ capital. Combine the two for a double treat of Sri Lankan culture, food and adventure followed by luxury downtime on a Maldivian beach. The country has also replaced its $50 visas with free e-visas for Australians, and its aged airport is finally getting a facelift to more than double its capacity.

Two Sri Lankan hotel groups continue to up their game. The family-run hotelier group Jetwing Hotels’ latest opening is Wahawa Walauwa, a restored 1870s manor house now a six-suite boutique hotel amid a coconut plantation. Meanwhile, Uga Resorts’ eighth property is the ultra-luxe, 15-villa Uga Ghiri in Ella, in the tea plantations of the Central Highlands. Train buffs note that its new villas have a view of the Nine Arch Bridge, a famous colonial-era viaduct that is a highlight on the spectacular rail journey from Ella to Kandy.

If you prefer a walking holiday, swap the train for shoe leather along the 300-kilometre Pekoe Trail from Kandy to Nuwara Eliya. The trail winds through the central highlands passing through tea plantations. The walking ranges from a gentle stroll to ridge walks and high elevations into the island’s cloud forests. Check out Intrepid Travel’s new 10-day Pekoe Trail trips. See srilanka. travel; jetstar. com; thepekoetrail. org; intrepidtravel. com- Belinda Jackson

FINNISH FEST

Expect to hear more Aussie accents in the saunas of Helsinki in 2027 as a flight to Finland becomes the hottest ticket in town, boosted by two new flight routes from Australia.

Finnair kicked off its daily Melbourne-Helsinki flights in late October, with a pitstop in Bangkok opening up the possibility of a sun-and-snow Christmas holiday. With both Finnair and Qantas in the Oneworld alliance, Australian travellers can use Qantas points to book seats, and unlike other carriers, the Nordic airline has kept its carrier charges at bargain-basement prices, for a genuinely good points deal.

While Finnair scooped the headlines, Emirates got in three weeks earlier, launching daily non-stop flights from Dubai to Helsinki, which means there are now two flight paths from Australia to the saunas and salmiakki (salted licorice).

On the ground, rail links with Sweden have been restored after a 38-year break, so train buffs can now ride the rails from northern Finland to southern Portugal, including its sleeper trains in Finnish Lapland, all on European booker Interrail’s rail pass network.

A feted design destination, Helsinki’s most stylish new statement is Kruunuvuorensilta Bridge. Finland’s longest, tallest bridge is also completely car free, for pedestrians, cyclists and light rail, cementing its position as the world’s most sustainable tourist destination on the Global Destination Sustainability Index.

With tree-hugging competitions and about 200 days of northern lights viewing, Finland’s hit the jackpot as a coolcation alternative to a sweaty, crowded Mediterranean holiday. No wonder it’s the world’s happiest country, according to the UN-sponsored World Happiness Report. See visitfinland. com; myhelsinki. fi; interrail. com- BJ

VIVA LAS VEGAS

From December 29, Qantas will operate Australia’s first seasonal non-stop flights from Sydney to Las Vegas, three times a week until March 12. Good news for bucks parties, hen weekends and anyone who has ever wanted to be married by an Elvis impersonator. Beyond the Strip, Nevada is one of America’s most spectacular and underexplored states, a place of vast desert highways, surreal rock formations, ghost towns and landscapes that seem borrowed from another planet. Just an hour from Vegas, the Valley of Fire State Park is a wonderland of blazing red sandstone, while Red Rock Canyon offers hiking trails through dramatic desert scenery. Further afield, Great Basin National Park has ancient bristlecone pines, limestone caves and some of the darkest night skies in America. And up north, Lake Tahoe delivers alpine scenery, ski resorts and impossibly blue water. All of which sound like excellent places to recover after a few nights in Sin City. See qantas. com- Justine Cullen

TAHITI LOOKS NICE(R)

Anyone who’s flown to French Polynesia from Australia knows that the journey usually involves a layover in Auckland followed by a late arrival into Papeete that necessitates spending a night in the capital. From mid-December, you can skip to the good part. Air Tahiti Nui is launching a twice-weekly non-stop flight from Sydney that not only saves travel time (it’ll be about seven hours instead of at least 10) but arrives just after 6am, allowing better connections to more chilled islands than Tahiti.

There’s a brand-new reason to head straight to the honeymooners’ haven of Bora Bora. Bloody Mary’s, a rustic restaurant that started trading in 1979 and quickly became a celeb hangout that attracted the likes of Jane Fonda and Marlon Brando, is opening a 53-room retreat. Choose suites or bungalows that are over water or face that famously Listerine-blue, fish-filled lagoon.

Another option is to hop on a 50-minute flight from Papeete to Tikehau to reach Motu Tianoa – a pink-sand islet that houses Le Tikehau by Pearl Resorts, a member of the Relais & Chateaux portfolio. It has unveiled its horizon over-water suite in a prime position at the end of a pontoon. Even more far-flung is its sister property, Le Nuku Hiva, in the Marquesas; its hillside bungalows have had a glow-up. Only 8165 Australians visited French Polynesia in 2025, but more bountiful numbers now seem assured for this South Pacific idyll. See airtahitinui. com; bloodymarys. com; letikehau. com; lenukuhiva. com- Katrina Lobley

Where to next? Visit these places before everyone else does

Sydney Morning Herald November 27, 2026

This is a modal window.

Beginning of dialog window. Escape will cancel and close the window.

End of dialog window.

This is a modal window. This modal can be closed by pressing the Escape key or activating the close button.

The bucket-list map is shifting, with familiar destinations finding new energy, and less obvious corners of the globe finally coming into their own.

You have reached your maximum number of saved items.

Remove items from your saved list to add more.

Our appetite for travelling to the locations that starred in series or movies shows few signs of abating. If 2027’s line-up of releases is anything to go by, Monaco will be at the top of our set-jetting wishlist. The Mediterranean principality plays a role in Bradley Cooper and Margot Robbie’s as-yet unnamed Ocean’s Eleven prequel and has transformed everywhere, from the legendary Hotel de Paris to the alleyways of Monaco’s old town, into the 1960s. Meanwhile The White Lotus cast has checked into Place du Casino for a part of their Cote d’Azur capers. Even Emily Cooper makes an appearance on the Monaco Grand Prix pit lane during the final season of Emily in Paris.

Plus there’s the effect of the Netflix documentary Drive to Survive. Formula One is ever-increasing in popularity thanks to the series and Monaco’s status as the most glamorous race of the season has only been bolstered by hometown hero Charles Leclerc, his fashionista wife, Alexandra and the couple’s miniature dachshund, Leo. Want to arrive in style?

The Venice Simplon-Orient-Express adds Monaco as a new destination for 2027, 50 years on from the Monte Carlo auction that helped breathe life back into the legendary train.– Chrissie McClatchie

Once the place you’d skip past on your way to the Gold Coast or Byron Bay, the word is well and truly out on the Tweed. Sitting on the border of NSW and Queensland, the region’s pristine coast and burgeoning dining scene have earned it a spot on Lonely Planet’s Best in Travel list and Expedia’s top 10 destinations for 2027.

Sign up for the Traveller Deals newsletter

Get exclusive travel deals delivered straight to your inbox. Sign up now.

Credit goes to that irresistible blend of stellar surf beaches, ancient volcanic landscapes, World Heritage-listed rainforest, luxe new accommodations and a wave of exciting and hatted dining options. Its culinary credentials – supercharged by a steady influx of capital city chef talent – are increasingly a major drawcard including the annual five-day Savour the Tweed festival, held in October, which has become a fixture on the national food calendar. Leading the charge is Pipit in Pottsville, where woodfired technique meets seriously inventive flavours over six courses, then there’s Potager, with its stunningly simple farm-to-table ethos, and Casuarina’s Bar Bruto, going full pelt on the tapas and Barcelona vibes.

Between whale spotting at Tweed Heads and long lunching in the breezy Hamptons-style dining room of Halcyon House’s Paper Daisy, there really areendless temptations to fill up a weekend. See visitthetweed. com. au – Katherine Scott

Lesser-known African countries and unfamiliar regions of favourite African destinations are attracting new attention.

Instead of just joining safaris in Kenya, travellers are also heading to its laid-back island of Lamu for the UNESCO World Heritage-listed old town’s winding alleyways, the striking fort and white-sand beaches. Similarly, Mozambique is increasingly popular for a combination of bush thrills and beach chills. And countries such as South Africa, Tanzania and Botswana face more competition from Namibia (above), a destination rich in desert-adapted wildlife, stirring adventure and spectacularly stark scenery.

In West Africa, there’s Ghana, Togo and Benin which are all becoming a much more trusted trio, with tours by World Expeditions, Intrepid Travel, G Adventures and On The Go. – Sue Williams

Strolling through the boutique-lined streets of Blloku, Tirana’s fashionable cafe-filled district, it’s hard to imagine that just 40 years ago, the city was the capital of one of the world’s most isolated totalitarian nations. Under Stalinist dictator Enver Hoxha, the regime banned everything from typewriters to facial hair.

Even by the Balkans’ standards, Albania’s post-communist transformation is extraordinary – an ideological, architectural and economic backflip that must be seen to be believed. Beyond the capital lies 450 kilometres of glorious coastline along the Adriatic and Ionian Seas, backed by a rugged mountainous interior. If you only do one hike, make it the 19-kilometre trail from Theth to Valbona, a rewarding trek over a 1795-metre-high mountain pass that delivers stride-stopping vistas of snow-dusted peaks and forested ravines. Intrepid Travel’s 10-day Hiking the Balkans trip includes this and other signature treks in the Dinaric Alps.

Most trips start or end in Tirana, a rapidly developing city with an intriguing clash of architectural styles – everything from 21st-century synagogues and Ottoman-era mosques to Italian Renaissance banks and brutalist Communist eyesores. Why visit now? Albania’s fast-tracked bid for European Union membership will inevitably bring more visitors and higher prices. Go soon to beat the rush. See intrepidtravel. com – Rob McFarland

Safety concerns that once deterred tourists are firmly in the past. The nation shares the same Smartraveller advisory rating as Morocco and the UK, yet receives a fraction of their visitors. Tourism remains in its infancy so don’t expect fine dining and five-star service. What you will find is heartfelt hospitality and a warm welcome.

What are some of the historical highlights of Africa’s largest nation? Extraordinary Roman ruins, like Djemila and Timgad – both sprawling UNESCO World Heritage sites with intricate mosaics, chariot-worn streets and yawning public forums. Elsewhere, there are colossal stone mausoleums built for Numidian royalty in the 3rd century BC and the remains of an ancient coastal Carthaginian trading post at Tipaza.

Head south into the Sahara Desert to see fortified hilltop settlements established in the 11th century by the Mozabites, a Berber people who retain their own distinctive dialect, attire and customs. And then there are the cities. The capital, Algiers, is a busy Mediterranean port with sweeping French colonial boulevards and a 1000-year-old UNESCO World Heritage-listed casbah. Meanwhile, 2000-year-old Constantine, known as the City of Bridges, occupies a dramatic hilltop setting with a dizzying collection of ravine-leaping spans.

Though France’s 132-year occupation of Algeria ended in 1962, its legacy lingers in the language, architecture and patisseries. Last year’s film adaptation of The Stranger, Albert Camus’s landmark novel set in 1930s French-colonised Algeria, offers an evocative recreation of this complex and controversial period.

Explore Worldwide is one of only a handful of companies operating in the region and its 10-day Wonders of Ancient Algeria and the M’Zab Valley trip ticks off all the highlights. For an even more immersive experience, check out the 16-day variant that includes five nights camping in the Sahara. See exploreworldwide. com. au – RM

No other South American country can compete with Colombia for scenic splendour and cultural diversity. Not content with having the world’s highest number of bird species (more than 1900), the planet’s tallest palm trees (found in the Cocora Valley) and the highest coastal mountain range (within the stunning Tayrona National Park), it’s also home to indigenous tribes that only came out of self-imposed exile in the 1990s.

Key urban stops include Cartagena, a steamy Caribbean stunner with a UNESCO World Heritage-listed old town, and Medellin, a misty, mountain-ringed metropolis famed for its parks and public art. Don’t overlook Cali, the world’s salsa capital, and the gritty port city of Barranquilla, famous for the country’s largest carnival, an exuberant four-day riot of parades and partying.

Outdoor enthusiasts can tackle a strenuous three-day jungle trek to the ruins of Ciudad Perdida (the Lost City) in the Sierra Nevada mountains, while the plantations around Salento produce some of the world’s best coffee.

Need another reason? Next year marks the 100th anniversary of the birth of Colombia’s most famous literary export: Gabriel Garcia Marquez. Several cities plan celebrations, including his birthplace, Aracataca, the capital, Bogota, and Cartagena, which inspired many of his novels. See colombia. travel – RM

It’s not just the affordable flights, visa-free entry and favourable exchange rates that drive travel to China. According to the Australian Bureau of Statistics, the country is now in the top five most popular destinations for Australians after Indonesia, New Zealand and Japan. With its ancient cultures, futuristic cities, UNESCO-listed sites, varied cuisine and underrated nature tourism, China is one of Asia’s most enticing destinations. In the last decade, high-speed rail has replaced traditional sleeper trains on a number of key routes across China, making the countryside more accessible than ever.

Cyberpunk city Chongqing in the south-east is on the doorstep of karst paradise Wulong National Park (above) and the UNESCO-listed Dazu Rock Carvings, and cooks up some of China’s most distinctive cuisine, such as Sichuan hot pot. Join a 22-day Discover China by Rail tour with Wendy Wu Tours, which includes two nights among the rice terraces of the minority ethnic Zhaoxing Village near Guizhou plus a visit to the mystical sandstone forests of Zhangjiajie National Park in Hunan. From $9690 a person. See wendywutours. com. au – Jennifer Hewett

Evora has long lingered in the shadow of Lisbon and Porto, which is odd given its historical significance as the capital of Portugal’s Alentejo region. Highlights within the cobbled streets of the UNESCO World Heritage-listed walled city include the Temple of Diana, a Roman Temple whose majestic Corinthian marble columns date from the 1st century AD, and Evora Cathedral, an imposing granite Gothic colossus that is Portugal’s largest medieval cathedral.

More unconventional sights include the skeleton-filled Chapel of Bones, built by 16th-century Franciscan monks as a reflection on mortality, and the nearby Almendres Cromlech, a prehistoric megalithic stone circle that’s older than Stonehenge.

Still not convinced? Next year Evora shares the title of European Capital of Culture with Liepaja in Latvia. Visitors can expect a busy schedule of music festivals, open-air theatre performances, art installations and international exhibitions.

The theme of the program is Vagar, a regional philosophy that promotes slow living, deep reflection and sustainable living. All of which sounds like the perfect excuse for a long lunch in a local taverna enjoying Alentejo’s acclaimed regional produce. Order the pork and clam stew with a glass (hell, make it a bottle) of the local, full-bodied tempranillo. See visitportugal. com– RM

This trio of countries – Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania – on the eastern shores of the Baltic Sea continues to grow steadily. Culturally rich, they blend medieval and crusader history, architecture and coastal towns. Cruise lines are increasingly porting in Baltic countries, such as small-ship Windstar Cruises, which offers Seven Gems of the Baltic which takes in Latvia’s UNESCO-listed old town Riga, as well as the World Heritage-flagged sand dunes of Curonian Spit National Park in Lithuania. Next year, Latvia’s Liepaja shares the honour of being European Capital of Culture for 2027 with Evora in Portugal and a program of events will encourage visitors to go beyond the seaside city’s beaches, music festivals and Soviet-era sites. The competition and cultural tourism initiative, Manor House Hackathon, aims to revive historic manors and rural estates in Kuldiga and South Kurzeme via art and multimedia projects. One of the winning creations includes a self-guided walking route that weaves in digital media at 19th-century neoclassical estate Kimale Manor. Seven Gems of the Baltic from $12,231 a person. See windstarcruises. com – JH

Everyone knows South Africa offers absorbing wildlife encounters. In Greater Kruger, India’s revered luxury hotel company Taj has opened a six-suite Bush Lodge, while MalaMala’s new nine-suite Khensani River Lodge will welcome guests beside the Sand River in December. Ulusaba’s rebuilt lodges in Sabi Sand return in April, 2027.

Pairing the bush and Big Five with a different kind of stay is becoming more enticing. Cape Town, the country’s prettiest city, welcomes The Cape Town Edition, an ultra-luxurious stay on the V&A Waterfront. Safari specialist Sabi Sabi’s Claremont hotel ups the glamour ante, with Kirstenbosch Botanic Gardens and the Constantia winelands withineasy reach.

At Mount Nelson, a Belmond Hotel, a new suite and concept store by South African fashion design star Thebe Magugu brings contemporary fashion and art into the hotel experience. Meanwhile, Club Med South Africa, the country’s first resort from the French-founded brand, combines Indian Ocean beach days with a separate Big Five safari stay that allows uncrowded wildlife viewing. See southafrica. net– Julietta Jameson

Red dirt, rock-adapted ghost gums and towering terracotta quartzite cliffs paint the story of a forgotten landscape in this ancient wilderness in Central Australia. The “East Macs” begin just 15 minutes from Alice Springs (Mparntwe) and stretch 150 kilometres east, offering a remote outback immersion by 4WD or on-foot via rugged walking trails. These mountain ranges began life about 350 million years ago, but geological findings indicate that the landscape could date back more than 2.4 billion years. The ranges share the same cultural clout of the Red Centre’s most awe-steeped natural wonders, including the better-known West MacDonnell Ranges, but none of the big tourist buses and crowds. Meet Australia’s largest and oldest silver fox – a ghost gum estimated to be more than 300 years old – at Trephina Gorge Nature Park or view First Nations rock art at Yeperenye or Emily Gap, which tells the creation story of the Caterpillar Dreaming and how the Arrernte understand the ranges were formed. Eco-certified Spirit Safaris offers small-group day tours of the East MacDonnell Ranges in a luxury 4WD, which includes lunch and a visit to the petroglyphs at N’Dhala Gorge. From $297 a person. See spiritsafaris. com – Jenny Hewett

Israeli strikes kill 16 schoolchildren so far this month, Gaza ministry says

The Guardian Thu, 26 Nov 2026 20:33:07 GMT

Statement follows death of sisters, aged 15 and 13, in airstrike on residential apartment in Gaza City

Israeli strikes have killed at least 16 schoolchildren in Gaza since the start of November, as young people across the territory face intensifying bombardment and a struggle to find food, clean water and shelter.

On Wednesday, Gaza’s ministry of education said: “Palestinian students had been targeted for the third time in less than 24 hours, in an escalation reflecting the continued Israeli violations against children in the Gaza Strip. The number of schoolchildren killed since the beginning of November has now risen to 16.”

The statement follows the death of two sisters, Yusra, 15, and Jana Mohammed Abu al-Ouf, 13, in the early hours of Wednesday in an airstrike targeting a residential apartment in western Gaza City.

Yusra was a pupil at Kafr Qasim school, while her sister Jana attended al-Manar private school.

The ministry added: “The girls’ father, Mohammed Majed Abu Al-Ouf, and their mother, Noura Ezzat Abu Al-Ouf, were also killed in the strike which injured several other Palestinians.” The father was a director of internal security services for Hamas in northern Gaza.

Earlier this year, an independent UN inquiry found that Israel continued to commit genocide by deliberately targeting Palestinian children in Gaza.

On 6 November, Mohammed Nidal Barbakh, 15, was shot by Israeli forces in the Bir 19 area of al-Mawasi, Khan Younis, and later died from his injuries.

He was in the 10th grade at the Muscat school and dreamed of becoming a professional football player.

“That day, after lunch, Mohammed went to the sports academy at 1.30pm to take part in training,” his father, Dr Nidal Mohammed Barbakh, said. “An Israeli tank had advanced and positioned itself on a nearby hill before firing two rounds towards the pitch. One of them ricocheted after hitting a metal object, striking Mohammed in the back and exiting through his neck.

“He was talented and an excellent student. He was killed at the age of 15, on a sports pitch in al-Mawasi, an area where people had been told to go because it was considered safe. I do not absolve the Israeli army of responsibility for what happened. It kills every ambition within us and buries our children’s dreams before they have a chance to come true.”

On 13 November, Israeli artillery shelling killed three people in Deir al-Balah, central Gaza, including a father and his 12-year-old son, Ahmed Abu Daher, as well as a woman.

Ahmed dreamed of becoming an Arabic language teacher, like his grandfather Saleh, said his mother, Walaa Abu Daher.

“That day, my husband was heading to a condolence gathering in the al-Qastal area, east of Deir al-Balah,” Daher said. “Ahmed asked his father if he could accompany him. While they were at the gathering, they were targeted by Israeli artillery fire.

“Ahmed ran to ask the people attending the gathering for help. He then rushed back towards his father when a second shell was fired. Shrapnel struck Ahmed in his legs, abdomen and head. I cannot describe how deeply their loss has affected me. I feel as though my life stopped that day.”

Thousands of school-age children and hundreds of education workers have been killed in Israel’s war in Gaza, while tens of thousands of children have been unable to attend school regularly.

On Thursday, Israeli attacks killed at least nine Palestinians across Gaza, including Khaled Abu Nada, the undersecretary of Gaza’s ministry of education, and his wife, according to health officials, as attacks continued despite the ceasefire in the territory.

A few days ago, the ministry of education said Israel’s attacks against students, civilian leaders and teachers were “part of a systematic assault on the Palestinian education system”.

According to Unicef, 98% of school buildings in Gaza have sustained damage, with more than 93% requiring major rehabilitation or full reconstruction, while approximately 81% were directly hit.

Young Palestinians in Gaza face a fourth winter in overcrowded tents and makeshift shelters, with limited access to basic services as the humanitarian and public health crisis deepens.

Children and young people are among those most vulnerable to meningitis, for which Gaza’s health ministry issued an epidemic alert on Tuesday after a sharp rise in infections, with more than 270 new cases reported in October.

Health organisations attribute the rise in infections to the destruction of infrastructure, overcrowded shelters and the contamination of drinking water with sewage – a crisis made worse by winter flooding and restrictions on humanitarian aid.

At least 74,746 Palestinians have been killed in Israel’s war in Gaza over the last three years, according to the territory’s health ministry. More than 20,000 children have been reported killed by Israeli strikes.

The Israel Defense Forces said there was not enough information to comment on the incidents involving Ahmed and Mohammed.

It said that on the day Ahmed died it was carrying out operations that resulted in the killing of “10 terrorists” and “prior to the strikes, measures were taken to mitigate harm to civilians”.

Net migration to UK falls to lowest level since 1997 excluding pandemic

The Guardian Thu, 26 Nov 2026 20:01:47 GMT

Latest figures show difference between number of people arriving and leaving UK was ⁠77,000 in ​year ‌to ‌June

Analysis: How much of the fall in UK immigration is due to Labour’s policies?

Net migration across the UK has fallen to its lowest level since 1997 with the exclusion of the years of the Covid pandemic.

Figures released by the Office for National Statistics and the Home Office show that the difference between people arriving and leaving the UK was ⁠77,000 in ⁠the ​year ‌to ‌June ‌2026.

The ONS figures cover the year ending June 2026, down from an estimated 171,000 in 2025 and a peak of 944,000 in 2023. Annual net migration to the UK in 1997 was 48,000.

UK net migration is also for the first time in the “tens of thousands” since that target was set but never fulfilled by David Cameron’s government in 2010. An estimated 738,000 people immigrated to the UK in the year to June while 661,000 emigrated, according to the data published on Thursday.

The 62% fall over the past 12 months – from 204,000 in the year ending June 2025 – results from lower immigration. Net migration has fallen more than 90% since the peak of 944,000 in the year ending March 2023.

Immigration fell by 17% over the year to June 2026, driven by fewer non-EU citizens being granted permission to work, study, bring family members to the UK or apply for asylum.

Keir Starmer’s policies last year made care workers and some mid-skilled jobs ineligible for work visas, suspended family reunion for refugees and toughened restrictions for universities sponsoring international students.

Emigration remained relatively high but fell by 4% (-28,000) compared with the year ending June 2025.

Most people leaving the UK to live in another country were non-citizens who previously migrated for work or study, including those who moved to the UK as part of the “Boriswave” from 2021 onwards when immigration was unusually high.

Reacting to the figures, the home secretary, Shabana Mahmood, said Labour’s policies should be credited for the drop. It will be seen as a boost to Andy Burnham’s plans to keep hold of “red wall” seats in any future general election.

“The Conservatives lost control of our borders. Year upon year, they promised they would bring net migration down to the tens of thousands. Instead, they let it reach close to a million a year, overseeing four decades worth of migration in their last four years alone.

“This government has restored control. Where they failed, we have delivered for the British people,” she said.

Burnham said of the figures: “I think we are finally, as a country, getting into the position that the public has long wanted to see.”

Asked about the UK’s future relationship with the EU and whether freedom of movement should be up for discussion, he said the Channel crossings crisis “arose significantly in the post-Brexit years when we lost that ability to collaborate with our European partners, and we’ve had to work hard to catch up again … So, no, I don’t think you can say that Brexit did anything other than weaken control of immigration in this country.”

The drop has been driven by policies pushed through by Labour and Conservative governments.

Home Office visa data from January to June 2026 shows visa grants to international students fell by 38% (-39,200) and grants to skilled workers including those in the health and care sector and their dependants also dropped by 38% (-26,300) compared with the same period in 2025.

Sign up to Breaking News UK

Sign up for the Breaking News UK email to get newsletter alerts direct to your inbox

after newsletter promotion

The end of social care visas has caused numbers to fall from 108,000 at their peak to just 1,400 last year.

Migration remains a key political issue, with Labour’s 2024 manifesto promising to reduce net migration, and aiming to “smash the gangs” involved in irregular migration and bringing asylum seekers across the Channel in small boats.

Burnham’s arrival in No 10 has signalled a shift in the way the government views legal migration. Some Labour insiders say that policy is now being driven by economic demands rather than a fear of the rise of Nigel Farage’s Reform UK, which has suffered a dip in the polls.

The Conservatives claimed their policies under Rishi Sunak’s administration were responsible for the drop, including restrictions on family members that could be brought over by care workers and changes stopping dependants moving to the UK with international students.

Chris Philp, the shadow home secretary, said: “The fall in net migration is mainly a result of changes made by the previous Conservative government. We now need to go even further with a legally binding annual cap, set by parliament, at a far lower level.”

Ben Brindle, a senior researcher at the Migration Observatory at the University of Oxford, said net migration could drop even further next year, and may have a “fiscal cost”.

“We are entering an unusual period where immigration has come down and may still have further to fall.

“Falling net migration is not automatically a problem for the UK economy, especially in the long run. Falling asylum migration is expected to benefit public finances. On the other hand, the number of migrants on skilled work visas has fallen even more over the past year, and that is expected to have a fiscal cost,” he said.

Sunder Katwala, the director of the British Future thinktank, said the figures “will come as a surprise to most of the public” who still tended to believe that immigration was rising. “It must now be time for the political and media debate to catch up and start a new phase of the debate about what happens next,” he said.

Other data published by the Home Office showed the number of asylum seekers living in hotels was at the lowest level since records began in 2022, but there was a 9% rise of those in “dispersal” accommodation – privately managed houses, flats or rooms in properties of multiple occupancy. There has been a drop in the number of new asylum applicants and Channel crossings are down 39% year on year, with 23,983 people having arrived in the UK in small boats in 2026.

Éric Cantona: ‘If I regret something about the kung fu kick, it’s that I would love to kick him in another place’

The Guardian Thu, 26 Nov 2026 20:00:44 GMT

Before the release of a new documentary, the unrepentant Manchester United icon reflects on his deep bond with English football and his darker instincts

“I’m an angel and a demon,” Éric Cantona says intently during a gripping new documentary about his life on and off the football pitch. “And an angel or a demon, you love him or you hate him. I’m far from being the person with the greatest integrity. I’m far from being the person who always tells the truth. I’m far from being the person who has never been hypocritical. Maybe I’m a good person, but I can also be a flower of evil. It’s the first time in my life I’ve realised this. I am a flower of evil, and I find it very beautiful.”

It’s hard to know what to expect from the only written interview pinned to the release of Cantona: Flower of Evil. Joel Cantona has warned that his famous brother will walk out at any mention of the enduring crisis surrounding Manchester United, whether it’s a question about Mauricio Pochettino’s arrival or the Glazer family’s ruinous ownership of the club.

I prepare for a possible meltdown because rare archive footage, which opens the documentary, captures a televised standoff between Cantona and a few French journalists. He objects to the fact that L’Équipe had described his kung fu kick against a Crystal Palace supporter in 1995 as “unforgivable”. After asking who is truly “unforgivable”, and highlighting the historical sins of the Catholic church, Cantona sneers: “I piss on the pope’s arse. Just as I piss on the arse of certain journalists … including you and you,” he says, pointing to two outraged writers.

Now, 30 years later, Cantona emerges in his home city of Marseille, wearing a natty trilby. Within minutes I can tell that the flower of evil is elsewhere because Cantona is in a generous mood. As he recalls that bitterly sensational clash with the French reporters he smiles: “I’m a good client for the journalists – and they are a good client for me to express myself. We play a bit like the cat and the mouse. Sometimes we have good relationships, sometimes a bad relationship. But it’s always interesting and exciting.”

This might be Cantona at his most angelic, stretching the truth about the supposed thrill of his journalistic encounters, but it’s fitting that the film starts with the 60-year-old quoting Charles Baudelaire, the 19th-century French poet who, in his Flowers of Evil collection, wrote: “I am the wound and the knife/I am the blow and the cheek/ … The victim and the executioner …”

Cantona’s brilliance and spite defined his troubled time at six French clubs between 1983 and 1992. He could have “disappeared” from football because, despite being France’s most gifted player, he had fallen out with the national manager. The young Cantona said: “I hope people realise Henri Michel is one of the most incompetent coaches in world football.”

Michel Platini, who replaced Michel, persuaded Cantona to end his fleeting retirement in 1992 by moving to England. As Cantona says: “I knew it will be my last chance … and it’s really in England where I regain this passion for football … it’s a rebirth.”

The documentary provides a compelling account of his turbulent love affair with English football – but ignores a strange prelude at Sheffield Wednesday. Cantona tells me this forgotten strand of his story with amused incredulity. “I arrived at Sheffield Wednesday and we played a friendly. We won 4-3 and I scored three goals. And then I waited to sign the contract. At the end of the week they said: ‘You have to spend one more week on trial.’ I said: ‘No. I leave.’”

Who managed Wednesday then? “Trevor Francis – who was a great player,” Cantona replies. “Howard Wilkinson heard about that and asked me to come to Leeds. I arrived in Leeds and then we became champions and it was a great time.”

That deceptively simple last sentence fails to capture the seismic impact Cantona had on English football and especially on Leeds, who won the league title for the first time in 18 years in 1992. “It was old-fashioned football,” Cantona says. “It was interesting. There was also, for me, the feeling of adding something different.”

Was it disheartening playing antiquated football? “No, because I played with wonderful players. We had a great midfield with Gary Speed, David Batty, Gary McAllister and Gordon Strachan. And quickly [the following season] I arrive at Manchester United with Alex Ferguson. The club had the Busby Babes. That was wonderful football. Manchester United has always been a club where winning in a good way is important.”

This should be the moment to ask Cantona about the contrast with the current moribund state of United but, rather than falling out over his refusal to discuss the club now, it’s enough to hear him in full flow. “This club always loved people with different personalities. They loved George Best, Brian McClair, [Norman] Whiteside, [Roy] Keane …”

Cantona was adored at Old Trafford, as he had been at Leeds before his shock departure to United for a mere £1m in November 1992. He also led United to their first Premier League title, in 1993, after a 26-year drought.

There are great clubs in Italy, Spain and Germany so could he have resurrected his career in one of these countries? Cantona shakes his head: “I love Italian football. I love Spanish football. I love Barcelona. But nothing can compare to English football and the fans, the way they sing and express themselves. It’s so powerful.”

Cantona remembers that, when he arrived in England, “in the street, nobody knew me. I felt free for the first time in my life. I could go have a drink somewhere, listen to some music and it was always peaceful.”

Ferguson recalls that he asked Guy Roux, the wise old manager who nurtured Cantona at his first club, Auxerre, how to harness his volatile talent. Roux offered two words: “Love him.”

Cantona nods: “I’m instinctive. If I feel bad I go. If I feel good, I try to create a relationship. And when I arrive in Manchester I see the ghosts of the past. I felt this very strong energy and I thought: ‘Maybe this is the place where I will have the opportunity to express myself.’ I found in Alex Ferguson the perfect manager. I was very lucky he gave me this freedom. He understood me so well so I could express myself 100%. He’s a great manager.”

Everything changed when Cantona’s temper returned – culminating in the dark moment in January 1995 when, after he was sent off against Crystal Palace, he was insulted by a rival fan as he headed towards the tunnel. Cantona launched himself at the man and, in mid-air, caught him with a scything kung fu kick.

He faced a charge of criminal assault and was sentenced to two weeks in prison, a judgment which was reduced to 120 hours of community service on appeal. Cantona was banned from football for eight months and returned to France. He looks at me coolly: “I know people expect me to say: ‘Oh, I regret it.’ No, I don’t regret it. If I regret something, it’s that I would love to kick him in another [place].” Cantona points out that perceptions are always changing. “The kung fu kick was criticised a lot, especially by journalists. But now it’s a [more positive] symbol. So I change everything.”

Sign up to Football Daily

Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football

after newsletter promotion

Did much thought go into his cryptic comment after the court hearing: “When the seagulls follow the trawler it’s because they think sardines will be thrown into the sea.”

Cantona grins. “No. I didn’t want to speak to the press, but the lawyer said: ‘You have to say something.’ I could have said: ‘I walk on the moon and tomorrow I dive deeper in the ocean.’ It was good for everybody. We all enjoyed it together.”

Ferguson, with compassion and guile, enticed Cantona back to Manchester. It was a triumph as, in a young team including David Beckham, Ryan Giggs and Paul Scholes, Cantona was a model of brooding magnificence as he inspired United to another championship.

He left the game for good the following year, in 1997, after captaining United to a fourth league title in five seasons. “I was very passionate about other things,” he says, “and I didn’t want to waste time. I wanted to do something else.”

Cantona adds: “I left football because I lost passion for the game. I had to be honest with myself, and with the fans. I’m very proud of that [honesty].”

There is a deep bond between Cantona and the older men in his life. When we spoke this month, Ferguson was 84, Cantona’s father Albert was 86, Roux was 88 and Ken Loach, the film-maker, was 90. “I met a few people in my life,” Cantona tells me, “and Guy Roux, Alex Ferguson, Ken Loach and, of course, my father, are the most wonderful people I know.”

Two days after our interview, Cantona announced the death of his dad with a heartfelt message on Instagram accompanied by a black-and-white photograph of Albert smoking a cigar: “My father. My God. My master. Rest in peace.”

The importance of his father, a painter who nourished Cantona’s interest in art and acting, is rivalled only by Ferguson. There is a deeply touching segment in the film when Ferguson reads aloud the letter of gratitude he wrote to Cantona after the footballer retired at the age of 30.

We also talk about what Cantona might have done had he not worked so much in film, art and music. “I still would have been involved in football, maybe as a manager,” he says. “It’s very interesting and I would have liked to be a manager in an artistic way, trying to create something.”

Would he have been a good manager? Cantona laughs. “I don’t know. But I will have tried to find something that nobody tried before. Something original – like Johan Cruyff at Barcelona. Or Alex Ferguson at Manchester United. It’s a big club, a rich club, it could buy anyone. But he believed in a young generation and he created a way to manage players.”

Cantona rarely watches football but when did he last see an entire game? “I’m shooting a TV series in Marseille and last month I went to the stadium to see Marseille against Olympiakos in the Europa League. It was the first time I came back to Marseille since 1991 when I was a player. They lost 1-0 but I enjoyed it because Marseille is in my veins, like English football and the fans of Manchester United.”

The world is changing so fast and, after 45 minutes, we start talking about AI and the future. “Of course,” Cantona says when I ask whether he is concerned. “I try as hard as possible to stay away [from technology]. I can show you my phone.”

He brings out an old brick. “I never had anything else,” Cantona says cheerfully. “I never had a smartphone. I don’t want it. More and more people realise that they become a prisoner of it. If you use it well, it can be good. But I’m a bit excessive. So I prefer not to have it.”

I ask Cantona about the demon inside him. What is it? “My instinct. It’s my best friend but there is always a fight with a different little voice inside. This voice is still alive.”

Cantona tips his hat one last time and grins: “We are still fighting. But I win a lot of fights.”

Cantona: Flower of Evil is in UK & Ireland cinemas 7 and 12 December only, with Éric Cantona Q&A broadcast live from Manchester. Participating cinemas here and tickets for the event here

Slow internet? The best wifi extenders and mesh systems to boost your home network – tested

The Guardian Thu, 26 Nov 2026 20:00:43 GMT

Guardian journalism is independent. We earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link. Learn more.

We put 11 range extenders and mesh systems to the test to find the fastest and most reliable for streaming, gaming and working from home

The best office chairs

Fast fibre broadband is fantastic – if the wifi signal reaches the part of your home where you need it. Most of us use the router provided by our broadband provider, often tucked away in a hallway or corner of the lounge. Sadly, these often don’t have the range to cover every room in your home, leaving you high and dry when you’re trying to binge-watch TV or get work done in a distant home office.

Wifi extenders and mesh systems can help. Extenders plug in to a mains socket between your location and the router, then pass data backwards and forwards to extend your router’s reach. Mesh systems are even smarter, pairing a secondary router with one or two satellite units, which work together to extend the wifi coverage throughout your home. The mesh system can pass your connection from unit to unit to make sure you’re always getting the best possible link from your device to the internet, wherever you are in your home.

Extenders are cheap and cheerful, but often only extend your wifi coverage to one area. A mesh system, working properly, should cover your whole home. I’ve tested the best of both to find the fastest, most effective and most affordable ways to boost your wifi.

Best mesh wifi system overallEero Pro 7

Best budget wifi extenderNetgear EAX12

Best value wifi 7 extenderTP-Link RE225BE

Best mesh wifi system for all-round coverageTP-Link Deco BE68

Best wifi extender for gaming and high speedsAsus ZenWiFi BT10

I’ve spent more than three decades reviewing technology, covering PCs, printers, laptops, tablets, games consoles, projectors and more. In that time, I’ve also tested more than my fair share of network extenders, mesh systems, network storage devices and routers. I know what to look for in terms of features and performance, as well as ease of setup and use.

I tested 11 wifi extenders and mesh systems from the leading manufacturers, covering as many different product types and budgets as possible. Each product was set up for real-world testing in my three-bedroom, two-floor home. It’s a tough testing ground for wireless products, with an unusually wide floor plan that makes it hard to push a wifi signal to one side of the house, especially with thick interior walls and glass doors getting in the way.

I installed and configured each mesh system or extender and added any satellite units. I then ran bandwidth tests using network-testing software to see how fast data could pass back and forth between a wifi 7 laptop and a second laptop, connected via ethernet cable to the router. I also ran file-transfer tests to check connection speeds. Tests took place in the two most troublesome wifi locations in the house: the dining room, where I often work, and an upstairs room used as an office.

In addition to these tests, I streamed 4K video from YouTube to check for signs of an erratic signal or buffering, and streamed games from a PC running Steam, a gaming platform. Testing network products can be frustrating and demoralising since there’s nearly always something that doesn’t work the first time. Blasting demons to bits in Doom: The Dark Ages helped keep me sane.

After testing, all the products were either returned to their sources or donated to InFocus, a charity that supports young people with vision impairment and complex needs.

Amazon’s premium mesh system can give you high-speed wifi 7 just about anywhere across your home, without too much fuss or expense. You can buy the router unit solo (£209.99 at the time of writing) or with one or two satellites, with each slim white unit standing at 18cm. The Eero app handles setup and configuration, and the mesh can run across the 2.4GHz, 5GHz and 6GHz wifi bands, with a combined theoretical bandwidth of 10.8 gigabits a second (Gbits/sec), rated BE10800, although Eero lists a more realistic 3.9Gbits/sec maximum.

Why we love it It’s extremely easy to set up. The simple-to-follow instructions in the app offer advice on where to place the satellites, and information on what devices are connected to which satellite, as well as the amount of bandwidth they’re consuming. Each unit has two 5-gigabit ethernet ports (5GbE), making this system future-proof, too.

The three-unit setup was super speedy in both test rooms, with the fastest file-transfer test recorded in the office and dining room. Wifi 7 speeds peaked at 854Mbits/sec in the dining room and 755Mbits/sec in the office, and neither 4K video nor game streaming showed any sign of lag or buffering.

It’s a shame that … the most useful security features and parental controls are locked away behind an Eero+ subscription for an additional £9.99 a month or £99.99 a year. And you’ll be reminded of this at every opportunity in the app.

Maximum wifi standard and bandwidth: wifi 7, 3.9Gbits/sec Bands supported: tri-band 2.4GHz, 5GHz, 6GHzPorts and sockets: 2 x 5GbE ports, 1 x USB-C power port

There’s nothing fancy about this basic wifi 6 extender. It doesn’t push the frontiers of performance, even by wifi 6 standards, with a maximum speed of 1.6Gbits/sec. As far as features go, there’s just one 1GbE port. However, it’s affordable and does a good job of extending wifi coverage to distant rooms. And for that, it’s a simple, cost-effective pick.

Why we love it Placed strategically in a nearby wall socket, the EAX12 delivered solid and reliable wifi 6 coverage in both the dining room and the upstairs office. Speeds aren’t anything to write home about, but were perfectly respectable, peaking at 218Mbits/sec in the dining room and 201Mbits/sec in the office. Once set up, it just got on with the job, with no unexpected dropouts. I was also surprised by how well it handled 4K video streaming and cloud gaming, as long as other devices on the network weren’t streaming and gaming at the same time.

It’s a shame that … there’s a mismatch between Netgear’s quick setup guide and the actual setup routine, with no QR code to be found on the extender itself. Luckily, setup is more straightforward if you install the app and follow the instructions in there.

Maximum wifi standard and bandwidth: wifi 6 AX1600, 1.6Gbits/secBands supported: dual-band 2.4GHz, 5GHzPorts and sockets: 1 x 1GbE

The RE225BE supports the latest wifi 7 standard, but doesn’t cost as much as the high-performance models. That’s partly because it’s a dual- rather than a tri-band extender (read more about this in the buying guide below), with speeds of up to a maximum 3.6Gbits/sec across the 2.4GHz and 5GHz bands. The pricier RE405BE offers speeds up to 6.5Gbits/sec. Still, 3.6Gbits/sec isn’t to be sniffed at, and is more than enough for today’s wifi 6 devices, while leaving headroom for future laptops and smartphones.

Why we love itTP-Link has mastered easy setup, and following the instructions in the app, you’ll have this extender up and running in minutes. In my tests, it was noticeably faster than the wifi 6 models with my wifi 7 laptop, with speeds of 279Mbits/sec in the dining room and 278Mbits/sec in the office. Coverage was excellent in surrounding rooms, 4K video streamed flawlessly to the dining room, and I could kick demons around in Doom without any dropouts or lag spoiling the party. Considering its price, it offers impressive value and enough performance to see you through your next few device upgrades.

It’s a shame that … there’s only a 1GbE port rather than a faster 2.5GbE port, but that’s only likely to matter if you’re connecting a high-end desktop PC or laptop that supports the faster standard.

Maximum wifi standard and bandwidth: wifi 7 BE3600, 3.6Gbits/secBands supported: dual-band 2.4GHz, 5GHzPorts and sockets: 1 x 1GbE

TP-Link’s two-unit wifi 7 mesh system nearly scooped the overall prize. It delivers tri-band wifi 7 performance with a theoretical 14Gbits/sec speed across all three bands, while each unit has one 10GbE port for connecting to your router, one 2.5GbE port for PCs or consoles, and a 1GbE port for other devices. This should more than cater to any device upgrades you make in the next five to 10 years.

Why we love itOnly the Eero Pro 7 matched TP-Link’s hassle-free setup, while TP-Link’s app offers more features and fewer irritating prompts to subscribe for extras. The compact, cylindrical design is simple, stylish enough and easy to tuck away. Although I tested the two-unit system, coverage and performance came close to the three-unit Eero and Orbi setups in my most distant test rooms. I hit it hard with 4K video, game streaming and online gaming – and it handled it all without breaking a sweat.

It’s a shame that … it’s not as fast as rivals for close-range connections, and there are some intrusive ads in the app.

Maximum wifi standard and bandwidth: wifi 7 BE14000, 14Gbits/secBands supported: tri-band 2.4GHz, 5GHz, 6GHzPorts and sockets: 1 x 10GbE port, 1 x 2.5GbE port, 1 x 1GbE port, 1 x USB

This two-unit, tri-band Asus mesh system is another serious contender. The square-fronted units look a little chunky compared with the TP-Link and Eero models, but with a combined theoretical bandwidth of up to 18Gbits/sec, it’s hard to complain. It’s also packed with features, including dual 10GbE ports and a 1GbE port per unit, built-in security tools, a USB port for shared network storage, and a truly comprehensive app.

Why we love itThe Asus system has all the tools and features an enthusiast could hope for – and all the performance you’d want to make the most of the UK’s fastest fibre connections. It’s ludicrously speedy at close range, and testing it with 4K video and full HD game streaming isn’t really enough to stretch it. More advanced features and parental controls are accessible through the app or the browser-based interface, and you don’t need to pay extra to use them. The powerhouse spec makes the Asus a good investment for the future.

It’s a shame that … speeds and coverage at long range weren’t quite up there with the Eero and Netgear Orbi setups, especially in my distant upstairs office. You can buy a three-unit system, but it costs more than £900.

Maximum wifi standard and bandwidth: wifi 7 BE18000, 18Gbits/secBands supported: tri-band 2.4GHz, 5GHz, 6GHzPorts and sockets: 2 x 10GbE ports, 1 x 1GbE port, 1 x USB

For more, read the best gaming chairs for every player

Best for: cutting-edge speeds

Netgear’s three-unit mesh system makes an intimidating first impression, with each of its black and dark-grey towers standing nearly 30cm tall. And it has the performance to match, beating the Eero, Asus and TP-Link systems in some tests and matching them closely in others. When I checked coverage around the house, it was hard to find a spot where signal strength dropped below 80% to 90%, and the app and the browser-based interface provide access to a huge range of settings and features.

With one 10GbE port and two 2.5GbE ports per satellite unit, plus an additional 10GbE port on the main unit for the WAN, the Orbis are ready for the fastest fibre broadband connections and anything else you might want to plug in. Plus, they have a combined theoretical bandwidth of up to 27Gbits/sec across four bands – 2.4GHz, two 5GHz and 6GHz bands – with one 5GHz band dedicated to the “backhaul” connection for the mesh. That’s arguably more bandwidth than most homes could realistically use, making regular wifi 7 routers look puny.

It didn’t make the final cut because … two units cost nearly £900 at the time of writing, with three at nearly £1,600. I struggled to connect one of the satellites, and the speeds don’t quite justify the premium for all but the most demanding tech-heads.

Maximum wifi standard and bandwidth: wifi 7 BE27000, 27Gbits/sec; bands supported: quad-band 2.4GHz, 5GHz (x2), 6GHz; ports and sockets: 1 x 10GbE port, 2 x 2.5GbE ports on satellite units, 2 x 10GbE ports, 4 x 2.5GbE ports on router

Best for: wifi boosting on the cheap

There’s much to love about this budget wifi 6 extender. It’s super-cheap – you could pick it up for less than £30 at the time of writing – and it still gives you up to 1.5Gbits/sec wifi over the 2.4GHz and 5GHz bands. It’s easy to set up using the Mercusys app or by pressing the WPS button on the extender and your router. The smart signal indicator also makes finding the best position straightforward. Performance won’t match pricier setups, but I had no issues streaming 4K video or spreading demon guts around the scenery in Doom: The Dark Ages. Basically, it does the job.

It didn’t make the final cut because … it’s cheaper than the Netgear and TP-Link extenders, but also significantly slower. Speeds topped out at 137Mbits/sec in the dining room and 140Mbits/sec in the office. It’s a decent wifi booster for now, but it could hold you back in a few years’ time.

Maximum wifi standard and bandwidth: wifi 6 AX1500, 1.5Gbits/sec; bands supported: dual-band 2.4GHz, 5GHz; ports and sockets: 1 x 1GbE port

Best for: a more affordable wifi 7 mesh setup

This Devolo wifi 7 mesh is the cheapest three-unit mesh system I tested, and its compact router and satellites – smaller than the average paperback in height – also make it one of the least obtrusive. Unlike most budget wifi 7 systems, it has a BE6500 speed rating, meaning wireless speeds are about as good as they get with two bands. You can switch the system to use a combination of the 2.4GHz and 5GHz bands or the 2.4GHz and 6GHz bands. This leaves you with a conundrum if you want to run existing wifi 6 kit at a decent speed, as they’ll be stuck on the slower 2.4GHz band if you want to run wifi 7 devices on the 6GHz band. Still, it gives you scope to switch as wifi 7 support improves.

It didn’t make the final cut because … I found it difficult to position the satellites to achieve a good balance between fast connections to the router and a decent signal in my two test rooms. The result? Underwhelming speeds, particularly in the upstairs office where I couldn’t push the speed over 168Mbits/sec (I could get up to 877Mbits/sec at close range, though).

Maximum wifi standard and bandwidth: wifi 7 BE6500, 6.5Gbits/sec; bands supported: dual-band 2.4GHz, 5GHz, or 2.4GHz and 6GHz; ports and sockets: 1 x 2.5GbE port, 3 x 1GbE ports

Best for: gaming on a budget

The RE405BE offers a speed boost over the RE225BE above, particularly if your phone or laptop supports wifi 7. It’s still a dual-band extender, but its BE6500 rating means a bump to 5.76Gbits/sec on the 5GHz band and 688Mbits/sec on the 2.4GHz band. This isn’t just a difference on paper: bandwidth peaked at 408Mbits/sec in my upstairs office and 326Mbits/sec in the dining room. The four-aerial design – which makes it look weirdly like a robot roast chicken – ensures a good signal in nearby rooms, while the 2.5GbE port makes it a great match for high-speed PCs, media servers and wired networks. It could also double as a wifi access point for a fast wired network.

It didn’t make the final cut because … it was almost twice the price of the RE225BE at the time of writing, and the speed increase isn’t really worth it unless you’re a gamer.

Maximum wifi standard and bandwidth: wifi 7 BE6500, 6.5Gbits/sec; bands supported: dual-band 2.4GHz, 5GHz; ports and sockets: 1 x 2.5GbE

Best for: smaller homes

Devolo’s wifi 6 extender is a little faster than its Netgear and Mercusys rivals, offering up to 2.4Gbits/sec on the 5GHz band and 574Mbits/sec on 2.4GHz. The compact unit has a single 1GbE port, while the front LEDs double as a status indicator and a wifi signal meter to help find the best position. I had some issues connecting the Repeater 3000 using Devolo’s Home Network app, but once up and running, it provided useful info on connected devices and bandwidth usage.

It didn’t make the final cut because … I couldn’t get it to connect to my main test network, and it struggles to maintain a good connection at a distance, rendering its speed advantage almost moot.

Maximum wifi standard and bandwidth: wifi 6 AX3000, 2.97Gbits/sec; bands supported: dual-band 2.4GHz, 5GHz; ports and sockets: 1 x 1GbE

Best for: a speedy wifi 6 extender

The most unusual extender in my test, this one looks more like a compact router than a traditional plug-in unit, thanks to its separate power supply. That gives it more room for internal aerials and two 1GbE ports, while offering greater flexibility over placement. It was noticeably faster than every other wifi 6 extender I tested, with excellent signal strength in nearby rooms. In fact, it was faster in my office than some wifi 7 mesh systems. It sailed through my gaming and video streaming tests, too.

It didn’t make the final cut because … in everyday use, it sometimes lost the connection to the router, and it’s comparatively expensive.

Maximum wifi standard and bandwidth: wifi 6 AX5400, 5.38Gbits/sec; bands supported: dual-band 2.4GHz, 5GHz; ports and sockets: 2 x 1GbE

While they both improve wifi range, extenders and mesh systems do slightly different things. An extender (or repeater) works with an existing router, extending its wifi signal to a room or an area in your home. It receives packets of data from your router or the device you’re using, then repeats them to the router or device at the other end. This can reduce connection speeds, but you can get a solid connection in areas where you wouldn’t otherwise.

A mesh system replaces your existing router or works alongside your broadband provider’s router, using one or more satellite units placed around your home to create a single, seamless wifi network. These units communicate with each other to find the most efficient route to send data between your devices and the router, helping extend coverage throughout your home. The downside? Mesh systems are considerably more expensive than a simple extender.

A new wifi standard is introduced every few years as the industry works to stay ahead of the demands of newer devices and faster internet connections. Routers, extenders and devices such as smartphones, tablets, laptops and games consoles gradually adopt each new standard, ideally before the next one arrives. Wifi 5 is still usable, but it’s a bit old-hat these days and will limit newer devices, particularly with broadband speeds of 100Mbits/sec and above. Wifi 6 is faster, better at longer range and now supported by most new devices, making it a good fit for connections below 1Gbit/sec.

However, internet connections are getting faster, and we have more devices competing for bandwidth. That’s where wifi 7 comes in, offering more capacity for busy homes and support for the fastest internet speeds.

There are two things we should make clear, though. First, your wifi doesn’t determine your internet speed – that’s down to your provider, the connection infrastructure in your area, your service package and the router it supplies. Better wifi can remove bottlenecks between your devices and that router, but it can’t speed up the connection itself. Second, older devices will still work with newer wifi standards; a wifi 6 laptop will still connect to a wifi 7 mesh system, but it won’t make the most of the available speed and bandwidth.

There can be incompatibility issues between manufacturers in some instances, but otherwise yes. Wifi standards are backwards-compatible, although you’ll be limited by the slower connection speed between the extender and the router. However, this isn’t a problem with mesh systems, where the main unit connects to your existing router through a cable and creates a brand-new wifi network. Speeds may be limited if your existing fibre router only has a gigabit ethernet connection or you have a relatively slow fibre broadband package. A mesh or extender can make the most of what you’ve got, but it can’t make your actual broadband faster.

Gigabit ethernet (GbE) ports are now standard on most mesh systems and extenders, providing a fast wired connection to your router and a way to add wired devices, such as a desktop PC or network storage, to your network. Faster 2.5GbE and 10GbE ports are useful if you have ultrafast fibre broadband above 1Gbit/sec, or a high-end gaming desktop PC that supports those speeds.

USB ports can also be handy on mesh systems if they allow you to hook up an external hard drive or SSD, and to share files between PCs or other devices connected to your network.

Most wifi 5 and wifi 6 networks run over two frequencies or bands – 5GHz and 2.4GHz. This gives them more bandwidth to work with than they’d have over a single band, and also means that some devices can use the 5GHz band, which is less congested and less prone to interference. The wifi 6E and wifi 7 standards went one better by adding a third 6GHz band (though, strangely, not all wifi 7 routers or extenders support this). This doesn’t have the same range as the 5GHz or 2.4GHz bands, but there’s even less congestion, and it can be really speedy at close range. You get increased capacity, giving more devices more bandwidth to work with.

What’s more, in a mesh network, the third band can work as a “backhaul”, passing data between the different nodes on the network while keeping the other two bands free for connecting your devices. Those devices aren’t then competing for the same resources, and can connect at even higher speeds.

Tri-band networks, then, are faster, but you might not need that fast a network, especially if your real bottleneck is your fibre broadband connection speed. Also, there may not be a difference at long range. Think of tri-band as a nice-to-have for maximum performance, but not an essential if you’re on a budget.

Most routers or mesh systems are able to run more than one wireless network at once, and many use this ability to offer a guest network or a dedicated network for your IoT (Internet of Things) devices. That makes sense, as many smart lightbulbs, security cameras or appliances don’t receive regular updates, and a hacker might use them to get a foothold on your network and see what mischief they can do from there. Also, keeping all those devices on a separate network means they’re not clogging up your main network with unnecessary traffic. You may need to enable additional settings to properly isolate them.

It’s a similar idea with guest networks. You can offer them to visitors, with their own network name and password, but they can’t see or start investigating any laptops or devices that you have hooked up to your main network. Plus, this usually preserves bandwidth for your devices, and stops a guest hogging it all with video streams or massive downloads.

Sites and stores such as Back Market, CeX and Amazon Resale sell customer returns or preowned products. If they’ve been reset and prepared for a new setup, they’ll be perfectly fine so long as they’re compatible with your network and still receive security updates. I’d still steer clear of older wifi 5 systems and extenders, though; wifi 6 mesh systems should have plenty of life in them yet.

Extenders and mesh systems can be recycled like most other electronic products, either through local collections or recycling points. Follow the manufacturer’s instructions to reset the device before disposing of it, and check that the reset has completed successfully. While it won’t store personal files, it may retain your wifi settings and network passwords, which could be misused.

Stuart Andrews is a journalist with more than three decades of experience in computing and consumer tech. When he’s not messing around with PCs, laptops and projectors, he’s trying to tame his post-apocalyptic garden with the latest cordless gadgets. Likes arty movies, walking and devices that just work; hates things that won’t connect to his home network. This round of testing may have affected his blood pressure and increased his snack consumption

Nottingham man jailed for 12 years for drugging and sexually assaulting partner

The Guardian Thu, 26 Nov 2026 19:54:05 GMT

‘Depraved’ predator attacked victim while she was under the influence of sleeping tablets he had given her

A man has been jailed for 12 years for drugging his long-term partner and sexually assaulting her while she slept.

The man, who is in his 30s and from Nottingham, cannot be named in order to protect the identity of his victim. At a hearing in June, he admitted sexually assaulting the woman on multiple occasions while she was under the influence of sleeping pills.

He was sentenced at Nottingham crown court on Thursday for two counts of sexual assault, six counts of assault by penetration and one count of possession of a class B drug.

The man wept in the dock as Judge Watson told him his sex crimes were “depraved” and “playing out a disturbing fantasy”.

“For a number of months you abused the trust inherent in any relationship,” the judge said. “You made excuses and shrugged off her concerns. She built up trust in you slowly that you betrayed.”

The court was told the victim was “particularly vulnerable” because he had given her sleeping tablets and sometimes wine that he asked her to drink. This induced a deep state of sleep.

The judge said the man would be subject to a sexual harm prevention and restraining order for the foreseeable future because he presented a “danger to future partners”.

Isabel Wilson of the Crown Prosecution Service East Midlands said: “This man sought to gain power over a woman who should have been at her safest with him, treating her as an object for his own sexual gratification.

“These were deeply predatory offences that involved a shocking abuse of trust, and the devastating impact of that betrayal cannot be overstated.

“I hope this conviction provides some sense of justice for the victim and demonstrates that those who commit such appalling offences will be brought before the courts and held accountable.”
