The Guardian Thu, 26 Nov 2026 19:03:47 GMT

Notebooks, clothes and ritual objects taken by British forces in India in the 1930s go on show at Pitt Rivers Museum

In 1932, British forces in north-east India imprisoned a 17-year-old girl called Gaidinliu for leading an uprising against colonial rule. While pursuing the freedom fighter through hills and valleys in the homeland of the Naga people, colonial officers also seized some of her most treasured possessions.

They were sent to the University of Oxford’s Pitt Rivers Museum and kept in storage. Now, for the first time, the museum is exhibiting the collection of 27 items, including a basket of Gaidinliu’s notebooks believed to contain her prophetic visions as the leader of a Naga Indigenous religion, clothes, bracelets and amulets.

Also on display are protective ritual objects, taken by the British from Gaidinliu’s hiding places, which they believed she had used against them. These are a stick with a monkey skull used to ward off evil spirits, and small wooden clubs, traditionally used by Naga people to cast an omen on an enemy.

The exhibition, The Afterlives of Captured Objects, raises questions about the colonial extraction of artefacts from Indigenous communities, which were often originally catalogued using prejudiced and discriminatory language, according to the curator, Clare Harris, a professor of visual anthropology.

For example, Harris said Gaidinliu’s notebooks were derided as “meaningless scribbling” by the colonial anthropologist JP Mills, who collected them. But he also recorded that these writings “gave her immense prestige”, which suggests that they may have been seized as part of British efforts to suppress the religious and political movement that Gaidinliu led, called Heraka.

While most of the objects on display were taken by the British after Gaidinliu abandoned them while on the run, two items were more violently extracted. Textiles displayed on mannequins in the show were taken from a pair of male and female sacred clay figures from a Heraka temple in the village of Kambiron in 1931.

The textiles are shown along with a photograph taken by a British officer of another soldier kneeling with the sacred figures, which were destroyed along with the temple.

“By showing the photograph at the same time, you can make the equation visually about what was extracted by the British there,” said Harris. “The British destroy the temple and they destroy the figures, so they take away the potency of those things.”

The show follows a four-year project by researchers from India and the Universities of Edinburgh and Oxford to digitise the Gaidinliu collection and share it with Naga communities in Assam, Nagaland and Manipur. Their craftspeople have used the images to revive and revitalise traditional crafts such as basket weaving and textile making, with some of their creations included in the exhibition.

Arkotong Longkumer, a professor of anthropology and modern Asia at the school of divinity, University of Edinburgh, who co-led the project with Harris, said attempts were also being made to translate Gaidinliu’s notebooks in an effort to reconstruct a new Indigenous language for the Naga people.

He said: “There are some symbols which are recognisable within stories and myths. They may be untranslatable in a conventional sense but they are being used to try and construct a language system.”

Water levels fell sharply in world’s rivers and lakes in two hottest years on record, study finds

The Guardian Thu, 26 Nov 2026 19:00:41 GMT

Researchers say effects particularly felt in South America where levels plunged even as some areas had extreme rain

Extreme global heat caused an unprecedented decline in the water levels of lakes, rivers and reservoirs around the world in 2023 and 2024, an international study has found.

The analysis of global water systems, a collaboration led by the Chinese Academy of Sciences, found that the planet’s surface freshwater fell sharply during the two years, which were the hottest on record. Global river flows fell to about 5.7% below normal, while the water stored in lakes and reservoirs dropped by 9.5%. Together, this was the largest synchronised decline in surface water since at least 1991.

As the planet warms, the water cycle becomes more extreme. A warmer atmosphere pulls more moisture out of soils, rivers and lakes, and hotter land speeds up evaporation even further. That moisture then falls as heavy rain elsewhere, often over oceans, causing sharper swings between drought and flood. This meant that during 2023-24, rivers ran low even in places hit by severe flooding.

To reach their findings, the researchers combined river flow measurements from 150 of the world’s major river basins with satellite data tracking more than 1.2m lakes and reservoirs between 1991 and 2025.

Dr Sulagna Mishra, one of the study’s authors, said: “The findings highlight an important paradox of climate change: a warmer atmosphere does not necessarily mean more water is available on land. Although global precipitation increased during this period, much of the additional rainfall occurred over the oceans, while many land regions experienced significant deficits.”

The effects were particularly pronounced in South America, where river flows dropped by 17.8% and water in lakes and reservoirs fell by 16.5%, even as some areas experienced extreme rainfall and flooding.

Dr Yi He, an associate professor in hydrology and climate change research at the University of East Anglia, said: “Parts of South America experienced severe flooding in 2023-24, yet the continent’s rivers carried much less water than usual over those two years. A river can flood during a downpour and still run low for much of the year.”

Water supplies around the world are facing multiple threats, including the super El Niño, droughts driven by the climate crisis, pollution and overexploitation.

The study’s findings showed how exposed the world’s water supplies were, the authors said. They said changes to fresh water were one of the main ways the climate crisis affected people and nature, and as the planet continued heating, it was becoming harder to predict how much water would be available.

Prof Christian Dunn, the chair of the British Ecological Society’s policy committee, said: “What’s particularly worrying about these findings is just how quickly our freshwater resources can decline, even in parts of the world we traditionally think of as being wet. And, as this study shows, just because we’re experiencing floods doesn’t mean we’re water secure.”

The Guardian view on Russia’s war dead: the toll won’t stop Putin. Resolve in backing Ukraine remains essential

The Guardian Thu, 26 Nov 2026 18:53:47 GMT

New data offers shocking details of military fatalities. But without domestic accountability, only external pressure can end this conflict

The toll of Russia’s war on Ukraine is appallingly evident in the devastation of apartment blocks and hospitals, in the suffering of survivors and, above all, in the mourning of the dead, which included an estimated 150,000 soldiers and at least 18,000 civilians.

The toll on Russia’s population has been carefully obscured by Moscow. But a fuller picture has emerged from its own statistics after the hacking group Cyber Partisans, linked to the Belarusian opposition, and the Ukrainian hacker collective Silent Crow obtained 11m death certificates. Analysis by the Guardian offers disturbing insights into the deaths of almost half a million Russians in Ukraine since Vladimir Putin launched a full-scale invasion in 2022.

The scale of death is hard to conceive. The Soviet Union lost 15,000 soldiers in its nine-year occupation of Afghanistan. More than 5,000 Russian personnel died in a single week last year. Almost 90,000 were killed in the battle to take Pokrovsk – a city of just 60,000 people. More than 1,000 soldiers have taken their own lives. With mobilisation deeply unpopular, Moscow has relied on cash bonuses, which many are too poor to resist, and foreign nationals from as far afield as Colombia and Nigeria – more than 7,300 of whom have died. Many are lured under false pretences. North Korean fatalities – with 2,000 dead, on one estimate – are not included in the data.

Having eradicated political opposition and independent media, Mr Putin faces no domestic accountability. The state can’t hide all these losses, but futile deaths in a shameful cause are portrayed as glorious sacrifice. With soldiers drawn from poor, remote rural areas, the sons of St Petersburg and Moscow remain untroubled. The authorities need not fear instability.

Instead of persuading Mr Putin to seek an exit, these deaths may drive him to keep seeking a victory to justify them. With the frontline barely shifting, and as Ukraine further embarrasses him with high-profile strikes – on the Kerch Bridge in Crimea and on Russian vessels, including a new warship anchored in Libya – he punishes its cities. Civilian casualties have risen sharply this year, and the choking of the US Starshield satellite internet service has weakened Ukraine’s air defences.

Donald Trump posted on Thursday on Truth Social that he “would like Putin to pull back all military aggression against territories throughout Europe”. But the US president’s diplomatic embrace of “my friend” gives Mr Putin reason to hope that the US will abandon Ukraine. The mood in Europe has also shifted. A poll suggests that most Germans now oppose military aid to Kyiv. France’s far-right presidential frontrunner, Marine Le Pen, says that it cannot afford aid; the hard-left Jean-Luc Mélenchon is also more sympathetic to Moscow.

Ukraine’s supporters are battling to lock in support while they can. As EU leaders meet in Brussels, Germany’s Friedrich Merz has threatened to veto the next seven-year budget, including aid for Ukraine, unless a separate €45bn loan is approved. Berlin is also pushing for future decisions on funding to be agreed by a majority, rather than unanimously, to further insulate Kyiv from political changes. As the conflict escalates and Russia’s hybrid war across Europe mounts, it is essential that EU states – and other members of the “coalition of the willing” – show unity and determination in standing with Ukraine, not only for Kyiv’s sake, but for their own.

The Guardian view on fostering: ceremonies and sibling rights should help care leavers

The Guardian Thu, 26 Nov 2026 18:51:56 GMT

Ministers have recognised that young adults need more support. But children’s social care reform must go deeper

The first lifelong guardianship ceremonies, held in Northampton last week with Josh MacAlister, the children’s minister, among the guests, are the latest in a series of measures aimed at boosting support for care leavers. While the decision to register a link between a person who has been looked after as a child and another adult such as a former carer or friend does not carry legal obligations, those involved spoke movingly about what it meant for these relationships to be formally recognised. New rules requiring councils to support contact between siblings in the care system are similarly aimed at strengthening networks that could sustain them beyond childhood into adult life.

Belatedly, the government is acting on a mound of evidence that children who are taken into local authority care are frequently acutely vulnerable when they come out of it as 18-year-olds. Care leavers are over-represented in prisons and homeless shelters, and among those who are not in education, employment or training. In August, the Department for Education published an analysis of 112 deaths of care leavers aged between 18 and 24 in 2025, which made for devastating reading.

It explained how even young people who want to try living independently can end up socially isolated and out of their depth. At a time when only half of young people in England and Wales move out of their childhood home before they are 24, there is growing recognition that care leavers need ongoing support and continuity – just like their peers. The new entitlement to free prescriptions and eye care for care leavers aged up to 25, in the Children’s Wellbeing and School Act, was an important signal of acceptance by the state of its ongoing duties towards the people it has removed from their birth families.

But positive as such initiatives are, they will not alter the fundamental problems of rising costs and overspent budgets in children’s social care departments, leading to a perpetual sense of crisis. In a recent report, the Institute for Government (IfG) said that councils must get better at planning, give more support to foster carers and reduce their reliance on private providers, some of whom were judged by the Competition and Markets Authority to take excessive profits. The IfG has also highlighted the “stratospheric” cost of caring for a minority of children with highly complex needs.

An increase in children being cared for by relatives or friends, rather than foster carers, has taken some of the pressure off. A pilot scheme is trialling allowances for kinship carers. But since the decline in the number of fostering households, combined with a lack of council children’s homes, lies behind the current problems, much depends on the outcome of a recruitment campaign that aims to create 10,000 new foster places. In a grim irony, last week’s guardianship ceremonies took place in an area where the use of illegal children’s homes has recently risen.

Councils need support and investment to take the more active role that is required of them; Mr MacAlister cannot make all the necessary changes from Whitehall. But his pledge to review the qualifications and caseloads of the personal advisers who support care leavers is welcome, as are efforts to reduce the churn of staff in social work departments. Ceremonies and new rights for siblings are important additions. But the children’s social care system needs rebuilding.

The defenestration of Marcus Bokkerink in the Keir Starmer-Rachel Reeves era is half-forgotten now – but the saga was a big deal in January 2025 and should still matter to those at the top of today’s government.

Bokkerink was chair of the Competition and Markets Authority (CMA) until he was turfed out because, it seemed, he was deemed insufficiently aligned with the Starmer-Reeves idea that regulators should “support growth”. Bokkerink hit back by warning of the dangers of political interference and competition authorities becoming “vulnerable to short-term expediency or vested interests”.

The exchange pointed to a philosophical divide. Did the government see a tension between growth and competition? Was it worried that business investment would suffer if the competition regulator was too active?

One piece of context was the epic whine by a senior Microsoft executive about the “darkest day in our four decades in Britain” after the CMA – entirely reasonably in this column’s view at the time – gave a thumbs-down in 2023 to his company’s planned $69bn (£53bn) takeover of the video games firm Activision Blizzard.

Those events are chewed over in a punchy paper this week from two former senior Treasury officials of yesteryear, John Kingman and Shriti Vadera (the latter was also a minister in Gordon Brown’s government). Top lines: strong competition is unambiguously good for growth; we need new firms to break through and make the economy more productive. The problem is that the value of competition and disruption has become “the blind spot of current UK economic policy”, the paper says.

Fair point. About 60% of the fall in the UK’s productivity rate since 2007 can be attributed to less dynamism, argue Kingman and Vadera, citing statistics from the government’s own Industrial Strategy Advisory Council. Firms under five years old made 18% of all business sales in 2005; by 2021, the figure was only 10%. That decline is huge.

Here’s the gist of the paper: “It appears that ministers of both parties have become noticeably less interested in competition and disruption as a source of growth, and noticeably less supportive of robust, independent competition policy. They have also tended to look for the approbation of incumbent businesses and investors in their decision-making on policy.”

Note the “both parties” reference. The authors are not making a party political point. Significant pro-growth, pro-competition interventions have happened under both Tories and Labour. Big bang in the City was under Margaret Thatcher. The indefensible BAA airports monopoly in London, which saw Heathrow, Gatwick and Stansted owned by a single firm, was broken up in 2009 when Brown was at the helm. The fintech revolution was born from getting tougher on banks after the 2008 crash. It has only been more recently that governments “have come to see active pro-competition policy as a threat to growth, rather than a driver of it”, as the paper put it.

To be fair to the CMA, it would be hard to say it has gone wobbly under pressure. Doug Gurr, Bokkerink’s replacement, was regarded in some quarters as big tech’s patsy because he came from Amazon. In practice, the CMA has been lively with its “strategic market status” designations that can impose “conduct requirements” on tech firms. Google has been designated in search and search advertising; Apple in mobile phones; and Microsoft may be added in business software.

All the same, political signals are important. They flag whether the government believes active competition policy boosts growth. In the age of AI, that is more important than ever. We don’t want AI giants to entrench an oligopoly before anybody notices, which is roughly what happened in the last tech revolution.

Encouragingly, the “public control” speech this week by Louise Haigh, the de facto deputy prime minister, included a mini-reference to competition policy. “Where competition exists, it should be left to thrive,” she said, supported by a “strong, independent” CMA.

Sign up to Business Today

after newsletter promotion

Was that a change of tone? Hard to say because ministers, even when they are sending mixed messages, always remember to mention the independence of the CMA. To clear things up, Haigh and Andy Burnham could adopt a few of Kingman and Vadera’s recommendations.

For example: say out loud that you want more competition and more disruption in the economy. Publish a scorecard of dynamism. Abolish the political “steer” to the CMA, which is a source of half the confusion. Reassert the primacy of its competition mandate. Give the body’s chair and chief executive single eight-year terms, as the governor of the Bank of England gets.

None feels incompatible with the “public control” stuff. All would send a clearer message about boosting growth and competition than we’re used to hearing.

What would happen if Russia detonated a nuclear weapon in space?

The Guardian Thu, 26 Nov 2026 18:13:33 GMT

⁠Sputnik-S, a nuclear-enabled satellite, has been assembled by Russia and could be launched in 60 days, reports say

Russia is reportedly preparing to launch a nuclear-armed satellite into space later this year, in a scenario that could pose a significant threat to global communications.

German media outlets have reported, citing western intelligence agency assessments, that such a satellite could be launched within 60 days and would be operational shortly afterwards.

Here we look at the implications of a nuclear weapon being detonated in space.

A report by the German broadcasters NDR and WDR and the newspaper Süddeutsche Zeitung said western intelligence services, including Germany’s Bundesnachrichtendienst (BND) intelligence service and armed forces, had exchanged information showing that a nuclear-enabled satellite, named ⁠Sputnik-S, was assembled several years ago and is stationed in ⁠the Moscow region. It could be launched this year. A German government spokesperson said it was taking the intelligence reports “very seriously”.

In space, where there is no atmosphere, there is no mushroom cloud. Instead, the energy from a nuclear explosion is released as radiation. A detonation would be particularly damaging in low Earth orbit, or up to 1,200 miles above Earth, where most satellites operate.

Jonathan McDowell, an astrophysicist and honorary professor at the Durham University Space Research Centre in the UK, said the main effects were twofold: everything within line of sight of the detonation could be zapped by X-rays and other forms of radiation which could knock out or damage satellites within thousands of miles; secondly, radiation particles could be emitted into the lower atmosphere and form a new “Van Allen belt”, the term for two belts of radiation that circle the Earth and shield it from the impact of solar storms.

It would be a replay of an event in 1962 when the US detonated a thermonuclear bomb 250 miles above Earth’s surface – in low Earth orbit – in an event called Starfish Prime. There were many fewer satellites then but it shortened the life of two craft: the Telstar 1 and Ariel-1 satellites.

“Starfish caused severe radiation over a period of months to at least half the satellites then working on orbit, which was not very many at that point,” said McDowell.

Keith Ryden, a professor of space engineering at the University of Surrey in the UK, said low Earth orbit satellites were vulnerable to bursts of radiation.

“Since natural levels of radiation are relatively low in this region, satellites located there are not designed for high radiation levels so they would be vulnerable to unexpected increases,” he says.

There are about 17,000 satellites in lower Earth orbit, including satellites important to weather forecasting, climate monitoring and the military as well as Elon Musk’s network of satellites that form the Starlink broadband network. The latter is crucial to assisting Ukraine’s efforts in repelling the invasion of Russia.

The International Space Station, in which Russia is a partner, is also in low Earth orbit. Musk’s proposed constellation of space datacentres would operate there as well.

Satellites handling TV broadcast, GPS and other communications are in higher orbits that are less easy for a nuclear weapon to affect.

McDowell said the artificial Van Allen belt caused by Starfish Prime was around for five years.

“There will be immediate impacts from a detonation but there are lasting environmental effects that will damage satellites in the longer run. It could take several years, up to a decade, for the trapped particles to diffuse out of the radiation belt,” he said.

Ryden added: “Just as important, the space industry would not have the capacity to rebuild and launch the required number of spacecraft in a short time.”

Hundreds of miles below the Starfish Prime explosion, streetlights in Hawaii were knocked out, burglar alarms were set off in the area, and phone calls were disrupted.

“There might be an impact on computers and electronic systems in the region of earth where the explosion is visible,” said McDowell.

Ryden added that Starfish and other nuclear tests took place over sparsely populated areas so the location of the detonation was key.

“It does depend a lot on where the detonation happens,” he said.

Starfish Prime also created stunning aurora effects as the sky was lit up in shades of green, yellow, red and, according to one report, “tremendous white rainbows”.

“There would be huge auroral effects. It would not be a subtle thing. It’s hard to be subtle with nukes,” said McDowell.

A European security official told the Guardian that they were doubtful that Russia would detonate a nuclear device in space. They said it could cause significant damage to western economies, but that it stood to significantly harm Russia as well. Such an explosion would be hard to control and would probably damage Russia’s own satellites, as well as, potentially, China’s. “It would be shooting themselves in the leg,” they said.

They pointed at Russia’s nuclear blackmail earlier in its war in Ukraine, including when Russia put its nuclear forces on high alert in 2022, followed by movements of troops and weapons. “They were bluffing then – and this looks like a bluff now,” said the official. McDowell said he was sceptical about Russia detonating a nuclear weapon in space, because it was “such a stupid idea” to commit what would be viewed as an act of war.

Is local democracy all it’s cracked up to be?

The Guardian Thu, 26 Nov 2026 18:02:10 GMT

Readers respond to an article by Simon Jenkins on why rural parish councils need to be granted powers over their future

Simon Jenkins presents continental Europe as a model of local democracy (The UK government ridicules villages such as Piddington – but it’s these ‘Nimbys’ who show us the way, 20 November), but similar issues happen all over the place.

In 2024, seven communes in the department of Rhône, France, lost the power to approve blocks of flats because they fell short of social housing targets. In 2016, it was reported that the French town of Cessy was knocking down historic architecture for more housing with the local mayor’s approval.

The countries that Jenkins praises have the same overrides over local concerns, whether from the state or mayors. On the flip side, in Sweden, despite local control over planning, more than 80% of municipalities reported housing shortages.

The desire to preserve the past is admirable, and local plans that ignore local character are a problem. But it’s unreasonable to argue against a plan purely because of the high numbers.

Aditya Chakrabortty’s article (The moral panic over Neets needs to stop. The problem is bad jobs, not young people, 20 November) particularly resonated with me. Many young people are desperate for a job, and a council housebuilding boom could help to lift many families out of poverty and help young people gain valuable skills.

Some of this will have to come from existing towns. Brownfield sites with no transport links or jobs are not a substitute. The evidence is clear: low supply is one of the main factors in high house prices.

There are two lessons to take from Europe. The first is German-style binding local plans – residents voice their concerns while the plan is agreed, and every development that meets the rules is then approved by default. The second is large-scale social housing, as in Vienna. Nazar RomanivMaidenhead, Berkshire

Simon Jenkins makes the case for local parishes to make decisions on housing development. But local democracy needs to go further. It is not just central government that overrides local democracy. Shire counties do it too. In Buckinghamshire, we have a council opposed to reducing speed limits in residential areas.

Unlike in neighbouring counties, only 2% of roads in Buckinghamshire have a 20mph limit. The fact that parish councils call for action to create livable streets is ignored. We are obliged to watch as children are forced into cars to get to school because the roads are deemed too dangerous with speeding traffic.

Time to devolve power to local representative bodies that are genuinely in touch with local needs. Jan WalmsleyWingrave, Buckinghamshire

My village beats Moreton-in-Marsh, mentioned in Simon Jenkins’ article. We have around the same number of homes, but Buckinghamshire council is planning to build 7,000 extra houses.

Central government could be more flexible on housing targets for places like Buckinghamshire, Brighton, the Cotswolds and Cumbria, where large areas are protected natural landscapes or national parks. But the national target does need to be shared around fairly, with some level of mandatory targets, or we will always fall short on the houses we need to build.

Buckinghamshire has good sites for new towns at Denham in the south, with rail connections to London, and Steeple Claydon in the north, with rail connections to Oxford, Milton Keynes and perhaps an HS2 station as well. Matthew HuttonHaddenham, Buckinghamshire

Don’t price EU students out of UK universities

The Guardian Thu, 26 Nov 2026 18:02:05 GMT

Widening pathways for disadvantaged youngsters from Europe should be top of the agenda in discussions about fees, says Angela McRobbie

It is dispiriting to hear arguments against young people from the EU being able to attend British universities with fees reset to home student level (EU nationals will pay higher tuition fees than UK students, Burnham indicates, 25 November).

Fees for international students are horrendously high at approximately £25,000 a year, and that does not include living costs. This means that only very wealthy families can afford to have their children study for a degree in the UK.

Until the end of 2020, when Brexit was fully implemented, EU students from average- and middle-income backgrounds could manage the costs, and they didn’t need fancy accommodation because (in my own experience at Goldsmiths, University of London) many could take a cheap bus to get back home to Poland, Berlin, Milan etc every few weeks. I even recall that they made little use of the NHS, instead preferring to see doctors in their home towns.

Some of the voices that have joined the discussion in recent days have suggested that the call to lower the fees was for the benefit of EU officials in Brussels who would like to be able to send their children to top-ranked universities in Britain, but find the high fees prohibitive. And Russell Group vice-chancellors have weighed in with the losses that would accrue from these proposed changes. Both of these discussions occlude the mainstream of the university sector, the new and post-1992 universities.

At Goldsmiths, our teaching in areas such as creative industry studies, art therapy and post-colonial theory appealed to EU students because they were largely unavailable at home. It is therefore a matter of widening pathways for disadvantaged youngsters that should be top of the agenda in the discussions about fee levels and access to the full range of our higher education provision. Angela McRobbie Professor emeritus, Goldsmiths, University of London

Palantir has created bespoke tech solutions for the NHS

The Guardian Thu, 26 Nov 2026 18:01:40 GMT

Stephen Childs responds to a letter that said the US software firm was not the right fit for Britain’s health service

Prof Caroline Mitchell is right that US systems designed for an insurance market are rife in the NHS (Letters, 18 November). But Palantir’s software isn’t among them – and should not be confused with a range of other systems, some designed as far back as the 1970s for billing and then exported to the NHS over the following decades.

Our story is different. Each application built on the federated data platform – which connects information across the NHS – is bespoke to the NHS and to the healthcare trust that uses it. The NHS is a highly complex, loose association of healthcare trusts and commissioners, with data that is rich, but often unstructured and frustratingly disconnected.

Through the national federated data platform, our software is helping to fix that with a range of tools purpose-built for the NHS, which perform functions like speeding up cancer diagnosis – not one of which has been adopted from the insurance market.

I speak from experience, having worked for the NHS for more than 30 years and having been responsible for building one of these unique applications in partnership with Palantir to tackle delayed discharges.

How data is managed in the NHS is a critical debate. We need to get the facts right or patient care and taxpayer value for money will suffer. Stephen ChildsSpecial adviser, Palantir

Ofsted’s pedagogically pinheaded approach to inspections

The Guardian Thu, 26 Nov 2026 18:01:34 GMT

Ian McCormack and Sid Cumberland respond to a letter from the FDA union

Remarkably, Helen Kenny’s defence of Ofsted (Letters, 18 November) dodges the central criticism of Simon Jenkins’ article. She offers no response to his criticism that inspections are menacing and based on a damagingly reductionistic idea of education. Neither does she address the stress that results from fear of Ofsted, not only for teachers but children, too.

The FDA public service union’s own research finds that only 18% of inspectors believe “educators perceive them ‘positively’”. Why might that be?

What strikes me most forcibly about the current practice is that it’s pedagogically pinheaded. If teachers took this approach in the classroom – spending too little time with the learners, filling them with anxiety, publicly shaming them for “failure”, telling them to improve and leaving them to it – it would be catastrophic.

Jenkins is right to talk about local control of schools. Inspectors I knew who worked for the old local education authorities took a very different approach: long-term, collaborative, supportive, human. Surely an education system that respected the professionalism of teachers and saw them as partners in the development of the art, craft and science of teaching would produce better outcomes and a happier, healthier nation. Ian McCormackLeicester

Helen Kenny objects to Simon Jenkins’ article, saying that “blaming the inspectors for the system is wholly unfair” and that “Jenkins dismisses the work of HMIs as merely a ‘sniff’ of the air and a stroll back to Whitehall”.

Jenkins does not refer specifically to HMIs but to “inspectors”. There are about 430 HMIs, and more than 2,000 additional Ofsted inspectors, and having worked in a variety of schools in my career I can assure you that HMIs and OIs are not the same. There is nothing quite so demoralising as having your work examined by someone who does not know exactly what they are looking at. (I shall never forget the inspector who came into the nursery where I was working and said: “Goodness me, aren’t they little!”)

Kenny also says that “74% of educators believed their most recent inspection was accurate”. I look forward to seeing the full results of that survey, especially given that another recent (2025) YouGov poll says that 74% of school and college leaders were unsatisfied with the new multigrade report card system. Sid CumberlandLydbrook, Gloucestershire

Poundland staff fear they’ll be left out in the cold for Christmas. When will workers have a say in their future?

The Guardian Thu, 26 Nov 2026 17:48:25 GMT

High streets and ultimately the taxpayer will suffer from the chain’s liquidation. Who will benefit? The company that snapped up this institution for just £1

When the bad news came through on his mobile on Wednesday afternoon, the manager of Poundland’s store in Camden, north London, Aboud, summoned all his staff. “One lad, been here 11 years, was in tears and ran out of the store, he was so upset. This is home and family for many of them.”

They are among 11,000 staff whose jobs are now at risk, but some shops might get bought by other chains. “Do you know,” Aboud asks me, “can we find out if this store might be saved?” I can’t, and the liquidators are only just starting work. He can no longer get through to his senior regional manager: “He doesn’t pick up now.”

He was told that day to keep the shop looking neat (“As I always do”), but more shelves are bare, the Christmas glitz a mockery to those fearing they’ll have no job by then. Now he is worrying about pay. “They paid us early this week and I don’t know why. Does it mean that’s it, no more?” Will stock deliveries stop? On Thursday, a conference call reassures them wages will be paid and he tells his staff to hang in there – to “have faith” that this store survives.

In this largest retail bust for a decade, 600 high streets stand to lose an anchor store. Many will join the boarded-up shopfronts that destroy a sense of thriving community. How did it come to this?

In 2025 Gordon Brothers, a company that specialises in buying and restructuring distressed companies, bought Poundland for £1. As part of the terms for taking over the company, it inherited a shareholder loan, and as such was owed £22.5m. Gordon Brothers rejected various offers to buy the business because of concerns the deals would not pay off that loan. Despite Poundland management taking the store into profit last year, the parent company argued that it was “still vulnerable” to inflation and any downturn in profits. However, Gordon Brothers restricted access to funds for day-to-day operations, meaning that stock was not being replenished, affecting sales.

Sign up to Matters of Opinion

Guardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and more

after newsletter promotion

Gordon Brothers said after the news broke this week: “First and foremost, our thoughts are with Poundland colleagues. We recognise how difficult the continued uncertainty is for them.” But Poundland staff feel their concerns are being placed neither “first” nor “foremost”. Poundland’s founder, Steve Smith, who started with one shop in Burton-on-Trent 36 years ago, warns that of the 2,000 suppliers due to be affected, most only supply to Poundland, so he expects more collapses and job losses, leaving a long trail of disaster. Critics have said Gordon Brothers stands to make its loans back and more from any insolvency process, however.

Andy Burnham’s Makerfield constituency has a large Poundland distribution centre. “Poundland is part of the fabric of high streets and communities up and down the country,” the prime minister said, with Downing Street promising to do all it can. But that’s hardly reassuring when the voices of government were ignored during the process of trying to save the company. Liam Byrne, chair of the business select committee, has summoned Mark Newton-Jones, the European director of Gordon Brothers, to a public hearing, keen to find out why it turned down offers, including one from Martin Property Group, owners of National Car Parks. Byrne gives me some estimates relating to where the money has gone. “They already made £18.3m in fees and charges. They will get the return of their £22m loan. They have starved Poundland into administration by denying access to its £63m bank account to restock and trade” – though Gordon Brothers denies it. Byrne adds: “This is not only terrible for the workers but for taxpayers too, as the state picks up any potential unpaid redundancy entitlement or tax.”

Lessons must be learned, he tells me. “Do we want ‘greed is good’ market supremacy?” It’s a “morality tale” that demands reform of company law, he says. He would change Section 172 of the Companies Act that gives primacy to shareholders. These laws enable private equity and restructuring firms to overload businesses with debt, as well as extract “proxy dividends” through debt repayments, and break up companies at the expense of high-street jobs. It’s time, he says, to put employees on company boards, German-style.

Despite firms lobbying about “over-regulation” of business, time and again we get a jolting reminder of where the power lies. Here’s a small but telling anecdote. Last week the business committee was due for a long-arranged visit to an Amazon “fulfilment centre”, letting the company display its working conditions. But the committee pulled out at the last minute when Amazon refused to let it speak to GMB union reps there, who might have had a different story to tell. This came just weeks after the union had applied for access rights to allow its reps to recruit inside the Coventry warehouse, under new powers within the Employment Rights Act. This may be an augury of friction to come. Coventry is where the GMB campaigned hard at Amazon for 12 years for union recognition, but lost a vote after the company subjected staff to six-hour union-bashing seminars and flooded the place with obedient new workers, amid threats of delayed wage rises.

Labour’s attempt to restore and rebalance the muscle of workforces against the steel of capital faces a drumbeat of business lobby objections to new employment rights that both the Tories and Reform UK have pledged to abolish. Put that into the context of how weak workers’ rights have become since Margaret Thatcher’s 1980s assaults. Union membership fell from 13m in 1979 to 6.5m by 2024. Loss of influence led to a sharp fall in pay as a proportion of GDP, from 72% in 1975 (the most equal year in history) to 59% last year.

Unions sprang into action as soon as their new rights came into force on 30 October, giving them legal access to every workplace to recruit: half have no union presence. Unionism has faded into the background of national life, so many workers have no idea how to join one, though when asked most say they want that collective bargaining, and rightly so since, as of last year, union membership brings a pay premium of 5.3%.

Gordon Brothers merits a term coined by Edward Heath: “the unacceptable face of capitalism”. But with Labour in power under a strong prime minister, this latest marauding looks likely to spark company law reform that tilts the scales a little more in favour of employees, communities, citizens and taxpayers. But that’s small comfort to Aboud and his team.

Polly Toynbee is a Guardian columnist

Man who stabbed passengers on train to London guilty of attempted murder of 14 people

The Guardian Thu, 26 Nov 2026 17:43:24 GMT

Anthony Williams stabbed two boys before assault on rail passengers in ‘ferocious and frenzied’ attack over 25 hours

A 33-year-old man has been found guilty of attempted murder in a “ferocious and frenzied attack” in which he stabbed 14 people, including 10 passengers at random on a London-bound train last year.

Anthony Williams of Peterborough admitted stabbing 14 people, including two boys, in 25 hours on 31 October and 1 November 2025. Ten people were attacked on an LNER service from Doncaster to London.

After a six-week trial at Cambridge crown court, a jury found Williams guilty of all 14 counts of attempted murder on Thursday.

British Transport Police (BTP) said the investigation had been “one of the most significant and complex in our history”.

The head of BTP’s major serious and organised crime team, Det Supt Sam Blackburn, said: “Passengers boarding that train had the right to travel safely and every reason to expect ordinary journeys home.

“Instead, they found themselves caught up in a ferocious and frenzied attack, which left multiple people seriously injured and passengers in fear for their lives.”

Williams, who psychiatrists said was experiencing “acute psychosis as a result of his schizophrenia” at the time, previously admitted wounding with intent to cause really serious bodily harm to 12 people and attempting to do so to two others, but denied attempted murder.

He had a history of mental illness and criminal convictions, prompting questions about whether the attack could have been prevented.

The NHS has said it will commission an investigation into the care provided to Williams to “identify any opportunities for learning and improvement”.

The Independent Office for Police Conduct (IOPC) is also investigating two Cambridgeshire constabulary officers over alleged failures to investigate an alleged assault a month before the stabbings on the LNER train.

During the trial, the court was told how passengers on the train from Doncaster to King’s Cross on 1 November 2025 were subjected to a “storm of violence” that left some with serious injuries and many fearing for their lives.

In the 24 hours before the train attack, Williams had attacked three people in Peterborough and a 17-year-old boy on the Docklands Light Railway in London in the early hours of 1 November, jurors were told.

Christopher Paxton KC, for the prosecution, told the court: “Williams, armed with a knife, caused terror and fear on an unimaginable scale, moving up and down a busy train from which there was no escape, stabbing several people as he did so.”

Paxton argued that Williams’s intention to kill was laid bare “not just in his words, some of which I’ve reminded you of, but in the slashes and stabs he inflicted not on the devil but on real people”.

The prosecution said this was evidenced when Williams asked the passenger Stephen Crean, aged 61 at the time, “Do you want to die?” before he stabbed him.

Crean was one of several passengers praised during the trial for their “extraordinary bravery” when trying to wrest the knife from Williams. Among Crean’s injuries was a stabbing to the left side of his scalp within “0.79cm of the brain”, jurors were told.

Another passenger, Scott Green, was also stabbed while he attempted to grab the knife from Williams. A member of the train crew, Samir Zitouni, was stabbed several times as he tried to use a frying pan to stop Williams, jurors heard.

Speaking after the conclusion of the trial, Zitouni said he wanted to “express my deepest gratitude” to police and medics who responded to the incident.

Paxton said: “In the face of that threat and the defendant’s sheer brutality, some stood tall to protect others trying to de-escalate his rampage, defending themselves and putting themselves in harm’s way to protect strangers.”

Gillian Jones KC, for the defence, said Williams had been “in the clutches of an acute psychotic episode” and that he “didn’t intend to kill, he didn’t intend to bring about death”. Williams was not called on to give evidence during the trial.

Dr Bernard Chin, a psychiatrist instructed by the defence, said Williams had been experiencing “paranoid persecutory delusions, meaning he had ideas and beliefs that people were going to harm him and that this was an organised conspiracy that came about due to … the devil”.

Chin told the court that a report written a day after the train attack by another psychiatrist, Dr Alan Smith, showed Williams had thought there was a “conspiracy organised by the devil against him and everyone was part of the conspiracy against him”.

Jones also told the court Williams had contacted his GP on 30 September 2025 and “had done so highlighting his deteriorating mental state”.

The GP, who did not see him in person, “established he had only been taking 100mg and needed to take 200mg” of his medication. Williams contacted his doctor again nine days before the train attack but did not respond thereafter.

Jones told the court: “He didn’t simply leave his house on 31 October and 1 November as a man intent on cold-blooded murder.”.

Williams is due to be sentenced at a later date.

‘Not really the thing to take a victory lap in’: the meaning of Jensen Huang’s new jacket

The Guardian Thu, 26 Nov 2026 17:30:40 GMT

Nvidia’s boss has returned in a new uniform. But what does swapping leather for cotton say about power and leadership?

Don’t get Fashion Statement delivered to your inbox? Sign up here

It’s been a big week for the stock market and the leather jacket-wearing community.

Nvidia founder Jensen Huang, who had resigned as chief executive of the chipmaker after reports of multiple affairs, was reinstated as CEO. But as he returned to the company’s Silicon Valley headquarters surrounded by clapping employees chanting his name, one thing was amiss. Jensen was back, but the black leather jacket that had been his trademark piece for nearly two decades remained absent from its former power position. In its place? A navy cotton jacket.

In his first post-return company all-hands meeting, Huang apologised to employees, telling them he had made some “terrible mistakes”. He also said: “I’m going to be a better CEO the second time around … I take this responsibility with the greatest humility and renewed commitment.”

What better than a humble cotton jacket to emphasise Huang’s newfound morality? A leather jacket comes with in-built bravado. It walks a fine line between confident and cocky, whereas its cotton cousin is much more subtle. It suggests modesty and restraint.

The internet was quick to weigh in.

“I changed my jacket. I’m different now,” read one comment below a photo of a leather-less Huang. “Someone in fashion needs to make ‘The Jensen’ jacket right now,” read another.

The Cut described it as his “listening and learning jacket”. Vogue posited it was his way of saying “I’m sorry.”

Johnny Davis, the luxury director of Esquire magazine, wasn’t surprised to see Huang switch up his look. “A black leather jacket is not really the thing to be taking a victory lap in,” he says. Instead, Huang needed a garment “to signal some degree of contrition”.

Huang’s zipped deep blue gabardine jacket brings to mind the popular chore jacket, which is rooted in workwear. While in the leather jacket club you’ll find everyone from Marlon Brando to Brad Pitt, chore-jacket fans include the likes of Monty Don. A leather jacket creates drama. A cotton jacket is very much “doing the work” in therapy speak.

Huang’s new jacket is less flashy than his Tom Ford leather numbers, but it is still a designer jacket. It appears to be Dior’s £2,400 “zipped shirt” – not cheap but Huang is worth over £100bn. He previously wore it on a visit to Seoul in June where he paired it with white jeans. This time, he teamed it with black jeans and slip-on Hermès shoes.

Andrew Groves, director of the menswear archive at the University of Westminster, suggests Huang has attempted to “materially soften his image” with his new look.

Sign up to Fashion Statement

“Leather carries associations of protection and rebellion,” Groves says. “Cotton feels more everyday and approachable. That shift registers before anyone notices it’s actually from Dior.”

Davis describes the cotton jacket as somewhere between a Harrington and a workwear jacket in “a very respectable colour” which brings to mind school uniforms and corporate dress. It says: “I’m getting back to work, but I’m still not a suit.”

With Huang facing two congressional hearings next week, we may be waiting a while before we see him back in his leathers. And with a collection of up to 40 variants, it’s unlikely his leather-jacket era is permanently over. Perhaps, like Colette Kress, who served as Nvidia’s interim chief executive for just 11 days, the cotton jacket is very much just in a temporary position, too.

Public service broadcaster services should be top of TV app menus – Ofcom

The Guardian Thu, 26 Nov 2026 17:09:14 GMT

UK regulator’s code of practice on streaming platforms is intended to give prominence to iPlayer and similar offerings

Public service broadcasters’ streaming services such as BBC iPlayer should appear first on app menus on smart TVs to give them an “appropriate degree of prominence”, according to Ofcom.

In addition, the regulator has said public service shows should rank higher on voice and text searches on televisions connected to the internet.

In an increasingly fragmented media world, TV guides and app menus act as gatekeepers to content and vary according to which set viewers have, with users often having to scroll for some time to find the traditional broadcasters.

So as part of the 2024 Media Act – which modernised the framework for making public service broadcasting content easier to discover on connected TVs – Ofcom has announced a new code of practice that it hopes will help audiences locate PSB shows more easily and standardise prominence on TV screens.

The code includes ensuring that the PSB’s streaming services “should be immediately visible” and “appear with the first nine” app icons or “tiles” on smart TV main app menus.

Ofcom said they should appear “in the following order … BBC iPlayer, ITVX, Channel 4 player, Channel 5 player, S4C Clic and STV player”, with the positioning changing depending on where the user is in the UK.

The regulator added that when searching for shows (including voice searches) via connected TVs, “public service programmes should be more prominent than other programmes where they are the most relevant results for a user’s search”.

Other recommendations include “public service programmes should be clearly attributed to the designated PSB service in which they are included” so it “helps audiences identify the content provider and make informed viewing choices”, and improving the “experience of disabled people” through labelling and enabling accessibility features such as subtitles or audio description.

Although the code is not mandatory, Ofcom hopes its recommendations could be in place within the next 12 to 18 months and said platform providers that follow it “will be treated as complying with the relevant prominence and accessibility duties”.

This issue is separate to that of greater prominence for established broadcasters and media companies on digital platforms such as YouTube and TikTok, the debate over which is continuing.

⁠Gérard Depardieu to face trial on charges ‌of raping ​actor Charlotte ⁠Arnould

The Guardian Thu, 26 Nov 2026 16:26:57 GMT

Arnould first accused Depardieu ⁠in 2018, saying assaults occurred at his Paris home on two separate occasions when ⁠she was in her early 20s

Gérard Depardieu has been ordered to stand trial on a charge of raping a female actor at his Paris home in 2018, after an appeals ⁠court rejected his attempt to avoid having the case tried.

The film star, 77, had appealed last year against an investigating magistrate’s ruling that he should stand criminal trial on charges of raping and sexually assaulting Charlotte Arnould on two occasions, but judges said on Thursday proceedings should go ahead.

The court said the star would be tried for allegedly raping Arnould on 7 August 2018, but dismissed a second allegation of rape said to have occurred the following week, on 13 August. Depardieu, one of the best-known names in French cinema, has denied wrongdoing.

Arnould, then 22, first accused Depardieu, whom she had known since childhood, in 2018, ⁠saying the assaults had occurred when she went to the actor’s Parisian townhouse to informally rehearse a play.

He could face a prison sentence of 15-20 years if convicted.

The initial indictment, partly upheld on Thursday, ruled that Depardieu should be tried for rape committed through “moral coercion, resulting from a state of shock that prevented Charlotte Arnould from protesting and fleeing”.

In its appeal against that decision, the actor’s defence argued that there was no evidence of sexual penetration, and denied any “criminal intent” on the part of the actor, formerly a towering figure in the French film world since the mid-1970s.

Earlier this month, Depardieu dropped his appeal against a 2025 conviction for sexually assaulting a set dresser and an assistant director on a film set in September 2021, accepting an 18-month suspended prison sentence and issuing a public apology.

“On film sets, I have long hidden behind provocation and crude humour. I believed my words and some of my actions had no consequences,” he said in his statement. “But they did, particularly coming from someone who held as much power as I once did.”

His sentence in that case will now stand, and his name has been added to France’s sex offender register. He is also under investigation over allegations that he and the writer Michel Houellebecq gang-raped and assaulted a woman during a 2018 film shoot. Houellebecq has not responded publicly to the accusation.

Carine Durrieu Diebolt, a lawyer for Charlotte Arnould, described Thursday’s appeal court ruling as a relief for her client. “She has been waiting for this moment for a very long time,” Durrieu Diebolt said. “She ⁠is fully prepared for it.”

Arnould had been “the first woman to denounce Gérard Depardieu”, Durrieu Diebolt told reporters after the appeal court decision, adding that the referral for alleged rape, after the actor had been convicted of sexual assault, “promises to be historic”.

The appeal court said Depardieu could ​turn to ​France’s highest court, the Cour de Cassation, which examines only whether the law was applied correctly and does not retry cases. His lawyer, David-Olivier Kaminski, said he was considering doing so.

Kaminski told Agence France-Presse that Thursday’s ruling was “a first victory for Gérard Depardieu”, adding: “The other half of the legal process remains to be completed to definitively establish Gérard Depardieu’s innocence.”

Depardieu is one of France’s best-known cinema actors and has starred in more than 200 films, including The Last Metro and Jean de Florette. He was nominated for an Oscar for Cyrano de Bergerac and won a Golden Globe for Green Card in 1990.

But accusations of sexual misconduct have increasingly overshadowed his cinematic legacy, and he has become the highest-profile figure to be caught up in France’s response to the #MeToo movement.

In 2023 the French president, Emmanuel Macron, drew sharp criticism from women’s groups after saying the actor, who was already under formal investigation for rape, “makes France proud” and that he would not participate in a “manhunt”.

Labour’s split over Rosebank oilfield exposed by letter from nearly 100 MPs

The Guardian Thu, 26 Nov 2026 16:13:09 GMT

Exclusive: Frontbenchers join scores of party colleagues urging Burnham not to let ministers approve project

Opinion: Why Labour MPs are opposing Rosebank

Podcast: are resignations next?

Labour’s internal divisions over the giant Rosebank oilfield have spilled into the open, with nearly 100 Labour MPs – including a handful of frontbenchers – writing to the prime minister to express their opposition to the project.

Ninety-two backbenchers and at least four frontbenchers have signed a letter to Andy Burnham urging him not to let his ministers approve the scheme for the biggest undeveloped field in UK waters.

It is the clearest sign yet of the deep rift the issue has caused within the Labour party. The chancellor, John Healey, and many Scottish MPs are pushing for it to go ahead, while dozens of others argue for it to be rejected on climate grounds.

Feelings are running so high that more than one frontbench ministerial aide is considering resigning if the project is approved, the Guardian has been told.

Catherine Fookes, the MP for Monmouthshire who helped organise the letter, said: “Concern about this project is widespread within the parliamentary Labour party. Some 92 people have signed our letter, and there are more who are worried about Rosebank who haven’t signed it.

“I know the prime minister is a good listener. I hope he will see these names and see the letter and take note and think carefully about oil drilling.”

In a separate article for the Guardian, she writes: “Our continued dependence on fossil fuels is driving up bills, fuelling deadly extreme weather and causing widespread harm to people in this country right now.

“Rosebank will do nothing to reduce energy bills for our constituents. The oil belongs to private companies who will ship it away to the highest bidder.

“If Rosebank is approved, champagne corks will pop in the offices of oil giants. But it will not make an iota of difference to our constituents’ energy bills.

“And it will accelerate the climate crisis, which is already pushing up food bills, dealing devastating floods in winter and in summer turning our green and pleasant land into a parched, burnt-out expanse.”

Rosebank and the smaller Jackdaw gasfield have become the focus of a growing political battle over industrial policy and net zero that threatens to become Burnham’s first major political crisis since entering Downing Street.

Many Labour MPs are already concerned about Burnham’s commitment to fighting climate change, given decisions such as cutting green projects and proposals to water down electric vehicle targets.

With the Conservatives promising to scrap the Climate Change Act and Reform UK saying it will cancel all government green spending if it comes to power, many Labour MPs want their administration to do everything it can to promote the green agenda.

The Conservatives initially gave the oil companies Shell and Equinor permission to operate Rosebank and Jackdaw, but they were forced to resubmit their environmental applications after a landmark ruling last year which found companies should account for the carbon emitted by burning the oil and gas they produce, rather than just what the fields themselves emit.

Labour promised in its 2024 manifesto not to grant any more licences for North Sea oil or gasfields. Ministers approved Jackdaw last month, however, and could approve Rosebank without breaking that promise, given the projects already have their licences and are waiting for the separate environmental permission to be granted.

after newsletter promotion

The energy secretary, Miatta Fahnbulleh, approved Jackdaw last month, arguing that the additional carbon it produced would be offset by the additional energy security it provided.

She made it clear though that the same arguments would not apply for Rosebank, given it would generate far greater emissions – an estimated 1m additional tonnes of carbon dioxide by 2042 – and most of its oil would be shipped abroad.

She is understood to be leaning against approving the bigger project. But she is under heavy pressure from trade unions and some cabinet colleagues – including Healey – to give the go-ahead, given it would create about 500 jobs and generate as much as £500m a year in tax revenues.

Burnham has insisted it will be up to Fahnbulleh to make the decision, but Labour MPs believe she will have little choice but to approve the project if the prime minister makes it clear he is in favour.

Now the dozens of Labour MPs who oppose the scheme because of the carbon emissions it would generate are hoping they can persuade Burnham to back Fahnbulleh in opposing the scheme – even if it causes a rift with the Treasury.

They write in their letter: “Approving Rosebank risks becoming an irreversible ‘point of no return’ for the party’s climate credibility, and risks alienating members of the electorate who have put their trust in our message of hope and positivity.

“We urge you to show that Labour is on the side of the people experiencing climate change’s impacts, not those fuelling it.”

Many argue that creating an additional 500 jobs should not outweigh the damage done to the climate, and that the hundreds of millions of pounds in lost revenue could easily be made up from elsewhere in the government’s budget.

Many, but not all, of the MPs who have written to the prime minister are in seats which are under threat from the Green party.

One said blocking Rosebank had become even more urgent in the wake of the collapse of climate talks at the Cop31 summit in Turkey.

“Britain’s role in the world is really important,” they said. “If a country like Britain cannot make a decision like this, what hope is there for the rest of the world?”

Woolly hats, battered bodies and big TV numbers mark rugby union’s new festival finale

The Guardian Thu, 26 Nov 2026 15:44:58 GMT

Nations Championship finals weekend can cement concept for future as players and coaches enjoy chance to let loose

It would be a stretch to describe the Nations Championship finals weekend as the “Glastonbury of Rugby” quite yet. Cher will certainly need to wrap up warm if she is planning to make a cameo appearance; with forecast temperatures of 3C, plenty more thermal vests and woolly hats will be in evidence than at Worthy Farm in June.

There will also be significant gaps in the Allianz Stadium moshpit when Italy and Fiji and Ireland and Australia kick off the three-day finals extravaganza beneath the Friday night lights. Even the organisers concede that Friday has been “a challenge” in terms of ticket sales and that’s without factoring in rush-hour traffic and public transport disruption.

But, whisper it, Test rugby’s newest vehicle has been appealing to viewers sitting comfortably at home. The organisers say the tournament is set to attract a total broadcast audience in excess of 100 million people, comparable to the 118 million fans in core markets who tuned in to this year’s Six Nations. The Nations Championship will clearly have spanned many more games – 42 compared to 15 – but the hope is that ITV will have seen enough to renew for future tournaments.

Stadium attendances are also said to be up by 4% compared to previous November international windows, although punchy ticket prices this weekend seem to have deterred plenty with Christmas around the corner. The stadium will not be filled to capacity on either Saturday or Sunday and, as Andy Farrell, Ireland’s head coach points out, it is not as simple as scheduling a game and expecting tens of thousands of green-shirted fans to drop everything. “Nobody knew until last weekend when we’d be playing,” said Farrell. “The Irish can’t buy flights over here because they’re £1,000 so that doesn’t work really.”

There is also the small matter of player welfare; on top of the summer travel travails of some northern teams can now be added some visibly shattered southern bodies. “I can only imagine how the southern hemisphere boys are feeling now at the back end of their season,” agrees Scotland’s captain Sione Tuipulotu, himself now sidelined with a minor knee problem.

On the flipside, Tuipulotu and others have enjoyed the amended format in other ways. Scotland, for example, have been to South Africa and Argentina and hosted New Zealand and Australia inside five months. “I’ve loved it,” says Tuipulotu, who should be back fit early next month. “Scottish teams don’t normally get those summer fixtures.”

Even New Zealand’s Dave Rennie, whose side are crawling to the end of a year in which they will have played 13 of their 17 games (including provincial tour matches in South Africa) away from home, likes the change. “I like the concept. The interesting thing is you’ve got the northern hemisphere teams coming down to us at the end of their year and vice versa when we come up here. I just think our [Nations Championship] year is a little bit different to what it will be in two years’ time when it is on again.”

England’s Steve Borthwick, for his part, is also upbeat ahead of this weekend’s rematch with the All Blacks. “There’s jeopardy in it, you start thinking about things which you weren’t thinking of previously in the autumn. I would suggest that is a real positive aspect.” Farrell, meanwhile, shares Rennie’s view that 2028 should be less stressful for all involved. “This is a little bit different because the World Cup is next year. People are always going to have one eye on that. I think everyone’s still trying to figure it out but it’s certainly interesting. Let’s see how this weekend goes.”

South Africa’s captain, Siya Kolisi, always someone with an eye on the bigger picture, is another fan regardless of whether his team edge out France in Sunday’s grand final. “I think it’s giving [the November Tests] more drive and more fans are excited about it. We’ve enjoyed it certainly as a team and I’m sure the other guys have all enjoyed it. Hopefully it continues.”

More attention-grabbing games this weekend would further cement the concept.

The venue for the 2028 edition will not be confirmed until the spring and it would not be a big surprise if Paris or other French cities emerge as strong contenders. There remains a vision, too, for future promotion/relegation playoffs for each hemisphere; not every union fancies it but to allow the world’s top dozen sides to remain unchallenged for ever would be a catastrophic look for the game’s global profile.

That is not to say aspects of future editions cannot be finessed. The north-south trophy for the winning hemisphere was on precisely nobody’s lips on Wednesday evening when all the head coaches – bar South Africa – were speaking simultaneously in the Spirit of Rugby suite in Twickenham, temporarily transformed into an oval-shaped Tower of Babel. A Glastonbury festival vibe deep in a European winter might also be more practicable over a two-day weekend, or at least at a venue where large numbers of fans can party inside in the warm.

Rhys Carre and James Botham return for Wales as Steve Tandy makes five changes for the Nations Championship finale against Japan.

Carre was named Wales player of the year in September after an outstanding 2026 Six Nations campaign, but the Saracens loosehead prop has not made a Test start this autumn. Botham was player of the match in Wales’ first victory over New Zealand since 1953, but was omitted for the defeat to Australia last weekend. He is back as openside flanker.

The Exeter lock Dafydd Jenkins takes over the captaincy as Dewi Lake moves to the bench and Ryan Elias starts at hooker. Adam Beard joins Jenkins in the second row.

Scrum-half Reuben Morgan-Williams makes his first Test start, with Tomos Williams – who has started 14 out of 15 matches under Tandy, including the past 11 – on the bench.

Wales B Murray (Scarlets), L Rees-Zammit (Bristol), E James (Scarlets), M Llewellyn (Gloucester), J Adams (Cardiff), S Costelow (Scarlets), R Morgan-Williams (Ospreys); R Carre (Saracens), R Elias (Scarlets), A Griffin (Bath), D Jenkins (Exeter, capt), A Beard (Montpellier), A Mann, J Botham (both Cardiff), A Wainwright (Leicester).

Replacements D Lake (Gloucester), G Thomas (Ospreys), D Lewis (Dragons), T Plumtree (Scarlets), J Morgan (Gloucester), T Williams (Saracens), J Hawkins, E Mee (both Scarlets).

This weekend, regardless, already means different things to different people. Kolisi, as you would expect, is purely focused on winning yet another trophy for South Africa. “Everything that happened before that final game doesn’t matter. It’s all about whether you can rock up on the day and play to the best of your ability. And that’s what we want to do.”

One or two of rugby’s other modern-day rock stars, though, sense the chance to let their hair down. “I love how we’re all playing in London this week,” says Tuipulotu. “There’s a lot of rugby boys in one city … I think there’ll be a few beers drunk after the game. Hopefully we can get through the weekend drama-free.”

But how do Scotland, who face Argentina on Sunday, feel about merely being an aperitif ahead of the grand final between the Springboks and France? “I’m not too sure,” shrugs Tuipulotu. “But if you’re coming for both games you’ve got five hours to drink as much beer as you can.” Both on and off the field a lively weekend awaits.

The man, who cannot be named to protect the anonymity of his victim, looked gaunt and red-faced as he gave evidence in a trial of nine other men who are alleged to have raped or sexually assaulted the woman, or encouraged the abuse online.

He held his head in his hands at times, sighed heavily, and fought back tears as the prosecutor Louise Oakley KC read out a list of the 62 charges he had pleaded guilty to, all of which relate to his wife of four decades.

His wife watched him give evidence via a live stream from a different courtroom in the same building at Manchester Minshull Street crown court, flanked by several members of her family.

The man said he wanted to give evidence “so the court knows the truth of what happened to my wife, so my wife knows, my children”.

The man, who is in his 60s, initially denied the offences after his arrest in October last year, but later pleaded guilty to some, and then all, of the charges, which span a period of more than 20 years.

He said he initially pleaded guilty to only some of the charges “because I felt guilty, I felt I needed to let people know that I was guilty”, but had denied some of them because he wanted to be able to participate in the trial to “tell the truth of what happened”.

Oakley asked him whether his wife had known “any of the men you invited round”, to which he replied: “No she didn’t” and added that “none of them ever spoke to her”.

When he was asked whether his wife would “ever have consented to swinging”, the man responded: “No, not at all.”

He said he had posted on internet sites to connect with people who were local to his home in Stockport, Greater Manchester, “to come and see [my wife] and abuse her”.

London Broncos are targeting Super League fixtures in new territories and new Australia-friendly kick-off times after returning to the top flight as part of their plan to grow rugby league, before campaigning to the NRL to be part of a unique double-header at Wembley in 2028 too.

London will have a Super League presence in 2027 after the Rugby Football League awarded the Broncos the 15th place in a newly expanded competition. That includes initiatives to boost their own profile and that of Super League, including the prospect of some of London’s home games being played in new areas for the sport. Wechsel has already floated the idea of playing a game against Wigan at Fulham’s Craven Cottage, the first venue for professional rugby league in London in 1980.

But he now wants to go further with games in cities across the south, and potentially even Wales, to try to grow the game. “We will definitely be doing something,” Wechsel told the Guardian. “I can’t guarantee it would be Fulham because if you play at a football stadium, the pitch has to be renovated and this has happened quite late.

“But we will take at least one game somewhere to a southern city in England or perhaps into Wales. We’ve seen that Wigan and Warrington are taking a game to Dublin [in April] and we want to do the same, and try to grow rugby league as much as possible, both in London and farther afield.”

Super League will align closely with the NRL in 2027 in a number of areas before an official partnership with the Australian governing body begins in 2028, which will see it take control of Super League. That includes spreading kick-off times to reduce clashes and put more eyeballs on the game, and Wechsel has volunteered London to take a new time-slot.

“Thursday nights in London will be great because everyone works from home on a Friday, so they could be tempted out on Thursdays,” he said. “But I’ve thrown up the idea of playing at 12.30pm on a Saturday lunchtime, like in the Premier League. Connect the dots; that’s 9.30pm on Saturday night in Australia. Both sides of the world can tune in.”

It’s the “choice of a lifetime”. The stakes have never been higher. Do you waste 15 minutes of your life reading the second issue of the Reformer, the official monthly newspaper of Reform, every word of which has been written by me, Nigel Farage?

Make no mistake. If “Backwards with Burnham” gets his way, the EU will insist that every future issue of the Reformer will be written in German. His so-called EU reset “deal” will make every household in the country at least £200,000 worse off each week.

Don’t let the government try to fool you by pointing out that net migration has fallen to its lowest level since 1997. What’s really happening is that foreigners have wised up and are staying away because they don’t want to pay the extortionate amount of money the EU is demanding from the UK. We will only know we have the EU on the run when net immigration is back up over 1 million. Er, hang on …

A UK back in the EU should be unthinkable to every true-born Englishman. So, I’m afraid that rather counts Suella Braverman out. But for the rest of us, the idea of being made to speak French and eat mayonnaise with our chips is an insult to the memory of King George V. A more British king you could not hope to find in a man who was basically German. I didn’t fight in two world wars to take orders from Brussels.

On a side note. Just a month too late, I would like us all to observe a two-minute silence to honour all those Brits who fell in combat. It’s also a time to remind you of my own heroism. On 1 July 1916, I was in command of a regiment on the frontline of the Somme. Shortly before zero hour, I reminded them all of the sacrifices we had to make to save our country. It was just rotten bad luck that as the whistle blew to go over the top, I noticed that one of my shoe laces had become untied. “Dash it, chaps. You go ahead,” I said. And as I bent down, I could feel my back go and I was basically out of combat until 11 November 1918. For my services to the country, I am proud to say I awarded myself the VC and the MC and Bar. Here’s a photo of how I might have looked at the time.

Time now for a change of tone. Enough about me – for the moment. We now move on to our occasional series, Apprentice of the month, in which one of our members recounts their start in life. Today, we hear from Richard “Dicky” Tice, one of our interns at Reform HQ.

“Gosh, yes, it was really exciting. My first day out with all the lads digging trenches on the building site. ‘This is really fun,’ I said to them, as they sat down to drink cups of tea. Or a ‘brew’ as they put it in their charming regional accents. And then, guess what? After three weeks, I must have been doing so well because it turned out that my grandfather ran the company and wanted me to be managing director. So with a bit of hard work, you can get on in life.”

Right, back to me. Here’s a photo of me with the brave women of Piddington. Up until a few months ago, Piddington was a sleepy Oxfordshire village with just 350 inhabitants and a US airbase on its doorstep. The women used to walk around with not a care in the world, mingling with 1,200 airmen, any one of whom could have been a rapist. Now the airbase is being repurposed as a detention centre for migrants from Afghanistan, all of whom could be murderers and rapists, and the village is up in arms. So well done to Piddington for declaring independence from the UK. We look forward to the villagers building their own schools and hospitals.

Here in the Reformer, we – I mean, I – am not afraid to deal with the big issues, including climate change. This is one of the biggest hoaxes being perpetrated on the British people since Brexit. Worse still, it seems that even our fish are being duped. I have personally spoken to several blue-fin tuna and they tell me that they were persuaded to move back to British waters because they were told that the seas around Cornwall had warmed up. But after swimming hundreds of miles north, they found they were still freezing so they jumped into the back of a fishing boat in the hope of getting a hot bath.

Time also for a shout-out to our vetting department. As you know we take vetting very seriously here in Reform. Unlike the Tories who have allowed any number of Cameron cuties – by the way I never said Kemi Badenoch was a Cameron cutie except in this week’s Telegraph – into their party. Brexit, my arse. Excuse my French. The only Brexit betrayer you’ll find in Reform is Robert Jenrick.

That just leaves space for yet another photo of me. This time with my faithful poodle. Dicky likes nothing better than to lie on the floor of my garage while I ignore him. The labrador, of course, sleeps on the bed.
