Mandelson tried to set up meeting between Trump adviser and lobbying firm he held shares in

The Guardian Thu, 26 Nov 2026 15:12:36 GMT

Then ambassador to US wanted to discuss alternatives to World Trade Organization in ‘under the radar’ meeting, documents reveal

Peter Mandelson sought to organise an “under the radar” meeting between a member of his former lobbying firm, Global Counsel, and an economic adviser to Donald Trump, while he still held shares in the company, newly released documents reveal.

Mandelson’s attempt to organise the meeting followed a Foreign Office proposal of a “light-touch way” to protect him “against perceptions of benefiting [Global Counsel] in some way while in public office”.

In April 2025, while ambassador to Washington, Mandelson wanted to hold a lunch to discuss “alternative options” to the World Trade Organization and on how “like-minded partners come to terms with China and its practices”. He told the economic adviser he wanted to bring “a former trade colleague of mine” with “interesting views” who could “lead off”. He added: “It would be best to keep this under the radar.”

Mandelson then forwarded the emails to a Global Counsel employee to ask for their availability.

Mandelson had already refused to dispose of his shares in the company after he was appointed ambassador because, according to an official’s letter, the firm had “not made an offer that Lord Mandelson considers commensurate with the fair value”. One July 2025 email reveals his frustration in response to media queries about his continuing shareholding: “They [Global Counsel] should pull their fingers out and buy my shares.”

By the time Mandelson was trying to arrange the lunch with the presidential adviser and the Global Counsel employee, the top civil servant in the Foreign Office, Olly Robbins, had told him in a letter that he needed to “avoid any perception that he is consciously or even unconsciously furthering [Global Counsel’s] commercial interests”.

In a covering email to a draft of the letter to Mandelson, Robbins said: “If this looks sensible to you, I will sign and send and we can get this up and running in a light-touch way.”

Mandelson, however, continued to consult his former colleagues on his work as ambassador while holding shares, sharing a draft of a speech to the Ditchley Foundation with a Global Counsel director for comments. After receiving feedback, Mandelson said he would “soften the lecture on China”.

Addressing the Commons on Thursday after the latest publication of documents, the security minister, Dan Jarvis, said the government planned to strengthen its policy on conflicts of interest.

Andy Burnham said there was a need for “political reform” so that “vested interests aren’t running large within the system”, in order to restore public confidence in Westminster and Whitehall. He said these issues would be addressed next month in a 10-year plan.

Several crucial documents about Mandelson’s appointment to Washington continue to be withheld from the public. They include his conflict of interest declaration form and a summary document produced by vetting officials about his security clearance.

The Guardian revealed in April that Mandelson had failed the developed vetting process after Keir Starmer announced in December 2024 that he would be the next British ambassador to Washington. The Foreign Office overruled vetting officials’ recommendation that Mandelson be denied clearance, clearing him to take up the post.

Among the vetting agency’s concerns, according to sources, were his associations with senior figures in China, Russia and Israel, as well as a £1m loan. Those concerns were separate to Mandelson’s relationship with the convicted child sex offender Jeffrey Epstein, the issue that led to Mandelson’s sacking in September 2025.

Starmer also sacked Robbins, who told MPs investigating the issue that he believed vetting officials considered Mandelson to be “borderline” and so he could be cleared with “mitigations”, but no documents have been disclosed to back up his claims. He told them his office had been under “constant pressure” from Downing Street to get Mandelson in post as soon as possible.

Robbins went on to receive a six-figure payout from the government for his dismissal.

Sign up for the Breaking News UK email to get newsletter alerts direct to your inbox

after newsletter promotion

In February, parliament passed a motion known as a humble address requiring the government to publicly release “all papers” relevant to Mandelson’s appointment.

But some documents were held back from disclosures in March and June at the request of the Metropolitan police, in case they could “potentially prejudice” its investigation into Mandelson. Ministers previously revealed that these documents included “vetting information and conflicts of interest process material”.

A Met police spokesperson said: “Our investigation into alleged misconduct in public office is ongoing.”

Police sources expect the investigation to take months rather than years but the Met is yet to receive unredacted documents from the Epstein files held by the US Department of Justice that could be relevant to its inquiries.

The newly released documents include an email from Ian Collard, the Foreign Office security chief, to his line managers noting Mandelson had been given clearance. Collard said Mandelson’s “private sector engagements” were being handled through the conflict of interest process and that Mandelson had been sent a letter about his responsibilities regarding personal conduct as an employee.

Collard said questions about Mandelson’s “overseas contacts” would be reviewed by other authorities responsible for higher levels of security clearance.

In July, the foreign affairs select committee concluded that Mandelson’s appointment was “nothing short of disastrous”, “highly damaging” for the British government and “painful and offensive to the victims of Jeffrey Epstein”.

Mandelson has been approached for comment. On Thursday he published an article about how British negotiations to rejoin the European Union might unfold.

Champions League review: Lille monster Bayern, De Bruyne’s sad return and more United chaos

The Guardian Thu, 26 Nov 2026 15:00:39 GMT

The French side earned their first group win over troubled German giants as Bellingham and Betis also caught the eye

Bayern Munich have hit a snagging point, with injuries wracking Vincent Kompany’s squad just as the head coach returns to work following his own health scare. For Lille’s winner, to exact Bayern’s first loss of the season, Aleksandar Pavlović had an own goal for the ages, desperately chasing back to then somehow direct the ball into his own net. Bayern are 15th in the Champions League table, and with Harry Kane out until well into 2027 and 18-year-old Lennart Karl asked to lead the line, resources are stretched. Jamal Musiala, subject of club grandees Uli Hoeness and Karl Heinz-Rummenigge’s gripes over his contract in the light of his neurological condition, could also play only 15 minutes.

Praise instead is due to Lille, coached by Davide Ancelotti to their first win of the group stage. They are captained by 36-year-old Benjamin André, who played one of the best matches of his long career. “Underrated” in the view of Ancelotti, who worked at Bayern under his father, Carlo. “Tonight was something special, we played like a monster.”

Soccer’s world-leading content delivery machine continues to supply a high grade of entertainment. While critics carp against the group stage’s baggy format, Manchester United have supplied the thrills, the spills, the pratfalls. Following the pathos of Atlético Madrid and Como, a comedy of errors at Sporting, with Senne Lammens saving a penalty from Luis Suárez, being unable to save Suárez’s next spot-kick and then dropping the ball for the same player to equalise for a 2-2 scoreline that undersold the chaos. United’s second goal, Bruno Fernandes’s second, also came via farcical means, beating Kaique Pereira, the Sporting keeper, after a bobble off a divot in the Estádio José Alvalade’s surface that Fernandes had himself created when trying to keep his footing. A word, too, for Szymon Marciniak, who gave a strange, overly-fussy referee’s performance, ruling out two seemingly legitimate United goals.

Were United improved? It was difficult to gauge. “With a performance like today it’s the best medicine to prepare the next game,” said Mauricio Pochettino, possibly still jet-lagged yet already deep in the United reeds. His team are 19th in both the Champions League and Premier League.

Kevin De Bruyne’s return to the Etihad brought yearning from both player and former club. Manchester City’s struggles continue and De Bruyne, now 35, is not performing as desired for Napoli, while those from within City continue to push the idea of business as usual amid the limbo of those guilty charges, two empty tiers of the renovated stadium cast telling shadows. Playing in an unfamiliar orange kit for reasons of partnership with a fashion firm best known for football casual “clobber” only added to the surrealism.

“When you don’t win, you question everything,” Erling Haaland said following a 2-2 draw rescued by some Rayan Cherki magic. Among those questions is how Enzo Maresca is dealing with the succession and legacy of Pep Guardiola. Recent signs are unpromising.

In late 2026, the year of Harry Kane, another Englishman is setting controls for the Ballon d’Or. Jude Bellingham has never played a Premier League match but who in the world’s richest league could afford him? At half-time against PSV Eindhoven, Real Madrid were 1-0 down, and then José Mourinho threw on Bellingham. He scored only one of the five his team ran in, though it was spectacular; a volley bearing a light comparison to Madrid legend Zinedine Zidane’s goal in 2002’s final in Glasgow. “I think Zidane is much better than me, he’s much more elegant and he’s my idol,” said a humble Bellingham, while also dismissing talk of inheriting Kane’s crown.

Only their second season in the competition, their previous campaign coming in 2005-06, when Marcos Assunção, Ricardo Oliveira and Joaquín were the star names, Betis are sixth in the table with four wins from five. The knockouts beckon.

after newsletter promotion

The 2026 vintage is full of experience, with Manuel Pellegrini, 73, coaching a team captained by Isco, 34, and still as inventive as ever. The star man in defeating Slovan Bratislava was the Colombian striker Cucho Hernández, previously of Columbus Crew. Two towering headers made sure Slovan remained bottom on zero points.

“I was convinced it was going to be a magical night for me personally,” said Hernández, who was returning after over a month’s absence. Troy Parrott faces a fight to get back in, having been the match-winner in Betis’s opening defeat of Lille. Wednesday was another night where Antony, a Manchester United escapee flourishing elsewhere was a major threat.

“We don’t need to sign players in the transfer window, it’s not our style to sign a player for just six months. Above all, we’re not afraid of anything. We’re confident in our abilities and our resilience … Are we going to start crying and complaining? No, that’s not how a team operates.” – Paris Saint-Germain’s chances of a third title in succession were lowered when Désiré Doué joined Khvicha Kvaratskheliain the ruptured ACL club. Their coach, Luis Enrique, remains unbowed but Wednesday’s 2-2 draw with Roma suggested certain vulnerabilities. A new-look front three of Maghnes Akliouche, Ferran Torres and Senny Mayulu started against the Serie A club.

Liverpool, following a 3-0 win at Club Brugge that belied the scoreline, are the highest-ranked English team in the standings in fifth and host Porto next time out. Arsenal, in seventh after their shaky draw with Dortmund on Tuesday, host Real Madrid in two huge Premier League-La Liga summits; Manchester City travel to Barcelona. Two top-eight surprise packages, Betis and Como, also meet.

I spent 69 hours building Lego – here are the best sets for Christmas

The Guardian Thu, 26 Nov 2026 15:00:38 GMT

Guardian journalism is independent. We earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link. Learn more.

From Bluey and KPop Demon Hunters to Star Wars, Hogwarts and a working pinball machine, there’s a build to delight everyone

The best Christmas gifts for 2026

Lego may have been around for almost a hundred years, but it’s as popular as ever. Don’t take our word for it: we asked kids, teens and tweens what they wanted for Christmas this year, and Lego made it on to every single list. But with a range of collaborations with Star Wars, Harry Potter and other classic nerdy franchises, there’s plenty for (not so) grownups to get excited about as well. So when I was asked to try out some of Lego’s latest and most exciting launches, I jumped at the chance.

I’ve spent the last few months turning my flat into my own personal Legoland. I built set after set until my fingers were sore and my patience thin (69hrs 31mins in total), all in the name of finding the best sets for all ages. From KPop Demon Hunters to Lando Norris’s helmet and even a retro-style pinball machine, here are the best Lego gifts for 2026.

Build time: 2hrs 37minsAge: 10+Number of pieces: 700

This mini Hogwarts is small but mighty, with lots of fun little details, like a mini Chamber of Secrets and a hidden room containing the Mirror of Erised. The perfect set for Harry Potter fans, even ones who aren’t massively into Lego … yet.

Build time: 2hrs 10minsAge: 10+Number of pieces: 873

The dials of this set, complete with a rosy-cheeked Santa peering out from the chimney, can be changed daily to count down to the big day. It’s a set that’s destined to be built every year and become part of the recipient’s festive traditions. This was one of my favourites.

Build time: 8hrs 36minsAge: 18+Number of pieces: 2,274

Cast them back to the golden age of gaming with this retro-style pinball machine. This set took me the longest to build, but once finished, it was fully functional. This will keep them entertained for hours.

Build time: 3hrs 50minsAge: 9+Number of pieces: 882

From Lego’s Technic range, this intricately designed car is a masterpiece, with lots of little elements slotting together to create moving parts, such as pistons that go up and down as the car moves. Some sets in this guide I could build with my mind half elsewhere (this isn’t a brag – some of these were designed for children aged two and over), but this one needed my full attention, and I enjoyed the challenge. This would be well received by car and Lego enthusiasts alike.

Build time: 2hrs 32minsAge: 18+Number of pieces: 1,194

This wreath is so pretty, it’s worthy of hanging on the wall, and luckily it has built-in holes to do just that. It’s quite a repetitive build, but the end product is worth it. I also loved the creativity involved with arranging the various accessories.

Build time: 3hrs 17minsAge: 10+Number of pieces: 1,028

Darth Vader in Lego figure form is undeniably cuter than the real thing. This set was quite robust, so it is well suited to clumsier hands, and truly satisfying to click together. Star Wars fans would no doubt love to build and display this one.

Build time: 1hr 33minsAge: 18+Number of pieces: 791

This set from Lego’s Art range is based on Robert Indiana’s LOVE sculpture. I love that it’s split into two parts, with two separate instruction booklets, making it an ideal present to give to a loved one and build together. Each person can build two letters, and when they’re complete, they slot together.

Build time: 5hrs 8minsAge: 14+Number of pieces: 1,228

This half-electric, half-acoustic guitar in Olivia Rodrigo’s signature purple is an imaginative build. It opens to reveal a stage for the Rodrigo minifigures to perform on, and has a hidden compartment that conceals a dressing room. It’s a little smaller than I expected, about half the size of a real guitar. One for the diehard Rodrigo fans, particularly tweens and teens.

Build time: 30minsAge: 6+Number of pieces: 179

Perfect for stockings, these ornaments make a wholesome Christmas morning activity and can be hung on the tree as soon as they’re built. The glow-in-the-dark elements on the tree bauble are a fun touch.

Build time: 1hr 5minsAge: 10+Number of pieces: 502

One of Minecraft’s best-known characters, this skeleton model comes complete with a bow and arrow and a helmet. If they enjoy digital building with Minecraft, they’re sure to enjoy analogue building with Lego. It also comes with a QR code to redeem an in-game Minecraft item.

Build time: 1hr 57minsAge: 18+Number of pieces: 749

Lego’s Botanicals range is one of my favourites, with everything from woodland mushrooms to bonsai trees. This pink bouquet is a classic – so much thought has been put into every detail of the flowers. It’s quite fiddly and repetitive to build, but the final product is beautiful. This is a set that even the uninitiated would enjoy.

Build time: 3hrs 35minsAge: 14+Number of pieces: 793

This set is very cleverly designed, with lots of little parts coming together to make the spherical shape of the helmet. It’s fiddly and delicate, so I wouldn’t recommend it for really young kids or those with a heavy hand. I loved the included minifigure of Lando Norris.

Build time: 5hrs 11minsAge: 10+Number of pieces: 2,164

This set was my favourite. It’s a bigger build that took me 5hrs 11mins – that’s just under the combined running time of Philosopher’s Stone and Chamber of Secrets. It comes with a generous number of minifigures (13), including more niche ones, such as Moaning Myrtle, and changeable faces and hair for Ron and Harry so they can transform into Crabbe and Goyle. There are also lots of interactive elements, my favourite being a sink that slides back to reveal a chute down to the Chamber of Secrets. This is a set that will encourage play and impress Potterheads.

Build time: 51minsAge: 10+Number of pieces: 314

This one is quite an easy, low-commitment build, so it would be great for Lego novices. It includes three minifigures, which is generous for a set of this size, and the end result is quite dynamic. It also includes a redeemable in-game item for Fortnite.

Build time: 5hrs 14mins (to build the koalas)Age: 10+Number of pieces: 1,536

Lego’s 3-in-1 sets can be built into three different models. The star of this one is a koala mother and baby perched in a tree, but it can also be transformed into sea turtles or kangaroos. The way each block is given a new lease of life within each model is so clever, and the end results are super cute.

Sign up to The Filter

Get the best shopping advice from the Filter team straight to your inbox. The Guardian’s journalism is independent. We will earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link.

after newsletter promotion

Build time: 1hr 18minsAge: 9+Number of pieces: 433

Marvel Avengers: Doomsday is premiering on 16 December in the UK, so this is a timely set. The minifigures’ accessories are great, such as Sam Wilson’s Captain America wings, and the Thing comes with big hands you can add to the minifigure. It’s a smaller set that won’t take up too much room, but it was still an engaging build.

Build time: 17minsAge: 3+Number of pieces: 131

This is more of a play set, taking me only 17mins to put together. Made for children three and over, it has much simpler, step-by-step instructions. Once it’s finished, there’s plenty for kids to explore. The woodland animals are adorable, and the little red and blue lenses can be used to reveal different images on some of the bricks.

Build time: 2hrs 17minsAge: 8+Number of pieces: 534

This was the set that excited me the most. Taking inspiration from Brand New Day, the latest Spider-Man film, the tower block is constructed so the Hulk can burst through the walls without destroying the entire build. It comes with five minifigures and a big Hulk figure, and there are mini guns that shoot Lego coins. Getting the part of the building that the Hulk bursts through to sit properly is a bit fiddly, so I’d recommend it for children eight and over, just as Lego does. This set is quite tall, but not very wide, so it won’t take up too much space.

Build time: 1hr 8minsAge: 6+Number of pieces: 400

Lego launched Smart Play this year: the sets revolve around an electronic brick that flashes and makes sounds in reaction to different prompts. For this set, the brick can be inserted into Pikachu to make him more interactive. If you hold the Lego sandwich up to him, he’ll make chewing noises; if you lie him down, he’ll snore. I love how the Smart Brick adds a fresh twist while still being screen-free.

Build time: 1hr 50minsAge: 9+Number of pieces: 825

KPop Demon Hunters was an instant hit with tweens when it came out in 2025, and now the hunters’ favourite furry companion is available in Lego form. Derpy Tiger was straightforward to build and comes with his sidekick Sussie Bird to perch on his head.

Build time: 23minsAge: 4+Number of pieces: 115

One of the smallest sets on this list, this is a very quick build, but it’s a fun play set once complete. Inspired by The Lost World: Jurassic Park, it includes a truck with a cage, a quad bike, two minifigures and a baby T rex. I love the little hotdog dangling from the quad bike as bait.

Build time: 1hrAge: 4+Number of pieces: 382

Bluey’s family home was easy to put together, with simplified instructions written with younger children in mind. It feels like a classic doll’s house, with lots of nooks and crannies to explore when complete.

Build time: 3hrs 18minsAge: 9+Number of pieces: 1,005

I found this comic book and game store with female figures a breath of fresh air – a far cry from the hyper-feminised play sets of my youth. It’s part of Lego’s Friends collection, which has lots of different doll’s house-style sets with repeat characters, and there’s even a TV show. The highlight of this one for me was the fun Comic-Con-style costumes the Lego figures are wearing, and the working vending machine.

Build time: 1hr 32minsAge: 6+Number of pieces: 581

In another of Lego’s Smart Play sets, the interactive brick reacts to the object it’s placed on. For example, if it’s placed on the ship, it flashes and makes whooshing sounds, and if you press it to R2-D2, it makes his signature bleeping noises. As well as Luke and Leia figures, this set includes a stormtrooper and a rebel crew member for re-enacting a battle between the two sides. I also love the mini lightsaber.

Build time: n/aAge: 4+Number of pieces: 484

Lego’s creative box puts the builder in charge; they can use the bricks to make whatever they want. There’s a booklet of suggestions included, though, in case they need some inspiration. I love that it comes in a brick-shaped tub that can be used to store the Lego.

Build time: 3hrs 11minsAge: 10+Number of pieces: 904

Move over, Santa. This charming Mrs Claus model was a straightforward build thanks to the chunky bricks, and it’s quite robust, making it ideal for heavy-handed kids and adults. Once built, she can be posed into different positions and added to the recipient’s festive decorations.

Build time: 1hr 16mins (to build the dolphins)Age: 9+Number of pieces: 542

This may be one of the more affordable sets on this list, but you still get a lot of bang for your buck. It’s another of the 3-in-1 sets that uses the same bricks to create three different models. This time, the recipient can transform the blocks into dolphins, a seahorse, or a crab and jellyfish.

Build time: 1hr 40minsAge: 7+Number of pieces: 691

This sleek, hi-tech fire truck has lots of fun little details, including the ability to shoot water (or at least a blue spear that’s supposed to represent water). I love that it includes two male and two female firefighters. It’s part of the City range that includes lots of sets that can be put together to build your very own Lego world.

Build time: 10minsAge: 2+Number of pieces: 57

Another build-and-play set aimed at younger kids. It comes with cute Duplo characters and a motorised train that can drive around the tracks. Pair it with other sets from the range to create your own Lego world.

Build time: 2hrs 5minsAge: 12+Number of pieces: 713

Bring everyone’s favourite elf to life with this newly released model. Building Buddy was fairly straightforward, but I made a few mistakes that I needed to fix along the way, which explains why Lego rates it 12+. This one will definitely get the recipient in the festive spirit.

a-ha’s Morten Harket: ‘My Parkinson’s diagnosis wasn’t devastating. I have a new appreciation for the human organism’

The Guardian Thu, 26 Nov 2026 15:00:37 GMT

As the Norwegian pop trio’s frontman releases his new album Human Grace, he answers your questions on the devastating effects of fame, living in squalor in London, 80s nostalgia – and a certain bandmate’s denim underwear

You’ve described your new album, Human Grace, as revealing more of yourself than your previous work. Was there anything you found unexpectedly difficult to express through these songs, or anything that surprised you about yourself during the creative process? BarefootJaxNo. It’s an exploratory process, the activity of making new music. It’s about quieting yourself, being available to hear tiny little differences in vibes, to pick up a seed that will blossom into something – and then it goes from being nothing to becoming a thing, instantaneously. That has never changed for me. With a-ha, there wasn’t much time and peace for songwriting. Being the frontman takes a lot of focus.

What has changed is my access to the skilled tools – singing and guitar – due to the Parkinson’s medication side-effects. For this album, we found old recordings of my voice, some from over 10 years back. It hasn’t been devastating for me to get this diagnosis – it has been a blunt and impactful instrument to stop everything I was doing. I had to reassemble myself first, to understand what it is. Losing access to parts of myself I’ve taken for granted all my life, but also a new appreciation for the architecture of ourselves as an organism – it’s so impressive. It’s mind-blowing.

In the early days of a-ha, you spent time living and recording in Sydenham, south London. Was it a formative, fun time for all of you? Any stories about that period? mrskiteIt was tough going, but it didn’t matter to us, because we were so excited about being where we were, doing what we were doing, feeling the freedom that comes with that. But we were on the brink of needing serious intervention: we didn’t have money to sustain ourselves, and we didn’t know how long that would last.

The living quarters were on the squalid side. There were only two beds, so we had to take turns sleeping on a mattress where springs would pop out. We all had pollen allergies, especially Magne [Furuholmen] and me. There was a gas leak, and we all woke up with massive headaches. After that, we heated the room using the electric cooktop coils. We once made an attempt at painting one of the walls, but it soon developed boils that popped, with yellowish-brown goo pouring out.

Take on Me took a few attempts, and a groundbreaking video, before it became the hit it so deserved to be. What was that period like for you and the band? Did you think you’d make it or did you get the sinking feeling that you’d never quite break through? 11LFO11I never doubted it – that was my touch of naivety. The other guys did, but I didn’t accept it, although they probably had a better understanding of reality and what was likely to happen than I did.

Since the first time I saw them, live at a gig, it hit me: I knew they needed me, to be complete, I didn’t have any doubt. I just saw them, and I knew. A crazy, gracious feeling, not egotistical. I’d discovered them, and I knew they just had to discover me.

a-ha: The Movie [in 2021] made it seem as if being in the band was not much fun for any of you – until you were suddenly playing the incredible unplugged version of Take on Me. Was that actually the case? RalfyJYes and no. We had exhausted parts of ourselves, and had too limited access to each other, and ourselves, as a result. We knew what the potential was between us, but we couldn’t access it because playfulness recedes when you don’t communicate. There were also rewarding moments, and I’ve always enjoyed touring, but in itself that’s nowhere near enough.

Paul McCartney says that when he writes, he still mentally asks John Lennon for advice about whatever he’s working on. When you’re writing songs, do you have an imaginary Paul [Waaktaar-Savoy] and Mags sitting on each shoulder? TommyG33No. But maybe the other way around – I think they’ve both written songs with my voice in mind.

You support Stoke City? How the hell did that happen? laithaljanBit of a stretch, really, that was said half as a joke. It’s mostly my younger brother who was an avid fan. We shared a room as kids, and it was plastered with his posters of Stoke City players. My own posters were of butterflies.

I remember being impressed as a kid with an interview you gave to (I think) Smash Hits, in which you said that if you hadn’t been a singer, you would have been a priest. Is that true? catmodermI knew it was not for me to be ordained as a priest, that kind of service, but I’ve been very interested in discussing faith with people who, according to them, have no faith. But I don’t want to do that with a Bible in my hand. I was curious as to whether I could find a language to talk about faith, theology, religion – which are all different things.

I’ve always been very curious – that’s the core aspect of me, and it has led me to go on searches, trips inside myself, and towards philosophical concepts and systems. I’ve always wanted to know what lies behind anything; even as a kid I had to investigate how things looked underneath and inside. Lately I’ve been fascinated by the profound work of [British psychiatrist] Iain McGilchrist, on the different roles of our two brain hemispheres.

After recording The Living Daylights, did you ever get to meet James Bond? GirlyouknowitstrueWho is he again? I’ve yet to even meet myself, and I’m fucking real.

I was wondering how the idea came about to have two of your daughters participate in your new album, and why you decided to do so? Virginie91It wasn’t planned. We knew from the outset that two songs were lacking something; they needed either me singing some bits, or someone else. There were voids. We started thinking of who it could be, and someone came up with the idea of my daughters, maybe [manager] Harald [Wiik], maybe me.

When it came up, I thought: are they prepared to be part of something that could bring attention, that could impact their lives for a period? Tomine is well acquainted with media and public appearances, but I had more concern for Karmen, although she’s very active with music and theatre, and is part of a band. They are very strong singers. I never tutored them at all: they’re completely self-taught, they just listened in the background to what I did with my voice. It took no time at all, in and out of the studio. It was fun, being there and hearing them, how precise they are. The timing and phrasing is excellent. And this isn’t even really their kind of music.

With the 1980s having another revival via gen Z, who feel nostalgia for a time they never knew, what do you think today’s young people are searching for? Apart from our fabulous hair? Christine_RousseauGen Z are searching for leadership they can believe in, but for themselves they’re looking for human relations, belonging, and finding that lacking today. For the last 15 to 20 years, the leaders of the world have been asking the youth for advice, and that may look good on the surface, but it should set off alarm bells, because it means they don’t really know. Our civilisation has been in the process of undoing itself for quite some time, due to negligence and lack of responsibility.

In life, the moment you become aware of something that is not OK, you’re immediately responsible for it. It’s no different from driving past a car accident: you need to stop, you remain 100% responsible and accountable.

I remember reading in a magazine in the late 80s that Paul wore denim underwear. Was that true? OnionfeverI’ve never looked at his underwear. It simply doesn’t interest me.

Through all the different versions of yourself that life has brought about, what is the one thing you feel has remained fundamentally unchanged about you? And what, if anything, have you had to let go of along the way? velvetroadsI suppose I would say my heart. I possess a kind of … naivety, at the base of my system, that is linked to the purity of the essential emotional being, and that influences all the things that I’m doing.

There’s only ever been one big change for me: fame. From being an actual member of society, to having that revoked when instant fame hit me. It’s a colossal change, a profound personal loss, surpassed only by that of losing a loved one. I hate fame, but I love people, and the potential in us. But I don’t like people, or the human race, very much, because we keep on making the same primitive mistakes, and in the end you lose patience for that. But I love the potential of what we can do, that spark in people, young or old. That moves me a lot.

I helped organise the letter from Labour MPs urging Andy Burnham to reject Rosebank. This is why

The Guardian Thu, 26 Nov 2026 15:00:37 GMT

Approval would be celebrated by the oil giants, but it wouldn’t help our constituents who worry about the climate crisis, and their bills

Catherine Fookes is Labour MP for Monmouthshire

Labour split over Rosebank oilfield exposed by letter from nearly 100 MPs

This week it was confirmed that millions of households are facing yet another winter of unaffordable energy bills, just as we learn that this summer’s heatwaves were linked to more than 5,000 deaths in the UK.

The cost of living and climate crises are two sides of the same coin: our continued dependence on fossil fuels is driving up bills, fuelling deadly extreme weather and causing widespread harm to people in this country. It was one year ago that Storm Claudia’s floods swept through Monmouthshire, devastating hundreds of homes, businesses and livelihoods. I know, as flood season is upon us again, how sick residents feel every time it rains.

This is why I, along with my colleagues on Labour’s backbenches, have written to the prime minister urging that his government makes the right decision and rejects the Rosebank oilfield.

As backbenchers, we are reflecting the concerns of our constituents who watched in horror as wildfires tore through countryside and communities this summer and who now face a winter of worrying about how they will afford to put the heating on.

Voicing these concerns is our job as MPs. We are not “rebels”, nor is this a “civil war” inside the Labour party, as some headlines have tried to make out. It is a reflection of the reality that is playing out in our communities.

After last month’s approval of the Jackdaw gasfield, my colleagues and I felt uneasy but understood the reasons for that decision – it is relatively small, short-lived and could displace some polluting imported gas at the margin.

However, we are clear that the Rosebank oilfield is a different proposition. It contains mostly oil for export, and it is far, far larger than Jackdaw. Most importantly, Rosebank will do nothing to reduce energy bills for our constituents. The oil belongs to private companies who will ship it away to the highest bidder. Claims on its tax benefits are overinflated, rarely accounting for the significant rebates companies claim for developing and decommissioning projects. And in a depleted basin, it will not turn the tide on jobs, which have been in decline for decades.

If Rosebank is approved, champagne corks will pop in the offices of oil companies. But it will not make an iota of difference to our constituents’ energy bills. And it will accelerate the climate crisis, which is already pushing up food bills, causing devastating floods in winter and in summer turning our green and pleasant land into a parched, burnt-out expanse.

Rejecting Rosebank is the right thing to do domestically, but it is also critical in the wake of last week’s failed climate talks. Cop31 collapsed because some countries refused to accept the imperative to phase out fossil fuels. It is not enough to just accelerate the adoption of renewables. The science shows that we already have more oil and gas in existing projects globally than can ever be safely burned.

This means that countries, such as the UK, that are committed to climate action need to act accordingly. Rosebank signals something important, at home and abroad, about our intent. If we cannot make the right decision on this field, which offers so little, then there will be questions about our commitment to dealing with even thornier climate problems.

We know that the majority of people in this country support action to protect people now and in the future from escalating climate change. And as we enter our fifth consecutive winter of painfully high bills, our answer cannot be, as the Tories’ was, more drilling. It didn’t help then, and it won’t help now.

Sign up to Matters of Opinion

after newsletter promotion

As MPs, we can see the harms of a warming planet play out now in our communities. Climate change is affecting workers who keep our public transport systems, hospitals and schools running during extreme weather, not to mention our under-resourced firefighters. But it is future generations who will ultimately experience the worst of what is to come.

I was proud to stand on the Green Prosperity Plan in our 2024 manifesto. It was one of the pledges that really resonated with people on the doorstep across Monmouthshire – they could finally see a party willing to take on profiteering oil companies and deliver a brighter future of community-owned energy, ample cheap domestic energy supplies from wind and solar and an end to the fuel poverty that blights the lives of so many.

As Labour MPs, we are bound to champion working people against the vested interests of the few. In 2026, that means standing with ordinary people living through the reality of the climate crisis and not the private oil and gas supergiants profiting from it. We urge the government to make the right decision.

Catherine Fookes is Labour MP for Monmouthshire

I’m an AI leader at a tech giant. Our industry has stopped taking safety seriously

The Guardian Thu, 26 Nov 2026 14:06:10 GMT

We’re developing the most powerful tech in history – but trust, safeguarding and privacy are being sidelined in favour of huge profit

I’m a senior AI leader at one of the world’s biggest tech companies, and the products we put out into the world are increasingly being recklessly rushed, without proper consideration. The tech industry used to take safety and privacy seriously, but lately I have become worried by how rash we have become. In a sector that is obsessed with being first, ethical hesitation is now viewed as a luxury we can’t afford.

If you want to properly understand the actions of big tech, you have to look at the industry’s culture. It moves fast and there is a mindset of constant one-upmanship. Being first matters financially. But just as importantly, competition is believed to bring out the best in people.

We are encouraged to see ourselves as though we are in a race not just against other companies and even against entire countries, but also against other teams within our own company. Relationships between teams have moved from competitive to actively adversarial. The AI teams are the most siloed, the most secretive and the most separated. That’s where the race is fastest and fiercest.

People are becoming paranoid about colleagues stealing their work, reluctant to share information, secretive about the models they are developing, and worried about job security if they don’t deliver.

The natural response to these conditions is to push back against the in-house guardrails. Checks around privacy, data protection, trust and safety exist to ensure that our products don’t cause harm or break the law. But they also slow us down and restrict our work.

If a tech firm launches a new AI chatbot, the company’s trust and safety staff might consider how its users’ data is protected, or what mechanisms are needed to prevent it from encouraging self-harm or crime. They might also think about what data is being used to train the model, and where that data comes from. But those teams are increasingly being slimmed down or sidelined. And if they do raise concerns, it often doesn’t result in material changes to the final product.

In AI in particular, product-safety managers are being sidelined and the biggest companies are reducing the number of people in these roles. This depletion has been taking place gradually over the past 15 years or so, but recently it has really accelerated. It has been happening in my company and, when I look at peers in other firms, I see it there too.

Sign up to Matters of Opinion

Guardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and more

after newsletter promotion

This is undoubtedly resulting in more dangerous products being released. And now, the prevailing attitude within companies is that the legal teams should only worry about negative responses to our products once they are out in the world, rather than trying to consider those concerns as they are built.

The underlying belief is that our stock price will be driven up by “the next big win”, more than it will from a strategy of steady, company-wide improvements. And, even if that big win comes with legal or safety problems, the bottom line will ultimately have benefited.

At the same time, the leadership and management within tech firms has become more arrogant, with senior figures becoming more disconnected from the reality of the rest of society. This is not just the well-known CEOs but also the people a few rungs down, who are now earning salaries that mean they never have to engage with the issues most people have to face.

I still love the tech industry. But in the midst of constant restructures and redundancies, the message being sent to staff is that the biggest prize awaits as long as you compete and win. This is the culture we’re working in while handling the most powerful technologies ever developed. AI doesn’t have an ethics problem, but the people running the companies do.

The writer is an AI expert working in the tech industry. A version of this piece originally appeared with the Bureau of Investigative Journalism as part of its Secret Source series, a regular column featuring industry whistleblowers

I’m not interested in having sex with near strangers. As a newly single man, how do I navigate dating?

The Guardian Thu, 26 Nov 2026 14:00:38 GMT

You don’t have to have sex because it’s ‘what’s expected’, advice columnist Eleanor Gordon-Smith writes. But you may want to be explicit about what you do want

Read more Leading questions

How do I navigate being single when I’m not interested in sex with near strangers? I don’t judge anyone, consenting adults can do whatever they like – but, for me, sex has to come with trust and, frankly, love, or at least the potential of love. I’m recently single after a long and toxic relationship, and I’ve never dated – I got on the dating scene and found that if I don’t try to get in someone’s pants by the third date, no matter how much of a nice time we’re having, they disappear – and in fact I’ve had some women do the old “call yourself a man” at me, in one memorable case, after they specifically said “not tonight” and I said “no problem” (the response was a frustrated “don’t you have needs?!”).

I’ve tried to go along with it and do what’s expected but I don’t enjoy it, it just feels a bit wrong, and when I’ve done this it kills the vibe we had, probably because I can’t get into it properly. I’ve always been into the person, not just the body, but it takes time to get to know someone enough to feel comfortable being intimate. So how can I keep a nice relationship going, so that I can develop the trust I need for sex, without them losing interest because I’m not doing (what I assume) everyone else on the dating scene is doing?

Eleanor says: I’ll say what should go without saying: it’s sad and horrible to have sex when you don’t really want to; the force of social expectations shouldn’t overrule what you want; and you don’t have to have sex because it’s “what’s expected”.

Someone reacting with gendered blowback or emotional pressure when you don’t want to have sex with them is telling you something important. They’re telling you that they’ll insult you in gendered ways when they feel ego-bruised; that they expect you to mind-read whether they’re being sincere; and that they’re mean. These are not traits that make for a good sex life. Or a good partner.

I can join you in asking how to avoid losing nice relationships but I want to be really clear about the difference between people who react to your preference badly, and people who just might wrongly infer that you’re not interested. Only one is a candidate for a nice relationship.

The trick to not losing the otherwise nice ones might be to separate not wanting to sleep together from what they think that symbolises.

The dating world runs on symbols. It’s all semaphore and signals and signs. Everybody’s meant to know that this action means that thing – texting back, kissing at the end of the date, meeting the friends.

For better or for worse, one sign of mutual interest can be sex at a certain pace. To someone who understands that to be the way “we” indicate interest, you not wanting it at that pace can look like someone who just isn’t interested.

Importantly though, people using the Dating Signal Handbook to say things and decode others doesn’t necessarily mean they have a particular attachment to the signal itself. I might still be mad that you didn’t get me a present on Valentine’s Day even though I know I don’t ultimately need a stuffed bear, and even though I agree that bought trinkets on designated days shouldn’t be a measure of love.

We often have very real feelings about things because of what they mean in our social signal world, even when we’re ambivalent about whether that symbol should be the way of communicating that thing.

So it may not be as simple as everybody wanting sex for sex’s sake; trying to “get in the pants” of “near strangers”. Sometimes people want to kiss or text lots or have sex for what that says about the relationship in the signal world, as much as because they want those things for their own sake.

It’s a stupid handbook that says that, unless people want to have sex, they aren’t interested. But if that’s the one the people you’re interested in are working from, you want a way to say “I don’t want that yet” without being heard to say “I don’t want you”. That might mean finding ways to dispel the interpretation that you’re not interested (Flowers? Really investing in romantic follow-up plans?), exploring other kinds of intimacy that build trust and show early-stage attraction, or just being vulnerable enough to say the whole of what you’ve said to me.

We rely on symbols instead of words to communicate in dating because words leave us no plausible deniability. But, for clear communication, saying it explicitly works precisely because it leaves us so vulnerable. If you’re worried about people wrongly inferring you don’t want to keep seeing them, your best bet might be to be explicit and vulnerable about the fact that you do.

‘Trucks on fire and drones overhead’: the Russians risking the long road to Crimea

The Guardian Thu, 26 Nov 2026 14:00:36 GMT

Kyiv’s destruction of the road section of the Crimean Bridge has left drivers facing hazardous journeys through occupied southern Ukraine

Russians once packed their swimming trunks and sunscreen for summer holidays in occupied Crimea, or hiking boots for trips in the colder months to the picturesque Black Sea peninsula annexed by Vladimir Putin in 2014.

Now, travellers swap advice on first-aid kits and how to avoid drones as they drive through a war zone to the peninsula.

For millions of Russians who until recently could reach Crimea with ease, the new reality comes after Ukraine destroyed the road section of the Crimean Bridge, opened by Putin in 2018 as a symbol of Moscow’s grip on the peninsula.

Russian officials have yet to provide a timetable for restoring road traffic across the bridge, which was repeatedly struck by Ukrainian drones and rockets.

Tellingly, Russia’s transport ministry has removed one of the two arches from its official image of the Crimean Bridge, leaving only the railway crossing.

This leaves Crimea-bound motorists facing the prospect of months, if not years, of hazardous journeys along a road through occupied southern Ukraine littered with burnt-out trucks.

Before the full-scale invasion, the Crimean Bridge was the sole link between Russia and illegally annexed Crimea, carrying tourists, food and fuel, as well as troops and military equipment.

But Russia’s occupation of parts of southern Ukraine in 2022 opened up a new land corridor to Crimea, along a highway that Moscow calls the Novorossiya route.

The roughly 390-mile (630km) road runs from Rostov-on-Don in southern Russia through the devastated city of Mariupol, along the Sea of Azov coast through Berdiansk and Melitopol, before entering Crimea.

The highway had already become a vital supply route for Russian forces in southern Ukraine, allowing Moscow to reduce its reliance on the Crimean Bridge for military logistics.

But that has also made the road an increasingly frequent target for Ukrainian attacks.

“What we saw was pretty apocalyptic,” said Anatoly, who had travelled to Crimea from Russia to visit his parents.

“Trucks on fire and drones overhead that our boys were trying to shoot down. It was quite an adrenaline rush, but I wouldn’t recommend making the journey,” he added, asking for his surname to be withheld.

About 5 million Russians visit Crimea each year, according to the peninsula’s tourism authorities, although they have yet to publish figures for this year. The bridge was also the main road link for Crimean residents travelling to Russia for cheaper groceries and petrol.

Passenger trains continue to cross the Crimean Bridge, though Kyiv has vowed to strike it again. A ferry service also operates across the Kerch strait, but carries passengers rather than cars and is frequently disrupted by winter storms.

With no easy alternative, drivers have begun compiling their own rules for surviving the journey.

A guide posted in one popular Telegram group, titled “How to drive the land route fast and alive”, opens with a stark warning: “Unless it’s a matter of life and death, don’t go.”

Drivers are urged to avoid travelling at night, because when “you’re alone on the road, the air defence teams can’t see you and you can’t see the drone”.

They are told to keep between 50 and 100 metres apart, stop only in designated areas and never shelter behind a lorry.

“A truck isn’t cover, it’s a target. A fuel tanker especially.”

after newsletter promotion

Drivers are also advised to carry spare fuel – as much as 240 litres – along with two fire extinguishers, tourniquets and haemostatic dressings to stop severe bleeding.

They are further instructed to tune into local FM radio stations, whose broadcasts are interrupted by warnings when drones are spotted. Mobile air defence teams hang flags along the roadside, with white signalling the all-clear, red an alert and yellow a drone threat.

Even Russian state television has acknowledged the danger. On Sunday’s edition of the flagship Vesti news programme, a presenter said the road “passes through three frontline regions and comes under attack”.

Drivers were advised to stock up on food and water, and take a first-aid kit “and know how to use what’s in it”.

According to the programme, up to 20,000 vehicles a day travel along the highway.

Beyond threatening Crimea’s summer tourist season and the businesses that depend on it, the bridge’s destruction risks deepening hardship on the peninsula.

Ukraine’s air campaign to isolate Crimea has already caused fuel shortages and disrupted water and electricity supplies, prompting local authorities to declare several states of emergency over the summer.

Kyiv says its strikes are aimed at Russian military logistics rather than civilian vehicles, and the drivers’ guides acknowledge that ordinary cars are rarely hit.

However, the highway’s heavy use by Russian forces and lorries transporting fuel and other supplies to Crimea makes it a key target for Ukrainian strikes and puts civilian motorists at risk of getting caught up in the attacks.

Ukraine carried out an average of two strikes a day along the highway corridor in the first six months of 2026, according to the Armed Conflict Location and Event Data Project, an independent conflict-monitoring organisation. About 90% of the strikes involved drones.

Some truck drivers have shared accounts of narrowly avoiding drones lying on the road and say they now wear bulletproof vests.

“Guys, watch out. When it gets dark, drive straight into the bushes,” one driver warned in a message shared online on Sunday.

“Yesterday my car ran over a lurking drone on the road. It was already dark, and the thing was just waiting there on the highway.”

Dmitry, a truck driver from Rostov who often crosses to Crimea, said he had recently considered quitting his job because of the risks, but was struggling to find other work and still had a mortgage to pay.

“For my birthday last month, I was given a tactical first-aid kit last month. I toasted that I would never have to use it.”

Banton’s ascent to England leadership role vindicates all-in approach to white-ball game

The Guardian Thu, 26 Nov 2026 12:09:28 GMT

Batter assumes vice-captaincy and is set to step in as skipper in Canberra, with appointment a potential pointer to side’s future limited-overs direction

When Will Jacks broke his hand at the MCG last Saturday night – his birthday ruined and his tour of Australia over – there were a few directions England could have turned as regards the vice-captaincy. Plenty of teams happily do without an official deputy, of course. But with Harry Brook jetting off to join the Test tour of South Africa after the fourth of these five T20 internationals, a replacement will be required when the series wraps up in Canberra.

Phil Salt was one option. For all of his unfettered aggression, powered by those tattooed, Popeye-like forearms, the opener is an intelligent, thoughtful cricketer very much in tune with the rhythms of T20. As well as two seasons captaining in the Hundred, most recently with Welsh Fire, Salt previously deputised for Jos Buttler against Australia at home two years ago.

And then there was Sam Curran, who has captained in the T20 Blast, the ILT20, the Hundred and, given its intensity and profile, most notably the Indian Premier League. Player of the tournament during England’s T20 World Cup win here back in 2022 – Sam Curran MBE, no less – the all-rounder could easily have been asked.

England have instead turned to Tom Banton, eight years since he led the England Under-19s during a home summer series against South Africa and with just a handful of matches in charge of Taunton in the West of England Premier League in between. It says something about a cricketer whose stock is currently on the rise in the eyes of Brook and head coach Brendon McCullum.

“I was pretty emotional when I got told a few days ago in the airport,” said Banton, ahead of Friday’s third T20 at the Gabba. “To captain your country is a great honour and something I’m looking forward to. Baz [McCullum] told me in the airport, he just pulled me aside and told me. I didn’t know how to react if I’m honest.”

While it was McCullum who broke the news, this initial promotion to vice-captain is as much about Banton’s tight relationship with Brook and Jacks. Former teammates during the 2018 Under-19s World Cup, they are clearly the new core of this white-ball set-up. Banton made his senior debut first, seven years ago, but it is only over the past 18 months that he has become as central as the other two.

Test ambitions also flickered at the start of 2025 when Banton’s epic 371 against Worcestershire broke Somerset’s record first-class score, previously held by Justin Langer (342). Key to that innings was his decision to dispense with dog-stick throwdowns in the nets, which he personally felt had led to bad habits.

However, last summer Banton put red-ball cricket on hold to go all-in on white-ball cricket. Whether causation or correlation, he has struck a rich run of form since, averaging 53 across 20 limited-overs internationals and finishing player of the series during England’s recent 2-1 win in the one-dayers. In this T20 series, a strike rate of 216 again underlines how big he is seeing the white Kookaburra.

It is a sabbatical of sorts, with Banton honest about his desire to seek overseas franchise cricket outside of England commitments but keen to return to four-day cricket in time. Equally, if approached by a younger teammate considering the same move, the 28-year-old said he would “definitely advise pursuing it”.

Banton’s own mentor is the currently sidelined Buttler – “To have him at the other end of the phone is something I don’t take for granted,” he said – while Kevin Pietersen’s recent presence in the England set-up as a “special mentor” during the first fortnight on tour was another welcome source of input.

“To have an idol of mine – and I’m sure many of the others – has been pretty awesome,” Banton said. “He put a real emphasis on not just turning up to training for the sake of it. It has been really testing the nets.

“It is challenging and it can be quite scary at times. But as a group we’re definitely seeing the rewards. The 10-day training block we had [in Perth] before the 50-over series … I’ve never seen an England team train as hard as that.”

That final observation is an interesting one, coming in Brisbane and exactly a year since Ben Stokes drove a push for England’s players to undergo extra training in response to going 1-0 down in the Ashes. McCullum then famously argued they were in fact “over-prepared” after this became a ruinous 2-0 at the Gabba.

It was the first clear sign of a captain and coach going their separate ways by way of outlook and the rest, as they say, is history. For now, though, albeit on a much lower-profile white-ball tour, England’s leadership appears on the same page.

Faulty electrical goods returned to UK supermarkets ending up on Ghana ‘megadump’

The Guardian Thu, 26 Nov 2026 12:00:34 GMT

Mountains of household items are burned and stripped down at the tip by workers without protection such as masks, investigation alleges

Electrical goods that were returned as faulty to leading British stores including Tesco, Argos and Asda have been found dumped on a waste tip in Ghana, an investigation has found.

The faulty electrical appliances, including toasters and slow cookers, had been returned to major UK supermarkets. They were found at Agbogbloshie, one of the world’s largest e-waste sites, in Ghana’s capital, Accra, a joint investigation by Unearthed and Greenpeace Africa has found. The findings raise serious questions about e-waste export rules.

Mountains of household items are burned and stripped down at the tip by workers without protection such as gloves and masks, the investigation alleges.

Exporting broken electrical goods to Africa is illegal under UK waste export rules in almost every circumstance.

Tesco own brand slow cookers, toasters and Crockpot branded slow cookers, including at least one with a Tesco label, were found on the Accra dump.

Tesco said on Thursday it had suspended its third-party electronic waste management providers with immediate effect while it completed a full audit of them and their practices.

“We’re extremely concerned about these claims … We remain committed to removing or reducing the waste across our operations wherever we can and we work closely with experts to ensure we handle materials responsibly, in line with legal requirements and our own robust standards,” the store said.

Argos items including its own brand Cookworks products, slow cookers, toasters and food slicers were found at the dump.

Argos also said it was mounting an investigation into how the items had ended up there.

“As a responsible retailer, we have processes in place for products returned to Argos. We take these findings seriously and are reviewing the information provided to establish what further action is needed to ensure our requirements are met,” Argos said in a statement.

The investigation found dozens more British items bearing returns labels for sale, including many marked as faulty, being sold in secondhand shops in the area.

Shopkeepers said they had bought the items from brokers in the UK, who provided them as mixed shipments of home electrical equipment.

“The percentage of unusable products varies [by shipment] but sometimes it can be about 10%,” one vendor said. “What do I do with the broken ones? I put them in this box and the Agbogbloshie boys come to collect it.”

All major UK retailers who sell electrical goods operate a take-back scheme which requires them to accept and recycle disused items – for example, a shopper who brings in their old toaster when they buy a new one. The goods should be logged as e-waste and contribute to stores meeting their government-mandated recycling targets.

Under the waste electrical and electronic equipment (WEEE) regulations, the goods should be passed on to approved processors. They can only be exported if the shipper can prove they will be handled in high-quality facilities.

No facilities in west Africa are approved to receive British WEEE, according to the Environment Agency.

“Ghana is not a dumping ground for broken appliances or failed retail returns from the UK,” Joshua Awuku-Apaw, a Ghanaian environmental consultant, told Unearthed. “Shipping faulty, non-functional kitchen appliances abroad under the cover of ‘reuse’ or ‘second-hand trade’ shifts the financial, environmental, and health costs of overconsumption on to Ghanaian communities and workers … Ghana’s communities should not bear the health burden of UK retail waste.”

The investigation traced the route by which the products could have ended up in Ghana. When recently bought items are returned to shops for a refund, even when they are being returned because they are faulty, they can enter a separate stream, the liquidation market, along with other consumer returns, the investigation found.

“Just because somebody in the supermarket says it’s not working, doesn’t always mean they’ve technically declared it as waste,” said e-waste expert Mark Sayers.

Many of the items Greenpeace found in Agbogbloshie and second-hand stores had stickers labelling the goods as “untested return”.

The investigation alleged that returned goods are often sold off in bulk, at a fraction of their shop shelf-price. Sometimes this takes place via the retailers’ own stock liquidation channels where pallets of returns, including job lots of small household electricals, are sold.

The lots are bought by “jobbers” – individuals and small businesses who buy the goods by the palletload and set about extracting any value they can – whether by listing items individually on eBay or Vinted, selling them in bargain-bin stores or exporting them.

Jim Puckett, founder of Basel Action Network, which campaigns against the export of e-waste to poorer countries, said that treating untested returns as anything other than waste was a “major loophole”.

“It should be considered waste until proven otherwise,” he said. “Especially if people are buying it at auction or whatever and shipping it all around the world.”

An Environment Agency spokesperson said: “Illegal waste exports are a serious crime. There is no excuse for exporting waste to be dumped or landfilled overseas. Waste leaving England must be sent for legitimate recovery or recycling.

“New controls mean exports of waste electrical and electronic equipment must be notified and approved before they leave the country. The Environment Agency is using intelligence to intervene earlier, target suspicious shipments and disrupt the criminals behind illegal waste exports.”

“Anyone who breaks the law risks having shipments stopped, facing prosecution and financial penalties. Waste criminals should be in no doubt, we are watching, we are acting and you will face the consequences.”

Greenpeace UK’s chief scientist, Dr Doug Parr, said: “Customers will be appalled to learn that, instead of being repaired or recycled, these faulty returns ended up in a notorious megadump leaching toxic run-offs that poison entire communities. This isn’t the circular economy, but long-range fly-tipping, and it’s shameful.”

Asda referred approaches to the British Retail Consortium. The BRC said in a statement: “Retailers take their responsibility to tackle electrical waste seriously, so reports of faulty electronics being dumped in Ghana are deeply concerning.

“Used electronics should only be exported for legitimate reuse where they are safe and functional and must not place the burden of dealing with UK waste on communities overseas. We also need greater investment in the UK’s recycling infrastructure so more electrical waste can be safely reused and recycled here.”

Human flamethrower Aaron Rodgers lays bare the cultural rot at the once-great Steelers

The Guardian Thu, 26 Nov 2026 10:00:52 GMT

The quarterback’s spectacularly messy exit from Pittsburgh could herald an overdue collapse at one of the NFL’s most famous franchises

Nobody in the world, except maybe Pittsburgh Steelers owner Art Rooney II, is surprised that the franchise’s marriage of convenience with Aaron Rodgers ended in spectacular flames. Despite their own elevated idea of themselves, Pittsburgh have been one of the NFL’s messiest soap operas for a solid decade. When they linked up with the league’s messiest quarterback, it seemed certain we would get … even more mess. When they doubled down last offseason by hiring the coach with whom Rodgers had fallen out in Green Bay in the late 2010s, the mess became inevitable. We’d seen hints of the approaching drama in the season’s first 11 weeks.

“What the fuck … call it!” Rodgers yelled at McCarthy as he looked for a play in early October.

“Fucking asshole,” his head coach barked on the sideline.

But give this to the Steelers, and to Rodgers: no matter how trashy each party has been for however many years, the show they gave us on Wednesday was special – right up there with the Hindenburg’s final moments. The league’s most dramatic, selfish quarterback collided with the NFL franchise that has the most outdated and over-inflated view of itself, and the result was the greatest explosion in modern history between a team and their QB.

The story began to come to a head on Tuesday, when Rodgers and McCarthy had their latest relationship breakdown. That night, the Steelers said that Rodgers would be inactive for Friday’s game against the Broncos and that his backup, Mason Rudolph, would start. A 6-4 team don’t voluntarily start Mason Rudolph – a man whose NFL career could generously be described as mediocre – unless something has gone horribly awry, and indeed, the details of the Rodgers-McCarthy blowup ended up being absurd.

As the Steelers are messaging it through Pittsburgh media, Rodgers wanted full play-calling authority or to be released, and the team chose the latter. (That’s the report from the Pittsburgh Post-Gazette’s Gerry Dulac, a longtime team insider, citing anonymous sources.) As Rodgers told it in a genuinely surreal television interview with his friend Pat McAfee, the standoff came after the QB confronted his once-and-present head coach over some pretty wild accusations. Rodgers accused McCarthy of falling asleep in team meetings, not watching film until at least two days after a Sunday game, failing to form relationships with defensive players (McCarthy’s background is on offense), and breaking a huddle by saying “1-2-3 Packers!” during a loss to the Eagles last weekend.

Rodgers, who isn’t known for his humility, has strange tendencies on his best days, and if you don’t find him a reliable narrator, you’re well within your rights. But McCarthy admitted to the “Packers” mishap during his own news conference on Wednesday, and various Steelers players had the chance to support their coach during media availabilities after practice and decided not to. “It’s all true,” one source told ESPN’s Brooke Pryor, whose story on Wednesday appeared to corroborate many of Rodgers’s claims about McCarthy.

During his call with McAfee, Rodgers made clear he didn’t expect players or coaches still with the Steelers to back up his version of events. Rodgers put Pat Freiermuth in a difficult spot by telling McAfee that it had been the tight end, not a Steelers higher-up, who informed him he’d been benched. “I can’t believe they’re doing this” was how Rodgers relayed Freiermuth’s words to him.

“I was just checking on a close friend,” the tight end said Wednesday. Good lord.

The Steelers releasing Rodgers may well have ended his career – he turns 43 next week, and had said this summer he plans to retire at the end of this season. The team move forward with Rudolph, who takes over a squad in contention to once again lose in the first round of the playoffs.

One of the day’s cattiest pieces of gossip was Rodgers telling McAfee that McCarthy had told a Steelers staffer he blamed the quarterback for his firing by the Packers in 2018, eight years after he and Rodgers won a Super Bowl together. We may never know for sure what’s in McCarthy’s head right now, but it was already well known that his relationship with Rodgers had deteriorated in the years after the Super Bowl win (against the Steelers, as it happens) in the 2010 season. The Steelers thought wrapping the two of them in their terrific organizational culture would smooth things over, I guess?

If only any of the 8 billion people on earth who knew this was a bad idea had told the Steelers’ leadership. But passing on Rodgers would have required the Steelers to take a risk on acquiring a younger quarterback. Instead, they rolled with the oldest one in the league, who had been in decline ever since he won back-to-back MVPs in 2020 and 2021. As an old man in a young man’s game, Rodgers was mostly immobile and borderline inept this season. A terrible receiving corps didn’t help, but a good running game covered up some of the deficiencies that come with age.

Wednesday was one of the most embarrassing days in the history of a once-great franchise that I grew up rooting on from the stands at Heinz Field. Could it be a turning point? The Steelers have needed one for a while. Longtime coach Mike Tomlin’s departure after last season could have been that turning point, but the Steelers ensured it wouldn’t be when they hired McCarthy. The now 63-year-old was out of the league after he left the Cowboys in 2025, and his main qualification for the Steelers job appeared to be that he was from Pittsburgh’s Greenfield neighborhood. This made for an emotional introductory press conference and a coaching tenure that is going downhill, fast.

The Steelers built their reputation for greatness in the 1970s, when they won four Super Bowls under founding owner Art Rooney. The family business had some down times in the 1980s but continued to be great under Rooney’s son, Dan, under whose leadership the club won two more championships in the 2005 and 2008 seasons. The Steelers’ devolution into their current status – a solid but unspectacular team that produces headlines worthy of TMZ – came after Dan’s son, Art Rooney II, assumed control of the franchise in 2017.

For a club once lauded for its stability – the Steelers had just three head coaches between 1969 and 2025 – it is obvious they are in the midst of cultural rot. They have ranked in the bottom 10 in the league most years since 2022 in the NFL Players Association’s “report cards”, which measure what players think of their teams. This year, they reached new depths by finishing dead last.

The franchise has seen a great deal of tabloid-style drama in the past 10 years, most of that under Tomlin, who kept putting a decent (but rarely good) product on the field despite the locker room chaos. (You may remember highlights such as Antonio Brown’s beef with Ben Roethlisberger, the scandal over JuJu Smith-Schuster being too online, or the time Steelers players raided Le’Veon Bell’s locker during his contract standoff with the team.) That is but a small sample of recent Steelers drama, and all of it falls well short of this week’s fiasco. Kudos to Pittsburgh on finding new frontiers in team culture every year.

Is this catastrophe public enough, or embarrassing enough, to prompt change? Ideally, Art Rooney II would sell the team to someone who has proven themselves more capable of running a large organization and isn’t just coasting off a family inheritance. But failing that, the Steelers cannot in good conscience bring back McCarthy for a second year, and they probably ought to look seriously into firing general manager Omar Khan as well. The team haven’t had a losing season since 2003, and their 6-4 start means they may not have one this year, either. But with an expensive, aging defense and an offense that just got beheaded, a long-overdue collapse and rebuild seems more plausible.
