We may all be eating too much protein. But that won’t stop the influencers and big business

The Guardian Thu, 26 Nov 2026 08:00:50 GMT

Protein is the food industry’s current nutritional good guy. The fact that it’s often added to ultra-processed food makes it anything but

When I was growing up in the US in the 1980s and 90s, fat in foods was demonised. Low-fat yoghurt, low-fat desserts and low-fat margarine were all the rage, with the message that fat was bad for our hearts and arteries. By the early 2000s, concern had moved to added sugar and its apparent links to obesity and type 2 diabetes, driving food reformulations.

Sugar was replaced with artificial sweeteners such as aspartame and acesulfame K, which have their own health impacts. Aspartame is classified by the World Health Organization as possibly carcinogenic in humans, while observational research such as a 2022 study of about 102,000 adults has linked acesulfame K with increased cancer risk. Then carbohydrates came into the spotlight, with pasta, rice and bread becoming the bad guys for our diet and blamed for weight gain. There is a fashion cycle in nutrition, where each food group or ingredient takes its turn being blamed for our poor health.

In recent years, protein has emerged as a nutritional good guy, with social media influencers blaming its deficiency for your fatigue or the fact that you don’t have the body you want. Go into a supermarket and you can find protein yoghurts, protein cereals, protein breads, protein drinks and even protein chocolate bars.

When I spoke about my last book on good health to the Edinburgh international book festival, the first question was how many grams of protein I recommended eating each day, and which supplements and powders to take. The same question was asked of Chris van Tulleken, a physician and leading UK expert on nutrition, when he spoke at the Hay festival.

Yes, protein is essential for our bodies to repair and build muscle, produce enzymes and hormones, and maintain normal bodily functions. Severe protein deficiency can cause conditions such as kwashiorkor, a severe form of malnutrition found in parts of Africa, where some children live with conflict, drought and extreme food scarcity. But those are extreme cases of food deprivation.

In the UK, the recommended daily intake is 0.75g of protein per kg of body weight. So if you weigh 75kg, that’s 56g of protein per day. Requirements differ based on age, pregnancy and how much physical activity – especially strength training and performance sport – someone does.

The evidence suggests that the rest of us are already eating enough protein. Indeed, the British Nutrition Foundation found that average protein consumption in the UK already exceeds these recommendations. They report an average daily intake of 85g for men (above the recommended intake of 56g) and 67g for women (above the recommended intake of 45g). Protein is part of the foods we eat every day: not just in chicken or burgers, but in wholemeal bread, rice, eggs, milk, beans, yoghurt, porridge, pasta and lentils.

Yet the “protein industry” has created the widespread impression that we should all be eating more, and has created a whole line of foods and marketing with “protein added”. Many of these products are ultra-processed (which we know isn’t good for our health) with very high levels of sugar and salt, plus all the additives and preservatives to keep them from going off for years. Simply adding protein doesn’t improve the overall nutritional quality of a food product.

In August 2026, a review of more than 350 studies looked at the relationship between protein intake, metabolism and ageing. The researchers found that for some people who don’t do much exercise, consuming less protein may be better for their metabolic health and longevity. As Prof Dudley Lamming said: “Because most people are relatively sedentary, many people are likely consuming more protein than they actually need, which probably has negative health consequences.”

The researchers suggest several biological mechanisms to explain this, including one focused on the hormone FGF21, which increases in the body when protein intake falls. Experiments in mice have linked increased FGF21 activity with longer lifespans, given that this hormone contributes to regulating energy expenditure, glucose metabolism and metabolic health. As a caveat, much of the evidence linking longevity with eating less protein in the paper comes from testing in animal models such as mice, rats and fruit flies. Nonetheless, the study challenges the idea that more protein is always better for healthy ageing, especially for those who aren’t very active.

Sign up to Matters of Opinion

Guardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and more

after newsletter promotion

What does this mean for all of us, trying to wade through the ever-changing dietary advice on social media and the multitude of products in the supermarket? For me, it’s another reason to avoid treating nutrition like fashion, with trends coming and going. Demonising or idolising individual nutrients and foods doesn’t help. Pasta isn’t the enemy. Protein powder isn’t the hero.

We should be eating a diverse and balanced diet, including a range of food groups such as vegetables, fruits, wholegrains, healthy fats, and plant and fish/meat-based protein sources. My only real rule is about reducing the amount of ultra-processed foods in our diets. This is largely to do with the ways these products are formulated and manufactured (just read the ingredient list and see if you could make it in your kitchen), and the emerging evidence on the harm they can do to our health.

And remember that at its heart, protein has become commercially attractive. Adding it to an existing product increases profit margins and gives consumers the impression that a solution has been found to a problem (I would argue) that never existed. It’s a clever marketing strategy, but not necessarily a nutritional improvement.

Prof Devi Sridhar is chair of global public health at the University of Edinburgh

I am staunchly pro-choice – but abortion statistics in the latest sexual attitudes survey shocked even me

The Guardian Thu, 26 Nov 2026 06:00:47 GMT

Deprivation is behind the sharp rise highlighted in the Natsal study, and that’s an outrage. High energy bills should never be a factor in reproductive choice

The National Survey of Sexual Attitudes and Lifestyles (Natsal) is the crowdpleaser of the data world. Nerds love it because of its extraordinary thoroughness. It’s one of the largest studies of sexual behaviour in the world, surveying nearly 7,000 people in the UK between the ages of 16 and 59, once a decade. Everyone else loves it because they get to talk about sex. Some of the statistics speak for themselves – among 25- to 34-year-old women, the number who say they never want children has gone up fourfold, a sad, completely understandable reflection of the outside world.

Other figures, though, are mysterious: the number of women aged 16 to 24 who are on the pill has dropped precipitously, from nearly half to less than a third. Over the same period, the online space has been flooded with information about hormonal contraception, some of it better than it has ever been – more accessible, more accurate – and some of it plain wrong. Is there strategic, funded disinformation coming from Christian fundamentalists, such as we have already seen in the abortion space, where anti-abortion activists hose money at putatively “grassroots” online influencers? Or is it a quirk of the algorithms that once you go down the rabbit hole of “has the pill made me depressed?”, you will be shown endless influencers who have experienced that very (improbable) thing? It’s hard for a young person to navigate what’s real, and it’s hard to distinguish superstition from preference.

What we can say for certain, though, is that everyone is having less sex. Natsal started in 1990, but the face-to-face fieldwork was interrupted by Covid. Instead, researchers released interim statistics, which described a sex drought from a number of different angles – fewer new encounters reported, more celibacy, particularly among the young, less sex within relationships. It felt at the time like the least bad side-effect of a global pandemic, but that picture has persisted. Under-45s typically have sex twice a month; in 1990 the average was four times. And one in three under-25s have never had sex at all.

Researchers, commentators, radio phone-in participants – everyone tends to find the thing they like least about modern life and project it on to this panda-like cohort. In the past 20 minutes (I’m not exaggerating), I’ve heard that it’s all down to the prevalence of porn; and that it’s all because of the vexed relationship between young men and young women, who are too anxious about consent and miles apart in their gender politics. A guy on LBC just said that it was because the stigma had been lifted on asexuality, and young people were simply expressing their desire not to have sex by not having it. Others cite a Covid hangover, a generation that didn’t learn how to socialise and so finds it more comfortable to conduct their intimacy from behind a screen.

Any of those things could be true, or none of them could. Even if respondents were called on to explain their sexual behaviour – and the survey tends not to ask questions that amount to “why are you weird?” – a lack of sexual encounters is not a thing you could readily explain. Did you not go out enough, or get drunk enough, or drop your inhibitions enough, or did others fail to disinhibit around you? Is that because none of you want it any more, or because the have-a-go jeopardy feels greater?

I could wade in here and talk about economic precariousness and the impact that may have on Jungian libido and animal magnetism, but I’d simply be trying to mould the low-sex phenomenon into my own talking point.

Very solid correlations do exist, however, when we look at the reproduction and contraception data from the same study. The proportion of women aged 16–54 who have had an abortion in their lifetime rose from 16% to 21% over the past decade, an increase mainly seen among those over 35 (the persistent idea of teenagers driving unwanted pregnancy rates has been wrong for years). What is really stark is that the rise is heavily determined by deprivation – MSI Reproductive Choices (formerly Marie Stopes) went so far as to state that the rise is accounted for entirely by women without a university degree (rising from 16% to 25%), and/or living in the most deprived areas (rising from 14% to 26%).

MSI’s deputy medical director, Dr Sarah Salkeld, underlined to me that, while Natsal wouldn’t ask why, MSI legally has to ask women why they want an abortion, so these statistics come as no surprise to them at all. It’s not only that larger families have become an impossibility with the cost of living crisis. Everything has become more difficult; if you struggle to find a GP appointment, still less a walk-in service, and your work isn’t flexible and your caring responsibilities won’t wait, the unwanted pregnancy itself is an economic effect.

I have been pro-choice all my life, never more so than after I had my (much loved) children, and realised the truth of how they shred your self-determination. So I’m staggered to find myself sayingthat these abortion numbers, rising in a very specific demographic, are not OK. This is not reproductive choice: it’s a eugenics programme quietly imposed by energy bills and childcare costs.

The bleph lady: Britain’s backstreet cosmetic surgeon

The Guardian Thu, 26 Nov 2026 05:00:46 GMT

Luyen Vu’s discount eye surgeries represent the dangers of an unregulated beauty industry. But for her fans, she is a folk hero

Robert Laycock, a facial plastic surgeon at Aintree University Hospital in Liverpool, first knew that something was up when a patient came to him in early 2024. She was a woman in her 40s who had undergone a blepharoplasty, a procedure that involves making an incision just below or above the eyelids and removing small amounts of skin and sometimes fat and muscle. The point of the surgery is to make the patient’s face look more youthful. This woman’s stitches, however, had started coming apart, leaving an open wound right above her eyes.

It is not unusual for botched private cosmetic surgeries to be fixed on the NHS. Laycock estimates that he sees three or four patients a year who need surgical intervention after too much tissue has been removed in a blepharoplasty. But something was different about this woman. “The surgery was done in a very odd way,” Laycock told me. The incision, he explained, had been made just beneath the eyebrow rather than on the crease of the eyelid. “[It’s] not the way that we would generally do a blepharoplasty in the UK.” He asked the woman where she’d had the work done but she was evasive and he dropped the subject.

A year later, Laycock was ordering a coffee in the hospital atrium when he noticed that the woman serving him had exactly the same scarring just beneath her eyebrows. He asked her about it. (He was familiar with the staff, who often came to him with questions about cosmetic procedures.) The woman said that someone called Luyen Vu had performed the surgery in a house just outside Liverpool. On her phone, she showed Laycock the Facebook page advertising the procedure.

Vu offered facelifts, necklifts, chin implants and labiaplasty. However, her most popular treatment – judging by the women who were very happy to share their results on social media – was blepharoplasty. It was easy to see the appeal. An upper blepharoplasty in the UK usually costs between £2,000 and £8,000, depending on the hospital and how experienced the surgeon is. Vu’s fee was £850.

After his encounter, Laycock contacted the General Medical Council (GMC), the independent body that regulates doctors, to ask what they could do to find out more about Vu and potentially stop her from working. The answer seemed to be very little: Vu was not registered with them and as such they had no remit to investigate her. The GMC told him to contact the police but the Merseyside police, he told me, said it was an issue for the GMC.

The confusion might have arisen from a loophole in the law: in the UK, it is technically legal for anyone to carry out surgery. What is against the law is pretending to be a registered surgeon when you are not. The law is also clear that any healthcare provider must be registered with the Care Quality Commission. Laycock spoke to the CQC but he reached a dead end there too: Vu was not identified as a healthcare professional so they had no remit to take further action.

It wasn’t just Laycock who discovered Vu’s work in 2025 – so did dozens of women across Liverpool. Initially, they had found her through word of mouth or her Facebook page. By April 2025, she had become sufficiently well known to attract the attention of Nip Tuck, a beauty and lifestyle podcast. In one episode, the two hosts sound the alarm about a woman in Liverpool whom they believed was charging too little for her work and was possibly operating in an unsound environment. (They also claimed that Vu was “sedating” her clients, which isn’t the case.) A clip of their outraged reaction was posted on TikTok; in response, women started uploading their own videos, partly in defence of Vu, whom they saw as unfairly maligned.

One woman, who looked to be in her 30s, shared a slideshow of images of her eye after having an upper blepharoplasty with Vu. If you compare the before and after photographs, her face looks younger and refreshed. It appeared as if Vu had done a pretty good job. The comment sections of these videos were filled with people asking for Vu’s details, affectionately referring to her as the “bleph lady”. “Girl the details we need the details,” posted one TikTok user.

Soon Vu was attracting the attention of the mainstream media. In July 2025, a reporter from Channel 5 News wore a hidden camera and posed as a client, meeting Vu and her assistant in a flat above a Thai restaurant in central Liverpool. The undercover reporter attempted to get Vu to admit whether she was or wasn’t a surgeon, but Vu dodged the question. In the same news package, another reporter followed Vu down the street, asking whether she was “putting some of [her] clients at risk”. Vu did not respond, and tried to hide her face from the camera. She subsequently moved her services out of the city; from October 2025 to August 2026, she popped up in Manchester, London, Dublin, and even Germany.

To her fans, Vu is a folk hero, a kind of Robin Hood for cosmetic procedures: not so much taking from the rich and giving to the poor, but offering to the poor what had until now only been accessible to the rich. To her detractors, Vu’s success is evidence that women are willing to risk serious injury to pursue ever more unrealistic beauty standards. To them, she represents everything that is wrong with a cosmetics market in the UK that has shifted in recent years from offering women superficial “beauty” treatments to pushing invasive, quasi-medical “aesthetic” procedures. It is a new grey area that is under-regulated, dangerous – and, in some cases, lethal.

In October 2025, a few months after the Channel 5 story, a woman based in Bury, Greater Manchester, began advertising Vu’s work on Facebook. “The transformation speaks for itself,” Cheryl Hogan wrote on the page of her salon, Fleek Aesthetics. “Brighter, smoother, and more youthful eyes with precision artistry that only she can deliver. Limited spaces available – don’t miss your chance to book with her while she’s back in Manchester!”

One person who visited Vu at Fleek Aesthetics was Laura (not her real name), a support worker for people with longterm disabilities. Laura is in her late 20s and wanted the loose skin above and below her eyes removed. “I lost weight and developed eye bags,” she told me on the phone. “No one else probably would have noticed my eye bags, but I did. So every time someone looked at me, I thought they were looking at [them].” A friend of hers who’s a paramedic had seen Vu for surgery herself and suggested Laura book in a lower blepharoplasty. Laura was persuaded by the personal recommendation and the £850 price tag. In late December 2025, she was sent the address of Fleek Aesthetics on WhatsApp. She was told to walk around the back of the building, where, she claims, Hogan let her in. Laura paid in cash and was asked to hand over her phone before heading upstairs.

There she met Vu, a neat-looking, middle-aged east Asian woman with a sharp bob haircut. She was wearing blue surgeon’s scrubs. Vu said hello in English, but then stepped back and let her assistant, a younger east Asian woman, translate. The room looked clean and orderly, which put Laura at ease. She sat down at a table and was injected in the arm with a test dose of the anaesthetic lidocaine; this was to check for any allergic reactions before a larger dose would be used during the surgery. Vu checked Laura’s blood pressure and began the consultation via her assistant.

Laura wanted a lower blepharoplasty but wondered if she should also have an upper one. Vu told her that she would be best sticking with just the lower, a response that made Laura feel comfortable. If Vu were a scammer, she reasoned, she would be pushing for her to have more procedures. Vu’s assistant pulled Laura’s hair back into a bun, tied a surgical gown around her neck and sat her on a reclining beautician’s chair. Vu indicated that all her tools were sterile by showing them to Laura in their vacuum-sealed packages. Then the local anaesthetic was injected into her lower eyelids and Laura waited for the operation to begin.

To understand what a lower blepharoplasty involves, put a finger on your lower eyelid. Sometimes this area has “bags”, puffy looking skin that droops downwards. Beneath the surface layer of skin, there are three layers of muscle, one layer of membrane and then three pads of fat. When people are young this area is smooth and plump, but over time, the top layer of skin becomes looser, the muscles weaken, and the layer of membrane becomes thinner allowing the fat to bulge outwards and downwards.

Now imagine a surgeon holding a scalpel just beneath your lower eyelashes. She makes a cut through the top of the skin, another cut through the dark pink muscle and then she reaches the thin white layer of membrane. The membrane is cut in three places; this makes the little yellow cushions of fat visible, which are repositioned or removed. The goal is to create an even amount of volume across the lower lid. The surgeon sews back together all the cuts in the membrane and muscle. Any excess skin is removed and the original incision is sewn back together. Finally, the surgeon stitches the lower outer corner of the eye to support the lid’s muscles as they heal. It’s a complex procedure and can take anywhere between 30 minutes and two hours. The surgeons that I spoke with speculated that Vu carried out a simpler version of this procedure in which only excess skin was removed, with no muscle or membrane cut, and no fat pads removed or repositioned.

During her procedure, Laura could hear Vu cutting the skin beneath her eye with scissors (different cutting tools can be used for the procedure). “I was like, what am I doing?” she recalled. “You’re trusting that she’s a qualified surgeon in her country, but you don’t know that … You’re just trusting this random person with a scalpel just to rip open your eyes.” Many of Vu’s supporters online asserted that she had received medical training abroad, but this has not been verified by her or anyone acting on her behalf. In fact, Vu and Hogan had been very careful never to clarify the fact. (I reached out to Hogan through the Fleek Aesthetics business email to ask for an interview over the summer. I then contacted her for comment via a personal email and Instagram. I also tried to reach Vu through Hogan. I didn’t receive a response from either.)

When the operation was complete and Laura was handed a mirror, she felt absolutely petrified. The way Vu had cut and sewn the skin back together meant that her lower lids were pulled downwards, revealing the reddish inside of her lower eyelids. She asked Vu if this was normal, but the assistant told her not to worry. Her lower eyelids, she said, would revert to their normal position as she healed.

Laura was given some tablets and creams in Vietnamese packaging and was shown out of the salon. At home she looked up the medication using Google Translate. There were antibiotics for five days; suppositories for the pain for two days; antibiotic ointment to use after day seven and steroid tablets to take for seven days. (It is against the law to dispense prescription medication if you are not a registered healthcare professional.)

In the first few days some bruises developed but Laura continued to go about her routine. She told her friends and family about the surgery. By day five she was back working. On day nine she took her own stitches out, something surgeons usually prefer to do once they’re happy the wound is fully healed. After that, no one would have noticed that she’d had an operation at all. Looking at the photos she sent me, the bottom of her eyes looked less puffy and overall more well rested. Laura is young so, to my eyes, the difference was minimal; but it gave her a huge confidence boost.

Like Laura, many of the women having blepharoplasties in Britain are young. You might say that these are not people who “need” surgery to address signs of ageing. And yet the desire to go under the knife is intense. As one TikTok user posted: “Does anyone on here have the Liverpool bleph ladies contact details, because I’m 29 tomorrow and we need this fixing immediately, cut and snip me immediately.”

The modern story of cosmetic surgery is sometimes said to have begun during the first world war, when new techniques were honed to deal with soldiers’ facial injuries. Another landmark in the field was the invention of breast implants in 1961 by two surgeons in Houston, Texas. But to understand why women are willing to take such risks today with backstreet blepharoplasties, it would suffice to begin the story in 2010. This was the year when Apple introduced a front-facing camera on the iPhone 4, allowing people to take closeup selfies while seeing themselves on a screen. It was also the year that Instagram launched, allowing users to share those images with friends and strangers. By 2026, a majority of British people who use the app say that it has made them feel insecure about their appearance.

If Instagram created a problem for its users, it also gave a huge platform to someone who embodied the supposed solution: Kylie Jenner. Kim Kardashian’s little sister first appeared on British TV screens in 2007 in Keeping Up With the Kardashians. She was a normal-looking teenager; since then she has transformed into a woman whom Vogue described in 2024 as “strikingly beautiful in a way I’m not sure cameras – or comment sections – do justice”. From around 2016, a meme started to do the rounds summing up how drastically Jenner’s appearance changed over the years. It’s a before and after photo of her face with the caption, “You’re not ugly, you’re just poor.”

In 2015, amid much speculation about what procedures Jenner had undergone, she reluctantly admitted in an episode of Keeping Up With the Kardashians to dermal filler injections in her lips, saying they were something she had always been insecure about. Filler is hyaluronic acid, a gel-like substance, which is injected into the face to give it a plumper and more sculpted look. Immediately after the episode aired, one cosmetic clinic in the US reported a 70% increase in filler inquiries; in the UK, clinics also reported a rise in filler bookings.

A new type of “look” began to emerge in western online spaces and, in 2019, it got a name: Instagram Face. “It’s a young face, of course, with poreless skin and plump, high cheekbones,” wrote Jia Tolentino in the New Yorker. “It has catlike eyes and long, cartoonish lashes; it has a small, neat nose and full, lush lips.” Instagram Face was a product of what British sociologist Rebecca Nash described in an academic paper in the same year as a “dynamic, global beauty landscape”, a place in which a globalised beauty standard could be established and widely disseminated.

But as many British women started getting dermal fillers in pursuit of Instagram Face, they ended up with what was quickly derided as “Love Island Face”. In its most extreme form, the look was less finely sculpted Kardashian and more blow-up doll – a caricature of what a conventionally attractive face might look like. “Duck lips” – lips that had been overfilled – became so recognisable that Saturday Night Live did a sketch in which Phoebe Waller-Bridge pretends to be a Love Island contestant. “Just got me lips done,” she says. “I asked the doctor for an allergic reaction look.”

But Love Island Face wasn’t supposed to be natural. The obvious artificiality was part of its appeal – a way to demonstrate how much time, effort and money had been spent on one’s appearance. As Ruth Holliday, a professor of gender and culture at Loughborough University, told me: “It’s a perfectly logical thing to want to invest in your body in order to earn more money in the labour market when you work in a service job, or maybe even to get a better relationship.” In my conversations with women who had gone for surgical and non-surgical procedures, a wide range of motivations were discussed, but one recurring theme was self-worth. As one woman in her early 20s from Merseyside put it: “I don’t do it for anyone else, I don’t do it to impress a boy, I don’t do it to impress other girls, I do it purely for myself. I think as well you’ve got one life, invest in yourself.”

With demand came supply. In the UK, businesses providing dermal fillers were making “high profits in an era when all other commercial income is stalling,” according to a 2013 Department of Health report into the subject. To walk up and down any British high street is to see the evidence of this. Alongside vape shops and barbers, you’ll likely find a salon offering fillers – alongside Botox injections, micro-needling, CO2 laser skin resurfacing, and chemical peels. These painful-sounding cosmetic procedures are now referred to as “medical aesthetics”; beauticians have transformed into “aestheticians”.

In the US, Australia and Canada, dermal fillers have to be injected by doctors, nurses or dentists – but in the UK filler syringes can be administered by anyone. The British aesthetics industry is a “wild west”, said a recent Chartered Trading Standards Institute report. One woman told me that she preferred filler administered by unqualified high-street aestheticians. “I liked how they did the work, they did it more doll-like,” she said, referring to a style called the Russian Lip, which adds volume vertically and emphasises the cupid’s bow. The registered nurses, she said, made lips look too natural.

It wouldn’t be long before fillers fell out of fashion, not least because people noticed they started migrating across the face and absorbing water, leading to “pillow face”: a wide and less-defined face with a puffy appearance. A 2025 survey of UK clinics by the industry accreditation body Save Face reported 70% fewer patients asking for dermal filler compared with 2024. In 2021, the influencer Molly-Mae spoke on a podcast about her decision to undo her filler work; this involves injecting the substance hyaluronidase into the face, dissolving the acid. Afterwards, her inbox filled with girls telling her they had followed her cue.

In the early 2020s the emphasis shifted from adding volume to the face to “rejuvenating” it. Sought-after treatments started to include polynucleotides – most commonly an injection of salmon DNA that tells your cells to jump start the production of collagen and elastin in the skin. “Stacking” has also become popular: after some microneedling, in which small pricks are made to the face to stimulate the release of collagen and elastin (proteins that give strength and elasticity to the skin), “active” substances such as retinol (which also boost collagen) are applied for deeper penetration into the skin.

High-street treatments have their limits. They can make your skin seem fresh and smooth but they can’t radically change how you look. Only surgery can do this. Once again, it was a member of the Jenner family – in this case Kylie’s mother, Kris – who became a model for the best surgical intervention money could buy. In 2025, the 71-year-old Jenner appeared in Paris for Lauren Bezos’ hen do; she was sporting what New York Magazine would describe as the “Forever-35 Face”. She looked smoother, tighter and plumper – young, but in an uncanny way. A week later a representative for Jenner confirmed she had undergone a facelift. There was much speculation about what technique was used – the conventional method or the increasingly popular, more risky deep plane facelift, in which surgeons work on the deepest layer, right above the bone, to reposition the entire face.

after newsletter promotion

A deep plane facelift can fetch price tags of £30,000 or more depending on the skill, or fame, of the surgeon. This is where the blepharoplasty comes in. The procedure is, in many ways, a budget facelift: one retired plastic surgeon told me that surgery is seen as the “best value cosmetic procedure you can do” in terms of reducing the signs of ageing for the smallest price tag. Most cosmetic surgery is expensive because it involves a surgeon, anaesthetist and an overnight stay in a hospital. A licensed blepharoplasty starts off at about £2,000 because it can mostly be done under local anaesthetic and doesn’t require an overnight stay. Recovery times are quick and the healing can be discreet – all you need is a large pair of sunglasses.

In 2022, blepharoplasties overtook nose jobs as the most popular facial plastic surgery procedure in the US; in the UK, it’s occupied the top slot since 2019 when the British Association of Aesthetic Plastic Surgeons began its yearly audits. Until recently, customers were mostly in their 40s and above. However, Colin Vize, an oculoplastic surgeon based in Hull, confirmed to me that many patients are now younger. “In the younger age group,” he said, “it appears to be a social-media-driven thing.” In the US, people under 35 represent the fastest-growing group getting the procedure done.

Some British women opt to travel overseas. In the Netherlands, the clinic Faceland offers upper blepharoplasties for just £585. It’s able to offer these low prices due to the volume of patients it sees, but a BBC report from this year detailed some patients seeing their stitches come apart or becoming unable to close their eyes. (Faceland told the BBC it offers “safe and quality” treatments and that “less than 1%” of procedures have led to a complaint.) Speaking generally, Vize told me that the main issue with some overseas appointments is too much skin being taken away: “[Patients are] trying to close their eyes and they’re struggling.”

It was in this context that Vu emerged. If people wanted cheaper cosmetic surgery options and were willing to travel abroad, why couldn’t someone from abroad offer surgery in the UK? Vu’s online defenders see her as exactly the type of skilled migrant the British government claims to want. After all, she saw a gap in the market and filled it. “She is amazing and so is her work don’t get y people r putting her down,” said one woman in her 50s from Liverpool, replying to my request for an interview.

What I have gleaned about Hogan and her relationship to Vu comes from her prolific social media posts. Hogan is an attractive middle-aged woman with brown eyes, full lips and hair pulled into a ponytail. She seems to be an astute businesswoman who knows how to use social media to promote her services and doesn’t shy from using her platforms to talk about her faith in God or her political beliefs.

She’s a member of the British Traveller community and, in October 2025, posted that she’d seen a woman from the community receiving abuse online about her appearance, following botched lip fillers. Hogan wrote on a crowdfunder: “No woman should be made to feel unworthy because of her looks.” At the time, Hogan reached out to Vu to see if she would give the woman an upper and lower blepharoplasty surgery for free as part of a makeover – and she did. This appears to be where the women’s friendship and business partnership began.

Later that month, Hogan began advertising Vu’s services on social media and hosting her at her salon, a premises that is not registered with the CQC. She also defended Vu from the negative stories that had appeared about her in the press. Posting on Facebook, she said: “Let’s get one thing straight – titles mean NOTHING if the skill, knowledge, and passion aren’t there. The Liverpool lady is a perfectionist whose results speak for themselves. Her clients trust her for a reason – and this right here proves that it’s not about the title, it’s about the talent.”

Not everyone is such a fan. This year, a woman set up a Reddit page called r/Support4LuyenVuVictim. She had visited Fleek Aesthetics for an upper blepharoplasty. When she was handed a mirror at the end of the surgery, she said she felt her soul leave her body. “I knew I had a lifetime of repair and misery,” she told me. “I’d actually been so deformed.” She felt that her eyebrows looked like they were in the wrong place, pulled too low. As she processed what had been done in the days after the surgery, she messaged asking for aftercare. She said: “You basically receive a ‘who dis?’ back … and that’s if you’re lucky. You will be ghosted too.” She is now on a waiting list to see an NHS consultant for corrective surgery.

One reason that people have differing opinions of the quality of Vu’s work is because she appears to use a technique more suited for east Asian than Caucasian eyes – this was the “odd” method that the doctor in Liverpool noticed. Instead of making the cut in the crease of the eye, she often appears to make it just below the brow. This approach is not suitable for all patients – especially older ones. Eyebrow muscles weaken and descend as we age. If tension is directly introduced to this area by removing excess skin, the brow muscles can descend even further. To avoid this, a UK registered surgeon would usually lift the brow muscles with a stitch and then cut excess skin away from the crease of the eyelid further away from the brow. It would appear that Vu was using a one-size-fits-all approach to an area of the face that varies from person to person.

To enter the world of extreme aestheticians is to encounter individuals for whom beauty has become an overwhelming obsession. Take Jordan James Parke, the self-titled “Lip King” who briefly hosted Vu’s work from his home. In 2016, Parke appeared on the daytime chatshow This Morning above the words: “My obsession with Kim Kardashian could kill me”. He had an androgynous look: his glossy lips, defined eyebrows and tiny nose looked feminine, but his shaved head was distinctly masculine. On the sofa, he listed all the work he’d had done: two nose jobs, a chin implant, neck liposuction, eyebrow tattoos, lip filler, cheek filler, smile line filler, jawline filler, a non-surgical thread facelift and botox.

He also appeared on a US reality TV show called Botched, in which patients hoping to have previous surgery corrected visit two doctors in Los Angeles. Unlike the usual patients, Parke liked his exaggerated appearance. He explained: “Looking fake, you walk into a room and people want to know you, and you’re just up. I love attention.” However, he wasn’t happy that his huge lips had started leaking filler. The doctors advised him to have the filler dissolved in case his lips fell off.

Parke took it easy on the lip filler for a while, but then he started to administer filler injections himself. In September 2024, Alice Webb, a 33-year-old aesthetician, arranged to have a liquid BBL (Brazilian butt lift) from Parke – a procedure that involves injecting filler into the buttocks to add volume. Webb passed out and was taken to hospital, where she died the following day. An inquest found that Parke had used seven times the recommended amount of filler; traces of it were discovered in Webb’s heart, lungs, brain and kidneys. Parke was arrested on suspicion of manslaughter in October 2024 and, as part of his bail conditions, he was banned from carrying out any cosmetic treatments. But there wasn’t anything preventing him from setting up appointments for other people.

We don’t know how Parke first connected with Luyen Vu, but in December 2025 he was taking deposits for bookings for Vu and letting her use his living room in Manchester as an operating theatre. Another Channel 5 journalist went undercover and attended an appointment. In the footage, you can see a woman lying flat on what looks like a massage table as Vu works over her. Keeping Up With the Kardashians plays in the background.

The headline on This Morning would turn out to be prophetic: this year, Parke died while undergoing a cosmetic treatment in a London hotel room. The police have arrested two people in connection with his death but no one has been charged yet.

There were other aestheticians willing to host Vu, too. There was the Clinic Club, whose owner was banned from carrying out liquid BBLs until 2028 because of the risk of serious harm from the procedure, including sepsis. And there was Luxury Medical Aesthetics, a company that was reportedly hosting Vu in December 2025. Its owners had previously been exposed in 2024 for offering non-surgical “fat reduction” training courses, when in fact they were training people in surgical liposuction. Luxury Medical Aesthetics did not respond to ITV News at the time of the report. I also reached out to one of the owners via her new business but she did not respond.

The government is proposing to close the loopholes that have until now allowed people like Vu to operate in the UK. In the future, the Department of Health and Social Care told me, “only GMC-registered doctors working for CQC-registered providers would be able to offer and provide cosmetic surgery and the CQC will be given enforcement powers in cases where this legal restriction is breached”. The department also pointed out that, although it is technically legal to perform surgery if you are not a surgeon, other legislation and offences could apply to people who do, such as breaches of the Health and Safety at Work Act or even assault.

In the meantime, over the summer of 2026, Fleek Aesthetics was publicising blepharoplasty, facelifts and other procedures with someone called the Real McCoy, in Dublin and Manchester. There was no mention of Vu in the seemingly AI-generated Instagram posts. However, when one woman from Liverpool asked over WhatsApp if it was the Liverpool bleph lady doing the work, the answer was a simple “yes”.

In August, Luyen Vu made an appearance in full on the Instagram account of Fleek Aesthetics. Hogan had flown to Vietnam; she was planning to have Vu give her a second brow lift. It looked like a girls’ holiday. In one of her stories, she posted a video of Vu taking her to a nail salon and then at a restaurant. Hogan wrote under one story: “Love this woman.” Towards the end of her time in Vietnam, Hogan posted a message to her salon’s Instagram followers: “If anyone is interested in coming in November, comment ‘info’ and I will DM you.”

For a while, it seemed as if Vu’s story would end in Vietnam. But this month I came across a new video on TikTok. A woman with a Mancunian accent, who says she’s now homeless after her house was petrol bombed, discusses recovering from an lower blepharoplasty. On day eight of her recovery she posted a video with the caption: “Pretty impressive work Liverpool blepth [sic] lady”. In another post she encourages anyone who is interested to DM her, but to not share the number on social media. “Evil eyes are watching,” she says.

Dan Carney Has Died. He Co-Founded Pizza Hut and Then Made It Ubiquitous.

The New York Times November 26, 2026

Advertisement

Supported by

The franchise with the iconic red roof began small, in a tiny brick hut in Kansas. Little more than a decade later, it was the world’s biggest pizza chain. He was 95.

By Steven Kurutz

Dan Carney, who founded Pizza Hut with his brother Frank, transforming a single location in Wichita, Kan., into one of the most recognizable restaurant chains in the world, thanks to ambitious franchising and a distinctive red roof, died on Nov. 13 at his home in Wichita. He was 95.

The cause of death, his son Michael said, was chronic obstructive pulmonary disease.

The Carney brothers, who were of Irish descent, became pizza kings by happenstance. In 1958, Dan was 26 and running his family’s corner grocery, Carney’s Food Market, when the owner of a tiny brick building nearby came in with a copy of The Saturday Evening Post and a proposal.

She wanted to oust her tenant, a tavern that sold burgers and beer, and showed Mr. Carney an article in the magazine about a new culinary trend.

“She said, ‘How would you like to go into the pizza business?’” he recalled in an interview for the 2025 documentary “Slice of Life: The American Dream. In Former Pizza Huts.” “And I said, ‘Yeah, OK.’ We knew nothing.”

He brought in Frank, who was then 19 and attending the University of Wichita (now Wichita State University), and they borrowed $600 from their mother to open the restaurant. They found their first pizza chef through their sister Sally: Her neighbor, an airman named John Bender, had worked at a pizzeria in Indiana. Mr. Bender, who developed Pizza Hut’s early sauce recipe, became the third partner. (Several years later, he sold his share of the business to the brothers.)

That first restaurant, at the intersection of Bluff and Kellogg Streets, was around 500 square feet. (The building is now a museum on the campus of Wichita State.) Dan’s wife Beverly made the curtains and tablecloths. The pizza ingredients came straight from Carney’s Food Market. And the pizza oven was found discarded behind an Italian restaurant.

Despite its humble beginnings, Pizza Hut was an immediate success, in part thanks to the Carneys’ community ties, but also because of the novelty of a Neapolitan dish in a meat-and-potatoes Midwestern city. They opened five restaurants in just over a year.

How The Times decides who gets an obituary. There is no formula, scoring system or checklist in determining the news value of a life. We investigate, research and ask around before settling on our subjects. If you know of someone who might be a candidate for a Times obituary, please suggest it here.

Within a few years, as the brothers sold franchises, Pizza Huts spread — from Kansas to surrounding states, including Missouri, Oklahoma, Colorado and Nebraska, and eventually across the United States and as far away as Australia and China.

The story of Pizza Hut is not about that first successful restaurant, but about the second one, and the third and the fourth, and so on, Jay Price, a professor of history at Wichita State, said. The brothers were early adopters of the franchise model, Dr. Price said in an interview: “The idea of having another one, another one, another one. The food is consistent; the service is consistent.”

Frank, the more outgoing brother, was the front-of-the-house guy and unofficial spokesman, while Dan preferred the back-of-the-house role dealing with logistics, contracts and other details related to business growth.

It was Dan who gave the American landscape the two-tiered red roof — as iconic a piece of roadside architecture as the golden arches of McDonald’s.

The first Pizza Huts were a hodgepodge of architectural styles based on available space. But by the early 1960s, Dan recognized the need for a branded building that would set Pizza Hut apart from competitors like Shakey’s Pizza.

He hired an architect, and the resulting design — a red roof topped by a cupola, with unusual trapezoidal windows below, said to have been inspired by the shape of pizza slices — was “conspicuous, noticeable and standardized,” Philip Langdon, an architecture and design writer for The Atlantic, told The New York Times.

It was also enduring. Forty years later, that design had become the architectural equivalent of comfort food.

“People walk into these buildings and straightaway know it’s a Pizza Hut,” said Matthew Salleh, who co-directed “Slice of Life,” about the repurposing of former Pizza Hut buildings to house other businesses, including churches and marijuana dispensaries. “What an amazing achievement of design to make a building that owns a common shape.”

Michael Daniel Carney was born on Oct. 6, 1931, in Kansas City, Mo., one of seven children of Mary Frances (Compton) Carney and Michael Carney, a meatpacker who opened a grocery store in Wichita.

When he was a teenager, his father died and he stepped in to run the business. At some point, Mr. Carney’s son Michael said, he reversed the order of his first and middle names, becoming Daniel Michael Carney.

After graduating from the University of Wichita in 1953 with a degree in business administration, Mr. Carney spent two years in the Air Force. During his downtime, he studied the concept of franchising. His eventual ambition, he told the “All Things Pizza” podcast in 2021, “was to put as many Pizza Huts in as I could.”

By the mid-60s, there were 145 Pizza Huts across the country. By 1971, Pizza Hut had become the world’s largest pizza chain, with some 1,000 restaurants around the world.

Mr. Carney prized personal relationships and favored handshake deals, and the business had in some ways outgrown his skill set and capital: Going global requires corporate structure and marketing power. In 1977, he and his brother sold the company to PepsiCo for $300 million (the equivalent of about $1.7 billion today).

Frank stayed on with the company until 1980, and then tried various other business ventures that mostly failed, losing millions. Later on, much to Dan’s dismay, Frank became the owner of a Papa Johns franchise and appeared in a commercial for the rival chain. He died in 2020 at 82.

Dan went from founder to franchisee, for a time owning Pizza Huts in Florida and Mexico. As a prominent business and civic leader in Kansas, he also served on charitable boards and backed younger entrepreneurs.

Mr. Carney married Beverly Singleton in 1954. She died in 1998. He married Gayla Coulter in 2001. In addition to his son Michael, she survives him, along with another son, Matthew; three daughters, Karen Carney, Tricia Kaufman and Polly Vickers; 15 grandchildren; and 22 great-grandchildren. A fourth daughter, Kay Carney, died in 2008.

In recent years, Pizza Hut has struggled to attract customers. In June, a private-equity firm bought the restaurants in the United States and around the world, except those in mainland China, which were sold to another company.

Nevertheless, generations of diners remember the chain fondly as a destination for family nights out, where bonding took place over breadsticks and deep-dish pan pizza. The affection is such that the locations that retain their original red roofs and familiar décor have become a popular draw.

Throughout his life, Mr. Carney remained humble about his business achievement. It was the right time and the right place, and they had a good product, he told interviewers.

On coming up with the name, he told the “Slice of Life” filmmakers, “The little hut we had was, in fact, a hut. So it didn’t take big brains to call it Pizza Hut.”

An alert to this obituary misspelled the name of the company that Mr. Carney founded. It is Pizza Hut, not Pizza Hunt.

Macy’s Parade Postponement Upends Plans and Adds Costs for Marching Bands

The New York Times November 26, 2026

Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade

Advertisement

Supported by

Nine marching bands were set to perform in the Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade. The decision to move the event to Saturday posed new logistical challenges for them.

By Ed ShanahanClaire Fahy and Mack Liederman

Ryan Demkovich, the director of the Pride of Pearland Marching Band from Pearland High School in Texas, was at a matinee of “Wicked” with his entire 500-member ensemble on Wednesday when word came through that the Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade was being postponed.

Mr. Demkovich said that the tour director for the trip “jetted out” of the theater to immediately assess, and try to address, the financial and logistical challenges that moving the festivities to Saturday had created for the band’s “once-in-a-lifetime” opportunity to march in the parade.

For one thing, the group, from Pearland, Texas, just south of Houston, could not extend its stay at its hotel, the New York Marriott Marquis in Times Square, because it was booked up for the coming weekend, Mr. Demkovich said. So the band, about 1,500 children and parents, would gather in the ballroom there on Thursday for a Thanksgiving feast, which would now be fuel for a Saturday showcase instead of a celebratory meal for a job well done. Then they headed to the Meadowlands in New Jersey — which was where they could find the closest hotel to extend their trip.

The band, which flew to New York from Texas, has chartered buses to return to Texas, since the group could not get on another flight home.

“The financial component is the part that’s the hardest,” said Mr. Demkovich, who estimated the total cost of bringing the band north for the parade at $2 million. The musicians and their families had paid for some of that; various fund-raising efforts had covered the rest.

“These kids have worked so hard for so long,” he added, noting that the band’s repertoire for the parade was scheduled to include a Herald Square performance of two Beatles songs, “Magical Mystery Tour” and “Eleanor Rigby.”

At about 7:30 p. m. on Wednesday, he said the Pearland band had made the decision to stay — at a cost of $350,000, an amount the band raised over the course of about six hours, Mr. Demkovich said.

“We have a lot of people who have reached out to help,” he said.

The Pearland band was one of nine marching bands scheduled to appear at the 100th Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade this year, and one of several that had traveled a considerable distance to do so. At least one marching band, the University of Alabama, had to make the decision to miss the parade because of a scheduling conflict with a football game in Tuscaloosa, Ala.

Bryan Golden, the music director for the 215-member Concord Marching Minutemen of Concord High School in Elkhart, Ind., faced less of a crisis: The group had already booked its rooms at a hotel near Newark Liberty International Airport through Friday night.

“We think we can work it out,” Mr. Golden said. He added that “the kids have been in great spirits” and that “another day for these guys in New York is not a bad thing.” (They planned to perform a rendition of Led Zeppelin’s “Stairway to Heaven.”)

Mr. Golden said he had already planned a dinner cruise on the Hudson River and around the Statue of Liberty on Thursday night for band members and the families who had traveled with them. What to do with the wide-open day on Thursday was the big question.

The University of Connecticut Marching Band’s 320 members had been staying at a Midtown hotel since Tuesday in advance of what would be the group’s parade debut.

Jessica Dickerson, the band director, said that roughly a quarter of the band remained in the city with parents who were able to extend hotel stays or went to their homes in New York and New Jersey. The rest of the band returned to campus in Storrs, Conn., with plans to come back to New York City on Friday night, she said.

The band was initially told that the parade would proceed on Thursday, with the start time moved up half an hour. The parade will now start at 8:30 a. m. Saturday, and the band is scheduled to do a run-through in Herald Square at 3 that morning.

“There’s a lot of buildup of energy and excitement, and certainly this announcement has kind of jarred all of us,” she said. “We have really been talking about flexibility and perseverance and how we show up when things don’t go the way we expect all year long as a band program.”

At about 6:45 p. m. on Wednesday evening, dozens of tuba players with the Marching Illini of the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign, followed by hundreds of other brass players, snaked into Times Square for a scheduled pep rally for the band, whose rehearsal version of the song “Chicago,” by Sufjan Stevens, was widely shared on social media this week.

In a social media post asking for donations, the band said the additional costs for staying until the do-over would be roughly $175,000. The band — still unsure whether it would perform on Saturday — stuck to its original itinerary for Thursday, without the morning parade.

But before hitting the town for an evening performance of the Radio City Music Hall Christmas Spectacular, Barry Houser, the director of the Marching Illini, gathered the band in its hotel lobby at around 12:30 p. m. to announce that the 436 members could, in fact, stay for the Saturday parade.

“Many of them, I think, saw some opportunities that were going to be lost, thinking that we’re not going to be able to do this,” Mr. Houser said in an interview. “So they’re elated — smiles, some tears of happiness — that they get to see this through and really take in this phenomenal experience.”

Miles G. Cohen contributed reporting. Sheelagh McNeill contributed research.

Ed Shanahan is a rewrite reporter and editor covering breaking news and general assignments on the Metro desk.

Claire Fahy reports on New York City and the surrounding area for The Times.

The Army Knew Much Earlier of the Explosive Risk in Iowa, Evidence Suggests

The New York Times November 26, 2026

Controlled Explosion in Iowa

Advertisement

Supported by

Efforts to get rid of unstable explosives at an Iowa plant began more than a year ago but weren’t completed at that time, setting the stage for Wednesday’s controversial blast.

By Hiroko Tabuchi

Hiroko Tabuchi earlier reported that the Army had rejected a cleaner alternative for neutralizing the explosives in Iowa.

In the days leading up to Wednesday’s extraordinary decision to intentionally blow up tons of unstable explosives at a munitions factory in Iowa, Army officials repeatedly said they had only just discovered the problem in March.

But evidence is mounting that the Army was aware of the problem for far longer.

More than a year ago, the Army contractor that runs the factory solicited expert help to deal with concerns over the unstable explosives at the site in Middletown, Iowa, records show. Those efforts were never completed.

And as far back as 2009, the Army knew the barrels of explosives were becoming dangerous. That’s when the military had moved them to the Iowa plant from another facility, according to Robert Cekada, director of the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives. They were “already old, degraded lead azide explosives, and already a concern for the military,” Mr. Cekada said on Wednesday.

All of this set the stage for Wednesday’s detonation, in which the Army blew up a cache of highly unstable lead azide bomb-making material. The Army said the controlled blast avoided the risk that the material would spontaneously explode, potentially causing far more damage.

The Army celebrated what Maj. Gen. Eric P. Shirley called Wednesday’s “tremendously successful” detonation. Sensors set up by the government around the blast site did not detect noticeable levels of lead in the air; water and soil testing continues.

But elected leaders in Iowa were asking how the Army had allowed nearly five tons of lead azide to deteriorate until it felt it had no choice but to trigger an enormous intentional explosion, risking contamination of homes and farmland.

“I will be using my position in the U. S. Senate to get answers as to why these failures took place, including investigations and hearings,” Josh Turek, the Democratic senator-elect from Iowa, said Wednesday on X. “Iowans, as well as the American people, deserve accountability and the peace of mind to know that this will never happen again.”

Wednesday morning’s explosion of the toxic material was the latest in a series of crises at the Iowa plant dating back decades. The facility is also a Superfund cleanup site contaminated with heavy metals, depleted uranium and other pollutants.

Lead azide is a highly sensitive explosive used in detonators. To be maintained properly, it must be kept in a bath of protective liquids. But if those liquids evaporate, lead azide can crystallize and is then at risk of spontaneously exploding if simply moved.

That’s what happened in Iowa, forcing the Army on Wednesday to conduct the intentional explosion of nearly 70 barrels of the dangerous material.

According to documents reviewed by The New York Times, in September 2025 the Army contractor that manages the Iowa plant, a firm named American Ordnance, sought quotes from MuniRem Environmental, a waste management company, to use its technology to chemically neutralize more than 9,700 pounds of dangerous lead azide explosives stored in Iowa.

MuniRem submitted a bid in October 2025, according to documents reviewed by The Times. But American Ordnance later told MuniRem that the government had decided not to award the contract for “safety reasons,” the documents showed, and would instead look for ways to solve the issue internally.

By January 2026, the Army had set up a team to evaluate treatment alternatives, according to a document prepared by Amy L. Borman, a deputy assistant secretary of the Army, and included in its application for an E. P. A. permit for the detonation. The team was instructed to develop a plan “that considered the acute explosive hazard” of the lead azide, the document shows.

But as the Army and American Ordnance began looking for ways to remove or neutralize the lead azide, its risks weren’t publicly disclosed. And all the while, the protective liquid — a mixture of water and ethanol that was keeping the lead azide submerged and stable inside 68 barrels — was evaporating, according to a timeline later provided in court filings.

On March 11, a further inspection confirmed crystallization of the lead azide on the lids and rims of the barrels where it was stored. Crystallization can occur when the protective liquid evaporates, and it makes the lead azide dangerously sensitive to friction or shock, according to Army statements.

In other words, simply moving the barrels could have caused the lead azide to spontaneously explode. Experts issued a “do not move” directive.

A day later, the Army publicly announced a “pause” in operations at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant but made no mention of the dangers of the crystallization emergency.

Instead, plant officials said the material would be safely neutralized and posed “no immediate danger to the public.” The Army then convened a panel of experts to review alternative remediation methods. It again considered MuniRem’s chemical neutralization technology and this time hired the firm to do the work. But shortly thereafter, the contract with MuniRem was canceled.

It was more than six months later, on Oct. 15, that U. S. Army officials hosted an open house at the Armed Forces Reserve Center in Middletown. It described a plan for an intentional detonation of explosive material, and invited residents to review blast-radius maps of a planned detonation and learn about safety measures.

Such a detonation threatened to send a cloud of lead dust across homes and farmland nearby. There are no safe levels of exposure to lead, a neurotoxin that is particularly dangerous to children and pregnant women.

Still, key state and local leaders said they remained in the dark. Gov. Kim Reynolds of Iowa said that she did not learn of the planned detonation until last week.

President Trump called the event a success and sought to blame the Obama administration for failing to resolve the issue of the deteriorating explosive material.

The lead azide crisis was the latest chapter in a decades-long history of fatal accidents and environmental contamination at the 19,000-acre Iowa Army Ammunitions Plant.

Less than three weeks after the plant began operations in 1941, its TNT melting unit detonated, rattling windows five miles away. Thirteen people died. About three months after that, another explosion killed at least 15 more workers.

In all, 70 employees have died over the decades in on-site industrial accidents, according to the Army, including two American Ordnance workers killed in 2006 while testing a high-explosive charge. That incident resulted in serious safety violations from the Occupational Safety and Health Administration.

The site is also heavily polluted.

From 1947 to 1975, the Atomic Energy Commission assembled and disassembled nuclear weapons components at the plant, leaving behind depleted uranium and toxic beryllium, according to Department of Energy and U. S. Army Corps of Engineers records. Former workers and their survivors have since received nearly $400 million in federal health compensation and medical bills.

Unlined wastewater lagoons also leached explosives like TNT and RDX into the soil and local groundwater, according to E. P. A. and Iowa Department of Natural Resources filings. In 1990, the E. P. A. designated the base a federal Superfund site.

In December 2024, the E. P. A. fined the Army and American Ordnance $39,311 for alleged federal hazardous waste violations, including improperly detonating explosives and burning munitions beyond permitted limits.

The stockpile of lead azide that was destroyed on Wednesday dates back to the Vietnam War, when the military mass-produced it for use in weapons known as scatterable gravel mines. In the early 1980s, surplus lead azide was stored at the Lone Star Army Ammunition Plant in Texarkana, Texas.

By 2004, the Defense Department expressed concerns that aging stockpiles of explosives like these risked deteriorating. The Army also moved away from using lead azide, because of how sensitive it was and how difficult it is to maintain in storage.

When the Lone Star plant was slated for closure under a 2005 base realignment order, the Army transferred the stockpile to Iowa in 2009, according to Army filings.

The Army logged the material as usable “industrial stock,” and workers placed the material into 68 drums filled with the protective water-and-ethanol mixture. They stored the drums inside two earth-covered concrete bunkers in Iowa.

Technicians were supposed to check the fluid levels every month through viewing ports and unseal the barrels each September to replenish any evaporated liquid, said Mr. Cekada of the ATF. They completed what would be their final routine check in September 2025.

Quinn Glabicki contributed reporting from Middletown, Iowa, and John Ismay contributed reporting from Washington.

Hiroko Tabuchi covers pollution and the environment for The Times. She has been a journalist for more than 20 years in Tokyo and New York.

Cuts to Food-Stamp Program Threaten Free School Meals

The New York Times November 26, 2026

Trump Administration

Advertisement

Supported by

The Trump administration’s cuts and proposed regulatory changes to the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program would have consequences for school lunch and breakfast.

By Linda Qiu

Reporting from Washington

Millions of children are at risk of losing access to free school meals after cuts and proposed changes to the largest antihunger program in the country under the Trump administration.

It would be a significant reversal from a decade-long push to expand universal school meals, leaving students to rack up debt over meals or simply go hungry at a time when food costs remain high and charitable resources are strained.

Because the nation’s social safety net programs are often intertwined, changes to one can have cascading effects on others. In this case, cuts to the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program that Republican lawmakers enacted under the sweeping domestic policy bill last summer have pushed an estimated two million children off food stamps. That, in turn, has curtailed access to free lunch and breakfast in countless school districts across the country.

Even more children may stop receiving free school lunch starting next year as parts of the tax cut law take effect, schools reach the end of funding cycles and a new proposal by the Agriculture Department, which runs SNAP, limits eligibility further.

“As children fall off SNAP rosters, schools’ ability to continue offering free school meals to all students is going to decrease, and has this really negative ripple effect throughout the school and the household,” said Erin Hysom, the senior child nutrition policy analyst at the Food Research & Action Center, an anti-hunger nonprofit. “Hunger is going to rise.”

Critics have countered that the program is vulnerable to “widespread fraud and abuse.”

A 2024 proposal by conservative House Republicans called for eliminating a provision in a 2010 law that “allows certain schools to provide free school lunches regardless of the individual eligibility of each student.”

The community eligibility provision, as the policy in the 2010 law is known, made it easier and cheaper for high-poverty schools to serve school meals for free. Schools and districts where a significant proportion of students receive public assistance like SNAP can also receive federal funding, at reimbursement rates on a sliding scale, for providing free lunch or breakfast to all. About 55,000 schools adopted the policy in the 2025-26 school year, providing free meals to more than 27 million students.

But critics have argued that the policy is wasteful and subsidizes meals for children who are not truly needy. Project 2025, a set of conservative policy proposals outlined by the Heritage Foundation, also endorsed the elimination of the community eligibility provision and called on future Republican administrations to reject universal school meal programs.

The Trump administration’s cuts to SNAP and other safety net programs like Medicaid are, in effect, a step toward accomplishing those goals. Declining enrollment in those programs has led children to lose automatic certification for free school meals, which, in turn, has reduced schools’ ability to participate in the community eligibility provision and provide free school meals for all.

It is difficult to ascertain how many schools have stopped doing so and how many children are affected because schools opt in to the policy every four years and can choose to renew before their funding cycles are complete. But many — including some of the country’s largest urban districts and those in rural and remote places — have already announced an end to the program.

In Houston this fall, the Spring Branch Independent School District stopped offering universal free school lunch at 22 schools, or about half the district. More than 50 percent of students in the district qualify for free school lunch, but even a small decline in the number of students at one school can push the federal reimbursement rate below a financially sustainable level, said Michael Francis, the district’s director of school nutrition services.

“We’re going to continue looking for ways to make sure we provide quality meals to our students, and that’s never going to change on our end,” he added. “But this does make it harder and harder.”

In Laveen School District near Phoenix, 500 fewer students qualify directly for free school meals this school year in a district of about 8,000 students, said Jennifer Gordon, the district’s director of child nutrition. Should the number of eligible students continue to decline, Laveen may be forced to end its free meal program in two years. Arizona is the state where SNAP enrollment has fallen the most sharply.

Ms. Gordon listed the operational changes that would necessitate: shifting resources and personnel to handle paperwork and verify eligibility, navigating parental anger and confusion, managing meal debt and serving meals at a slower pace to account for payment processing.

“It would have a very drastic and unpleasant impact,” she said. “We would be focusing our efforts more on collecting applications and money for lunch accounts versus just feeding the kids and feeding them that high-quality meal that we’ve really worked so hard to make.”

This month, the Agriculture Department also proposed a regulation that would restrict SNAP eligibility further and, as a result, remove nearly 1.8 million children from automatically qualifying for free school meals. The vast majority of those children would still be eligible for the program, the agency estimated. But just how many will continue to receive free school meals is unclear.

Cindy Long, who oversaw nutrition programs under the Biden administration, said at a recent panel that the effects of the regulation, coupled with existing law, would be momentous.

SNAP cuts and further restrictions to food stamp eligibility “could be the last, frankly, the nail in the coffin for universal programs,” she said.

Linda Qiu is a Times reporter who specializes in fact-checking statements made by politicians and public figures. She has been reporting and fact-checking public figures for nearly a decade.

Connections: Sports Edition

Connections: Soccer Edition

Connections Coach

Dozens of Brazilians have joined the Russian army, some say lured by a pair of recruiters promising money and adventure. Here is one soldier’s story.

Chairon Vitor Sepulvida de SouzaCredit... Santos family

Supported by

By Ana Ionova

Ana Ionova, a correspondent in Brazil, spent months interviewing Brazilians who were recruited into the Russian military and their family members. She reported this story from São Paulo.

On the ragged outskirts of São Paulo, Chairon Vitor Sepulvida de Souza spent his days delivering packages and his nights working as a security guard. Still, money was tight.

Then Mr. Souza, 22, stumbled on an opportunity that he saw as life-changing, his mother said. Russia was paying generous salaries and bonuses, an Instagram video claimed, to foreigners who joined its military for a year. The two Brazilians who posted the video claimed to live in Moscow and offered to help any Brazilian willing to enlist in the Russian Army.

Mr. Souza started saving for a plane ticket to Moscow in early 2025.

“We were against him going,” recalled his mother, Charlaenne Sepulvida dos Santos. “But he’s so stubborn,” she said. “His mind was made up.”

On March 25, 2025, Mr. Souza, dressed in Brazil’s yellow soccer jersey, said goodbye to his family at the airport, according to his mother and photographs taken that day. He promised he would be back in a year, with enough savings to start his own business.

Months later, Mr. Souza vanished in eastern Ukraine, his mother said.

“My biggest hope is that he was captured,” she said. “My worst fear is that he was killed.”

Ms. Santos said her son had been lured by the two Brazilian recruiters with promises that he could stay far from the front lines. Instead, she said, the men skimmed money from Mr. Souza’s bank account and he was sent to fight in Ukraine. Dozens of other Brazilians have fallen for the same scam.

Until his disappearance, Mr. Souza spoke to his mother often, sending her photos, videos, voice notes and texts detailing his experiences as a foreign soldier. This material, which was shared with The New York Times, offers a glimpse into what recruits experienced once they joined the Russian Army and were sent to fight in Ukraine after just weeks of training.

Some 24 hours after her son left home that day in March, Ms. Santos still had not heard from him. Then, a message came from an unknown WhatsApp number belonging to one of the two men who had recruited him online, she said.

“Chairon already arrived here,” the sender, later identified in legal documents as Artur Michel Kreff Avalone, apparently wrote to Ms. Santos. Her son would be in touch soon, he said.

When Mr. Souza did get in touch, his mother demanded frequent video and audio messages as proof he was safe. “Don’t write,” she texted. “I want to see you.”

Mr. Souza replied with a teasing voice note. “There are no Russians here who speak Portuguese,” he said. “I’m OK, Mom.”

When Ms. Santos fretted about the risk, her son assured her that he would not be in harm’s way. “He said he was going to be far from the front lines,” she said.

Just over a week after arriving in Moscow, Mr. Souza told his mother that he had been sent to a training camp. He shared mundane details about daily life, complaining about bad food and bone-chilling cold. Ms. Santos scolded him for looking gaunt. He told her he had passed his physical exams.

After his head was shaved in early April, he sent a selfie. “I look like Buzz Buzzard,” he wrote, referring to the vulture from the Woody Woodpecker cartoons. When he was transferred to what he identified as an army base in Crimea, he sent a video of himself playing the guitar, stretched out on a bed in a room filled with other soldiers.

In early June, Mr. Souza told his mother he had been sent to the Donetsk region of eastern Ukraine. Their exchanges grew more somber.

“I’m alive,” he wrote in response to panicked texts from Ms. Santos, following days of silence. “I can’t talk much, or a drone will pick it up.”

After returning from the front lines one night, Mr. Souza, still clad in fatigues and a helmet, sent a 19-second video to his mother. “I love you,” he said, his face streaked with sweat and dirt. “It’s already night here. I’m all dirty, I’m going to take a shower.”

After a particularly grueling mission in early July, Mr. Souza sent his mother a string of texts saying he was considering deliberately breaking a leg, so he could be discharged.

“War is hell,” he wrote.

Then, on July 11, Mr. Souza told his mother he was preparing for an assault on an enemy target. “Mom, I’m going to the front lines again,” he said in a voice note, over the sound of Brazilian funk music.

Three days later, Mr. Souza sent another audio message. He was silent, but the crackling sound of gunfire echoed loudly. Shortly after, his mother said, he stopped responding to her texts.

“Something bad happened to him,” Ms. Santos said in her home in São Paulo. “Otherwise, he would find a way to text me.”

More than a year after her son vanished, Ms. Santos traveled to Russia in a desperate attempt to find him, but had no luck. “I still came back without answers,” she said.

Lis Moriconi and Leonardo Coelho contributed reporting.

Ana Ionova is a correspondent for The Times, covering Brazil and neighboring countries.
