Connections: Sports Edition

Connections: Soccer Edition

Connections Coach

From virtual agents on A. I. platforms to store helpers like Walmart’s Sparky, consumers are using the technology to save money and time.

Credit... Nick Little

Supported by

By Kim Bhasin and Aruni Soni

Artificial intelligence has fundamentally changed how people shop and redefined how retailers compete for customer attention and dollars this holiday season.

With many Americans struggling with higher prices for food and gas, they’re leaning on A. I. to help them find discounts and save time.

About 58 percent of Americans said they would use A. I. tools such as Google Gemini or Perplexity for shopping during the holidays this year, up from 51 percent last year, according to a survey by Goldman Sachs. Nearly a third said they would use these methods more than last year. The push is being led by Gen Z and millennial shoppers, who are looking for discounts, comparing prices and switching to cheaper brands.

“This is that budget-conscious, very savvy consumer that is leveraging A. I. to help them save money this holiday season,” Michael Brown, the principal U. S. economist at Visa, said.

Virtual agents can help consumers research items, compare prices, curate lists of selections, check availability, track prices and check out on their behalf. They allow people to bypass search engines, salespeople, product reviews, online listings and digital shopping carts.

Personal A. I. agents, such as Meta Muse and OpenAI’s dots, are third-party assistants that can refine broad requests and an individual’s budget and preferences to develop shopping plans and narrow down choices.

Holiday shopping with A. I. begins with the input of basic details, such as your budget and a gift recipient’s age and preferences. You can figure out how a new painting would look in a living room with a room visualizer, or use a photo of a pair of shoes you saw to find a similar pair. From there, the agents are able to build a shortlist of recommendations.

The bot could then spit out product reviews, compare gift suggestions with similar items from other brands, track prices over time and find the best deal at the right moment. Consumers can also view product specifications, shipping speeds, return policies and inventory availability in real time.

The way A. I. crawls websites and pulls recommendations has changed the way brands think about how their customers are finding them. Because there’s no longer an infinite set of links to scroll through, the trend has pushed retailers to invest more in “A. I.-engine optimization.”

Just as search-engine optimization strategies boost website links to the top of a Google search, retailers are working on ways to prioritize their products in an A. I. bot’s answers. That includes making sure their online catalogs are listed in such way that makes it easy for an A. I. agent to read inventory and pricing information.

“I do think this is a top-of-mind issue for all retailers, but I have seen varied levels of investment, focus, prioritization in this space,” Ali Furman, the U. S. consumer markets industry leader at PwC, said.

Consulting firms like PwC are building tools to help retailers compete when it comes to A. I. agents. And some companies have already developed their own specialized A. I. capabilities.

Walmart, the world’s largest retailer, has its own A. I. agent, called Sparky. This year, it has a voice and is able to not only aid online shoppers but help customers find items in stores, by flashing lights on digital shelf labels for the things they want in the app. Use has grown about 129 percent this year, according to Tracy Poulliot, executive vice president of e-commerce and marketing for Walmart U. S.

“If you think about traditional shopping, we still have a lot of products in front of a customer and expect them to do the work to figure out which one meets their needs,” Ms. Poulliot said. “What we’re seeing is customers are expecting A. I. tools to help narrow that funnel.”

Target’s assistant, Ask Target, is still being tested. Michael Fiddelke, the chief executive, told investors in November that he was “encouraged by early results” and that the company would add capabilities in the coming months. He said customers purchased at twice the rate through A. I. as they did through traditional methods.

Amazon has Alexa for Shopping, a merged version of its old Rufus shopping helper and Alexa+, its virtual assistant. It answers product questions, keeps price history and shares personalized guidance.

Retailers have been careful over access to their online ecosystems. In September, Amazon cut off Meta’s Muse from its e-commerce site, citing privacy and security risks.

Some A. I. agents are able to complete the transaction, though many consumers still don’t trust A. I. to check out. About 7 percent of Americans said they would use A. I. to complete transactions, according to a survey from PwC. Agents for Walmart and Target don’t offer automatic checkout yet.

Shoppers are also reluctant to admit to their friends and family that they used A. I. to pick out a gift. According to Visa, 41 percent of Americans said they wouldn’t tell someone that they had handed that task off to an A. I. agent rather than picking out the gift themselves.

But even if shoppers won’t divulge their secret bot use, they’re going to make these holidays a turning point for A. I. assisted shopping, forcing retailers to keep up.

“If you are a retail executive or a brand executive, you need to go where the customers are,” Jack Trotter, a partner at McKinsey & Company, said. “This is significant and a little bit of a paradigm shift.”

Kim Bhasin is a business reporter covering the retail industry for The Times.

Aruni Soni is a business reporter and a member of the 2026-27 Times Fellowship, a program for journalists early in their careers.

Developers Wanted to Build a High-Rise Data Center. Kansas City Blocked It.

The New York Times November 26, 2026

Artificial Intelligence

Advertisement

Supported by

The facilities that power A. I. and other big data needs are in high demand but widely despised. Some developers are trying to build them up instead of out.

By Tiffany Hsu

Reporting from Kansas City, Mo.

In the largely low-slung historic downtown of Kansas City, Mo., near a school, a cabaret theater and a fur shop turned eatery, an investment fund from out of town proposed to build a 20-story data center.

Far from the data centers of public imagination, where flat boxes sprawl horizontally across rural fields, the brick-clad tower would be the 10th-tallest property in town, designed by an architecture firm responsible for some of the loftiest structures in the world. To make room, a squat landmark that has occupied the block for 126 years would be demolished.

Locals were put off by the idea of a data center — possibly the least popular category of building globally. They were also unsettled by the idea that it would be built upward instead of out. They soured further when some suspected that the project might be a smokescreen, a private equity maneuver that uses federal incentives for heritage preservation.

The Kansas City government received more than 400 letters in opposition to the tower over the summer — one calling it “an absolutely dystopian idea” and another saying that “the data center bubble is nearing a pop.” This month, the City Council unanimously rejected the project.

Proposals for vertical data centers, however, will continue amid rising demand for computing power in the age of artificial intelligence. Other novel formats are being considered for data centers, including offshore and subsea facilities, former nuclear sites and solar-powered hubs in space (an idea backed by tech titans including Elon Musk).

Data center towers “illustrate an emerging question for city centers confronting both obsolete commercial buildings and growing demand for computing infrastructure,” according to the Council on Vertical Urbanism, a group offering expertise on tall buildings.

More than 3,000 data centers already operate nationwide, and more than 1,500 were in development as of the spring — the vast majority of them planned for the South and the Midwest, according to the Pew Research Center.

Public attention has been consumed by several enormous data center projects planned or under construction in more rural locales, many of them designed to address the immense power needs of A. I. However, more than 97 percent of data centers reside inside urban cores and their immediate surroundings (including hundreds of acres for Google and Meta in northern Kansas City), according to a report from the engineering school at New York University. The rest are, on average, 8.5 miles from the nearest urban edge.

Meta has an 11-story riverside data center in Singapore. A permit for an 11-story data center near the convention center in San Jose, Calif., is under review. In downtown Los Angeles, a proposed 13-story data center promises to serve the “entertainment and technology industries’ growing data needs.” Plans for a data center in central Chicago involve converting half of a 12-story, 99-year-old landmark. This month, activists stormed the construction site for a Microsoft data center in Amsterdam, where three high-rise towers are planned.

There are benefits to building soaring urban data centers, architects said. In cities with intensifying demand for digital services such as financial trading, telehealth and A. I., having heavy-duty computing infrastructure nearby can help users more quickly gain access to data. Building vertically is often the only option in places like Taiwan, where land is limited. In cities like New York, data centers are sharing refurbished skyscraper space with other tenants.

But keeping servers cool is a trickier proposition in a tower, where heat can rise and concentrate. Heavy equipment must be maneuvered into higher floors, requiring careful engineering to manage extreme weight. The same concerns that accompany ground-level centers also apply: How much power and water will the site extract, and how much heat and noise will it expel?

Projects around the country were thoroughly rebuked by voters in the recent midterm elections, and three communities in Kansas alone voted to ban large-scale data center construction.

In Kansas City, home to dozens of data centers but also new regulations on how they are classified and zoned, the vertical data center proposal became public in June. The developer was Revitalization Unlimited, a real estate private equity fund based in Miami, which describes itself as “enhancing investor returns through preservation of certified historic structures” by tapping “powerful tax incentives.”

The architecture firm was Skidmore, Owings & Merrill, known as SOM and based in Chicago. It designed the Willis Tower there (the tallest building in the world for decades), One World Trade Center in New York (the tallest building in the Western Hemisphere) and the Burj Khalifa in Dubai (the tallest building in the world).

For Kansas City, SOM envisioned a 384-foot downtown tower, whose height would exceed all but a handful of local buildings. The 141,000 square feet would include systems for cooling and power generation. The ground floor would feature retail space.

The proposal did not mention “artificial intelligence” or “A. I.” And no tenant was named.

The proposal called for the demolition of the Western Newspaper Union Building, which was built in 1900 and listed on the National Register of Historic Places. In January, Revitalization said it had purchased the recently renovated site, adding that it planned “to continue the careful preservation of the building’s architectural features.”

The mayor publicly opposed the plan. A preservation group called the proposal “peculiar” and questioned why the data center could not be built on a parking lot or an abandoned site.

Critics also questioned the motivations for the project. A theory took hold that Revitalization was less interested in building a data center and more intent on using a complicated federal tax maneuver to increase the value of its property and maximize income for investors.

Steve Austin, Revitalization’s chief executive, explained the process in a video posted on YouTube last year. The firm can arrange for a legally binding agreement called a historical preservation easement to be placed on a historic property, which permanently protects the building from future work. The firm can donate the easement to the government or a preservation-focused nonprofit group and file for a charitable deduction, whose amount is based on the fair market value of the property if it had been redeveloped rather than preserved. (President Trump has used a similar tactic involving tax deductions through conservation easements on his golf courses.)

Revitalization’s proposal to the city imagined the Western Newspaper Union property reborn as a data center tower — an expensive undertaking. Mr. Austin told one trade publication that, at $183 million, he expected construction to exceed the average cost of building a suburban facility. But the firm had made those plans legally difficult to execute by setting up an easement for the building, critics suggested.

“They basically protected the building from the very thing they’re proposing,” said Brooke Bowlin, a community organizer with the advocacy groups Kansas City Data Center Watchdog and Sunrise Movement Kansas City. Sitting down the street among the elegant 120-year-old marble columns of the Kansas City Public Library, she called the data center pitch a form of “predatory development,” capitalizing on Kansas City history.

“There are a lot of parallels with a real data center — a wealthy company coming in and extracting from locals and their resources,” she said.

Mr. Austin said in a statement that Revitalization had ended up not taking a deduction on the property, and that the deduction was not contingent on the city’s approving the data center. The company deemed a residential, office or hospitality building too expensive to build. A data center, he said, “was the most economically viable development that would not require any incentives from the city or county.” Mr. Austin added that the tower would have created $15.7 million in local spending each year.

“The suggestion that this proposal existed to inflate an appraisal is baseless and misleading,” he said. The company, he said, was “evaluating next steps.”

In a recent YouTube video, Mr. Austin says that “right now, there’s nothing that’s more profitable in real estate, as a landlord, than building a data center.” He added that Revitalization planned to use federal historic tax credits to help convert an unoccupied former courthouse in Miami — a four-story building that is more than 100 years old — into a data center.

“You can go take these beautiful historic buildings and you can use these various tax incentives to kind of breathe new life into them,” Mr. Austin says in the video, extolling the idea of converting old structures into “something as modern and high-tech as a data center.”

“I don’t know that there’s anything more poetic in real estate,” he said.

Tiffany Hsu reports on the information ecosystem, including foreign influence, political speech and disinformation

Democrats Confront a Familiar Question: How Are You Going to Pay for That?

The New York Times November 26, 2026

120th U. S. Congress

Advertisement

Supported by

Many Democratic plans are unlikely to become law under President Trump. But the party is still grappling with the difficult budget math of its agenda.

By Andrew Duehren

Reporting from Washington

Democrats have made no secret of the agenda they plan to pursue when they control the House and Senate next year. Reversing President Trump’s cuts to the social safety net, reining in his tariffs and restoring health insurance subsidies are all primed for votes in the opening days, if not hours, of the new Congress.

Largely left unsaid is if — or how — they’ll pay for those plans.

As long as Mr. Trump remains in the White House, many Democratic proposals are unlikely to become law and, therefore, would not have any actual effect on the budget. Nevertheless, Democrats are starting to confront the difficult math of both unraveling Mr. Trump’s policies and pursuing a proactive agenda of their own. The deliberations are an early window into the fiscal challenge the party will face if it wins total control of Washington in 2028.

Democrats have had to puzzle together a way to finance their agenda after past election victories. But the nation’s fiscal situation is much more challenging now. Mr. Trump’s tax cuts piled on to a federal deficit that has remained much larger than it was before the coronavirus pandemic. Interest rates have also stayed elevated, fueling investors’ fears that the government’s debt load could, in the not-so-distant future, make it more expensive for Americans to borrow money.

“It’s a really big hole they’re inheriting,” said Ben Ritz, a budget analyst at the Progressive Policy Institute, a center-left think tank. “Whatever Democrats do today sets the stage for the next time they have a trifecta, which could be in two years.”

Many Democrats support the idea of raising taxes on companies and the wealthy, and Democratic lawmakers and their aides have been dusting off revenue plans in preparation for next year. But translating populist, tax-the-rich talk into policy changes that become law has been a challenge for the party. In California this month, voters rejected what would have been the first wealth tax in the nation, a blow to the progressive tax agenda.

Democrats’ ambitions are also large enough that the tax increases that may already be palatable to many in the party, like modestly raising the income tax rates on corporations and high-earning individuals, would likely not pay for the full scope of their plans.

Just rolling back the parts of Mr. Trump’s agenda that Democrats spent the election campaigning against could cost more than $4 trillion over a decade, according to an estimate from the Committee for a Responsible Federal Budget, which pushes for a smaller deficit. More sweeping changes Democrats are considering, like an expansion of Medicare or a more generous child tax credit, could add trillions more.

“We should be exploring those sorts of things, and I think that we have to remind the American people: Are you willing to pay for them?” said Representative Richard E. Neal of Massachusetts, the top Democrat on the House Ways and Means Committee, which writes tax legislation. “Many of those items can be and are pricey.”

Those potential costs are set to renew a debate among Democrats about whether the national debt is an urgent problem and how far to go in raising taxes. Historically, the party’s centrist members have been both the most concerned about the country’s fiscal situation and the most hesitant to support substantially raising taxes. Progressives, on the other hand, see raising taxes on the rich as a political asset but chafe against letting bean counters dictate the party’s agenda.

A potential wild card is how the party’s new lawmakers, especially those elected from historically red districts and states, approach budget questions. For instance, Annie Andrews, the South Carolina Democrat elected to the Senate, included a pledge to cut taxes in her campaign platform alongside support for a constitutional amendment requiring a balanced budget.

There are also tactical considerations about how to use control of Congress under divided government. Some in the party believe that going through the process of drafting tax increases could help Democrats seem more substantive, all while preparing them for their next potential turn in power. But including tax increases would reduce the likelihood that any Republicans support the legislation. And others in the party worry that fiscal considerations could overcomplicate straightforward votes on bills that are meant to unify Democrats — and that won’t likely become law, anyway.

“Democrats ran on addressing the cost-of-living crisis that is affecting ordinary Americans, and they should not hold back on those proposals out of a manufactured fear of debt,” said Kitty Richards, a senior fellow at the Groundwork Collaborative, a progressive group that favors higher taxes on the rich.

The conversations could start to come to a head in the coming weeks. Some House Democrats have started organizing an effort to impose a House rule requiring that the cost of legislation brought to the floor be covered by tax increases or other spending cuts. The rule, called “pay as you go” or PAYGO, would not apply to all spending, and versions of the rule adopted by previous House Democratic majorities have been easy to waive. But whether the rule is adopted will be an early indicator of how Democrats approach their fiscal dilemma.

“We just have to have this conversation,” said Representative Scott Peters, a California Democrat who is among those pushing for the inclusion of the rule. “PAYGO forces us to go in that room and have that conversation like adults.”

Much of the fiscal challenge for Democrats stems from the tax cut Republicans passed last year. The G. O. P. tried to offset the cost of those tax cuts with steep cuts to health care and food stamp programs. But the law still cost more than $4 trillion over a decade. Democrats have so far rallied around repealing those spending reductions, though doing so is expensive enough that some in the party are exploring the possibility of preserving some elements of the Republican spending changes. One option is to leave in place limits Republicans put on Medicaid provider taxes while rolling back other cuts the G. O. P. made to the program.

Mr. Trump’s tax cuts are a different question. Democrats may be able to easily reverse some of them, including by raising the top marginal individual income rate, which is now at 37 percent. But many of the Republican-passed tax cuts, like an expanded standard deduction, provide benefits to working-class Americans that Democrats are unlikely to want to claw back since such moves would amount to de facto tax increases. Even some of the law’s provisions that primarily benefited the rich, like a larger deduction for state and local taxes, enjoy Democratic support.

The new majority party will also be forced to grapple with Mr. Trump’s campaign promises to not tax tips, overtime or Social Security. When Republicans turned those catchphrases into law, they did so only temporarily, setting them up to expire at the end of 2028. Many Democrats have supported the tax breaks, which are largely targeted to middle-class Americans. One of the few areas of potential bipartisan compromise next Congress may be a deal between Democrats and Mr. Trump to extend those tax cuts, which could cost more than $400 billion over a decade.

Democrats would likely be able to attract Republican support for such a deal, meaning it would be able to pass the Senate easily. But bills repealing Mr. Trump’s cuts to Medicaid, canceling his tariffs or expanding Obamacare subsidies would face hurdles. Even though they won a 56-seat majority in that chamber, Democrats are still short of the 60 votes needed to overcome a filibuster for most legislation.

That means Democrats may resort to a special budget process, called reconciliation, to pass tax and spending legislation. Reconciliation allows lawmakers to avoid the 60-vote threshold in the Senate, but it also includes a number of fiscal rules, including that long-term changes to the budget be paid for. Those rules would require Democrats to come up with enough tax increases to cover the long-term cost of their agenda, even for a bill that Mr. Trump would veto. That procedural requirement may ultimately shape how they proceed.

“I expect any of this stuff to eventually be paid for, regardless,” said Bobby Kogan, a budget analyst at the Center for American Progress, a liberal think tank.

Andrew Duehren covers tax policy for The Times from Washington.

Gérard Depardieu Is Ordered to Stand Trial Over Rape Accusation

The New York Times November 26, 2026

Advertisement

Supported by

The actress Charlotte Arnould has accused the French movie star of raping her in 2018. He has denied any wrongdoing in the case.

By Catherine Porter

Reporting from Paris

The Paris appeals court on Thursday ordered the French movie star Gérard Depardieu to stand trial over an accusation that he raped a young aspiring actress eight years ago.

If convicted, he could face up to 15 years in prison.

The case was brought by Charlotte Arnould, a family friend of Mr. Depardieu who went to his Paris home twice in August 2018 seeking help on breaking into the movie industry. She filed a complaint later that month accusing Mr. Depardieu of raping her during both visits.

The police opened an investigation but dropped the case the following year, citing insufficient evidence. Prosecutors picked the case back up in 2020, after Ms. Arnould invoked a legal measure to have it resumed.

The court ruled that Mr. Depardieu should be tried over Ms. Arnould’s accusation that Mr. Depardieu raped her during the first visit to his home. But it did not order him to stand trial over Ms. Arnould’s accusation that Mr. Depardieu also raped her during the second visit.

“It is a victory for her, given that Gérard Depardieu is going to stand trial for rape,” Carine Durrieu Diebolt, Ms. Arnould’s lawyer, said outside the courtroom on Thursday. “We are eagerly awaiting this trial.”

Mr. Depardieu, 77, can still appeal before France’s highest court, the Court of Cassation. If that fails, it would be the second sexual abuse case against him to go to trial. On Thursday, his two lawyers characterized the court decision as a partial win because the second rape charge was dropped.

The actor has starred in over 230 movies and won dozens of awards and accolades, but he has faced a series of accusations of sexual abuse in recent years, tarnishing his image and putting him at the center of France’s fraught debates over the #MeToo movement, especially in the movie industry.

Mr. Depardieu has said that his encounters with Ms. Arnould, then 22, were consensual.

“A woman came to my house a first time, light-footed, going up to my room of her own free will,” Mr. Depardieu wrote in an open letter in Le Figaro newspaper in October 2023. “Today she says she was raped there. She came back a second time. There was never any coercion, violence or protest between us.”

More than 20 women followed in Ms. Arnould’s wake and accused Mr. Depardieu of sexual abuse, mostly by talking to the news media.

He has consistently denied the accusations, although in one separate case earlier this month he admitted his guilt and apologized for his actions.

In that case, a court convicted him last year of sexually assaulting two women who worked with him on the set of the 2021 film “Les Volets Verts.” Mr. Depardieu received a suspended sentence of 18 months, and his name was added to the national sex and violent offender registry. He had initially appealed the conviction but dropped the appeal last week.

The victims in that case, a set decorator and an assistant director, both said in court that Ms. Arnould’s case and her decision to go public with her accusations had propelled them to go to the police.

Despite the accusations against him, Mr. Depardieu has been publicly defended by prominent and powerful people in France, including President Emmanuel Macron. In 2023, Mr. Macron condemned what he called a “manhunt” against the actor, and said that Mr. Depardieu “makes France proud.”

Giulia Imbert contributed reporting from Paris.

Catherine Porter is an international reporter for The Times, covering France. She is based in Paris.

Recruiters Lured Brazilians to Fight Russia’s War, Then Stole Their Money

The New York Times November 26, 2026

Russia-Ukraine War

Dozens of Brazilians were sent to the front lines with little training, and the high salaries they were promised, they say, turned out to be illusory.

“They were scammed and sent out there to die,” said Hélade de Oliveira Madeiros. whose son disappeared in Russia’s war. Credit... Victor Moriyama for The New York Times

Supported by

By Ana IonovaLeonardo Coelho and Lis Moriconi

The reporters, who cover Brazil, interviewed soldiers and their family members, obtained documents and analyzed visual evidence for this story.

Igor Pereira Santos, a small-time stock trader, yearned for some excitement. Browsing YouTube, he recalls, he spotted a video offering him the adventure of a lifetime — along with a dizzying amount of cash.

Mr. Santos could earn thousands of dollars a month, the video said, serving in an army 7,000 miles from his sleepy hometown in Brazil’s northeast. Two men claiming to be Brazilians living in Moscow promised, in a video viewed by The New York Times, to help foreigners join the Russian Army.

The Brazilian recruiters, Mr. Santos said, later assured him and others that, for a fee, their associates in the military could get them jobs in kitchens or fixing weapons —far from the front lines of the war in Ukraine. Their pitch convinced Mr. Santos, 37, a history buff with a weakness for war films and combat video games. “I bought a ticket and just went for it,” he said.

But within weeks of arriving in Moscow last year, he said, he was sent to the front lines with little training, while the $25,000 he received for joining the army disappeared from his bank account. Months later, Mr. Santos was badly wounded in both legs by shrapnel during a mission in eastern Ukraine, medical records reviewed by The Times show.

“They promise you the moon and the stars,” he said in an interview. “But the reality is horrifying.”

Lured by the same pair of middlemen, dozens of Brazilians traveled to join the Russian Army, according to soldiers who signed up.

Once in Russia, they were duped into signing documents in a language they didn’t understand that gave the recruiters control over their bank accounts and military salaries, according to nine Brazilian recruits, the relatives of three others and documents reviewed by The Times.

Some said they or their comrades were wounded in combat, accounts verified through medical records. At least three went on missions and never returned, their families and fellow soldiers said.

The Times conducted interviews with Brazilian soldiers and their relatives, and analyzed materials they provided, including documents, photos, videos, audio and text messages. The documents included power of attorney forms, military contracts and bank statements.

These accounts, together with online posts by the recruiters, offer a look at how these men were enlisted and sent, largely unprepared, to fight in the war.

As the conflict has dragged on, Russia has sought volunteers abroad to bolster ranks depleted by soaring casualty rates. Generous sign-up bonuses, high salaries and even Russian citizenship have drawn foreign fighters from around the world.

But the rush to find new soldiers appears to have also opened the door, in Brazil, South Africa and elsewhere, to scam artists and middlemen seeking profits.

Mr. Santos acknowledged that he had been naïve to believe the recruiters. “We didn’t suspect anything,” he said.

Mr. Santos first started seeing calls to join the Russian army on social media in late 2024.

In online tutorials reviewed by The Times, two recruiters later identified in power of attorney documents as Artur Michel Kreff Avalone and Antônio Aguiar Neto explained how Brazilians could earn $50,000 to $100,000 by signing yearlong contracts with the Russian military.

“Attention, Brazilian people,” Mr. Avalone says in one video. “Come and enlist in the most powerful army on the planet. You don’t need to speak Russian or have proven military experience.”

All Brazilians had to do, the recruiters said, was buy a one-way ticket to Moscow. The videos, posted on YouTube, Instagram and TikTok, mostly ended the same way: “To learn more, reach out on Telegram.”

On that messaging app, Mr. Avalone and Mr. Neto shared instructions on becoming a foreign fighter.

The perks offered echoed brochures promoting student exchange programs. “What’s included?” the posts read. “Transport from the airport,” said one bullet point. “Introduction to Russian culture,” read another.

Mr. Avalone and Mr. Neto did not respond to multiple requests for comment. In recent months, their online campaign has gone silent and their whereabouts are unclear.

Russia’s defense ministry did not answer emailed questions about whether the two Brazilian men had links to the military or were recruiting soldiers on its behalf. Russia’s foreign minister, Sergey V. Lavrov, acknowledged this year that foreigners were participating in the fighting, but said his government did not trick people into joining the army.

The Brazilian and Russian authorities declined to say whether they were investigating the claims against the two recruiters.

The Brazilian government has not directly addressed recruitment into the Russian Army, but its foreign ministry has warned citizens against joining foreign conflicts. In emails reviewed by The Times, Brazil’s embassy in Moscow informed relatives of two missing Brazilian men that they had disappeared while in the Russian Army, but provided no details.

In South Africa, Kenya and Bolivia, officials have spoken out about citizens being duped into fighting for Russia.

At the United Nations in September, Ukraine’s president, Volodymyr Zelensky, said his country had taken people from 47 nations as prisoners of war. “People from your countries,” he said, “ended up in Russia through deception and tricks.”

Mr. Santos, one of the Brazilians recruited, said he had long harbored a fascination with family tales of a great-uncle who served in World War II. “I came to be part of history,” he said.

When Mr. Santos arrived in Moscow in February 2025, he said, he was greeted at the airport by Mr. Neto and taken to a hostel. Over the following days, he said, a handful of other Brazilians trickled in.

One, Anderson de Oliveira Ferreira, 24, was a ride-share driver from an impoverished neighborhood of São Paulo who, friends say, planned to buy a home and an electric car with money he earned in Russia.

On his first night in Moscow, Mr. Ferreira called his 5-year-old daughter over video to show her the frosty streets, said Gabriela Aparecida Oliveira Silva, his former girlfriend.

“Look, it snows here,” Ms. Silva recalled him saying to their daughter. He told Ms. Silva he was working as a bodyguard. “We didn’t know he was going to fight,’’ she said.

Fernando Mazzo, 45, also joined the group. He had gone to Russia, he said, after growing bored with his job in transport logistics in rural Brazil. “You know when you’re searching for meaning?” Mr. Mazzo said. “I felt this could be it.”

After arriving, Mr. Mazzo and Mr. Santos were taken to a drab office building in Moscow, where a clerk questioned them in Russian, a language they didn’t speak, they said. Mr. Neto translated, they said, explaining that they were being evaluated for service.

They were given documents in Russian, which were described as army admission forms, according to Mr. Santos. “We trusted them,” he said, “so we signed.”

Later, Mr. Mazzo and Mr. Santos said, the recruiters took them to a Russian bank, where they signed more paperwork to open local accounts so they could receive their paychecks..

Mr. Mazzo said that he, Mr. Santos and Mr. Ferreira were eventually sent to a Russian military training center on the outskirts of Moscow. “It was like a preschool for war,” he said. There, Mr. Mazzo said, they spent a few weeks learning to operate drones and shoot weapons, avoid explosives and decipher commands in basic Russian.

Through bank apps on their phones, Mr. Mazzo and Mr. Santos started noticing suspicious withdrawals from their new Russian accounts, they said. At the army base, they said they met other Brazilians recruited by Mr. Avalone and Mr. Neto who also suspected the middlemen of emptying their bank accounts. With the help of a lawyer, they learned that the documents they had signed were powers of attorney granting Mr. Avalone and Mr. Neto legal authority over their finances.

“By the time we realized the scam, we were already enlisted in the army,” Mr. Mazzo said.

After just 20 days of training, he said, he was sent to Crimea, then to the Kursk region. Mr. Santos said that he and Mr. Ferreira were sent to a Russian base some 25 miles from the eastern border with Ukraine.

In online comments, some social media followers of Mr. Avalone and Mr. Neto were starting to accuse them of running a scam. The recruiters denied this, blaming Ukrainian agents for smearing them. “It has nothing to do with money,” Mr. Neto said in one video, insisting he was helping the Russian cause.

Less than 10 miles from Russia’s eastern border with Ukraine, Mr. Mazzo’s unit was targeted by drones daily, he said. Then, in April of last year, he said, he fell ill with pneumonia and was evacuated to a military hospital in St. Petersburg.

“That’s probably what saved me,” Mr. Mazzo said.

He managed to escape the hospital, he said, desert the army and return to Brazil.

In eastern Ukraine, near the city of Volchansk, Mr. Santos’s unit was also under constant attack by Ukrainian forces, he said. He was wounded on June 18, 2025, he said, when he and six other soldierswere hit by gunfire and shrapnel.

Three weeks later Mr. Oliveira went missing in the same region of Ukraine, according to his family.

“They were scammed and sent out there to die,” said his mother, Hélade de Oliveira Madeiros.

Just before he was wounded, Mr. Santos discovered that Mr. Avalone had withdrawn nearly 2 million rubles — the equivalent of $25,000 — from his bank account, he said. “They are merchants of death,” Mr. Santos said. “They profit from the blood of others.”

By early August, Mr. Avalone appeared to have joined the war effort himself. In one video, he is seen in the back of what appears to be a troop carrier with other soldiers.

Months after her son disappeared, Ms. Madeiros went to a police building in São Paulo where a doctor swabbed her mouth. A forensics lab analyzed the genetic material, adding it to a database of missing persons.

Ms. Madeiros doesn’t harbor hopes of finding her son alive. But these genetic clues may help track down his remains, she said.

“I won’t leave him there, abandoned,” she said. “I want him back, even if it’s just his bones.”

Alina Lobzina contributed reporting.

Ana Ionova is a correspondent for The Times, covering Brazil and neighboring countries.

‘Pumpkin Pie Is Disgusting’ and Other Unpopular Opinions

The New York Times November 26, 2026

Advertisement

Supported by

The Conversation

By Frank Bruni and Bret Stephens

Mr. Bruni is a contributing Opinion writer; Mr. Stephens is an Opinion columnist.

Bret Stephens: Hi, Frank. My mother reminded me the other day that it was the 76th anniversary of her arrival, alongside her mother, as a 10-year-old refugee in the United States. It never fails to make me think of how much my family owes this country — the land of the still-free-despite-it-all.

Frank Bruni: My family, too. My paternal grandfather, Mauro Bruni, a stonemason, came here illegally, with nothing, from southern Italy — I wrote about that in this 2013 column.

Bret: Careful, lest Stephen Miller try to deport you. Although, if you have to be deported back to Puglia, there are worse fates.

Frank: My grandfather and my grandmother, Adelina Mazzone Bruni, also an immigrant from Puglia (though they met here), had minimal education and didn’t speak decent English until they’d been in the United States for decades. But they had drive and they had dreams. My father, the eldest of their three sons, became student body president at White Plains High School in New York and attended Dartmouth College on a full scholarship. That’s America, and no amount of messiness or ugliness or Stephen Miller-ness will erase my debt to — and gratitude for — this country.

Bret: Similar story on my paternal side. My grandfather arrived as a young boy escaping the pogroms of Russia. His father got off the boat and found work as a carpenter at the Brooklyn Navy Yard, earning about eight dollars a week for a family of eight, all so that his posterity could have the chance to rise in the world, think for themselves, be outspoken if they wanted, live mostly without want and completely without fear. It’s why I think few people appreciate this country more than immigrants, because for them our freedoms aren’t givens.

Frank: There’s another aspect of my father’s experience that’s worth mentioning in terms of what did — and can — make America so special. The White Plains school system that he attended had a robust mix of relatively poor children, like him, and middle- and upper-middle class ones, like my mother, Leslie Frier, whose Anglo ancestors included Johnny Appleseed, as I wrote early this week.

Bret: A detail about your ancestry that truly blew my mind.

Frank: My father’s parents didn’t know from college and the Ivy League — but my father had classmates like my mother to observe, learn from, emulate. That’s America, too: the communion of diverse people who come to speak a shared language of aspiration and possibility. In an era of increasing segmentation and fragmentation, we absolutely must dedicate ourselves to preserving that part of our heritage and character.

Bret: My mother moved to L. A. as a teenager in part because my grandmother had heard there was an excellent public school system there — which, in midcentury America, was true. Her high school classmates included the likes of Nora Ephron. That’s less-and-less possible in a world where upper middle class families tend to flee the public education system as soon as they can. I confess to being guilty of this, too, in the interests of my kids. But I’m also reacting to a broken system that, as our colleague Nikole Hannah-Jones detailed in an extraordinarily candid personal essay earlier this year, no longer operates in the interests of the children it is meant to serve.

Frank: One big reason that people of privilege retreat into social, residential and educational enclaves that are designed to preserve their privilege is a pessimism in America that didn’t exist to this degree just a quarter century ago. You see it in surveys: Many American parents no longer trust that their children will do better than they did, just as many American offspring have lost hope of measuring up to their parents. People of all ages don’t believe the country is headed in a positive direction. They worry that there won’t be enough to go around. So they huddle with their tribes and they hoard. That’s not America, and it’s crucial that we figure out how we turn that psychology around.

Bret: One of our most underappreciated presidents, George H. W. Bush, is also the last U. S. president who served in combat. What I always admired about him was that he was raised to believe his family’s affluence and social connections required greater, not fewer, sacrifices. He graduated from Andover, went straight to flight school, and barely survived getting shot down in the Pacific. Pretty much the opposite of Commander in Chief Bone Spur, who thinks service is for suckers and embodies the idea that success lies in whatever you can get away with. That’s why it’s so important that the country at last seems to be turning the corner on him — not simply for who he is and what he’s done, but for everything he embodies that’s coarse and wrong about America.

Frank: Maybe he has done us a kind of favor, Bret. (Mind you: If he has made a positive contribution, it’s entirely by accident.) On this day of thanks, I choose to believe that Donald Trump in all his grandiose depravity has given Americans a jarring, jolting glimpse of who we are when we forget our ideals, part company with all decency and surrender to our most puerile and pettiest impulses. Perhaps the story of the midterms is that Trump scared us straight. At least that’s the moral that pairs best with turkey, stuffing, cranberry dressing and pumpkin pie.

Bret: Pumpkin pie is disgusting. A culinary abomination.

Frank: Not if you suffocate it with whipped cream.

Bret: Um, Frank, that’s true of nearly everything.

Frank: Enough whipped cream would make even chopped toenails a delicacy.

Bret: Anyway … I think the point we are both circling is that what the country needs is more than just a political reset. It’s a cultural, moral and generational one. At the risk of upsetting a lot of our Boomer readers, America was not well-served by that generation’s Me-First, if-it-feels-good-it-is-good ethos; its veneration of youth over age; its soapy spiritualism descending to grabby materialism.

Frank: Are you not a Boomer yourself, Bret?

Bret: I turned 53 the other day, which makes me squarely Gen X.

Frank: Happy Belated Birthday and damn you for your youth. I am, sadly, the very last year of the Boomer generation, born in 1964. The first year was 1946, when, um, Donald Trump screeched into this world. He and I are Boomer-generation bookends and birth year anagrams. Make of that what you will.

Bret: One of the miracles of our time is that 53 is now considered young. I’m the same age that Lyndon Johnson was as vice president, by which time he’d already had a heart attack and looked like Methuselah.

Frank: Well, our era isn’t miraculous enough for me to feel young at 62, but then I have a lot more mileage on me than I expected to. I suffered a stroke of sorts about nine years ago that rendered my right eye useless. From August to October, I did a brutal dance with cancer. It’s hard to feel sprightly after that, though my prognosis is good and I should be fine.

Bret: Thank God. Fingers still crossed.

Frank: The upside, and I really do mean this: Surviving hardship and confronting limits can make you more conscious and appreciative of what remains — of your blessings — in a manner that’s not hokey or platitudinous, but genuine and deeply felt. That’s one of many poignant verities in an essay in Times Opinion this week by our gifted editor, Aaron Retica.

Bret: Aaron has had 12 separate knee surgeries over the last few years, making ordinary motion somewhere between excruciating and effectively impossible. It has led him to discover all that it means to live a life of disability, with its paradoxical combination of acute physical limitations, but also broadened emotional and spiritual horizons. The essay is extraordinary on many levels, not least in the reminder of how, even today with all the A. D. A. regulations and accommodations, disabled people are so often still treated shabbily by many people who ought to know better. But it’s also a reminder that our “disabled” editor has never missed a week over the past many years making the two of us look that much sharper to our readers than we really are.

Frank: Aaron has precisely what too many Americans have lost and what we’ve been saying in our back-and-forth today that the country must rediscover: true generosity of spirit. He roots and works for others as hard as he does for himself. He’s not rashly judgmental: In fact, he edits us in such a way that when you and I disagree, I often can’t tell whose side he’s on. He’s less interested in staking out his patch of ground than in making sure the entire landscape, in all its riotous diversity, is nurtured. More politicians should do that. More of us, too.

Bret: Along with my family — those present, absent and long-since departed — that’s who I’ll be giving thanks to today: Aaron as well as Nick Fox, my other genius editor, our team of fact-checkers and copy and photo editors, and the whole quiet band of people at The Times whose understated brilliance is matched with a drive to serve and preserve the greatest news organization on earth.

The E. R. Closed at 5 P. M. A Dying Woman Showed Up 11 Minutes Too Late.

The New York Times November 26, 2026

Advertisement

Supported by

In rural British Columbia, Courtney McCowan died after paramedics tried to help her in a hospital’s parking lot.

By Mark Colley

Courtney McCowan arrived at a hospital in Port Hardy, British Columbia, on Nov. 19, in respiratory distress. But the rural hospital’s emergency room had closed at 5 p. m. And it was 5:11 p. m. when she arrived, with the help of a friend.

Paramedics tried to save her in the parking lot. But by the time she was allowed into the small hospital, it was too late. Not long after, Ms. McCowan, 48, was dead.

Island Health, the public health authority that oversees the hospital, said in a statement that it was working “to establish and clarify the facts of what occurred,” adding, “All potential factors will be examined and considered.”

Hailey Schubert, Ms. McCowan’s daughter, said in an interview that she was searching for answers about why her mother had been denied entry to the hospital and instead had received care from paramedics on the ground outside the closed emergency room.

Port Hardy is a town of about 4,000 people in a remote part of the northern tip of Vancouver Island. Its emergency room has been closed from 5 p. m. to 7 a. m. every day for nearly four years because of staff shortages. The E. R.’s stripped-down hours are not unique to the town.

Doctor and nurse shortages across British Columbia have caused some 2,600 temporary E. R. closures over the past two years, almost all at remote hospitals, said Paul Adams, executive director of the B. C. Rural Health Network. Similar emergency department closures have occurred across Canada.

“We really don’t tend to understand the scope of the problem because it doesn’t hit the news until somebody’s dying in a parking lot,” Mr. Adams said.

That appears to be what happened on the night of Nov. 19. Ian Tait, a spokesman for the province’s ambulance paramedics union, said that a paramedic who had been at the hospital had seen Ms. McCowan in cardiac arrest at 5:11 p. m. and called for backup. The paramedics administered 10 rounds of CPR in the hospital’s parking lot, each taking three to five minutes, before staff brought Ms. McCowan into the hospital.

When people arrive at the hospital after hours, Island Health said in its statement, staff “assess the situation” to determine next steps, which can include administering emergency treatment or transferring the patient elsewhere.

Residents who need an alternative to the Port Hardy emergency department face a 30-minute drive down a dark road with no cellphone coverage or bus routes to Port McNeill, which has the closest 24-hour E. R., said Pat Corbett-Labatt, mayor of Port Hardy.

“The community’s very frustrated,” she said. “There’s a lack of understanding of why our hospital’s not open 24/7.”

A resident of Port Hardy for 13 years, Ms. McCowan was planning to move soon to Victoria, the provincial capital, to be closer to her daughter. Ms. McCowan loved gardening, often giving baskets of flowers to neighbors in the spring and summer, and had three cats, Ms. Schubert, 27, said.

Ms. McCowan fell sick with what she at first thought was a regular cold, her daughter said. When Ms. Schubert didn’t hear from her mother on Nov. 18, she had a neighbor check in. Ms. McCowan eventually answered the door but was barely able to keep her eyes open, Ms. Schubert said. The next day, Ms. McCowan’s friend took her to the hospital.

Ms. Schubert was on the phone with her uncle, who had driven to the hospital, shortly after 6 p. m. when a doctor interrupted.

Her uncle, sobbing, then relayed the news to her: “Hailey, your mom is dead.”

Of the limited Port Hardy hours, Ms. Schubert said, “It just simply does not make sense.”

Mr. Tait said many people in small communities went to the ambulance station after hours instead of the E. R.

Ryan Peterson, British Columbia’s newly appointed minister of health, said in a statement that the provincial government planned to hire and retain more doctors and nurses, and invest $50 million in an emergency fund to help address closures.

“British Columbians deserve better, and we are committed to delivering the reliable emergency care they need,” he said.

Ms. Schubert said that keeping the Port Hardy E. R. open 24 hours a day “needs to be priority No. 1,” adding, “You shouldn’t have closing hours on an emergency.”

Trump Lost My Brother!

The New York Times November 26, 2026

Advertisement

Supported by

Maureen Dowd

By Maureen Dowd

Opinion Columnist

It has been a scary year for our family, but we have a ton to be thankful for. My brother Kevin had a holiday miracle as schmaltzy and heartwarming as a Hallmark movie. I am relieved that, given how disappointed the former Trump fan is in the president now, I won’t have to sit through another Thanksgiving toast to the scoundrel in the White House. We’re even forgoing the Trump champagne! Here is Kevin’s annual offering:

I’m back to write again — and for a while that didn’t look like a sure thing.

For most of the spring I was trying to find the source of a constant cough. I spent my birthday in May getting a PET scan, which revealed that my kidney cancer had returned after 15 years, this time in my lungs. I was blessed to be accepted into the renowned immunotherapy program at Georgetown University’s Lombardi Comprehensive Cancer Center under the care of the exceptional Dr. Michael Atkins and his talented team. The results have been very positive, and I hope the miracle will culminate with the defeat of this odious disease.

In the meantime, the midterms produced a rare moment in which American voters demanded accountability, and may get it.

Republicans were swept out even in red states once thought invulnerable. All of that can be laid at the feet of President Trump.

His decision to bomb Iran set in motion events that were bound to raise gas prices and reintroduce the public to nasty inflation. Worse, his decision to grant Iran a 60-day negotiating period was a blunder worthy of Neville Chamberlain. Iran has proved over 47 years of theocratic rule that it uses these pauses to delay, not to negotiate.

Gas prices were a daily reminder of Trump’s failed boasts that the war would end quickly. And as he kept repeating that the United States economy was the envy of the world, credit cards were maxed out and we relied more on McDonald’s value meals.

Bill Clinton boosted his 1992 presidential campaign by telling voters, “I feel your pain.” Trump showed no interest in sharing any pain as he continued to profit from his Trump watches and Bibles and meme coin and as a Russian oligarch spent hundreds of thousands on two parties for Don Jr.’s wedding in the Bahamas.

An event that crystallized Trump’s disconnect from the working-class voters who had twice been the driving force in his election was his proposed makeover of Hains Point, home to several Washington, D. C., public golf courses that hosted 124,000 rounds last year. Some of Maureen’s favorite expeditions as a child were to its miniature golf course. There are picnic areas and a four-mile loop used by thousands of joggers and bikers. Trump brought in a top designer of luxury golf courses to create a world-class destination, which would eliminate the opportunity for an inexpensive round of golf and deprive runners and cyclists of their daily exercise routine.

The year that is ending with Trump’s repudiation began with his holding all the cards — to use one of his favorite metaphors. The economy was strong and gas prices were stable.

But Americans were still scrambling to pay bills, and the president exhibited no empathy for them as he, his family and his cronies got richer and richer.

The blue team is giddy with its success, but Democrats are gonna Democrat. Voters do not thirst for tax increases or huge social spending programs. Democrats should not be so foolish as to think that the public is ready to embrace impeachment and endless investigations to settle old scores.

Democrats and Republicans are demanding that a median income be able to produce a middle-class life — a right citizens came to expect. This election sent a strong message that the status quo is unacceptable and that the government will be held accountable for failing to live up to that standard.

The founders showed concern with one-party domination and gave us a Constitution designed to guarantee compromise for the greater good. That has been lost, and our survival as a functioning republic depends on a return to those tenets.

Thanksgiving has always been one of my favorite holidays, gathering with family to overeat, watch football and thank God for our blessings. When I got my diagnosis six months ago, my only hope was to stick around long enough to meet my new granddaughter, Mary Ellen. Now I have, and she’s perfect. She’s not wrinkly. In the grand scheme, family arguments over politics seem trivial. My three sons and two sisters drove me to Georgetown and sat with me every month. My wife, Ellen, who has M. S., was always there in spirit even if she couldn’t be there in person. Political figures and movements come and go, but your family is forever. Besides, you never know when you will need a ride to the hospital.

God bless you. God bless America. And God bless the oncologists and health care workers at Sloan Kettering and Georgetown, who have been, for me, the “Top Gun” pilots of the medical profession. And a special thanks to Dr. Jerome Groopman, who has saved our family more than once.

Happy Thanksgiving weekend!

The Iowa Lead Detonation Happened. Now the Real Work Begins to Study It

Wired November 25, 2026

On Wednesday morning, the US Army detonated nearly five tons of degraded lead azide outside of Middletown, Iowa.

Environmental Protection Administration chief Lee Zeldin told CNN shortly after the explosion that preliminary monitoring from the site detected no lead in the air around the site.

But the full extent of the fallout may not be certain for at least a few days. A barrage of government, university, and citizen monitoring and testing projects are underway. Air, soil, and water samples they’ve collected will determine the extent of lead exposure, if any, in Middletown and the surrounding area.

The lead azide has been on the base near Middletown for decades, but recently the Army deemed it unstable and too dangerous to move and remediate. Poor communication between the Army and towns in the path of the fallout led to a public uproar. While the federal government stepped up its mitigation measures—the Army dug a dam around the detonation site, while NASA stepped in with research jets and satellites for monitoring—universities had already been swinging into action due to the chaotic rollout.

Several departments at the University of Iowa kicked into gear to begin to set up air and soil monitoring stations late last week. “Initially we did not know that [the] EPA or Army or anybody else was going to be doing anything,” says Peter Thorne, a professor of environmental health at the university.

Scientists at Purdue University, nearly 300 miles away, also put out a call for soil samples from Middletown.

“We learned about the detonation late last week; once we learned of the initial delay in detonation date we decided to put forth the call,” says Ellen Wells, a professor of public health at Purdue who is helping lead the testing.

Surrounding towns were notified in late October that the Army wanted to conduct pre- and post-detonation soil sampling for “an intentional, controlled detonation” of a “quantity of lead azide”—seemingly the only notification that many towns in the initial modeled path of the fallout say they received before a press release issued by the Army days before the planned explosion.

The lack of communication has, understandably, instilled a lot of public distrust in the federal government, including agencies’ monitoring programs. Thorne says that efforts like the University of Iowa’s are not meant to displace federal monitoring, but rather to supplement and support it—and hopefully reassure the public.

“We and the EPA are doing similar exposure assessment efforts. If they agree, they can give us some confidence,” he says. “For people who might be concerned about the veracity of what the government tells them, if their findings are in alignment with ours, then I think that helps quell some of those concerns.”

Thorne says that the soil samples the University of Iowa scientists had measured before the detonation had low levels of lead. “If I saw something like a 10 fold increase in the amount of lead in the soil 20 miles downwind, I’d be concerned with that,” he says.

Some soil testing can be done instantaneously with devices that can image the soil’s surface, using a gun device that fires X-ray beams into a sample and measures the specific electromagnetic signature of lead atoms that bounce back. While Wells and her team don’t have those instruments in the field, they are planning on using them to analyze the samples they receive. More sensitive lab equipment can provide even more granular data, though Thorne estimates those results could take about a week.

In addition to monitoring being done by the Army and the EPA, which is maintaining a live website of air quality results, University of Iowa scientists are monitoring the plume to figure out where the highest concentration of lead may settle. They’re also collecting data on particulate matter in the air around the detonation site for analysis, sending air filters to the lab for more detailed results.

“As these data are compiled over the holiday week to the early next week, I think we'll start to have a bigger picture of roughly how much loading we have of the soil at various places downwind and what we can expect from that,” says Thorne.

A lot of concern online has centered around how additional lead in the soil may impact crops in Iowa, one of the central agricultural hubs for soybeans and corn. Jeffrey Catalano, a professor of earth and environmental sciences at Washington University in Saint Louis, says that there’s a large amount of research showing that plants like corn are actually pretty bad at absorbing lead.

“The hazard is more like, if soil with lead in it gets stuck to leaves, and you eat leaves that have lead-rich soil on them,” he says. “If you take some corn crops next year versus this year and measure their lead content, I don’t think you would see anything other than random variations. I’m not worried about food produced in Iowa.”

Municipal drinking water is also unlikely to be affected because most treatment plants are designed to remove lead from water supplies, says Patrick McNamara, a professor of environmental engineering at Marquette University. It’s more worrisome for private wells or streams on people’s property where livestock may drink. McNamara suggests that owners use at-home lead water tests for safety.

While the detonation and haphazard announcements leading up to it raised alarm bells, both Thorne and Catalano say that there are communities dealing with legacy pollution around the country that are exposed to dangerous levels of lead every day that deserve attention—and remediation.

“I've done work in places like East Chicago, Indiana, where they built a housing project and a school on the grounds of a former lead smelting plant—we were seeing soil lead levels that are roughly 10,000-fold higher than what we've measured in Iowa this week,” Thorne says. “There are a lot of places around the country where there's a much greater lead hazard than I'm going to anticipate what we’ll end up with here. I don't want to over-sell this one when we recognize that there are places where people are really suffering, and need to be remediated for the health of their children.”

How Jump-Roping Toy Soldiers Accidentally Took Over Your FYP

Wired November 25, 2026

Holidave, the stalwart leader of SeaWorld’s jump-roping toy soldiers troupe, is known for his ability to jump rope while sitting down, “a skill only shared by 0.1 percent of Earth’s population.”

He’s the most “laid-back” of all the toy soldiers, allowing fellow toy soldier Jackary Jingleson to take center stage. And “experts” and “recent polling data,” “fans believe it is Holidave who holds the most whimsy” out of all the SeaWorld toy soldiers.

This is all according to AI slop videos posted by @wejumprope_memes, a fan page devoted to the group of masked professional jump ropers, who perform an annual holiday show at SeaWorld Orlando. Per toy soldier lore, in addition to Jackary Jingleson there’s also Sugarsnookie, Soulja Toy, Big Chestnut, and Frosty McSleigh. And all of the edits are the same: an AI-generated narrator recites stats about the toy soldiers, such as their net worth and their vertical leap, as if they were elite athletes and not niche theme park performers.

For the past two weeks, fan page videos featuring the jump-roping toy soldiers have been going viral, with @wejumprope_memes’ most popular video garnering 1.2 million views. In the comments sections, fans debate the merits and deficits of each toy soldier, declaring their allegiance to their favorite as if they were a ’90s boy band: “Jackery Jingleson is having a banner year! His speed is incomparable, his style undeniable, and his technique is utterly flawless,” reads one comment. Another disputes this, writing “Soulja Toy the underrated gem.”

Mostly, people seem confused as to why these videos keep showing up in their algorithm and why they keep watching them. “I have a PhD and lecture at a university. And yet here I am,” one commenter writes on a video about whether Major Bounce, a new toy soldier, will show up for the 2026 season. (In a November 20 Reel announcing “major news for the jump-roping toy soldier community,” he finally did.)

As it turns out, there’s a simple explanation for the virality. @wejumprope_memes is run by Devin Meek, an Orlando-based professional entertainer who works for WeFlip, a production company that produces acrobatics shows. But he’s now perhaps best known as his alter ego—Holidave.

What started just a few weeks ago as him making memes to make his coworkers laugh has metamorphosed into an internet sensation, with the toy soldiers amassing a genuine, and ardent, fandom. “I really just made these videos for my friends in the jump-roping community,” Meek tells WIRED. “But I guess they resonated with more people than I thought.”

The videos are piggybacking on a larger—and increasingly absurd—trend of seasonal theme park employees going viral. In September, as WIRED previously reported, SeaWorld Orlando enjoyed a bump in ticket sales thanks to Just One More Chapter, a BookTok-themed Halloween scare zone at SeaWorld Orlando that featured swaggering bad boys from the romantasy genre flirting with guests. And last month, women on TikTok swooned over Archer and Fryboy, two performers at Hersheypark Halloween known for sliding around in kneepads wearing tactical streetwear and clown makeup, a practice known as “sliding.”

Meek, who has been jumping rope for the past 20 years, was inspired to create the videos featuring Sugarsnookie, Jackary, and the like after seeing the success of Archer and Fryboy, who have a combined more than 3.1 million followers on TikTok. “It was such an interesting phenomenon, because I’m somebody who is in a very similar position where I work a few months out of the year as a holiday-themed performer,” he says. “So I got a kick out of it.”

Meek already had an account, @wejumprope_memes, where he posted jump-roping fails and compilations. He posted one video on November 13 featuring old footage from SeaWorld Orlando, where he’s been performing with the other toy soldiers for the past six years. (The group got started during the height of the Covid pandemic—hence, why they wear masks during their shows.) “Fryboy who? Move over, Archer,” it begins, before introducing the lore of Jackery Jingleson, the most “light-hearted, nonchalant” of the toy soldiers.

To Meek’s surprise, the video received almost a million views and 588 comments, most of which were not from fellow members of the jumping community but from total strangers. So Meek posted more toy soldier lore on his meme page, introducing Big Chestnut (“a powerful jumper”), Soulja Toy (the developer of the “Christmas Ice Storm 261”), Sugarsnookie (“the girl’s girl of the group,” who is dating Big Chestnut) and Frosty McSleigh (“he has the fastest salute time of all the toy soldiers.”)

Though the lore is fictional, it’s also based on the jumpers’ actual skills and personalities: the jumpers who play Big Chestnut and Sugarsnookie are actually in a long-term relationship, and Jackery Jingleson, perhaps the most popular of the group, once held the world record for the fastest jump roper in the United States. “Honestly, that makes [the popularity of the memes] even funnier to us,” he says.

Though some fans have speculated in the comments that the toy soldier memes are a marketing campaign for SeaWorld Orlando, Meek denies that’s the case: He doesn’t tag SeaWorld in the comments, nor has he been in contact with the theme park about his page. (SeaWorld Orlando did not respond to WIRED’s request for comment.)

“This is something that is so targeted to people who are internet-brained and have this ironic sense of humor,” he says. “And that’s exactly the type of person who’ll tune out immediately if they feel like they’re being sold something on the internet.”

Others have even speculated that there is an actual feud brewing between the SeaWorld Orlando “jumpers” and the Southern California–based “sliders,” though Meek says the rivalry is playful, and he has even reached out to collab with them. (The sliders may view it differently: So far, he says, they “don’t seem super interested” in joining forces.)

What has surprised Meek the most, however, is that very few commenters suspect that the toy soldiers themselves are behind the memes. In fact, he’s been shocked by how many organic meme fan pages have popped up within the past week, with people drawing their own fan art of Holidave saluting or Jackery Jingleson jumping. WeFlip has also been deluged with business inquiries: “People are like, how can we get Jackery Jingleson out here?”

Essentially, what started as an inside joke within an extremely niche community has evolved into an inside joke for the internet at large. “I think people like the feeling of being in on a joke and being a part of it and building it up,” he says.

So what’s next for the SeaWorld Orlando jump-roping toy soldiers? The rotating cast typically performs at the park on the weekends, ramping up appearances as it gets closer to the holiday season. Meek also shares that the toy soldiers will “likely cross state lines” in the coming months, including a stint at the Christmas market in Cullman, Alabama. Frosty McSleigh, renowned for his 0.08-second salute, plus a slew of new, yet-to-be-introduced toy soldiers will also make an appearance.

Though it may come as a disappointment to some that the roots of the toy soldier phenomenon were inorganic, Meek isn’t concerned. “The people are real. The athleticism is real. The lore is real,” he says. “For all of these people, jump rope is their life, and we’re super-dedicated to teaching it and sharing it. And I think people can feel that.”

Airplane Turbulence Is Extremely Hard to Predict, but Maybe Not for Long

Wired November 25, 2026

In the early 1500s, an Italian polymath named Leonardo da Vinci took a good crack at exactly the phenomenon that makes nervous fliers clutch their airplane seats in fear and flight attendants push their carts back to the galleys with haste: turbulence.

Da Vinci was fascinated by swirling, chaotic eddies of water, movements so complex that he made hundreds of drawings of his observations. Why, exactly, did water—any fluid, really, be it atmospheric air or blood in the heart—move in that way?

Now the world has ChatGPT and self-driving cars and solar farms, and it still doesn’t exactly know how turbulence works. “It’s the hardest remaining problem in classical physics, and it’s one we need to fly through,” says Michael Murillo, a professor of theoretical and computational physics at Michigan State University.

Now a bumper crop of data-driven efforts to predict and avoid turbulence could get fliers closer to a smooth flight. Twenty terabytes of data are created by an airplane’s engine in one hour of commercial flying, according to the International Air Transport Association, with more broadcast by airplanes midflight: GPS position, altitude, speed. An “electronic flight bag,” basically a specialized iPad, is equipped with navigation charts and manuals and can transmit its own information, as long as the airplane’s internet connection cooperates. Satellites watch and collect it all.

“Air traffic has gone up, and communication costs and the costs of putting computers on aircraft have come down,” says Larry Cornman, a physicist with the National Science Foundation’s National Center for Atmospheric Research who has been studying turbulence for decades. “The time is now to work on these things because we can do them.”

This is good news for aviation safety. More than 200 people were seriously injured on US airplanes in turbulence-related incidents between 2009 and 2023, according to FAA data. Turbulence is also getting worse. Climate change alters the atmospheric conditions around the world’s jet streams, creating destabilizing wind shear. From the cockpit of an airplane, this translates into sudden, clear-air turbulence, difficult to see or predict. Historically, pilots’ only method of avoiding turbulence is heeding the warning of those who accidentally went through it before them, and hoping that nothing had changed.

But just in the past two years, Cornman’s decades of work on turbulence has been put into the field in ways it couldn’t be before, part of several projects coordinated by the US federal government and the airline industry. One breakthrough came when Cornman and an FAA air traffic controller determined that aircrafts’ federally required broadcasts of their positions, altitude, and speed could be used to spot unexpected turbulence, without requiring new hardware or software onboard. Researchers can use this crowdsourced, public data to make predictions about when and where turbulence will pop up.

In September, the National Science Foundation announced a $30 million award to nine universities to stand up a new center dedicated to predicting turbulence—in the air, but also in the charged particles inside a fusion reactor, and in the gas clouds that stretch across space.

“Turbulence is the reason we don’t have fusion energy yet,” says Murillo, who heads up the new center, called Transformative Explorations in Multi-Physics and Engineering of Scientific Turbulence, or Tempest. The chaotic swirling of superhot plasma inside a reactor allows heat to leak out, preventing the material from reaching the temperatures needed to allow nuclei to fuse. The US federal government wants to get closer to figuring that out.

“Closer,” because turbulence is impossible to perfectly predict, scientists say. For one thing, turbulence occurs at many different, small scales at the same time. Air swirling around an airplane breaks into eddies, then smaller eddies, and then even smaller eddies, with each interacting with each other—too many variables, happening too quickly, to mathematically account for. For another, tiny changes—wind speed, temperature—can eventually dramatically alter air movement, suddenly altering the turbulence once predicted. To make perfect forecasts, one would need a perfect picture of exactly what’s going on in the atmosphere at all times.

But increasing sophisticated applications of machine learning could allow scientists to get closer to knowing what’s going to happen when, says Murillo. And while brute, computational force can’t solve the turbulence problem, AI agents might give the effort a boost. OpenAI’s blockbuster announcement this fall that it had resolved the Navier-Stokes problem—equations that are the beginning of all turbulence models—suggests LLMs could help.

“Turbulence has been a problem only human minds could work on; as of this year, that's no longer true,” says Murillo.

To make flying better, the aviation industry doesn’t necessarily need to solve turbulence. It needs to get better at knowing what sort of conditions create it and not send airplanes there.

One company in Tel Aviv, SkyPath, uses those in-plane iPads and their accelerometers to collect and share crowdsourced data between different airplanes, even if they don’t fly for the same airline. (This sort of dating sharing can be a sensitive topic for competing companies; SkyPath says it assuages these concerns by ensuring that data is anonymized before it’s shared.) More than 40,000 of these devices have SkyPath installed on them, says CEO Maya Shpak; the company says that several major airlines, including American, use the technology. SkyPath combines that collected data with additional information, including weather forecasts, and uses machine intelligence to make predictions about the future state of the air. The app helps pilots avoid turbulent air and warn passengers and crew members that choppiness is coming, 10 to 15 minutes before it happens.

One pilot named Eric who uses SkyPath, who asked WIRED not to use his full name because he was not authorized to speak to the media, said the app is a helpful tool that allows him to warn passengers what to expect. His issue is the same as those studying turbulence: One can’t take measurements everywhere all at once.

“It’s like any crowdsourced software,” says the pilot. “It only works if everyone uses it, and no one wants to use it until everyone else is.” Today, several large operators are using the app, which makes it especially useful in areas with lots of flights, he says.

Cornman, the physicist, wants to keep all these advances in perspective. “No matter what people say, we’re not getting close to 100 percent, 90 percent, 80 percent [predictive accuracy] anytime soon,” he says. “It’s too complicated a problem.” Smoother skies, if not perfect ones, are ahead.
